[15] Title: Investigating the effects of formative assessment on EFL students’ achievement and motivation: a Self-Determination Theory perspective
    Authors: Zhang H. (2025)
    Source: Scopus / DOI:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1664871
    URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1664871
  [ABSTRACT ONLY — no PDF available]

Formative assessment in secondary school mathematics has been the subject of various studies examining its impact on student achievement. Here are some key findings:

1. **Confidence Assessment in Low-Stakes, Formative Mathematics Assessments**: A study involving 475 secondary-school students across four schools found that incorporating confidence assessment into low-stakes classroom mathematics formative assessments did not significantly affect students' attainment. The aggregated effect size was Cohen's d = -0.02, indicating no substantial difference between the intervention and control groups. ([eric.ed.gov](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1348640&q=cas-express&utm_source=openai))

2. **Promoting Socioeconomic Equity through Automatic Formative Assessment**: Research with 299 eighth-grade students demonstrated a positive effect of automatic formative assessment on learning achievement, with an effect size of 0.42. Notably, the effect size for students from low socioeconomic status backgrounds was higher at 0.77, suggesting that this approach may help reduce educational inequalities. ([eric.ed.gov](https://eric.ed.gov/?ff1=subGrade+8&id=EJ1413543&pg=4&q=%2C%E4%B8%AD%E5%9B%BD%E5%9B%BD%E9%99%85%E5%A4%A7%E5%AD%A6%E7%94%9F%E5%88%9B%E6%96%B0%E5%A4%A7%E8%B5%9B+2024&utm_source=openai))

3. **Impact of Formative Assessment Instructional Approach on Students' Mathematics Achievement and Metacognitive Awareness**: A study involving 164 grade 11 students in Kenya found that those taught using a formative assessment instructional approach outperformed peers taught with conventional methods in both mathematics achievement and metacognitive awareness, with effect sizes of η² = 0.38 and η² = 0.47, respectively. ([files.eric.ed.gov](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1341771.pdf?utm_source=openai))

4. **The Impact of Formative Assessment on K-12 Learning: A Meta-Analysis**: This meta-analysis examined 258 effect sizes from 118 primary studies worldwide and found that formative assessment has a positive impact on student academic achievement in K-12 classrooms. Formative assessments are tools used by educators to monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback, aiming to improve teaching and learning processes. Research has explored how these assessments impact various student subgroups, including English learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, and those with varying prior achievements.

**Overall Effectiveness of Formative Assessment:**

A meta-analysis encompassing 48 studies with 116,051 K-12 students found that formative assessments have a modest positive effect on reading achievement, with an effect size of +0.19. This suggests that formative assessments can enhance reading outcomes, though the impact is relatively small. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

**Impact on Specific Student Subgroups:**

- **English Learners and Students with Disabilities:** A study examining the effects of text-to-speech (TTS) technology as a universal design for assessment tool found that TTS usage was associated with improved math performance among English learners and students with disabilities who were granted extended time accommodations. This indicates that formative assessment tools tailored to specific needs can be beneficial for these groups. ([publications.ici.umn.edu](https://publications.ici.umn.edu/nceo/nceo-reports/453/a-summary-of-the-research-on-the-effects-of-k-12-test-accommodations-2024?utm_source=openai))

- **Low-Income Students:** Research on interim assessments in grades 3–8 found that the treatment did not significantly affect the achievement gap, suggesting that interim assessments may not be sufficient to address disparities among low-income students. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0883035516305985?utm_source=openai))

- **Prior Achievement Levels:** A systematic review of formative assessment in mathematics education found that low-achieving students benefited most from integrated formative assessment in self-regulated learning. This suggests that formative assessments can be particularly effective for students with lower prior achievement levels. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11858-025-01696-x?utm_source=openai))

**Moderating Factors Influencing Effectiveness:**

- **Differentiated Instruction:** The meta-analysis on formative assessment for reading achievement highlighted that integrating differentiated instruction during or after formative assessments significantly enhances reading outcomes. This underscores the importance of tailoring instruction to meet diverse student needs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

- **Type of Intervention:** The same meta-analysis found that studies with smaller sample sizes (250 or fewer students) yielded significantly larger effect sizes than those with larger samples. Additionally, formative assessments embedded with differentiated instruction and those integrating both teacher and student-directed assessments were more effective. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

In summary, formative assessments can positively impact student achievement, with varying effects across different subgroups. Tailoring these assessments to the specific needs of students, such as integrating differentiated instruction and considering prior achievement levels, can enhance their effectiveness.

Formative assessment plays a crucial role in enhancing educational outcomes for diverse student populations, including English language learners (ELLs), students with disabilities, and those from low-income backgrounds. Research indicates that formative assessments can positively impact reading achievement across various K-12 settings. A meta-analysis found a medium effect size (d = 0.18) of formative assessments on reading achievement, suggesting that these assessments are beneficial for improving reading skills among students. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9443994/?utm_source=openai))

The effectiveness of formative assessments can vary based on several factors:

- **Sample Size**: Studies with smaller sample sizes often report larger effect sizes, potentially due to more controlled environments and tailored interventions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9443994/?utm_source=openai))

- **Differentiated Instruction**: Implementing differentiated instruction alongside formative assessments has been associated with improved reading outcomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9443994/?utm_source=openai))

- **Student Characteristics**: The impact of formative assessments may differ based on student demographics. For instance, a study focusing on ELLs found that interventions targeting phonological awareness, reading fluency, vocabulary, and reading comprehension were particularly effective. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8461348/?utm_source=openai))

However, challenges exist in implementing formative assessments effectively. Teachers often face obstacles such as insufficient time, inadequate technical support, and unclear assessment criteria. A study involving Chinese EFL teachers highlighted that 76% of respondents cited heavy assessment workloads as a significant challenge, while 60% expressed concerns about the objectivity and fairness of self- and peer-assessments. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12478959/?utm_source=openai))

In summary, formative assessments, when thoughtfully designed and implemented, can serve as a powerful tool to support the academic growth of students from diverse backgrounds. Addressing the challenges associated with their implementation is essential to maximize their effectiveness.

Formative assessment, characterized by ongoing, interactive evaluations of student progress, has been shown to significantly enhance student achievement in K-12 education. By providing continuous feedback, formative assessments enable teachers to adjust instruction to meet individual student needs, fostering a more personalized learning experience. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2005/01/formative-assessment_g1gh4c28/9789264007413-en.pdf?utm_source=openai))

In contrast, summative assessments, which evaluate student learning at the end of an instructional period, primarily serve to measure what students have learned. While they are essential for accountability and program evaluation, summative assessments do not offer the immediate feedback necessary for instructional adjustments. ([amle.org](https://www.amle.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Formative_Assessment_Article_Aug2013.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Diagnostic assessments aim to identify students' existing knowledge and skills, helping teachers tailor instruction accordingly. Interim assessments, conducted periodically throughout the academic year, monitor student progress toward learning goals. Both types of assessments provide valuable information but may not offer the continuous, real-time feedback that formative assessments do. ([cde.ca.gov](https://www.cde.ca.gov/ls/he/hn/guidanceonassessments.asp?utm_source=openai))

Teacher feedback without instructional adjustment may not be as effective, as it lacks the responsiveness to student needs that formative assessments provide. Professional development packages that focus on formative assessment strategies can equip teachers with the skills to implement these practices effectively, leading to improved student outcomes. ([files.eric.ed.gov](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED572214.pdf?utm_source=openai))

In summary, while all assessment types have their place in education, formative assessments are particularly effective in enhancing student achievement by enabling teachers to make timely instructional adjustments based on continuous feedback.

You seem to be interested in the topic of K-12 formative assessment interventions and various factors influencing their effectiveness. Here’s a breakdown addressing key elements related to this topic:

1. **Effectiveness of Formative Assessment Interventions:**
   - Formative assessments are designed to monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback that can be used by instructors to improve their teaching and by students to improve their learning.
   - Research generally shows that formative assessment interventions have a positive impact on student achievement outcomes.

2. **Feedback Quality:**
   - High-quality feedback is timely, specific, and actionable.
   - Feedback should guide students on how to improve rather than just indicate right or wrong answers.
   
3. **Differentiation:**
   - Effective formative assessments account for students' diverse needs and tailor instruction accordingly.
   - Differentiation helps in addressing varying skill levels within the classroom.

4. **Teacher Training:**
   - Proper training is essential for teachers to effectively implement formative assessments.
   - Training helps teachers understand how to design, implement, and respond to formative assessments to maximize student learning.

5. **Dosage:**
   - The frequency and intensity (dosage) of formative assessments can influence their effectiveness.
   - Regular and sustained use is typically more effective than sporadic use.

6. **Use of Digital Tools:**
   - Digital assessment tools can facilitate immediate feedback and data collection.
   - They can support differentiated instruction and track student progress over time.
   
7. **Delayed Posttests, Retention, and Transfer:**
   - Evaluating retention and transfer through delayed posttests shows whether learning is durable and applicable beyond the immediate learning context.
   - Effective formative assessments can contribute to better retention and transfer of knowledge.

8. **Workload and Feasibility:**
   - The additional workload on teachers must be manageable to sustain implementation.
   - Feasibility depends on resources, time, and support available within the school environment.

9. **Implementation Fidelity:**
   - The degree to which formative assessment interventions are implemented as intended impacts their effectiveness.
   - Monitoring fidelity ensures the intervention is delivered properly.

10. **Achievement Outcomes:**
    - Success is often measured by improvements in student achievement scores.
    - Formative assessment interventions often lead to gains in academic performance when implemented effectively.

This research examined the use of Direct Behavior Rating-Single Item Scales (DBR-SIS) as a formative assessment tool in conjunction with a Daily Behavior Report Card intervention. [14] Title: The impact of assessment for learning on learner performance in life science
    Authors: Oyinloye O.M. (2019)
    Source: Scopus / DOI:10.29333/ejmste/108689

Formative assessment, also known as assessment for learning, involves ongoing evaluations that inform instructional decisions and support student learning. Research has demonstrated its effectiveness in enhancing student achievement across various subjects, including mathematics, science, and writing. Below is a summary of key studies and meta-analyses that provide evidence for the impact of formative assessment in secondary education:

**1. Meta-Analysis on Formative Assessment in K-12 Education**

A comprehensive meta-analysis examined the effects of formative assessment on K-12 students' learning outcomes. The study found that formative assessment positively influences student achievement, with an average weighted effect size of 0.19. Notably, the implementation of differentiated instruction by teachers during formative assessment was linked to stronger effects, highlighting the importance of tailored teaching strategies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9443994/?utm_source=openai))

**2. Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses on Formative Assessment**

An umbrella review systematically analyzed multiple meta-analyses investigating the impact of formative assessment on K-12 students' learning. The findings underscore the effectiveness of formative assessment in improving student outcomes, emphasizing its role in monitoring and enhancing student understanding and competencies. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/16/17/7826?utm_source=openai))

**3. Meta-Analysis on Teacher Professional Development and Student Mathematics Achievement**

A meta-analysis focused on the relationship between teacher professional development (PD) and student mathematics achievement. The study found that PD programs were most effective when they were under a year in duration, focused on geometry, combined content and pedagogy, targeted grades 6–8, used online video, were reform-initiated, and employed randomized designs. While this study primarily addresses PD, it highlights the importance of instructional strategies that can be informed by formative assessment practices. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/9/1156?utm_source=openai))

**4. Meta-Analysis on Teacher Professional Development and Student Mathematics Achievement**

Another meta-analysis examined the effects of teacher professional development on student mathematics achievement. The study discusses recommendations for improving PD program features and explores mechanisms of change that can enhance student mathematics outcomes. Although not exclusively focused on formative assessment, the findings suggest that effective PD can lead to improved student achievement, potentially through the adoption of formative assessment strategies. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/9/1177?utm_source=openai))

**5. Study on the Effect of E-Homework on K-12 Students' Academic Achievements**

A meta-analysis evaluated the impact of electronic homework (e-homework) on K-12 students' academic achievements. The study included 26 empirical studies and found that e-homework positively affects student performance. While not directly about formative assessment, the integration of technology in formative assessment practices, such as through e-homework, can enhance student engagement and learning outcomes. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1758739/full?utm_source=openai))

These studies collectively provide robust evidence supporting the effectiveness of formative assessment in enhancing student achievement in secondary education. Implementing formative assessment strategies, such as differentiated instruction and integrating technology, can lead to improved learning outcomes in mathematics, science, and writing.

A comprehensive meta-analysis titled "The Impact of Formative Assessment on K-12 Learning" was published in 2024 in the journal *Educational Research and Evaluation*. This study examined 118 primary studies, encompassing 258 effect sizes, to assess the influence of formative assessment on student academic achievement across K-12 classrooms. The findings revealed an overall effect size of 0.25 (Hedges' g), indicating a moderate positive impact of formative assessment practices on student learning outcomes. Notably, the effect size was consistent across various types of formative assessments, such as self-assessment and peer assessment, and across different content domains, including mathematics and science. The study also found that the mean effect size was significantly larger for studies conducted outside North America and Western Europe, for formative assessments targeting high school students, and for studies employing quasi-experimental designs. No publication bias was detected for studies conducted in North America and Western Europe. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13803611.2024.2363831?utm_source=openai))

Another meta-analysis, "The Effect of Formative Assessment Practices on Student Learning," published in 2021 in the *International Journal of Assessment Tools in Education*, analyzed 32 studies with 47 effect sizes. This research found a higher overall mean effect size of 0.72, suggesting a strong positive impact of formative assessment practices on student learning. The study highlighted that student-initiated formative feedback had the largest effect size (d=1.16), followed by mixed feedback (d=0.83), adult-initiated formative feedback (d=0.69), and computer-initiated formative feedback (d=0.42). These findings underscore the significant role of formative assessment in enhancing student learning outcomes. ([eric.ed.gov](https://eric.ed.gov/?ff1=subHigher+Education&id=EJ1329204&pg=11&q=+computer+security+in+the+school+classroom&utm_source=openai))

Additionally, a study titled "The Impacts of a Standards-Based Grading System Emphasizing Formative Assessment, Feedback, and Re-Assessment: A Mixed Methods, Cluster Randomized Control Trial in Ninth Grade Mathematics Classrooms," published in 2023, investigated the effects of a standards-based grading system that incorporated formative assessment practices in ninth-grade mathematics classrooms. The research employed a mixed-methods, cluster randomized control trial design, providing robust evidence on the effectiveness of formative assessment strategies in improving student performance in mathematics. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19345747.2023.2287594?utm_source=openai))

These studies collectively highlight the positive impact of formative assessment practices on student learning, particularly in secondary education settings, and emphasize the importance of incorporating such strategies into instructional practices to enhance educational outcomes.

Several meta-analyses have examined the impact of formative assessment on student learning outcomes, including subgroup analyses based on various student characteristics. However, specific subgroup analyses focusing on English language learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, and prior achievement levels are limited. Below is a summary of relevant studies:

1. **The Effectiveness of Formative Assessment for Enhancing Reading Achievement in K-12 Classrooms: A Meta-Analysis** (2022)

   This meta-analysis included 48 studies with a total sample of 116,051 K-12 students. The findings suggested that formative assessment had a positive effect (ES = +0.19) on students' reading achievement. Meta-regression results revealed that studies with smaller sample sizes (≤250 students) yielded significantly larger effect sizes. Additionally, formative assessments embedded with differentiated instruction led to an increase of 0.13 SD in reading achievement scores. The study also found that integrating both teacher and student-directed assessments was more effective than assessments initiated solely by teachers. Subgroup analysis indicated that effect sizes differed significantly between Confucian-heritage cultures and Anglophone cultures, highlighting the need for cultural adaptation in formative assessment practices. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

2. **The Impact of Formative Assessment on K-12 Learning: A Meta-Analysis** (2024)

   This meta-analysis examined 258 effect sizes from 118 primary studies worldwide. The overall effect size was 0.25 (Hedges’ g) for all studies and 0.22 for studies conducted within the U.S. The effect size was similar across different types of formative assessments (e.g., self-assessment vs. peer assessment) and content domains (e.g., English language, mathematics, science). Subgroup analyses revealed significantly larger effect sizes for studies conducted outside North America and Western Europe, for formative assessments targeting high school students, and for studies using quasi-experimental designs. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13803611.2024.2363831?utm_source=openai))

3. **The Effect of Formative Assessment Practices on Student Learning: A Meta-Analysis Study** (2021)

   This meta-analysis included 32 studies with 47 effect sizes that met specified criteria, such as using true experimental or quasi-experimental designs and measuring learning outcomes. The overall mean effect size was 0.72 (SE = 0.07, p < 0.05). Subgroup analyses showed significant differences based on the type of formative feedback. Student-initiated formative feedback had a large effect size (d = 1.16), followed by mixed feedback (d = 0.83), adult-initiated formative feedback (d = 0.69), and computer-initiated formative feedback (d = 0.42). However, the study did not report subgroup analyses based on student characteristics such as prior achievement, English language proficiency, or socioeconomic status. ([indexacademicdocs.org](https://www.indexacademicdocs.org/paper/1629/65134/870300?utm_source=openai))

While these studies provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of formative assessment, they do not specifically address how formative assessment impacts subgroups like English language learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, or students with varying prior achievement levels. Further research is needed to explore these subgroup effects to inform more targeted and equitable educational practices.

I searched for meta-analyses examining formative assessment with moderators such as English Language Learners (ELL), disability status, low-income background, and prior achievement. While I couldn't locate a specific meta-analysis combining all these moderators, several studies have explored related aspects:

(2020) proposed a model for language learning assessment based on higher-order thinking skills, emphasizing the role of formative assessment in language acquisition. ([scholar.google.com](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Ffryk-8AAAAJ&utm_source=openai))

These studies provide insights into formative assessment's role across various educational contexts. For a comprehensive understanding of how formative assessment interacts with moderators like ELL status, disability, low-income background, and prior achievement, consulting specialized educational databases or conducting a systematic review may be beneficial.

Formative assessment is a process used by educators to monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback that can be used to improve teaching and learning. It is distinct from other assessment types, each serving different purposes in the educational process.

**Formative Assessment**: Conducted during the learning process, formative assessments aim to monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback that can be used to improve teaching and learning. These assessments are typically low-stakes and may include activities such as in-class discussions, quizzes, peer reviews, and self-assessments. The primary goal is to identify learning gaps and adjust instruction accordingly. ([niu.edu](https://www.niu.edu/citl/resources/guides/instructional-guide/formative-and-summative-assessment.shtml?utm_source=openai))

**Diagnostic Testing**: Administered before instruction begins, diagnostic assessments help identify students' existing knowledge, skills, and potential misconceptions. This information allows educators to tailor their teaching strategies to meet students' needs effectively. ([niu.edu](https://www.niu.edu/citl/resources/guides/instructional-guide/formative-and-summative-assessment.shtml?utm_source=openai))

**Interim Assessment**: Also known as benchmark assessments, these are conducted at intervals during the instructional period. They evaluate students' progress toward learning goals and can inform instructional adjustments. While they provide valuable data, interim assessments are typically not as frequent as formative assessments. ([nwea.org](https://www.nwea.org/blog/2024/understanding-formative-interim-summative-assessments-role-student-learning/?utm_source=openai))

**Summative Assessment**: Administered at the end of an instructional period, summative assessments evaluate the cumulative knowledge and skills students have acquired. These assessments are often high-stakes and include final exams, standardized tests, and end-of-term projects. ([niu.edu](https://www.niu.edu/citl/resources/guides/instructional-guide/formative-and-summative-assessment.shtml?utm_source=openai))

**Graded Quizzes**: These can serve as either formative or summative assessments, depending on their timing and purpose. If administered during the learning process to provide feedback and guide instruction, they function as formative assessments. If given at the end of a unit to evaluate student learning, they serve as summative assessments. ([niu.edu](https://www.niu.edu/citl/resources/guides/instructional-guide/formative-and-summative-assessment.shtml?utm_source=openai))

**Ordinary Feedback**: This refers to informal, ongoing comments provided by educators to students regarding their performance. While not a formal assessment, regular feedback is crucial for guiding student learning and can be part of formative assessment practices.

**Professional Development Packages**: These are structured programs designed to enhance educators' teaching skills and knowledge. While not directly related to student assessments, professional development can improve instructional strategies, thereby indirectly impacting student learning outcomes.

Understanding the distinctions between these assessment types is essential for educators to effectively monitor and support student learning throughout the educational process.

Formative assessment is an integral part of the instructional process, aimed at monitoring student learning to provide ongoing feedback that can be used by instructors to improve their teaching and by students to improve their learning. It is distinct from other assessment types in several key ways:

**Diagnostic Assessment**: Conducted before instruction begins, diagnostic assessments identify students' existing knowledge and skills, helping to inform the planning of future lessons. In contrast, formative assessments are implemented during the learning process to monitor progress and guide immediate instructional adjustments.

**Summative Assessment**: Typically administered at the end of an instructional period, summative assessments evaluate the cumulative learning of students, often resulting in grades or scores. Formative assessments, however, are ongoing and provide real-time feedback to support continuous learning and improvement.

**Interim Assessment**: Also known as benchmark assessments, interim assessments are conducted at intervals throughout the academic year to evaluate students' progress toward learning goals. While they share similarities with formative assessments, interim assessments are often more structured and may not be as closely integrated into daily instructional practices.

**Feedback**: In the context of formative assessment, feedback is immediate and specific, aimed at guiding students on how to improve their performance. This contrasts with the feedback from summative assessments, which is typically less detailed and provided after the learning period has concluded.

**Professional Development**: Formative assessments can inform professional development by highlighting areas where teachers may need to adjust their instructional strategies to better meet students' needs. This ongoing reflection and adaptation are essential for effective teaching and learning.

Understanding these distinctions is crucial for educators to effectively implement assessment strategies that support student learning and development.

It looks like you are interested in various aspects related to K-12 formative assessment interventions, including their implementation features and effects. Here's an overview based on the terms you mentioned:

1. **Implementation Features:**
   - **Feedback Quality:** High-quality, actionable feedback is crucial for effective formative assessment. Feedback should be timely, specific, and constructive to help students improve.
   - **Differentiation:** Formative assessments should be tailored to meet the diverse needs of students, addressing different learning styles and levels.
   - **Teacher Training:** Effective implementation requires comprehensive teacher training to ensure educators understand how to design, administer, and use formative assessments to inform instruction.
   - **Dosage:** The frequency and intensity of formative assessments (dosage) can influence their effectiveness, with regular assessments generally yielding better outcomes.
   - **Digital Tools:** Integration of digital tools can facilitate efficient administration, immediate feedback, and data collection, enhancing the formative assessment process.
   - **Delayed Posttests:** Using delayed posttests helps in measuring retention and the long-term impact of formative assessments.
   - **Retention and Transfer:** Evaluating how well students retain knowledge and transfer skills to new contexts post-intervention is important for assessing effectiveness.
   - **Workload and Feasibility:** The implementation of formative assessments must consider teacher workload and practical feasibility to ensure sustainability.
   - **Implementation Fidelity:** Consistent and accurate adherence to the formative assessment protocols is vital for achieving desired outcomes.

2. **Effects on Achievement:**
   - Formative assessment interventions generally have positive effects on student achievement, particularly when the above features are optimized.
   - Positive outcomes include improved student learning, greater engagement, and better instructional adjustments by teachers.

Formative assessment interventions have been widely studied for their impact on K-12 student learning outcomes. Meta-analyses have generally found positive effects, though the magnitude varies based on several factors.

A meta-analysis by Xuan et al. (2022) included 48 studies with 116,051 K-12 students and reported an overall effect size of +0.18 on reading achievement. This suggests a modest positive impact of formative assessments on reading outcomes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

Another meta-analysis by Yao et al. (2024) examined 118 studies and found an overall effect size of 0.25, indicating a moderate positive effect of formative assessments on student achievement. This study also noted that the effect size was similar across different types of formative assessments and content domains. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13803611.2024.2363831?utm_source=openai))

Subgroup analyses have identified factors that influence the effectiveness of formative assessments:

- **Student Characteristics**: Studies focusing on at-risk students reported a higher effect size (0.27) compared to mainstream students (0.18), suggesting that formative assessments may be more beneficial for students facing challenges. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

- **Grade Level**: Effect sizes varied by educational level, with kindergarten students showing an effect size of 0.28, elementary students 0.16, and middle/high school students 0.27. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

- **Type of Intervention**: Student-directed formative assessments (e.g., peer or self-assessment) had a higher effect size (0.31) compared to teacher-directed (0.12) and integrated assessments (0.20), indicating that involving students actively in the assessment process may enhance learning outcomes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

- **Differentiated Instruction**: The inclusion of differentiated instruction in formative assessments was associated with a higher effect size (0.24) compared to assessments without such instruction (0.05), highlighting the importance of tailoring assessments to meet diverse student needs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

Regarding specific student subgroups:

- **English Learners and Students with Disabilities**: While the meta-analysis by Xuan et al. (2022) did not provide separate effect sizes for these groups, other research indicates that formative assessments can be particularly beneficial for students with learning disabilities and those from language backgrounds other than English. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1747938X25000958?utm_source=openai))

- **Low-Income Students**: The effectiveness of formative assessments for low-income students is not directly addressed in the available meta-analyses. However, studies focusing on at-risk students, which often include those from low-income backgrounds, have reported higher effect sizes, suggesting potential benefits for this group. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

In summary, formative assessment interventions generally have a positive impact on K-12 student learning, with variations influenced by student characteristics, intervention types, and instructional strategies. Tailoring formative assessments to the specific needs of diverse student populations, including English learners, students with disabilities, and low-income students, may enhance their effectiveness.

Formative assessment interventions in K-12 education have been shown to positively impact student learning outcomes. A meta-analysis encompassing 258 effect sizes from 118 studies worldwide reported an overall effect size of 0.25 (Hedges’ g), indicating a moderate positive effect on student achievement. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13803611.2024.2363831?utm_source=openai))

Subgroup analyses within this meta-analysis revealed that the effect size was significantly larger for studies conducted outside North America and Western Europe, for formative assessments targeting high school students, and for studies employing quasi-experimental designs. However, the analysis did not specifically examine the impact of formative assessments on subgroups such as English language learners (ELLs), students with disabilities, or students from varying socioeconomic backgrounds.

Another meta-analysis focused on the effectiveness of formative assessment for enhancing reading achievement in K-12 classrooms included 48 studies with a total sample size of 116,051 students. The overall weighted effect size was 0.18, suggesting a small positive impact on reading achievement. Subgroup analyses indicated that the effect size varied based on factors such as grade level, type of intervention, program duration, and differentiated instruction. Notably, studies involving differentiated instruction reported a significantly larger effect size (0.24) compared to those without (0.05). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9443994/?utm_source=openai))

While these studies provide valuable insights into the general effectiveness of formative assessment interventions, they do not offer detailed subgroup analyses specifically focusing on ELLs, students with disabilities, or students from different socioeconomic statuses. Further research is needed to explore how formative assessments impact these specific student populations and to determine the most effective strategies for their inclusion in formative assessment practices.

Here's a structured overview covering these topics:

1. **Formative Assessment Interventions in K-12**  
   - These are strategies and practices used by teachers to gather ongoing information about student learning to inform instruction and improve student outcomes.

2. **Implementation Features**  
   - Key features include the frequency and timing of assessments, integration with instruction, use of digital tools, and alignment with curriculum standards.
   - Dosage (how often and how much assessment is implemented) and duration (length of intervention period) affect outcomes.

3. **Tradeoffs**  
   - Balancing comprehensive assessment with teacher workload and feasibility can be challenging.
   - High-fidelity implementation might require extensive teacher training and ongoing support.
   - Digital tools can enhance scalability but may introduce technical challenges.

4. **Feedback Quality**  
   - Effective feedback is timely, specific, actionable, and supportive of student learning.
   - Quality feedback supports differentiated instruction by identifying individual student needs.

5. **Differentiated Instruction**  
   - Formative assessments help tailor teaching to diverse learner profiles.
   - Requires teacher skills in interpreting assessment data and adjusting instruction accordingly.

6. **Teacher Training**  
   - Critical for effective use of formative assessments.
   - Training should cover interpretation of assessment data, feedback delivery, and integrating assessments into instruction.

7. **Dosage and Duration**  
   - Optimal dosage varies; too little may be ineffective, too much may increase workload.
   - Duration of interventions affects retention and transfer of knowledge.

8. **Digital Tools**  
   - Can facilitate real-time data collection and feedback.
   - Need to consider access, usability, and alignment with instructional goals.

9. **Delayed Posttests, Retention, and Transfer**  
   - Assessing retention and transfer through delayed posttests measures long-term effects.
   - Formative assessments ideally support durable learning.

10. **Workload and Feasibility**  
    - Implementation should balance effectiveness with manageable workload.
    - Feasibility depends on school context, resources, and teacher readiness.

11. **Fidelity of Implementation**  
    - High fidelity ensures that interventions are delivered as intended.
    - Monitoring fidelity helps interpret outcomes accurately.

12. **Student Achievement**  
    - Formative assessments are linked to improved student outcomes when implemented well.
    - Impact depends on quality of feedback, instructional adjustments, and student engagement.

Formative assessment, also known as assessment for learning or formative feedback, is a teaching approach that involves gathering and using information about student learning to inform instructional decisions and improve educational outcomes. In K-12 classrooms, effective implementation of formative assessment can enhance student engagement, motivation, and achievement.

**Key Aspects of Formative Assessment Implementation:**

1. **Teacher Training and Professional Development:** Equipping educators with the skills and knowledge to effectively implement formative assessment is crucial. Professional development programs that focus on formative assessment strategies can lead to improved teaching practices and student learning outcomes. For instance, a study highlighted the importance of ongoing teacher training in formative assessment, noting that such professional development can enhance the effectiveness of these practices in the classroom. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/339634057_The_Effectiveness_and_Features_of_Formative_Assessment_in_US_K-12_Education_A_Systematic_Review?utm_source=openai))

2. **Integration of Technology:** Digital tools can support formative assessment by providing real-time feedback and facilitating adaptive learning experiences. The use of technology in formative assessment allows for more personalized and efficient monitoring of student progress. Research indicates that computer-based formative assessments can be effective, though they may differ from traditional paper-based assessments in their impact. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/339634057_The_Effectiveness_and_Features_of_Formative_Assessment_in_US_K-12_Education_A_Systematic_Review?utm_source=openai))

3. **Adaptive and Differentiated Instruction:** Formative assessment enables teachers to tailor instruction to meet the diverse needs of students. By continuously assessing student understanding, educators can adjust teaching strategies to address learning gaps and provide appropriate challenges, promoting deeper learning and retention.

4. **Student Engagement and Motivation:** Involving students in the assessment process through self-assessment and peer feedback can increase their investment in learning. Formative assessment practices that encourage student participation have been shown to enhance motivation and foster a sense of ownership over their learning. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2024.2371169?utm_source=openai))

5. **Sustained Feedback and Reflection:** Providing timely and constructive feedback allows students to understand their progress and areas for improvement. When feedback is integrated into the learning process, it can lead to better retention and transfer of knowledge. Research suggests that formative assessment, when coupled with immediate feedback, effectively promotes student mastery of content. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-023-02200-0?utm_source=openai))

In summary, implementing formative assessment in K-12 classrooms involves strategic teacher training, the integration of technology, adaptive instructional practices, and fostering student engagement. These elements collectively contribute to a more responsive and effective learning environment, supporting the continuous development of students' skills and knowledge.

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

Formative assessment in K-12 classrooms is described as a classroom practice that provides information about student learning to be used by teachers and by students’ peers as feedback and to modify teaching and learning activities [1]. It is also described as “assessment for learning,” “assessment as learning,” and classroom assessment used to inform decisions about instruction, feedback, grading, intervention, and placement [2, 3, 4, 5].

Black and Wiliam’s definition recurs across sources: “Practice in a classroom is formative to the extent that evidence about student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or their peers, to make decisions about the next steps in instruction that are likely to be better, or better founded, than the decisions they would have taken in the absence of the evidence that was elicited” [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. The definition is also repeated in the literature as “all those activities undertaken by teachers and/or by their students [that] provide information to be used as feedback to modify the teaching and learning activities in which they are engaged” [11]. Another formulation states: “assessment for learning is the process by which teachers and learners use and interpret assessment results in order to decide ‘where they are in their learning, where they need to go, and how best to get there’” [12].

**Questioning / checks for understanding / classroom dialogue**

Questioning is repeatedly identified as a common or core formative assessment strategy [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. In the snippet from *Informal Formative Assessment Conversations in Mathematics*, “Many studies also support conversational interaction-based informal formative assessments in supporting students’ learning, and suggest that questioning is the most common strategy to engage” [1]. In *Formative assessment in science education: Is it being practiced?*, teachers may use “the Socratic questioning or other evidence-eliciting techniques” and the ten dimensions include “questioning strategies that elicit evidence of student learning” and “feedback loops during questioning” [2]. In *The Application of Formative Evaluation Strategies in College English Classroom from the Perspective of Teacher Questioning*, teacher questioning is described as a way to collect important information about the current learning level of students so that teachers can better adjust their teaching strategies to promote students’ learning; it follows “teacher initiation-student response-teacher feedback/evaluation (IRF/E)” [13]. That source also states that “teacher questioning cannot be used as an evaluation tool under any circumstances” unless the questions help students understand what they are learning, the student response represents the student’s thinking level, and teachers take meaningful interventions to promote learning [13].

In *ESL Teachers’ Questioning Technique in an Assessment for Learning Context: Promising or Problematic?*, students in an AfL classroom “are exposed to the learning intentions at the very beginning of the learning and instruction process” and know “the learning intentions and criteria for success” [14]. The same source states that when criteria for success are established, teachers need to ask questions to ensure learning and progress toward learning intentions; “effective questioning technique plays an important part in student learning to enhance executive function ability to develop reasoning,” “challenge students’ beliefs and background knowledge,” and “strengthen their arguments and propositions” [14]. In *The use of formative assessments in traditional and hybrid lecture-labs of industrial engineering undergraduates and their motivational profiles*, “the five key strategies” include “engineering classroom discussions, questions, and learning tasks that elicit evidence of learning” [15].

The open web search summary also described questioning as helping teachers gauge students’ understanding in real time, with examples of “open-ended, focused, or reflective” questions; “quick, informal assessments like exit tickets, thumbs up/down, or short quizzes”; and “teachers use assessment data to make decisions about pacing, grouping, and instructional strategies” [16]. While this open-web source is less specific than the academic snippets, it aligns with the research snippets on questioning and checks for understanding [16].

**Peer assessment / self assessment / student agency**

Peer assessment and self-assessment appear repeatedly as key formative practices [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 14, 15, 17]. In *Formative assessment in science education: Is it being practiced?*, the ten criteria include “peer assessment” and “self-assessment,” and the paper states that formative assessment “underpins student involvement both as evaluators of their own learning and as resources to other classmates” [2]. It further says that through “providing descriptive feedback, the students gain an understanding of their strengths and weaknesses in connection with classroom learning” [2].

In *A systematic review on the formative assessment practice in teaching and learning in secondary school*, the first theme is “the diversity of assessments,” with three subthemes: “teacher assessment; peer-assessment; and self-assessment” [3]. The paper states that “the diversity of assessment in the classroom suggests that AfL three agent roles: teacher, student, and peer” [3]. It also says peers “play a role by helping each other to complete the group assignments given by the teacher,” “help each other understand the task,” and “high-achieving students help each other with their low-performing peers” [3]. The same source describes self-assessment as “a test question instrument, where the students can self-assess each concept, they learned” [3]. It also notes “Teachers questioning practices were also practiced as a measure to assess their students” and “Follow-up action on teacher feedback was also implemented by teachers” [3].

In *Basic psychological needs satisfaction as a mediator of the effects of a formative assessment practice on behavioral engagement and autonomous motivation*, formative assessment is described as teacher-centered, student-centered, or a combination of these [7]. In student-centered approaches, “the students are involved in peer assessment and peer feedback and/or self-assessment in order to take a more proactive role in the core formative assessment processes of identifying their learning needs and acting on this information to improve their learning” [7]. The same source states that “the teacher’s role is to help the students become motivated and proficient in carrying out these processes” [7].

In *Assessment for learning strategies: Amharic Language Teachers’ Practice and Challenges in Ethiopia*, the second section of the questionnaire included a sub-section on “self and peer assessment alternatives” with items such as “Lessons on new topics begin with pupils being invited to reflect on their prior learning,” “Pupils use each other as resources for learning,” and “Assessment techniques are used to create an environment in which pupils can be honest about areas where they are experiencing difficulty” [17].

In *Rethinking the Uses of Assessment in the Second Language Classroom*, students are “highly involved through direct participation in assessing their own or their peers’ work” [11]. That source also says “it involves students in self-assessment” and “it provides feedback, which leads to students recognizing their next steps and how to take them” [11]. In *Teacher Candidates’ Views On Self And Peer Assessment As A Tool For Student Development*, self and peer assessment help students become “active participants in their own learning and that of their peers,” and these practices support “professional development” [18].

**Feedback**

Feedback is one of the most consistently emphasized mechanisms in the findings [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 19]. In *Exploring Primary School Teachers’ Conceptions of “Assessment for Learning”*, “An essential feature of formative assessment is feedback” and Black (1993) considers an assessment formative when it provides feedback to students and teachers “about the learning that is occurring, during the teaching and learning, not after the learning ends” [11]. The paper further says “other researchers such as Clarke (2005) also agreed that feedback is seen to be the fundamental aspect of formative assessment interaction for the purpose to support learning” [11].

In *Formative assessment in science education: Is it being practiced?*, “ongoing and collaborative feedback is provided to the students to improve learning and teaching,” and “Through providing descriptive feedback, the students gain an understanding of their strengths and weaknesses in connection with classroom learning” [2]. That source also says “limited feedback to the students may not lead to improved student learning as suggested by a significant body of research” [2]. The ten criteria include “individualised descriptive feedback” [2].

In *Rethinking the Uses of Assessment in the Second Language Classroom*, assessment for learning “provides information that both teachers and students can use as feedback to adjust teaching and learning practices” [11]. It “helps teachers identify areas where further explanation or more practice is needed as well as which methodological changes can be implemented so that students are more successful in their learning” [11]. In the same source, feedback “provides specific suggestions to help achieve improvement” and self-assessment “encourages students to take responsibility for their own learning” [11].

In *The Application of Formative Evaluation Strategies in College English Classroom from the Perspective of Teacher Questioning*, “teacher feedback” is a formative evaluation strategy, and the paper emphasizes that teachers should “take meaningful interventions to promote students to achieve their learning goals” [13]. The paper also notes that “teachers should check the entire process of classroom questioning and ensure that each step cannot be separated from the purpose of learning” [13].

In *STUDENT TEACHERS’ CONCEPTION OF FEEDBACK WITHIN AN ASSESSMENT FOR LEARNING ENVIRONMENT: LINK TO PUPIL ASPIRATION*, feedback is “the key component of assessment for learning” [20]. Feedback is “information such as knowledge, skills or attitudes provided by teachers, peers, books, parents, self or experiences regarding one’s performance” [20]. The paper says teachers are expected to assess during teaching and learning so feedback can “improve students’ learning and also to enable teachers to modify their teaching strategies” [20]. It gives examples that teachers could do “questioning techniques to determine knowledge, skills and values of students” and use the information to “modify their lesson plan for the next class” [20]. It also states that “feedback during peer-assessment produces an internalize force in themselves regarding learning intentions and success criteria in the context of their peers work, which has more powerful effect on them” [20].

In *Shaping an Adaptive Path on Analytic Geometry with Automatic Formative Assessment and Interactive Feedback*, feedback is described as “probably the most distinctive and characteristic element of formative assessment” [21]. It must answer “Where am I going?”, “How am I going?”, and “Where am I going next?” [21]. The paper also states that feedback can work at “the activity level,” “the process level,” “the self-regulation level,” and “the personal level” [21].

In *How Formative Assessments Drive Instructional Decision Making in the Classroom*, “Feedback needs to be specific, concrete, and promote a change in learning for students” [4]. It says a majority of homework feedback showed “simple comments like ‘good job’ or merely a check mark,” and “The feedback provided on the homework documents lacked effectiveness” [4]. In *Quality of teaching at secondary schools in Nicaragua, South Korea, and the Netherlands*, feedback was identified as a dimension that may be missing or reduced to marks: “Many comments indicated a preponderance of feedback as marks on assessment” and “the inference is that feedback on student assessment was not always useful” [22].

**Success criteria / learning intentions / criteria**

Success criteria and learning intentions are central in the definitions and strategies retrieved [2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 20, 21]. In *Formative assessment in science education: Is it being practiced?*, the ten dimensions include “(1) learning goals” and “(2) criteria for success” [2]. In *Rethinking the Uses of Assessment in the Second Language Classroom*, one principle is “It involves sharing learning goals with pupils,” and another is “It aims to help students to know and to recognize the standards they are aiming for” [11]. In *Assessment for learning strategies: Amharic Language Teachers’ Practice and Challenges in Ethiopia*, the first sub-section covered “learning intentions and success criteria” including items like “Assessment techniques are used to assess pupils’ prior learning,” “Pupils are reminded of the learning intentions during lessons,” and “Success criteria are differentiated according to pupils’ needs” [17]. In *ESL Teachers’ Questioning Technique in an Assessment for Learning Context: Promising or Problematic?*, students “learn about the learning intentions and criteria for success as well as the scaffoldings they receive to achieve success” [14]. In *The use of formative assessments in traditional and hybrid lecture-labs of industrial engineering undergraduates and their motivational profiles*, the five key strategies include “Clarifying and sharing learning intentions and criteria for success” [15]. In *A playbill: Rethinking assessment in teacher education*, the five keys include “Clarifying, sharing, and understanding goals for learning and criteria for success with learning” [19]. In *An Intelligent Recommender System for Personalized Test Administration Scheduling With Computerized Formative Assessments*, the “primary goal of formative assessments is to provide students with timely and descriptive feedback based on the learning goals or criteria for success” [5].

**Instructional decisions informed by formative assessment**

Multiple sources explicitly state that formative assessment informs instructional decisions [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17, 21, 23]. In *An Intelligent Recommender System for Personalized Test Administration Scheduling With Computerized Formative Assessments*, formative assessments “are used during instruction to monitor student learning, provide students with feedback, and help them identify target skills that need improvement” and now include “monitoring student’s response to instruction, identifying at-risk students, and informing the instruction to address individual student needs” [5]. The paper says classroom assessments allow teachers to make “a variety of important decisions about learning outcomes (e.g., producing feedback, assigning grades)” and formative assessment should inform “on-going improvement of the curriculum” [5].

In *Exploring Primary School Teachers’ Conceptions of “Assessment for Learning”*, “the evidence of student understanding (and learning) as a result of one round of the formative assessment process should be used to adapt the teaching work to meet learning needs” [11]. The paper states that “substantial learning gains are possible when teachers introduce formative assessment into their classroom practices,” and that when teachers know how students are progressing and where they are having trouble, they can make “necessary instructional adjustments, such as reteach, trying alternative instructional approaches, or offering more opportunities for practice” [11].

In *From Classroom to Online: Comparing the Effectiveness and Student Academic Performance of Classroom Learning and Online Learning*, assessment is used to obtain information used to make decisions about “students, curriculum, and educational policy” [24]. The paper says “formative assessment enables teachers in making important daily instruction decisions” and teachers can “monitor and interpret students’ progress and give a constructive feedback to help improve the students’ learning and the teaching methods” [24]. It concludes that “the purpose of formative assessment in the classroom is to improve instruction” and assessment information is used “to inform subsequent teaching and learning” [24].

In *Assessment for Learning Explored in Grade 9 Applied Mathematics Classrooms*, formative assessment is valuable for struggling students and teachers should use it to see “where they are in their learning, where they need to go, and how best to get there” [10]. It says formative assessment “helps teachers identify areas where further explanation or more practice is needed as well as which methodological changes can be implemented so that students are more successful in their learning” [10]. It also says teachers and students use formative assessment information to adjust teaching and learning [10].

In *How Formative Assessments Drive Instructional Decision Making in the Classroom*, classroom activities such as mini-lessons and conferencing “provided students with feedback,” but “the activities were not connected to self-assessment or learning targets” [4]. Lesson plans often lacked documentation of formative assessment, and “The local district did not develop a system for teachers to correctly incorporate formative assessment practices” [4]. The paper says formative assessment “consists of asking three questions and incorporating seven strategies in a cyclical manner to improve student learning” [4].

In *Classroom Assessment as Co-Regulated Learning: A Systematic Review*, “Effective classroom assessment is used by teachers and students to articulate learning targets, collect feedback about where students are in relation to those targets, and prompt adjustments to instruction by teachers, as well as changes to learning processes and revision of work products by students” [23]. It also summarizes the regulation process in three questions: “Where am I going? How am I going? and Where to next?” [23].

In *The effectiveness of formative assessment for enhancing reading achievement in K-12 classrooms: A meta-analysis*, formative assessment is broadly defined as an active and intentional process in which teachers “continuously and systematically elicit, interpret and use evidence about students’ learning and conceptual organization (how) to guide their pedagogical plans (why), and/or students ... work with/without teachers or peers to adjust their current learning tactics ... with an effort to improve their achievements and self-regulate their learning” [25].

In *Students’ Voices on E-Portfolio-Based English Listening Assessment Using Google Sites*, formative assessment “directs teacher decision making about future instruction” and “teachers will also be able to check their learners’ development and decide on what they need to develop their mastery” [26]. It also says formative assessment helps the learner establish “an index to their own learning” and provides “instant feedback on understanding and learning” [26].

In *Analysis of instruction/decision making in a study on formative feedback and peer/self-assessment*, there is repeated emphasis that “evidence of learning is actually used to adapt the teaching to meet student needs” [27]. In *Shaping an Adaptive Path on Analytic Geometry with Automatic Formative Assessment and Interactive Feedback*, formative assessment is used to “make decisions about next steps in instruction” [21]. In *The Application of Formative Evaluation Strategies in College English Classroom from the Perspective of Teacher Questioning*, teacher questioning is used so that teachers can “better adjust their teaching strategies” [13].

**Delivery models / implementation forms**

The findings include several delivery models and implementation forms.

1. **Informal conversational classroom assessment**: *Informal Formative Assessment Conversations in Mathematics* emphasizes “classroom conversations,” “IRF sequences,” and assessment conversations “embedded in classroom teaching and occur spontaneously and informally” [1].
2. **Planned school- or unit-based formative assessment**: *Formative assessment in science education: Is it being practiced?* says “When formative assessment is integrated into classroom instruction, it is a planned process” [2]. It uses explicit dimensions and teacher/student self-reflection surveys [2].
3. **Teacher-centered, student-centered, or combined approaches**: *Basic psychological needs satisfaction as a mediator of the effects of a formative assessment practice on behavioral engagement and autonomous motivation* explicitly states that formative assessment practices may be teacher-centered, student-centered, or a combination [7].
4. **Computerized formative assessment**: *An Intelligent Recommender System for Personalized Test Administration Scheduling With Computerized Formative Assessments* says computerized formative assessments integrate computer technologies and measurement theory to manage and deliver classroom assessments [5].
5. **Automatic formative assessment in digital learning environments**: *Analyzing Interactions in Automatic Formative Assessment Activities for Mathematics in Digital Learning Environments* describes formative assessment as a key principle in physical or virtual learning environments and identifies teacher, student, and peers as principal agents [6].
6. **Rubrics and instructional rubrics**: *Beyond Fairness and Consistency in Grading: The Role of Rubrics in Higher Education* says rubrics support summative and formative assessments; instructional rubrics are a formative tool that promote student self-assessment, peer assessment, and feedback literacy [28].
7. **Homework as a formative assessment vehicle**: *How Formative Assessments Drive Instructional Decision Making in the Classroom* uses homework documents as a formative assessment context and finds the district had not created a system for incorporating formative assessment practices [4].
8. **Video-supported coaching / online coaching / instructional coaching**: Several sources discuss coaching models as delivery supports for formative assessment implementation, including online modules, peer study groups, classroom walkthroughs, teacher inquiry, video coaching, and instructional coaching [29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34].
9. **Mentorship / teacher education integration**: *Fostering Effective Teaching Practices: Integrating Formative Assessment and Mentorship in Indonesian Preservice Teacher Education* focuses on mentorship in guiding preservice teachers to use formative assessment practices [35].

**Professional development supports**

The sources give multiple forms of professional development (PD) support for implementing formative assessment and related coaching.

- *Investigating the Efficacy of a Professional Development Program in Formative Classroom Assessment in Middle School English Language Arts and Mathematics* reports a professional development program implemented in “state-identified, low performing middle schools from November 2005 through April 2008” [29]. In Year 1 it was “implemented by an assessment coach” in treatment schools and no PD was provided in control schools; in Years 2 and 3, PD was implemented by “an assessment coach or a relatively untrained facilitator” [29]. The program increased teacher assessment skill regardless of implementation by a trained coach or a relatively untrained facilitator, but students of teachers participating in the PD “tended to demonstrate lower achievement than a matched set of students whose teachers did not receive the professional development” [29]. The study also used a “multi-site, cluster randomized trial” in Year 1 and a “quasi-experimental design” in Years 2 and 3 [29].
- *How Formative Assessments Drive Instructional Decision Making in the Classroom* says “professional development workshops were developed to help teachers build their formative assessment knowledge,” and “professional development plan highlights strategies to increase teachers’ understanding of the formative assessment process and to apply learning targets, feedback, and student self-assessment when assigning homework” [4]. It also says “The formative assessment process consists of asking three questions and incorporating seven strategies in a cyclical manner to improve student learning” [4].
- *Promoting Student Ownership of Learning Through High-Impact Formative Assessment Practices* describes a “five-year professional development initiative” that “employs online modules, peer study groups, classroom walkthroughs, and teacher inquiry into their classroom practices and the beliefs that drive them” [19]. It says the initiative involved the Armstrong School District and the Center for Advancing the Study of Teaching and Learning at the Duquesne University School of Education [19].
- *Online Continuous Professional Learning: A Model for Improving Reading Outcomes in Regional and Remote Schools?* states that the online CPL was designed “to provide the schools with the knowledge, skills, and resources to ensure the school was able to maintain the program and instructional coaching practices once the online support from the researchers was no longer available” [30]. It says the online coach’s role was to “provide the literacy expertise and model appropriate interactions between coach and teachers,” while the in-school coach supported local implementation [30].
- *A Novel Approach to Professional Development in Middle School Science: Instructional Coaching by University Professors to Improve the Instructional Core* describes teachers submitting unit outlines to university coaches for review and feedback, making revisions, receiving “three real-time observations” via Adobe Connect, and participating in individual coaching sessions [31]. In year two there were six PD sessions embedded with instructional coaching over 27.5 hours of PD, with continuous feedback and revision opportunities electronically [31]. Teachers received additional exemplars and targeted focus on releasing control, integration of Common Core State Standards for Literacy, and the use of formative and summative assessments [31].
- *Development of Mathematics and Science Teacher Competencies through Coaching* used a coaching system implemented in a private primary school in Thailand; the coaching process lasted “twenty weeks,” included “an initial classroom visit,” “face-to-face conferences between coaches and coachees every other Saturday,” and “periodic video demonstrations” [32].
- *Teacher Video Coaching, From Design Features to Student Impacts: A Systematic Literature Review* says coaching is consistent with research-based PD features such as “a focus on content, active learning, sustained duration, coherence, and collective participation,” and the combination of video and coaching “seems particularly promising for in-service teacher professional development” [33].
- *Keeping Teachers Afloat with Instructional Coaching: Coaching Structure and Implementation* describes the coaching cycle as having a “reflection and feedback” stage or “improve” step that helps coaches and teachers identify improvement in teaching practices and student outcomes [34]. It says the cycle can continue if goals are not met, and that coaching activities in pre-conference, observation, and post-observation should be designed to accomplish the myriad purposes of each stage [34].
- *Principals’ Sensemaking of Coaching for Ambitious Reading Instruction in a High-Stakes Accountability Policy Environment* says literacy coaching is aligned with effective PD emphasizing “sustained, connected learning opportunities for teachers” and includes modeling and guidance/feedback as teachers enact new practices [36].
- *Considerations when using rating scales to support teacher professional development: A commentary on Weadman, Serry and Snow (2022)* says a recent meta-analysis concluded that instructional coaching has a pooled effect size of “.49 SD on teacher’s practice and .18 SD on child outcomes” [37]. It adds that effective coaching programs commonly include “observation, feedback, goal-setting, and reflection” [37].
- *Effective Teacher Professional Development for School-Based Mental Health Promotion: A Review of the Literature* states that “The delivery of performance feedback is also an opportunity to develop teachers’ motivation for change and to highlight and build on strengths” and that observation and feedback can take many forms, including live in-person observations with real-time feedback, video submissions with detailed written feedback and occasional video chat, or online reports [38].
- *A playbill: Rethinking assessment in teacher education* notes that formative assessment implementation required reforming assessment practices and that teachers used the “five keys” as a blueprint for reform [19].
- *Fostering Effective Teaching Practices: Integrating Formative Assessment and Mentorship in Indonesian Preservice Teacher Education* argues that implementing formative assessment depends on teacher, student, assessment, and context; it highlights the need for preservice teacher education and mentorship support [35].

**Mechanisms proposed to connect formative assessment to student achievement**

The mechanisms proposed across sources are consistent and recurring:

- **Adaptive instruction based on evidence**: Teachers collect evidence, interpret it, and use it to adjust teaching to meet student needs [5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 21, 23, 25, 26].
- **Feedback that moves learning forward**: Specific, descriptive, timely feedback is repeatedly described as a mechanism [2, 4, 5, 11, 12, 13, 20, 21, 28].
- **Goal clarity / learning intentions / success criteria**: Students need to know where they are going and what success looks like [2, 7, 8, 9, 11, 14, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23].
- **Student self-regulation and ownership**: Formative assessment supports students as owners of learning, self-assessors, and self-regulated learners [7, 8, 9, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25, 28].
- **Peer learning and peer feedback**: Students support each other’s learning through peer assessment and peer feedback [3, 7, 15, 18, 23, 28].
- **Teacher professional development and coaching**: Teachers need support to implement formative assessment with fidelity [4, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 36, 37, 38].
- **Coherence of assessment and curriculum/instruction**: Formative assessment is effective when assessment tasks align with learning goals and instructional sequence [4, 11, 29].
- **Classroom dialogue / questioning / IRF sequences**: Informal formative assessment conversations and questioning create evidence and allow responsive moves [1, 13, 14, 21].
- **Use of technology and computerized systems**: Computerized assessments, automated feedback, learning analytics, and online coaching were described as ways to support implementation [5, 6, 30, 33].
- **Metacognition and self-monitoring**: Assessment for learning supports students in goal setting, monitoring progress, and revision and adjustment [7, 11, 19, 21, 23].
- **Motivation and engagement pathways**: Formative assessment is suggested as a possible way to support student motivation, with satisfaction of basic psychological needs as one proposed mediator [7, 19, 38].
