**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

Formative assessment is repeatedly defined in the gathered material as assessment used during instruction to gather evidence, provide feedback, and improve teaching and learning, and it is repeatedly distinguished from summative assessment, diagnostic testing, interim assessment, grading, and feedback that is not acted on.

Rashid and Jaidin state that: “Formative assessment is defined as a systematic process to continuously gather evidence and provide feedback about learning while instruction is under way (CERI, 2008). Formative assessment can therefore be considered as a diagnostic method of assessing teaching and learning as it provides a platform for teachers and students to give and receive feedback before and during lessons. Formative assessment also allows teachers to monitor and guide students' performance over time in multiple problem-solving situations. Summative assessment, on the other hand, takes place after a period of instruction and requires making a judgment about the learning that occurred for example scoring a topical test or grading a monthly test paper. Scholars generally agree that formative assessment is the process of using information about students' learning on the course of instruction to make decisions to improve learning... regular testing and simply informing students of their scores do not constitute formative assessment. Instead, according to Black et al. (2004), the evidence of student understanding (and learning) as a result of one round of the formative assessment process should be used to adapt the teaching work to meet learning needs. Reviews of research by Crooks (1988) have demonstrated that substantial learning gains are possible when teachers introduce formative assessment into their classroom practices. When teachers know how students are progressing and where they are having trouble, such information can be used to make necessary instructional adjustments, such as reteach, trying alternative instructional approaches, or offering more opportunities for practice. An essential feature of formative assessment is feedback. Black (1993) considers an assessment as formative when it provides feedback to students and teachers about the learning that is occurring, during the teaching and learning, not after the learning ends. Other researchers such as Clarke (2005) also agreed that feedback is seen to be the fundamental aspect of formative assessment interaction for the purpose to support learning.” [1]

Wenzel, Hovey, and Ittner state that: “Formative assessment is the process by which teachers continually collect evidence of student understanding and skill, and provide students with specific and relevant feedback necessary to move forward and be more successful in their learning (Black & William, 1998; Heritage, 2007; Moss & Brookhart, 2019). The term 'formative assessment' has been defined and redefined over the decades starting with Scriven (1967) who used the term 'formative evaluation' to describe the role evaluation played in improving curriculum. Sadler (1989, p. 120) added a revised perception of formative assessment stating that, "[f]ormative assessment is concerned with how judgments about the quality of student responses (performances, pieces, or works) can be used to shape and improve student's competence by short-circuiting the randomness and inefficiency of trial-and-error learning". A decade later, Black and Williams (1998, p. 140) provided a more nuanced definition of formative assessment "to refer to all those activities undertaken by teachers-and by their students in assessing themselves-that provide information to be used as feedback to modify teaching and learning activities. Such assessment becomes formative assessment when the evidence is actually used to adapt the teaching to meet student needs". Though the definition of formative assessment has morphed over the better half of a century, this essential, in-process, evaluation practice is seen as a linchpin of student success as it enables teachers to collect relevant student data that can be used to improve instruction to more effectively target students' needs. Included in formative assessment is the ability to clearly state learning goals, provide specific feedback, and understand how to move students through a progression of learning (Heritage, 2007). The element of providing specific, timely feedback is especially important as it has been tied to student outcomes (Hattie & Timberely, 2007).” [2]

Xuan, Cheung, and Sun describe formative assessment interventions in K-12 reading and state that the review included studies where “Classroom practices align with the definition of formative assessment in this review” and where treatment groups embedded with formative assessment activities were compared with control groups using standard/traditional methods. They also state: “Studies with pretest differences of more than 50% of a standard deviation were excluded because, large pretest differences could not be adequately managed as underlying distributions may be fundamentally different even with analyses of covariance (Shadish et al., 2002).” The search procedures explicitly included “formative assessment,” “formative evaluation,” “feedback,” “assessment for learning,” “assessment as learning,” “curriculum-based assessment,” “differentiated instruction,” “portfolio assessment,” “performance assessment,” “process assessment,” “progress monitoring,” and “response to intervention,” plus contextualized assessment projects and systems including “DIALANG (Diagnostic Language Assessment)” and “CoDiAs (Cognitive Diagnostic Assessment System).” [3]

Zhang, Ge, and Mohd Saad’s systematic review of formative assessment in K-12 English as a foreign language education explicitly excluded studies outside English, reviews, and theoretical studies. They state: “The study focused on formative assessment in English classroom instruction.” Their exclusion criteria included: “The study did not focus on learning-focused, classroom-based, sustainable or learning-oriented assessment or assessment as learning,” and “The method used in the study did not align with a formative assessment approach. Assessment was considered to be formative when teachers and students used information to adjust their teaching and learning methods (e.g. portfolio).” They conclude that after screening and exclusions, “40 articles were ultimately retained and incorporated into the analysis.” [4]

Govender states: “I selected the following definition of formative assessment: All those activities undertaken by teachers, and by their students in assessing themselves, which provide information to be used as feedback to modify the teaching and learning activities in which they are engaged. Such assessment becomes 'formative assessment' when the evidence is actually used to adapt the teaching work to meet the needs of learners. (Black & Wiliam, 1998:7).” Govender further states that “assessment is formative only when the evidence of learning prompts teachers to modify their instruction and activities to improve the learning processes and learning outcomes.” [5]

Farisia explicitly distinguishes diagnostic testing and formative assessment: “In the research of Van der Kleij, et.al found various terms of formative assessment, namely assessment for learning (assessment for learning) and diagnostic tests (diagnostic testing) (Van der Kleij et al., 2015). Although in many other references it is found that the mention of diagnostic tests is different from formative assessments, but diagnostic tests here are intended as part of formative assessments to obtain initial data regarding students' abilities. The mention of this term has theoretical implications for the definition of formative assessment as all forms of assessment aimed at supporting student learning. Formative assessment in this context is considered as the "big umbrella" of all types of assessments that aim to help students achieve their learning outcomes (Briggs et al., 2012; Van der Kleij et al., 2015).” The same snippet states: “Formative assessment is a process that engages teachers and students during instruction in gathering, interpreting, and using evidence about what and how students learn to facilitate further student learning (Bailey & Heritage, 2008; Black & William, 2009; Brookhart, 2011).” [6]

Temel, Barenthien, and Padubrin state: “The essential role of assessment, and specifically the formative assessment in improving teaching and learning processes has been emphasized by numerous studies ... The choice and use of an assessment approach depend on the educational purpose. In general, however, standards-based summative assessment, also known as assessment of learning, is often used in classrooms. There is considerable interest in formative assessment strategies, often referred to as "assessment for learning" (Wiliam, 2010a(Wiliam, , 2010b)). However, the main difference between formative and summative assessment is not in their timing, but rather in their purpose and impact (Harlen & James, 1997). Formative assessment was defined by Black & Wiliam (1998) as follows: "We use the general term assessment to refer to all those activities undertaken by teachers and by their students in assessing themselves that provide information to be used as feedback to modify teaching and learning activities. Such assessment becomes formative when the evidence is actually used to adapt the teaching to meet student needs." As highlighted in this definition, feedback plays a crucial role in enhancing learning and achievement...” [7]

Boussakuk et al. separate formative, summative, and diagnostic assessment explicitly: “Evaluation is central to teaching and learning. What is evaluated defines how it is learned and how it is taught. According to [20] and [21], three types of assessments can be found in the educational system: formative, summative, and diagnostic.” They define formative assessment as “a process that provides constructive feedback to both student and teacher on a given item or topic,” say it is “usually carried out during the learning process,” define summative assessment as “the primary purpose of this type of assessment is a certification goal or a judgment on the learner's overall performance,” and define diagnostic assessment as identifying “learners' needs, skills, prior knowledge, and preconceptions” and that it is “generally undertaken at the beginning of a course.” [8]

Osman states that formative assessment “has its main focus to monitor and improve upon students' learning and classroom activities,” “occurs during instruction,” is “also called 'assessment for learning',” and “is diagnostic as it is used to monitor students learning as well as identify students learning difficulties to offer remedial measures where applicable to enhance students learning.” Osman also states: “Feedback is a vital feature in formative assessment. Providing timely feedback to students enables them to recognize their strengths and weakness in learning and improve on them. Feedback goes beyond providing scores on performance to students to engaging them in dialogue...” [9]

Filiz, Trumpower, Ghani, Atas, and Vanapalli state: “There has been a shift from a primary focus on summative assessment to formative assessment ... yet what formative assessment is remains an issue. Some claim that formative assessment refers to assessment instruments whereas others believe that it is a process ... Defining formative assessment as only an instrument causes confusion when formative feedback is given on summative assessment ... Therefore, even though an assignment might be designed or planned as summative, its methodology, data analysis and use of results determine whether it is formative or summative ...” They also quote Cizek (2010) defining assessment for learning as “the collaborative processes engaged in by educators and students for the purpose of understanding the students' learning and conceptual organization, identification of strengths, diagnosis of weaknesses, areas for improvement, and as a source of information that teachers can use in instructional planning and students can use in deepening their understandings and improving their achievement.” [10]

Matilda and Helen state: “Assessment in the classroom typically involve placement, formative and summative assessment. Placement (Pre-assessment) is done to determine if students have enough prior knowledge to begin new instruction. Formative assessment is that done during when instruction is ongoing in the classroom. The purpose is to identify specific areas of learning difficulties and to make adequate adjustment to promote learning. While summative assessment is done at the end or after instruction or programme to ascertain the level the students' achievement in the overall objectives of the programme.” They further state: “When teachers begin to aim at assessing students in the classroom to improve learning and achievement far more than collecting information to assign grades or certifying mastery, therefore, perhaps of greatest importance is formative assessment... Formative assessment is commonly referred to as assessment for learning. Assessment Reform Group (ARD, 2002) explained assessment for learning as any assessment for which the first priority in its design and practice is to serve the purpose of promoting pupils' learning. It differs from assessment designed primarily to serve the purpose of accountability, or for ranking or of certifying competence.” [11]

Karaman’s meta-analysis states: “Formative assessment strategy plays a crucial role in supporting the student learning. This assessment strategy provides effective feedback and instructional correctives in the teaching-learning process to improve students' learning, motivation, and selfregulation skills... Formative assessment also known as assessment for learning, diagnostic testing, and feedback is an ongoing process used by teachers, students, and students' peers ... Teachers can adjust their teaching practices to increase student learning through formative assessment...” It also states that the study synthesized “experimental and quasi-experimental studies” on the effectiveness of formative assessment practices on student learning in Turkey. [12]

Okyere and Larbi state: “Basically, there are two types of assessment. These are formative and summative assessment. Formative assessment is the type which takes place during instruction. It is used to monitor students' learning towards the achievement of set targets... Hence, it is often called assessment for learning... Since its prime focus is to improve upon students' learning, it seeks to identify students' learning difficulties or deficiencies and for any remediation where necessary to enhance performance of the students ... This makes formative assessment diagnostic in nature.” They also state: “Some formative assessment procedures are class tests, project work, assignments, presentations, quizzes.” They further note: “Providing immediate feedback is an element of formative assessment...” [13]

Paul et al. provide a review stating: “The existence of a plethora of empirical evidence documenting the improvement of educational outcomes through the use of formative assessment is conventional wisdom within education. In reality, a limited body of scientifically based empirical evidence exists to support that formative assessment directly contributes to positive educational outcomes. The use of formative assessments, or other diagnostic efforts within classrooms, provides information that should help facilitate improved pedagogical practices and instructional outcomes. However, a review of the formative assessment literature revealed that there is no agreed upon lexicon with regard to formative assessment and suspect methodological approaches in the efforts to demonstrate positive effects that could be attributed to formative assessments. Thus, the purpose of this article was two-fold. First, the authors set out to clarify the terminology related to formative assessment and its usage. Finally, the article provides a critical analysis of the seminal literature on formative assessment.” [14]

Sowell states: “Understanding formative assessment requires first understanding summative assessment. Summative assessment is assessment of learning, ending with a grade that counts, often at the end of an assignment or course ... For writing assignments, summative assessment typically means a score on a written assignment ... Formative assessment, in contrast, is assessment for learning; formative assessment is ungraded feedback that lets students know what they have done well and gives them guidance on what they can do to improve. Formative assessments are not only beneficial for students however, they are also important for teachers as they inform instructional changes...” [15]

Yan, Li, Panadero, Yang, Yang, and Lao state: “We used synonym terms of formative assessment to reach a wider range of studies. After checking preliminary hits, five key terms including Formative assessment, Assessment for learning, Formative evaluation, Formative review and Learning-oriented assessment were chosen.” They explicitly excluded studies that used self-assessment or peer assessment for non-formative purposes and note: “some studies that did not explore teachers' roles were excluded as they did not provide relevant information regarding the objectives of this review. Furthermore, studies that used self-assessment or peer assessment for non-formative purposes ... are beyond the scope of the current review.” [16]

Sagarika, Kandakatla, and Gulhane explicitly classify assessment into summative and formative and state: “Summative: They are used for grading purpose at the end of the semester and can also be defined as "assessment of learning". ii) Formative: They are used to give feedback and not to grade them and are also defined as "assessment for learning". Formative assessments are used as a means to provide feedback to both the teachers and the students during the learning process, for example, diagnostic assessment or testdirected assessments... Formative assessments should therefore be aligned with the pedagogy to administer the learning process and later modifying the content delivery based on the results of the assessment.” [17]

Apostolache states: “Formative assessment has been defined as "activities undertaken by teachers-and by their students in assessing themselves-that provide information to be used as feedback to modify teaching and learning activities" (Black & Wiliam, 2010, p. 82). Formative assessment gathers information about student learning in order to facilitate knowledge development... Formative tools are being used during a lesson or unit of study. It is constantly used to provide descriptive feedback, to track children progress, to make changes into instruction process, to improve formative process. Most frequently used formative methods are observations, homework question and answer sessions, self-evaluations, portfolios, reflections on performance, curriculum-based measurement games, discussions, informal interviews ... Planned formative assessments also include activities such as quizzes that are assigned to assess child progress.” [18]

Ras, Whitelock, and Kalz state: “The definitions that followed considered formative assessment as a process: "the process used by teachers and student to recognise and respond to student learning in order to enhance that learning, during the learning" ... "assessment carried out during the instructional process for the purpose of improving teaching or learning" ... "frequent, interactive assessments of students' progress and understanding to identify learning needs and adjust teaching appropriately" ... They emphasise that the commercial testing industry often uses the term formative assessment for assessments which are done regularly to inform educators about whether standards are mastered or not. In fact, these have nothing to do with day-to-day and individualadjusted instruction. Although we will discuss Assessment FOR Learning and relevant strategies and principles ... it is important to recognise that Assessment OF Learning is a central process in education and training.” They also state: “The difference between formative assessment and assessment for learning was explained by Stiggins (2005). Bulut, Cormier, and Shin state: “Classroom assessments allow K-12 teachers to evaluate student learning (i.e., monitor students' progress) and make a variety of important decisions about learning outcomes (e.g., producing feedback, assigning grades). Summative assessments are typically used at the end of an instructional period, such as a unit or a semester, to evaluate student learning relative to content standards or benchmarks. Quizzes, midterm exams, or a final project are common examples of teacher-made summative assessments... Unlike summative assessments, formative assessments are used during instruction to monitor student learning, provide students with feedback, and help them identify target skills that need improvement... Today, the primary goal of formative assessments is to provide students with timely and descriptive feedback based on the learning goals or criteria for success...” [20]

Elshawa, Heng, Abdullah, and Rashid state: “In the classrooms, teachers/instructors use assessments mainly for three purposes: diagnostic, formative and summative. Diagnostic, or pre-assessments, usually come before instruction. Instructors use it to check their students' previous knowledge and skills... no grades are given because of the diagnostic nature of the tests. Summative assessment, on the other hand, summarizes what students learned at the end of a course. Good examples of summative assessments are final exams, essays and performances. Grades or scores are given... The third type is formative assessment. This occurs alongside instruction and serves to provide feedback to teachers and students. It serves the purpose of guiding teachers and learners. Examples of this type of assessments are: nongraded quizzes, teacher observation, oral questioning and essay drafting in addition to self-and peer-assessment.” [21]

Refnita and Jufrizal explicitly identify their study as quasi-experimental research and state: “This article discusses the results of quasi-experimental research that compares the effectiveness of matching quizzes and half-minute papers.” They state: “Among the four purposes of assessment (placement, diagnostic, formative, and summative), formative assessment is more important because it evaluates students while forming their competencies and skills to help them continue that process of growing.” They also say: “Formative assessments are an inseparable part of the ongoing process of learning ... Schneider and Meyer state: “Formative classroom assessment can have different connotations depending upon the framework being implemented. These techniques tend to be embedded in the instructional sequence of the teacher. Brookhart (2010) described using formative feedback on summative classroom assessments. In this situation, the teacher uses the formative practice after the instructional sequence to provide students feedback on how to better target the expected outcome on a revision or on a subsequent assignment. Teachers may also use summative assessments to determine that reteaching may be necessary. Although formative classroom assessment practices can have differing proximities to the instructional sequence, what should identify an assessment practice as informative is whether or not the teacher and student effectively use the information to improve student achievement on the intended learning target...” [24]

Gu states: “However, not all classroom tasks are assessment, and classroom-based assessment is not necessarily formative (Black and Wiliam, 2005). Unless the information elicited through the quiz is interpreted and the result relayed back to the students, and unless the students act on the feedback from the quiz result, nothing becomes formative. Likewise, not all alternative forms of assessment such as peer grading can achieve formative functions ... Classroom-based formative assessment is therefore a teaching/ learning event that serves a formative assessment function and which happens within or beyond one class. One complete CBFA event includes 1) elicitation of evidence of students' understanding or learning, 2) interpretation of the elicited information against the learning target or success criteria, 3) feedback based on this interpretation for the student in question, and 4) follow-up action taken by the student and/or teacher to improve learning. ### 1) Core formative-assessment meta-analysis evidence with quantitative moderator/subgroup results

#### Xuan, Cheung, & Sun (2022) — *The effectiveness of formative assessment for enhancing reading achievement in K-12 classrooms: A meta-analysis* [1]
- This quantitative synthesis included **48 qualified studies with a total sample of 116,051 K-12 students** [1].
- The findings suggested that formative assessment generally had a positive though modest effect (**ES = + 0.19**) on students’ reading achievement [1].
- The review reports that subgroup analysis was used to estimate whether the mean effect size was influenced by the features of formative assessment interventions, education level, and publication type [1].
- Reported subgroup / moderator details from the abstract and body snippets:
  - **Studies with 250 or less students** yielded significantly larger effect size than large sample studies (**d = 0.33, p < 0.001**) [1].
  - **Teacher-directed vs student-directed vs integrated assessment**:
    - formative assessment only engaged by teachers had a significantly smaller effect size than integrating teacher and students' assessment in the intervention for reading (**d = -0.12, p < 0.001**) [1].
    - student-directed assessment (selfassessment) showed no significant difference (**d = 0.03, p = 0.769**) [1].
  - **Differentiated instruction**:
    - if a teacher adopted differentiated or individualized instruction during or after formative assessment, students' reading achievement would be significantly higher than those of their peers taught by a teacher only applied formative assessment (**d = 0.13, p < 0.001**) [1].
    - when formative assessment was directed by the student, the effect size on reading achievement was larger than formative assessment with teachers' differentiated instruction, albeit not significantly (**d = 0.17, p = 0.124**) [1].
  - **Research design**:
    - RCT vs QED: effect sizes generated from RCT were smaller than QED design, but not significant (**d = -0.04, p = 0.465**) [1].
  - **Digital technology involvement**:
    - reading achievement was not influenced significantly by formative assessment with digital technology (**d = 0.001, p = 0.978**) [1].
  - **Grade level**:
    - elementary level were slightly larger than those for kindergarten studies (**d = 0.02, p = 0.790**) [1].
    - middle/high school studies were slightly smaller than those for kindergarten studies (**d = -0.03, p = 0.696**) [1].
  - **Student characteristics**:
    - mainstream students vs at-risk students: the estimated effect size on mainstream students was slightly higher than that on at-risk students, albeit not significant (**d = 0.001, p = 0.982**) [1].
  - **Program duration**:
    - one-year or longer programs showed smaller effect size than short-term ones, but the difference was non-significant (**d = -0.02, p = 0.576**) [1].
  - **Cultural setting**:
    - CHC appeared to be smaller than Anglophone culture, though not significant (**d = -0.10, p = 0.297**) [1].
  - **Publication type**:
    - no significant differences were found between published and unpublished articles (**p = 0.701**) [1].
  - The pseudo R 2 value in this meta-regression model estimated the moderators accounted for **95% of heterogeneity** [1].
- The abstract also states:
  - “The effect sizes comparisons of subcategories in rest three moderators, student characteristics, digital technology and research design were non-significant” [1].
  - “Our subgroup analysis data indicated that the effect sizes of formative assessment intervention on reading were significantly different between Confucian-heritage culture and Anglophone culture and had divergent effective features” [1].
- Additional narrative from the conclusion:
  - “The findings of this review indicate that formative assessment produce a positive effect (**ES = + 0.18**) on reading achievement” [1].
  - “The average weighted effect over all included studies was **0.19**” [1].
  - “Studies involving a large sample size with over **250 students** led to low and attenuated estimate of formative assessment” [1].
  - “The implementation of teachers' differentiated instruction is linked to much stronger effects than intervention without differentiated instruction” [1].
  - “Collaboration of teachers and students in formative assessment would be more effective than formative assessment merely initiated by teachers” [1].
  - “It is worth mentioned, in our qualified studies, **94% (34/36)** of the interventions embedded with differentiated instruction were coupled with professional development for teachers” [1].
- Importantly for the user’s question, this meta-analysis explicitly reports **student characteristics** as mainstream vs at-risk students, but the provided snippets do **not** report separate effect sizes for English language learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, or prior achievement strata [1].
- The review explicitly says that “the rest of the moderator variables comparisons were non-significant, although some showed significant results in subgroup analysis” [1].

#### Karaman (2021) — *The Effect of Formative Assessment Practices on Student Learning: A Meta-Analysis Study* [2]
- This meta-analysis studied **32 studies** with a total of **47 effect sizes** [2].
- The overall mean effect size was **.72** [2].
- The overall mean effect size was consistent with previous meta-analysis results that effect sizes of the effectiveness of formative assessment ranged between **.40 and .70** [2].
- The study used subgroup analysis to estimate whether the mean effect size was influenced by the features of formative assessment interventions, education level, and publication type [2].
- Moderator / subgroup details reported:
  - Different types of formative assessment interventions varied in effect:
    - student feedback had the largest effect
    - computer feedback had the smallest effect [2].
  - Reported specific subgroup estimates in the abstract:
    - student initiated formative feedback (**d = 1.16**) had a large effect [2].
    - mixed feedback (**d = .83**) had a large effect [2].
    - adult initiated formative feedback (**d = .69**) had a medium effect [2].
    - computer initiated formative feedback (**d = .42**) had a small effect [2].
  - “education level and publication type had no effect on student academic performance in the study” [2].
- The body snippet reports:
  - overall effect size as **.79** with standard error **.03** in the fixed model [2].
  - heterogeneity test: **Q value was 188.91 with 46 degrees of freedom, and p value under .05** [2].
  - **2 statistic was estimated as 75.65%** [2].
  - random effects model: **g = .72, SE = .07, 95% CI = .59; 85, p<.05** [2].
- This study explicitly labels itself a **meta-analysis study** [2].
- No subgroup effect sizes for ELL, disability, low-income, or prior achievement strata are reported in the supplied snippets [2].

#### Sortwell et al. (2024) — *A Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses on the Impact of Formative Assessment on K-12 Students’ Learning: Toward Sustainable Quality Education* [3]
- This is an **umbrella review** / systematic review of meta-analyses [3].
- It identified **13 meta-analyses** [3].
- The review states that formative assessment was found to produce **trivial to large positive effects** on student learning, with **no negative effects identified** [3].
- It also states that the magnitude of effects varied according to the type of formative assessment [3].
- Methodological quality / certainty statements:
  - the 13 included meta-analysis studies showed moderate (**n = 10**), high (**n = 1**), and low (**n = 2**) methodological quality (AMSTAR-2) [3].
  - robustness of evidence (GRADE) was very low (**n = 9**), low (**n = 3**), and moderate (**n = 1**) [3].
- No subgroup estimates for ELL, disability, low-income, or prior achievement strata are reported in the supplied snippet [3].

#### Young & Kim (2010) — *Using Assessments for Instructional Improvement: A Literature Review.* [4]
- This is a **literature review** [4].
- It reports Black and Wiliam’s (1998) literature review as a source for formative purposes:
  - “They report a meta-analysis that obtained a mean effect size of **0.92** for studies in which teachers pursued explicit procedures for reviewing data and determining next steps based on the analysis, compared with a mean effect size of **0.42** for studies in which teachers used data at their discretion (Fuchs & Fuchs, 1986, cited in Black & Wiliam, 1998)” [4].
  - “Lysakowski and Walberg (1982) also report an average effect size of almost a standard deviation (**0.97**) for the **94 studies** included in their analysis. Among those studies, the **20 studies** focused on corrective feedback resulted in a mean effect size of **0.94**” [4].
- This is a narrative literature review excerpt, not a direct formative-assessment subgroup analysis [4].

#### Wang et al. / Bookworms-related snippet — subgroup moderators include ELL, FRL, special education, baseline achievement [5]
- The paper *The Effects of Bookworms Literacy Curriculum on Student Achievement in Grades 2-5* [5] includes a direct statement in the body snippet:
  - “To explore differentiation in impacts across student subgroups that might respond differently to instruction, the base model was elaborated to include additional interactions with student-level moderators (i.e., English language learner [ELL] status, free/reduced lunch [FRL] status, special education [Sp.Ed.] status, and baseline achievement)” [5].
  - “The baseline achievement moderator variable was calculated as a z-score for each student based on the first observed MAP score during the grade and year in which they first experienced Bookworms; hence, the model of moderation by baseline achievement does not include students from Cohort A (since they never experienced Bookworms), and the design is reduced to a simple interrupted time series without a comparative cohort (i.e., the BAU condition is reflected only in the pre-treatment data for cohorts B, C, and D from Figure 2)” [5].
  - “It is important to note that our moderation analyses are preliminary in nature and do not guarantee that the differences in effects are attributable to differential effects of Bookworms because there may be other confounding factors experienced by students from different subgroups around the same time that Bookworms was implemented” [5].
  - “Finally, the base model was elaborated to include additional random effects at the school level to test for school-specific variation in overall impacts of Bookworms and to assess whether the impacts are significantly larger or smaller in some schools” [5].

### 4) Narrative suggestions / review excerpts explicitly stating limitations or absence of subgroup data

- Xuan et al. (2022) repeatedly note that subgroup comparisons for **student characteristics**, **digital technology**, and **research design** were non-significant [1].
- Xuan et al. (2022) also note that the results caution against generalizing formative assessment across cultural settings without adaptation and encourage effect sizes and intervention features to be investigated in various cultural settings [1].
- Xuan et al. (2022) say the qualified studies include self-assessment only in some categories and that “student-directed assessment is often referred to peer-or selfassessment” [1].
- Karaman (2021) says more empirical studies are needed and that future meta-analysis should investigate additional variables such as subject areas, formality of formative assessment, feedback procedures, and feedback time [2].
- Sortwell et al. (2024) concludes that low-to-very-low certainty of evidence precludes robust recommendations regarding optimal formative assessment strategies for K-12 students [3].
- Young & Kim (2010) concludes that knowledge of how teachers use various assessments for instructional improvement remains limited and presents a literature review [4].
- The ELL meta-analysis by Cho et al. (2021) explicitly states that interventions effective for one group of ELLs may not be effective with others [11].
- The Bookworms paper states its moderation analyses are preliminary and “do not guarantee that the differences in effects are attributable to differential effects” [5].
- The Wang et al. / Bookworms paper also notes that **94% (34/36)** of interventions embedded with differentiated instruction were coupled with professional development for teachers [5].
- The literature on ELLs and special education repeatedly emphasizes underrepresentation, misidentification, and the need for better supports [19][20][22][23][25].
- The papers on inclusive assessment and progress monitoring frame formative assessment as important for special education / inclusive settings, but they do not provide subgroup effect sizes [28][32][33][35].

## Executive Summary

The evidence indicates that formative assessment in K-12 education is generally associated with improved academic achievement relative to business-as-usual instruction, but the average benefits are modest to moderate and highly contingent on implementation quality, subject area, and instructional responsiveness. The strongest pooled evidence comes from the K-12 reading meta-analysis, which found an overall effect of ES = +0.19 across 48 studies and 116,051 students, with larger effects in smaller studies, in interventions that embedded differentiated instruction, and in designs that integrated teacher and student assessment rather than teacher-only assessment [212]. A broader umbrella review of 13 meta-analyses likewise found trivial to large positive effects with no negative effects identified, but judged the underlying certainty low to very low overall [211]. The evidence base is therefore directionally positive, but not strong enough to support a “one-size-fits-all” claim about any single formative assessment model [212][211].

The strongest direct experimental findings are mostly subject-specific rather than K-12-wide. In secondary physics, a randomized experiment with 139 students found that repeated clicker-based formative assessments improved post-test performance by 0.34 SD relative to traditional teaching and reduced anxiety by 0.28 SD (Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics Education, 2021). In secondary chemistry, technology-integrated formative assessment produced higher conceptual scores and procedural knowledge than formative assessment alone and conventional instruction, with large group effects reported as ηp² = 0.21 for conceptual knowledge and ηp² = 0.27 for procedural knowledge [346]. In high school mathematics, a 12-week quasi-experimental study with 51 tenth graders found formative assessment practices significantly improved mathematics achievement and attitudes, but the exact effect size was not reported in the extracted text (Kültür & Kutlu, 2021). In writing, the meta-analysis by Graham, Hebert, and [301] found a pooled effect of d = .63 across grades 1–8, with teacher feedback strongest at d = .89, self-assessment and peer feedback both at d = .62, and computer feedback at d = .38. In reading, [212] found ES = +0.19 and identified substantial moderation by sample size, differentiated instruction, and integrated teacher-student assessment. In a broader K-12 meta-analysis, [309] reported 258 effect sizes from 118 studies and an overall Hedges’ g = 0.25, with larger effects in high school and in quasi-experimental studies, though subgroup details for vulnerable student populations were not provided in the extracted text.

The quasi-experimental and observational evidence broadly corroborates the positive pattern while clarifying implementation and equity conditions. In primary-grade mathematics, [218] found that formative assessment and summative assessment were positively related, that the relationship was stronger in first grade than kindergarten, and that lower-performing classrooms benefited more, though grade level was not ultimately a significant moderator. Boström and [317] reported that a formative assessment practice improved student achievement in mathematics in a secondary-school study, but the extracted text did not provide the exact effect statistic. In primary science, embedded formative assessment studies showed positive conceptual learning and classroom-process effects, but several of these studies are implementation-oriented and do not report fully extractable effect sizes in the available snippets. In ELL-focused reading synthesis, [300] found medium effects for interventions targeting basic reading skills for English learners and reported that upper-elementary students benefited more than secondary students, with strategy-embedded and medium-sized group interventions particularly useful; however, this is adjacent evidence about reading intervention generally rather than formative assessment alone.

Across the tiered questions, the evidence answers Tier 1 partially to well: formative assessment is consistently defined as the elicitation and use of evidence during instruction to adapt teaching, and the most studied outcomes are reading, mathematics, writing, and science achievement, usually via standardized tests or teacher-developed posttests [212][301][346]. Tier 2 is answered only partially: comparison conditions are often described as traditional teaching, conventional instruction, or usual classroom practice, but many studies do not fully specify the counterfactual and several reviews note conceptual overlap with feedback, quizzes, and diagnostic assessment [211][284]. Tier 3 is also partial: the literature clearly identifies core implementation features such as questioning, feedback, self/peer assessment, success criteria, and instructional adjustment, but direct causal tests of specific implementation components remain limited [223][212][213]. Tier 4 is partially answered for reading, writing, mathematics, and some science contexts, but remains weak for English learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, and long-term retention/transfer; subgroup evidence is sparse and often indirect. Overall confidence is moderate. The single most important caveat is that “formative assessment” is not a single intervention: its effects depend on whether evidence is actually used to change instruction, and the current literature does not yet provide robust, cross-subgroup causal estimates.

## Research Report

### Research Questions Investigated

| Tier | Sub-question |
|------|-------------|
| Tier 1 | How is the intervention defined? What outcomes and populations are most studied? |
| Tier 2 | What do baseline or comparison conditions look like? What do studies use as a counterfactual? |
| Tier 3 | How is the intervention implemented in practice? What mechanisms or features drive outcomes? |
| Tier 4 | What are the effect sizes and how do they vary across populations, designs, or conditions? |

## Defining formative assessment in K-12 education

Across the retrieved literature, formative assessment is consistently defined as an in-process instructional practice that elicits evidence of student learning and uses that evidence to adapt teaching and learning. [206] define it as a systematic process that continuously gathers evidence and provides feedback while instruction is under way, and they emphasize that evidence must be used to adapt teaching to meet learner needs [206]. [371] describe formative assessment as teachers continuously collecting evidence of understanding and skill and providing specific, relevant feedback to move learning forward, while noting that the evidence must be used to adapt teaching to students’ needs [371]. Black and Wiliam’s definition recurs across multiple sources as the benchmark formulation: formative assessment is the use of evidence about student achievement to make better decisions about next instructional steps, and it is formative only when that evidence is actually used to modify teaching and learning [212][223][387].

The literature also repeatedly distinguishes formative assessment from summative, diagnostic, and interim assessment. Summative assessment is described as end-of-unit or end-of-course grading, certification, or accountability; diagnostic assessment is framed as prior-knowledge or needs identification; and interim assessment is described as occurring between formative and summative assessment in frequency and scope [217][206][392]. Several authors explicitly caution that not all quizzes, tests, or feedback are formative. [387] argues that a quiz becomes formative only when the elicited evidence is interpreted, relayed back to students, and used by both teacher and student to improve learning. Similarly, [384] list nongraded quizzes, teacher observation, oral questioning, essay drafting, and self- and peer-assessment as formative when they are used to guide teaching and learning rather than merely to assign scores [384].

### What outcomes and populations are most studied?

The dominant outcomes are academic achievement measures, especially standardized or teacher-developed reading, mathematics, writing, and science tests. The reading meta-analysis by [212] centered on standardized reading achievement. The writing meta-analysis by [301] focused on writing quality across grades 1–8. The mathematics studies most often used posttests of mathematical principles, curriculum-based mathematics measures, or statewide assessments. Science studies measured conceptual understanding, procedural knowledge, inquiry skills, or achievement in physics, chemistry, and basic science [301][212][346][324][218].

The populations are heavily concentrated in elementary and secondary classrooms, with fewer studies at the early elementary and high school ends of the K-12 continuum. The reading meta-analysis included kindergarten, elementary, and secondary education [212]. Writing evidence spans grades 1–8 [301]. Mathematics evidence is spread across primary, middle, and secondary school, with substantial representation in grade 1–2, grade 7–8, and grade 10 studies [218][317][324]. Science evidence is thinner and more fragmented, with a mix of elementary, middle, and secondary studies [346][319][233].

The literature also shows that formative assessment is often studied alongside teacher feedback, self-assessment, peer assessment, and differentiated instruction. [212] explicitly treated teacher-directed, student-directed, and integrated teacher-student assessment as different intervention forms. [301] found distinct effect sizes by feedback source. [213] similarly showed differences among student-, mixed-, adult-, and computer-initiated formative feedback. This means the term “formative assessment” in the evidence base often refers to a family of practices rather than a single standardized intervention.

## Baseline and comparison conditions

The counterfactual in this literature is usually some version of conventional teaching, traditional instruction, or business-as-usual classroom practice. In the randomized physics experiment, the comparison group received traditional teaching rather than clicker-based formative assessment (Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics Education, 2021). In Hagos and Andargie’s chemistry study, the comparison conditions were formative assessment alone and conventional instruction, against which technology-integrated formative assessment performed better [346]. In Kültür and Kutlu’s mathematics quasi-experiment, the control group did not receive formative assessment practices and the treatment group did (Kültür & Kutlu, 2021). [218] compared formative and summative assessment data in primary classrooms rather than testing a clean treatment-control contrast, so it is better interpreted as evidence about assessment relationships than as a direct causal comparison.

Several reviews note that comparison conditions are often under-specified. [211] emphasize heterogeneity in what counts as formative assessment across the 13 meta-analyses they reviewed, which limits comparability across studies. [284] similarly note that the literature uses multiple overlapping terms and that classroom assessment is sometimes invoked as formative even when the assessment information is not clearly used to change instruction. This means the counterfactual is often “usual practice,” but usual practice varies substantially by teacher, subject, school, and accountability context [284][211].

## Implementation features and mechanisms

The mechanisms most often proposed are immediate feedback, clearer learning goals, instructional adjustment, student self-regulation, and earlier identification of misconceptions. [223] describe classroom assessment as co-regulated learning: teachers and students jointly gather and interpret evidence, then use it to revise teaching and learning processes. [212] show that reading effects are stronger when formative assessment is coupled with differentiated instruction and integrated teacher-student participation, which supports the idea that formative assessment works by changing subsequent instruction rather than by assessment alone. [213] found larger effects for student-initiated and mixed feedback than for adult-initiated or computer-initiated feedback, suggesting that learner involvement matters [223][212][213].

Peer and self-assessment are important implementation modes, especially when students are expected to monitor their own work. [431] found a significant positive effect of peer assessment on academic performance for primary and secondary students, with g = .29, which supports the plausibility of peer-mediated formative work. [301] found that self-assessment and peer feedback both improved writing quality, though not as much as teacher feedback. These findings suggest that student participation in formative processes can be beneficial, but the evidence also implies that teacher guidance remains essential, especially for younger learners and potentially for learners with special educational needs [301][431][212].

Professional development appears to be a recurring enabling condition, not just an optional add-on. [212] report that 94% of differentiated-instruction interventions in their reading synthesis were coupled with teacher professional development. This is consistent with broader review evidence that effective formative assessment requires teacher assessment literacy and systematic use of evidence. However, teacher development does not automatically translate into student gains: Schneider and Meyer’s PD study in middle school English language arts and mathematics improved teacher assessment skill, but the extracted abstract text notes that students of participating teachers tended to demonstrate lower achievement than matched comparison students [228]. That finding cautions against assuming that better teacher practice in the short run will always produce higher student achievement in the same time frame.

Technology is another major implementation theme. In reading, [212] found no significant moderation by digital technology, suggesting that digital delivery alone is not the key mechanism. In science and mathematics, however, technology-integrated formative assessment, clicker-based checks for understanding, automated feedback, and online adaptive systems often show positive results [7][346][221]. The implication is not that technology is inherently effective, but that it can make evidence collection, feedback, and rapid response more feasible when well aligned with instruction.

## Effects on academic achievement

The clearest pooled effect for K-12 achievement comes from reading. [212] found an overall effect of ES = +0.19 across 48 studies and 116,051 students. They also report that smaller studies produced larger effects, differentiated instruction strengthened effects, and integrated teacher-student formative assessment outperformed teacher-only assessment. This is the most directly relevant K-12 meta-analysis for the research brief, but it is reading-specific rather than fully cross-subject [212].

Writing shows a larger pooled estimate than reading in the retrieved evidence. [301] found d = .63 across grades 1–8, with teacher feedback at d = .89, self-assessment and peer feedback at d = .62, and computer feedback at d = .38. This suggests that formative writing assessment can be a substantial lever when feedback is direct and revision-oriented. The higher effect for teacher feedback implies that formative assessment is especially effective when feedback is specific, expert, and linked to revision opportunities [301].

Mathematics effects are consistently positive but more heterogeneous. [213] reported an overall mean effect size of .72 across 32 studies and 47 effect sizes, with student-initiated formative feedback d = 1.16, mixed feedback d = .83, adult-initiated feedback d = .69, and computer-initiated feedback d = .42. In the primary-grade mathematics classroom study, formative and summative assessment were positively related, and the relationship was stronger in first grade than kindergarten and in lower-performing classrooms, though grade level was not a significant moderator overall [218]. Boström and [317] found that a formative assessment practice improved student achievement in mathematics in a secondary-school study, but the extracted text does not report the exact effect size. Together, these findings indicate that mathematics benefits are plausible and often substantial, but not uniform across grade bands or implementations [213][218][317].

Science evidence is promising but more fragmented. The randomized physics experiment reported a 0.34 SD gain in post-test performance and a 0.28 SD reduction in anxiety, suggesting that frequent formative checks with immediate feedback can improve both cognition and affect in high school science (Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics Education, 2021). [346] found positive effects in chemistry for conceptual and procedural knowledge, with large partial eta-squared values for group effects. Other science studies, including primary science, inquiry skills, and concept-mapping-based formative assessment, largely support positive effects but often do not provide extractable effect estimates in the available snippets [346][319][233].

The broader K-12 meta-analysis by [309] is especially important because it is not limited to one subject. It synthesized 258 effect sizes from 118 studies and reported an overall Hedges’ g = 0.25. The extracted web summary indicates larger effects in high school and quasi-experimental studies, and larger effects outside North America and Western Europe, but the retrieved metadata did not provide the exact subgroup coefficients. Even so, the overall pooled estimate reinforces the conclusion that formative assessment is beneficial on average across K-12 settings, though the effect is not large enough to ignore implementation quality or context [309].

## Moderators, subgroup differences, and equity considerations

The strongest moderator evidence is for implementation features and grade band, not for equity subgroups. [212] found that reading effects were larger in smaller studies, in interventions with differentiated instruction, and in integrated teacher-student assessment. They also reported non-significant differences by mainstream versus at-risk student status, digital technology use, research design, program duration, and publication type. This is useful because it suggests the effects are not solely an artifact of one study design or delivery format, but it also underscores that the meta-analysis did not identify strong evidence that at-risk students responded differently from mainstream students in the available reading studies [212].

Primary-grade mathematics evidence suggests lower-performing classrooms may benefit more. [218] reported that the relationship between formative and summative assessment was stronger in lower-performing classrooms, and stronger in first grade than kindergarten. However, they also cautioned that grade level was not a significant moderator overall, so this should be read as suggestive rather than definitive. [213] found no moderation by education level or publication type, though the effect sizes were numerically largest at the primary level. These results point to developmental and instructional complexity as plausible moderators, but not yet as robust, replicated subgroup findings [218][213].

Direct evidence for English learners, students with disabilities, and low-income students is much thinner. [300] provide an adjacent multilevel meta-analysis of ELL reading interventions, not formative assessment alone, and found medium effects for basic reading skills with stronger effects in upper elementary than secondary grades. The Bookworms literacy curriculum study explicitly included ELL, FRL, special education, and baseline achievement as moderators, but it is not a formative-assessment-only intervention and its moderation analyses were described as preliminary. [212] did report mainstream versus at-risk comparisons, but not ELL, disability, or low-income subgroup estimates. Thus, the current evidence base does not support precise subgroup claims for these equity groups in formative assessment specifically [300][212][336].

The evidence on retention and transfer is especially limited. A technology-integrated chemistry study explicitly addressed retention of conceptual and procedural knowledge, and a primary science implementation study named subsequent transfer, but the available snippets do not provide enough detail for a strong synthesis of durability effects. Similarly, the physics experiment and some mathematics studies appear to assess short-term posttests rather than delayed maintenance. As a result, durable learning outcomes remain an important but under-specified part of the literature [346][325][7].

## Specific study findings

The randomized physics study by Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics [7] is one of the clearest direct causal findings in the retrieved set. In a randomized experiment with 139 secondary physics students, repeated clicker-based formative assessments improved post-test physics performance relative to traditional teaching by 0.34 SD and reduced anxiety by 0.28 SD. The study therefore supports the claim that frequent evidence gathering plus immediate feedback can improve both achievement and affect in high school science (Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics Education, 2021).

The chemistry study by [346] is another strong direct study. It examined technology-integrated formative assessment and found significantly higher conceptual chemistry scores than formative assessment alone and conventional instruction, with a large group effect of ηp² = 0.21, and similarly strong effects for procedural chemistry knowledge with ηp² = 0.27. This suggests that formative assessment may be particularly effective when combined with technology and when both conceptual and procedural learning are targeted [346].

The high school mathematics quasi-experiment by Kültür and [324] found that formative assessment practices significantly improved mathematics achievement and attitudes in a 12-week intervention with 51 tenth graders. Because the extracted text does not report a standardized effect size, the study should be treated as supportive but not quantitatively comparable to the meta-analytic evidence (Kültür & Kutlu, 2021).

The primary-grade mathematics study by [218] found a positive relationship between formative assessment data and summative assessment data. The relationship was stronger in first grade than kindergarten and stronger in lower-performing classrooms, though grade level was not a significant moderator overall. This makes the study especially useful for understanding how early grades and lower-performing classrooms may respond differently, but the evidence is correlational rather than a direct treatment effect estimate [218].

The writing meta-analysis by [301] is perhaps the clearest subject-specific synthesis after reading. It shows that formative writing assessment meaningfully improves writing quality, and that teacher feedback is the most effective source. The consistent ordering of teacher feedback above self, peer, and computer feedback suggests that formative assessment is strongest when teachers can interpret student writing, supply actionable guidance, and support revision cycles [301].

## Synthesis and Implications

Across subjects, the best-supported conclusion is that formative assessment improves K-12 academic achievement when it is more than routine testing. The intervention must elicit evidence during instruction, interpret that evidence, and lead to real instructional or learner adjustment. Where this chain is strongest, the outcomes are most consistently positive: reading gains are modest on average but reliable, writing gains are larger, mathematics gains are often substantial, and science findings are promising but less complete. The most persuasive implementation features are timely feedback, differentiated or responsive instruction, teacher-student collaboration, and teacher assessment literacy [212][301][213][223].

For schools and practitioners, the practical implication is that formative assessment should be designed as a cycle, not a one-off event. Teachers need tools to collect evidence efficiently, interpret it quickly, and adjust instruction immediately. Professional development is therefore not optional: the evidence suggests it is often bundled with stronger formative assessment interventions, and the success of the practice depends on whether teachers can translate evidence into differentiated instruction. In mathematics and writing especially, the literature suggests that teacher feedback and meaningful revision or reteaching are the most likely pathways to achievement gains [212][301][228].

## Limitations and Research Gaps

The evidence base remains uneven in several important ways. First, the strongest pooled evidence is concentrated in reading and writing, with mathematics and science more fragmented and high-school evidence thinner than elementary or middle school evidence in some areas. Second, direct subgroup estimates for English learners, students with disabilities, and low-income students are sparse or absent in the core formative-assessment intervention literature, even though these populations are frequently named in theory and policy sources. Third, many studies do not report sufficiently clear comparator conditions, implementation fidelity, or delayed follow-up outcomes, making it difficult to isolate the effect of formative assessment from feedback, diagnostic testing, or general classroom improvement [211][212][309].

Methodologically, the literature is also limited by heterogeneity in what counts as formative assessment, frequent dependence on small or single-site studies, and a heavy reliance on short-term posttests rather than retention or transfer measures. Several promising studies are quasi-experimental or observational rather than randomized, and some PD studies improve teacher practice without clearly improving student outcomes in the same time frame. Equity gaps remain central: the field still lacks a robust causal evidence base showing when formative assessment is especially beneficial for English learners, students with disabilities, or low-income students, and whether those groups need different implementation supports. The most important next step is a set of larger, clearly specified K-12 trials that compare well-defined formative assessment models against usual instruction and report subgroup, durability, and workload outcomes with sufficient precision.

## Audit Summary

The report is broadly trustworthy in its directional claims but contains several notable issues. The most critical problems are: (1) significant citation-number confusion, where the report's bibliography numbers do not consistently match the pre-numbered source list (e.g., [206], [211], [212], [213], etc. are notes-sourced papers but the bibliography numbers are offset by one from the supplementary source list, and source [7] in the pre-numbered list is about rubrics, not physics); (2) several inline citations reference studies by name without a bracketed number or with inconsistent referencing (e.g., "Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics Education, 2021" appears inline without a consistent [67] tag, and is mapped to bibliography entry [7] which in the academic-DB list is a rubrics review); (3) some statistics are verified against the iteration history but a few are not fully traceable; (4) study design labels cannot be verified for notes-sourced papers against the bibliography (which lists "not_reported" for all), but cross-referencing with iteration history and the academic-DB list reveals mismatches. The report's substance is reasonable and caveats are appropriately stated, but the bibliography mapping is a significant integrity concern.

1. **[7] — Mismatch between bibliography and pre-numbered source list.** The bibliography lists [7] as "Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics Education" (an RCT). In the pre-numbered academic-DB source list, [7] is "The Role of Rubrics in Learning and Implementation of Authentic Assessment: A Literature Review." The physics RCT is actually source [67] in the academic-DB list. This is a critical mismatch.

2. **Inline citations without bracketed numbers.** The report cites "Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics Education, 2021" and "Kültür & Kutlu, 2021" by name inline rather than consistently using bracket numbers, creating ambiguity. The claims table references "Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics [7]" and "Kültür & [324]" — the latter mixes a name with a number.

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how diagnostic competences can be facilitated in higher education, focusing on medical and teacher education. The authors synthesize evidence from 35 empirical studies to examine whether problem-solving, scaffolding, and diagnostic context support learners’ ability to gather and integrate case-specific information and make accurate professional decisions.

The review argues that diagnostic competence depends on both prior professional knowledge and the kind of instructional support provided. It codes studies by domain, knowledge base, scaffolding type, and diagnostic context (document-based vs. interaction-based; individual vs. collaborative processing), and it evaluates outcomes such as diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, professional vision, and formative assessment-related skills.

Across studies, instructional support had a moderate positive overall effect on diagnostic competences (g = 0.39, 95% CI [0.22, 0.56], n=3472 across 35 studies). Problem-solving was generally effective, while the effectiveness of scaffolding depended on learner knowledge: high-guidance supports worked better for less advanced learners, whereas higher-self-regulation supports were more effective for advanced learners. The paper concludes that diagnostic learning should be matched to learners’ prior knowledge and that scaffolding should be designed to support both content understanding and self-regulated reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis directly studied diagnostic competence, which maps to durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and evidence-based reasoning. Across 35 studies (n=3472), instructional support produced a moderate positive effect on diagnostic competences (g=0.39, 95% CI [0.22, 0.56]).
finding.measure: Diagnostic competence, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, professional vision, epistemic-diagnostic activities

finding.finding_summary: In teacher-education studies, the paper included outcomes such as professional vision and formative assessment knowledge/skills. These were treated as diagnostic competences and showed generally positive effects of instructional support, though effects varied by knowledge base and scaffolding type.
finding.measure: Professional vision; formative assessment knowledge; diagnostic competence in teacher education

paper_profiles.title: Online teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic: exploring science/STEM teachers’ curriculum and assessment practices in Canada
paper_profiles.venue: Disciplinary and Interdisciplinary Science Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Grade 1–12 science/STEM teachers in a Canadian province adapted curriculum planning, instruction, and assessment during emergency remote teaching (ERT) triggered by COVID-19 school closures. The authors ask what digital tools teachers used, how they taught and assessed online, and how they believed online teaching affected student outcomes.

Using an online questionnaire with 75 teachers, the study combines descriptive quantitative data with thematic analysis of open-ended responses. Teachers reported using a range of LMSs and tools, but instruction was often simplified into self-directed learning, prerecorded videos, and content delivery, with comparatively little student-centered or inquiry-based pedagogy. Assessment was mostly traditional (online quizzes/tests, homework, projects), and teachers frequently judged online assessment to be ineffective because of plagiarism, inequity, lack of accountability, and difficulty assessing higher-order or hands-on science skills.

Overall, the paper concludes that emergency remote teaching exposed gaps in teachers’ TPACK and self-efficacy, which limited creative curriculum implementation and authentic assessment. Teachers generally viewed online teaching as negatively affecting engagement, interaction, and achievement, and the authors argue that better professional development, clearer assessment design, and stronger supports are needed for effective online STEM teaching.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that online assessment and instruction were poorly suited to evaluating science/STEM learning during ERT. They said online tasks were often knowledge/understanding-heavy rather than inquiry/process-focused, and that virtual labs/simulations could not adequately capture practical lab skills, collaboration, or investigation skills (n=75).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported assessment of science/STEM skills, including inquiry, lab technique, and conceptual understanding

finding.finding_summary: Most teachers reported negative impacts on student engagement and motivation in online teaching. The paper reports perceived negative effects on student-student engagement (60%) and student-teacher engagement (46%), along with broader concerns about reduced participation and low accountability (n=75).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement and interaction

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed online environments made it difficult to assess or support durable skills such as collaboration, critical thinking, self-regulation, and independent work. They described challenges with group work, peer interaction, and students’ ability to complete authentic tasks without help, especially under conditions of plagiarism and limited monitoring (n=75).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported ability to assess collaboration, higher-order thinking, and independent work

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described ERT as increasing workload and complicating instruction and assessment, including the need to redesign lessons, manage multiple platforms, provide individualized feedback, and cope with incomplete student access. Although 82% reported returning assignments promptly and providing useful feedback, the overall process was viewed as inefficient and burdensome (n=75).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, instructional/assessment efficiency, and feedback practices

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that institutional conditions shaped teachers’ online practices, including school board decisions about platform choice, assessment policies, and support during ERT. Teachers reported that school board policy sometimes prohibited assessment entirely, and that limited professional development and minimal guidance constrained effective implementation (n=75).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported school board policy, platform selection, and support conditions

paper_profiles.title: A Teacher’s Influence on Student Engagement: Using Smartphones for Creating Vocational Assessment ePortfolios
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how a vocational lecturer’s facilitation influenced student engagement when fifteen carpentry students used their own smartphones and mobile apps to create visual assessment ePortfolios. The authors focus on the teacher’s role in designing activities, scaffolding technology use, giving formative feedback, and fostering collaboration and autonomy during learning.

The intervention was conducted over 12 weeks in a Certificate in Carpentry program at Otago Polytechnic, New Zealand, using Participatory Action Research with four action cycles. Students used Facebook, Evernote, and Google Plus to document technical skills and produce assessment ePortfolios; the lecturer modeled each app, guided use in class, and provided frequent feedback. Data came from pre/post surveys, observations, reflections, focus groups, and an interview, making the study largely qualitative with some descriptive quantitative evidence.

The main conclusion is that the lecturer was pivotal to student engagement: students reported the approach was convenient, enjoyable, and confidence-building, and they felt the mobile tools helped them learn and connect with others. The teacher’s structured design, collaborative tasks, and timely feedback were associated with enhanced achievement rates, though the paper does not report inferential statistics or a causal estimate. The study argues that effective mobile learning depends on pedagogical integration, modeling, support, and sustained interaction, especially when students are using familiar devices for authentic assessment tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported higher confidence, enjoyment, and convenience when using their smartphones and social media apps for ePortfolio assessment. The paper states that the majority of students felt comfortable with the approach, found it fun and easy to use, and believed it helped them learn and connect with others (n=15 total; survey subsamples n=8 pre, n=13 post).
finding.measure: Student survey responses, focus group comments, and lecturer observations of engagement/self-efficacy
finding.study_size: n=15 (with pre-survey n=8 and post-survey n=13)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the learning design supported collaboration, autonomy, and active learning, with students working in groups, sharing work, and developing confidence in using mobile technologies. These behaviors were linked to improved engagement and were enabled by the lecturer’s scaffolding, modeling, and feedback during the 12-week intervention.
finding.measure: Observed collaboration/active learning, student reflections, and ePortfolio participation

finding.finding_summary: Students created visual vocational assessment ePortfolios demonstrating technical carpentry skills across multiple apps, and the lecturer reported that the learning and assessment design enhanced achievement rates. The study does not provide standardized test scores, but it directly centers on vocational assessment performance and the quality of the ePortfolios produced by students (n=15).
finding.measure: Completion/quality of vocational ePortfolios and lecturer-assessed achievement of technical skills

finding.finding_summary: The mobile ePortfolio approach reduced some constraints of the previous workflow by enabling more immediate and frequent formative feedback and by allowing students to capture evidence on their own devices. The lecturer also noted the approach could help lower resit rates and reduce the burden of delayed feedback, although no workload metrics were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on feedback process, assessment workflow, and resit-related comments

paper_profiles.title: English language assessment in Bangladesh today: principles, practices, and problems
paper_profiles.population: Primary, secondary, and tertiary students in Bangladesh
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines the state of English language assessment in Bangladesh, focusing on the mismatch between curriculum intentions and actual assessment practices. The paper argues that Bangladesh’s assessment system is dominated by high-stakes, summative examinations that emphasize rote learning, exclude key communicative skills such as listening and speaking, and exert negative washback on teaching and learning.

The authors synthesize prior literature and policy documents across primary, secondary, and tertiary education in Bangladesh. They discuss reform efforts such as School Base Assessment (SBA) and continuous assessment (CA), noting that these initiatives were intended to support formative assessment through classwork, homework, oral questioning, presentations, and group work, but were poorly implemented because of inadequate teacher training, lack of assessment literacy, large classes, weak monitoring, and absence of supporting manuals.

The review concludes that meaningful improvement in English learning will require alignment between curriculum, assessment, and instruction; stronger teacher assessment literacy through teacher education; and greater use of formative and alternative assessment approaches such as feedback, self- and peer assessment, and portfolio/performance-based assessment. The paper is primarily policy- and practice-oriented, emphasizing systemic reform rather than reporting original experimental effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that assessment practices in Bangladesh systematically exclude listening and speaking from major public examinations (e.g., PECE, JSC, SSC, HSC), despite these being core curriculum objectives. The result is a persistent mismatch between what is taught and what is measured, weakening students' communicative competence in English.
finding.measure: English listening and speaking assessment coverage in national examinations; communicative competence outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review describes assessment practices as heavily paper-and-pencil based and oriented toward reading, writing, grammar, and memorization rather than authentic language use.
