Although literacy-related skills are measured in exams, the narrow test format is argued to distort learning toward rote performance rather than meaningful literacy development.
finding.measure: Reading and writing test content in public examinations; literacy-oriented assessment coverage

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that continuous assessment and classroom-based feedback can help students diagnose strengths and weaknesses, stay motivated, and participate more actively; however, high-stakes testing produces stress, anxiety, and poor self-concept, especially for low-performing students. Thus, the emotional and motivational effects of assessment are presented as mixed overall, depending on the assessment mode.
finding.measure: Student motivation, anxiety, participation, self-concept, and attitudes toward assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative practices such as oral questioning, group work, peer assessment, self-assessment, and feedback can support higher-order and self-regulatory capacities by helping learners reflect on strengths and weaknesses and adapt learning strategies. In contrast, the dominant testing regime encourages memorization and surface learning rather than collaboration, metacognition, or independent learning.
finding.measure: Use and perceived benefits of alternative/formative assessment practices (peer work, self/peer assessment, oral questioning, group presentation)

finding.finding_summary: Continuous assessment is presented as cost-effective and time-efficient in principle, helping teachers diagnose learning and modify instruction with minimal investment of time. However, the review also reports that it is difficult to implement because of large class sizes, heavy teacher workload, limited class time, lack of manuals, and difficulty checking homework and tests.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, time required for assessment, feasibility of continuous assessment implementation

finding.finding_summary: The central finding is a persistent systemic gap between curriculum-based assessment principles and actual practice across Bangladesh’s English education system. The review describes failed or weak implementation of School Base Assessment and continuous assessment, lack of teacher training and assessment literacy, and policy-driven reliance on high-stakes testing, all of which undermine curriculum reform and institutional alignment.
finding.measure: Policy implementation of SBA/CA, alignment between curriculum and assessment, teacher training and monitoring capacity

paper_profiles.title: Differentiating Instruction: Development of a Practice Framework for and with Secondary Mathematics Classroom Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article addresses the persistent gap between differentiated instruction theory and classroom practice, focusing on how teachers can implement differentiation in mixed-ability secondary mathematics classrooms. The authors argue that while differentiated instruction is widely endorsed, it is not used consistently or effectively in practice, in part because teachers lack sufficient pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), confidence, and sustained professional learning supports. The paper situates formative assessment as a central mechanism for informing instructional decisions and differentiating content, process, and product.

Rather than reporting an intervention trial, the article develops and describes a prototype practice framework intended to support teachers in collaboratively designing and enacting differentiated instruction. The framework is informed by prior literature, exemplar cases from mathematics education, Tomlinson’s principles of differentiation, and the REACH framework, and it is aligned with design-based implementation research (DBIR). The authors emphasize iterative co-development, generative dialogue, in-school professional learning, coaching, collaboration, and ongoing data use as supports for sustainable implementation.

The context is secondary mathematics in Australia, especially mixed-ability classrooms and regional settings where teachers may have limited access to subject-specific support. The paper concludes that effective differentiation depends on combining formative assessment, teacher reflection, collaborative professional learning, and system-level support structures. Its main contribution is conceptual and practice-oriented: it proposes a framework and implementation logic for bridging theory and practice, rather than testing student outcomes empirically.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report a new empirical evaluation of student mathematics achievement; instead, it argues from prior research that differentiated instruction supported by formative assessment can improve mathematical learning when implemented well. It cites previous studies showing that heterogeneous grouping and formative assessment can support stronger understanding and achievement, but the article itself provides no original effect size or achievement data.
finding.measure: student mathematics achievement / mathematical understanding (cited literature, not newly measured in this paper)

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes that differentiated instruction in mixed-ability mathematics classrooms is intended to support student engagement, self-esteem, and motivation alongside academic progress. These claims are conceptual and drawn from prior literature rather than from a direct study in this paper, so no original sample size or effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: student engagement, self-esteem, motivation (conceptual/prior literature)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses collaboration, reflection, and metacognitive adjustment as part of the differentiation framework, especially through generative dialogue and teacher-student interaction. However, these are presented as mechanisms and theoretical supports rather than as directly measured student outcomes in an empirical study.
finding.measure: collaboration, reflection, self-evaluation, metacognitive adjustment (theoretical framework)

finding.finding_summary: A major aim of the framework is to make differentiated instruction more workable and sustainable for teachers by improving planning, lesson delivery, and use of assessment data. The paper argues that collaborative, ongoing professional learning and framework-guided data use can help teachers streamline curriculum and make better instructional decisions, but it does not report empirical workload or productivity outcomes.
finding.measure: teacher planning, lesson delivery, data use, and implementation support (conceptual/practice framework)

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a whole-school, DBIR-aligned approach to building capacity for differentiated instruction through collaboration, co-creation, and ongoing professional learning. Its main institutional claim is that sustained implementation requires school and system supports, including coaching, on-site support, and distributed leadership, but the article does not present original outcome data on policy or organizational change.
finding.measure: whole-school implementation capacity, professional learning infrastructure, and collaborative school change (framework/proposal)

paper_profiles.title: Using Global Observation Protocols to Inform Research on Teaching Effectiveness and School Improvement: Strengths and Emerging Limitations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the strengths and limitations of widely used global teacher observation protocols for evaluating instruction and supporting school improvement. The authors focus on four major observation systems used in the Measures of Effective Teaching (MET) study: Danielson Framework for Teaching (FFT), CLASS, PLATO, and MQI. Rather than testing an instructional intervention, the paper asks whether these protocols can precisely discriminate lesson quality, measure separable dimensions of teaching, yield reliable ratings, reflect teachers’ own contributions to instruction, and capture tradeoffs among instructional practices.

Using video-coded lesson data from the MET study, the authors analyze score distributions, exploratory factor structures, inter-rater agreement, classroom-composition regressions, and correlations among protocol subdomains. The sample includes roughly 1,570 teachers for FFT/CLASS scoring and about 940 for MQI/PLATO, drawn from six large urban school districts and spanning grades 4-9. The observations were collected for research purposes, with raters trained and monitored, allowing the authors to compare normal and expert scoring conditions.

The paper concludes that global observation protocols have real strengths—especially comprehensiveness and alignment to teaching standards—but also important limitations. Scores often cluster in a few middle categories, subdomains are less independent than intended, reliability depends heavily on rater training and expert monitoring, and some protocols are sensitive to classroom composition, complicating causal interpretation in evaluation settings. The authors argue that fine-grained or automated observation tools may better support instructional improvement and produce more precise feedback than broad global rubrics.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that global observation protocols are useful for teacher evaluation and school improvement, but they have important structural limitations. Scores cluster in middle categories, subdomains are not very separable, and reliability depends strongly on rater training; classroom composition also predicts some scores (e.g., average prior achievement coefficient = 0.091 for FFT and 0.074 for CLASS), which raises concerns for high-stakes use.
finding.measure: Teacher observation protocol score distributions, exploratory factor analysis, inter-rater reliability, and regressions of observation scores on classroom composition
finding.study_size: FFT/CLASS: n=7,820 to 17,804 ratings; PLATO/MQI: n=5,526 to 17,524 observations depending on model

paper_profiles.title: The Role of Rubrics in Learning and Implementation of Authentic Assessment: A Literature Review
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of InSITE 2020: Informing Science and Information Technology Education Conference
paper_profiles.population: Not specified (primarily higher education and assessment contexts; not K-12-specific)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews literature on rubric design, rubric types, and the benefits and challenges of using rubrics in authentic assessment. Its central question is how rubrics function as scoring guides and learning supports, and under what conditions they improve assessment reliability, validity, feedback quality, and student performance.

The review synthesizes conceptual and empirical work across education contexts rather than reporting a new primary study. It contrasts generic, task-specific, holistic, analytic, single-point, and developmental rubrics, arguing that rubric choice should depend on the learning goal, task type, and assessment purpose. The paper emphasizes that rubrics can help students understand expectations, self-assess, use peer feedback, and support self-regulated learning, while also helping instructors design instruction and improve scoring consistency.

At the same time, the review highlights important limitations: rubric effects are inconsistent, depend heavily on user familiarity and training, and may not improve validity or achievement in all cases. The authors conclude that rubrics are useful pedagogical tools when well designed, aligned to outcomes, and paired with appropriate training and context-sensitive implementation, but they are not a universal solution for improving learning or assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that rubrics can improve writing quality and feedback for essays and other written tasks, but results are inconsistent. Some studies reported better papers or higher scores with rubric use, while others found no difference or benefit only in a subset of assignments; one cited survey found peer feedback based on rubric criteria improved the quality of papers in 1,026 observations.
finding.measure: Writing quality, essay performance, paper quality, and writing-task scores
finding.study_size: varies across cited studies; includes n=1026 observations in one survey and n=114 teachers in one scoring study

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that rubrics support self-regulation-related outcomes by clarifying expectations, reducing anxiety, and helping learners monitor progress. It cites literature suggesting rubrics can enhance motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, and self-regulated learning, although the review also notes that novice learners may need weeks of practice before they can use rubrics effectively for self- and peer-assessment.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, self-efficacy, engagement, motivation, anxiety, and self-monitoring

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that rubrics help students develop metacognition, calibration accuracy, and self-assessment skills. The authors report that analytic and generic rubrics can help learners track progress, identify strengths and weaknesses, and allocate effort strategically; however, interpretation differences between teachers and students can limit these benefits without training and exemplars.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-assessment, peer assessment, and ability to interpret criteria
finding.study_size: varies across cited studies; not_reported for a single pooled sample

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that rubrics can improve scoring consistency, reduce grading ambiguity, and save teacher time, especially when rubrics are well designed or task-specific. It also notes that rubrics can support instruction design and help instructors detect curricular misalignments, though creating high-quality rubrics can itself be time-consuming and may require expert involvement.
finding.measure: Scoring reliability, inter-rater consistency, teacher grading efficiency, and instructional design support
finding.study_size: varies across cited studies; includes studies with 114 teachers and multiple rubric-comparison datasets

finding.finding_summary: Beyond writing, the review argues that rubrics are useful across many authentic tasks such as lab work, presentations, performances, portfolios, artwork, internships, and problem solving. The overall conclusion is that task-specific rubrics improve reliability and validity for large-scale or high-stakes assessment, while holistic rubrics are better suited to summative judgment after learning has occurred.
finding.measure: Performance on authentic tasks across disciplines; reliability and validity of assessment

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating High School Student Success Through READ 180: Analysis of Program Impact Using Measures of Academic Progress (MAP)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines whether the commercial literacy intervention READ 180 improved student achievement more than traditional high school English instruction in a rural Title I high school in South Carolina. The motivation for the study was the school’s repeated failure to meet AYP under NCLB and the district’s decision to purchase READ 180 for students with weak reading performance. The author was especially interested in whether a literacy intervention aimed at reading could also influence mathematics performance.

The study compared two intact ninth-grade groups: students assigned to READ 180 and students assigned to traditional English language arts instruction. Both groups were pre- and post-tested using the Northwest Evaluation Association’s Measures of Academic Progress (MAP) in reading/ELA and math, and the analyses included dependent-samples t-tests and ANCOVA using pretest scores as covariates. The dissertation reports that the traditional instruction group showed statistically significant gains in both reading and math, whereas the READ 180 group did not show significant gains.

Overall, the findings do not support READ 180 as implemented at this school as a more effective option than usual English instruction for improving MAP reading or math scores. The study is presented as an independent, standardized-measure evaluation intended to inform district decisions about continuing the costly program and to contribute evidence on the relationship between literacy interventions and cross-curricular achievement. No subgroup analyses by English learner status, disability status, prior achievement beyond the intact-group assignment, or socioeconomic context are reported in the excerpt beyond the Title I/rural setting.

finding.finding_summary: In this quasi-experimental comparison of ninth graders (n=not_reported), the READ 180 group did not show statistically significant improvement in MAP reading/ELA scores from pretest to posttest, while the traditional English instruction group did show significant gains. The study used MAP reading/ELA RIT scores as the outcome and found no evidence that READ 180 outperformed usual instruction for reading achievement.
finding.measure: MAP reading/ELA (RIT scores)

finding.finding_summary: The study also examined whether READ 180 affected math achievement using MAP math RIT scores. The READ 180 group did not show statistically significant improvement in math, whereas the traditional instruction group showed statistically significant gains, indicating no positive effect of READ 180 on mathematics outcomes in this sample.
finding.measure: MAP math (RIT scores)

paper_profiles.title: Supported to Stay in School: How Students’ Perceptions of the Psychosocial Learning Environment are Related to Intentions to Quit Upper Secondary School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This PhD thesis examines why some upper secondary students develop intentions to quit school and whether those intentions are linked to how students perceive the psychosocial learning environment. The work is grounded in self-determination theory and achievement goal theory, and focuses on teacher support, peer loneliness, and mastery climate as possible antecedents of school-quit intentions.

Across three quantitative studies using self-report and register data from 1,379 students in Rogaland, Norway, the thesis found that perceived emotional support from teachers was consistently linked to lower intentions to quit school. Study 1 showed indirect negative associations for emotional support, autonomy granting, and feedback quality via emotional engagement and academic boredom, with emotional support also showing a direct negative association. Study 2 found that increases in emotional support were associated with decreases in quit intentions, while increases in loneliness among peers were associated with increases in quit intentions. Study 3 identified three emotional-support trajectory groups and showed that students in a decreasing-support group had more increasing quit intentions, an effect fully mediated by declining mastery climate. The thesis concludes that psychosocial factors in school matter for persistence in upper secondary education and may help prevent dropout-related motivational decline.

finding.finding_summary: The thesis directly studies students’ intentions to quit school as a persistence-related motivational outcome, along with emotional engagement, academic boredom, peer loneliness, perceived teacher support, and mastery climate. Across 3 studies with n=1,379 upper secondary students, perceived emotional support from teachers was consistently associated with lower quit intentions, while increasing loneliness was associated with higher quit intentions; Study 3 found that a decreasing emotional-support trajectory predicted greater increases in quit intentions through worsening mastery climate.
finding.measure: Intentions to quit school; perceived emotional support from teachers; emotional engagement; academic boredom; loneliness among peers; perceived mastery climate

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses formative assessment as a strategy to improve learning, with emphasis on how frequent low-stakes assessments and immediate feedback can support student progress. The authors frame formative assessment as a way to move beyond summative grading and argue that regular checks on understanding can help students identify gaps, reflect on performance, and improve before end-of-semester exams.

The empirical component is a survey of university students at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) about continuous assessment and the use of Blackboard (BB) online tests. Students responded to a 16-item questionnaire about frequent internal assessments, BB versus classroom tests, and teacher feedback. The paper reports that students generally favored BB-based formative assessment because it offered immediate feedback, flexibility, and the ability to study small topic chunks; Engineering students were more likely than Business and IT students to rate the BB option as very much needed. The paper concludes that technology-mediated formative assessment is perceived positively and may improve summative grades, but it does not report achievement test results or causal effects on academic performance.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent formative assessments and immediate feedback helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses, stay on track, and reduce uncertainty about their progress. The survey found strong support for continuous assessment because it was seen as helping learning occur in steps and providing constant feedback, although some students also noted stress from too many tests.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, feedback usefulness, and stress/pressure from frequent assessments

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and self-regulation by helping students reflect on feedback, recognize errors, and work toward improved performance. Students also said the approach helped them learn individual topics progressively and keep in touch with the subject throughout the semester.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of learning progression, reflection on feedback, and checking whether they were on track

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main academic claim is that formative assessment through weekly Blackboard tests may improve course learning and potentially summative semester exam performance. However, this conclusion is based on student perceptions and theory rather than direct achievement data; no test score gains, effect sizes, or causal comparisons with usual instruction are reported.
finding.measure: Perceived learning improvement and expected summative semester examination performance

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: ICPE 2013 – International Conference on Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether student-produced videos can serve as a formative assessment tool in high school physics. The authors argue that video production reveals student understanding, misconceptions, planning processes, and collaborative skills more effectively than traditional tests alone, and can help teachers adjust instruction while the term is still underway.

The activity was implemented in a Brazilian high school (Colégio Pedro II, Rio de Janeiro) across first-, second-, and third-year classes. After formal instruction in physics topics, students worked in groups of up to five to create short videos on studied themes and submit a brief written explanation; the teacher then reviewed, classified, and discussed the products in class. The paper analyzes 55 videos from 232 students and reports descriptive results on content accuracy, clarity, coherence, technical quality, use of experiments, and thematic distribution.

The main finding is that student video production appeared to be a useful and reliable formative assessment device. The authors report that 35% of videos were fully correct and 45% partially correct in physics content, 47% presented ideas clearly, 75% matched the proposal, and 87% had a logical sequence. They also report a strong correlation between technical quality and conceptual accuracy, suggesting that careful planning and production were associated with better physics understanding. No comparison group or causal estimate relative to standard instruction is provided; the study is primarily descriptive and correlational.

finding.finding_summary: In this descriptive study of 55 student-produced physics videos from 232 high school students, the videos were used to assess understanding of physics concepts and reasoning. The authors report that 35% of videos were fully correct and 45% partially correct in physical content, with 47% of presentations judged clear and 87% showing a logical sequence, indicating that the activity exposed students' conceptual understanding and misconceptions.
finding.measure: Accuracy and clarity of physics content in student-produced videos; logical sequence and proposal-product alignment

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly frames video production as eliciting metacognition, planning, collaboration, and project completion skills. The authors note that students had to plan, replan, and work cooperatively, and that video quality often reflected the care and effort students invested; 42% of videos were technically very well done, and 90% of those were entirely conceptually correct.
finding.measure: Observed planning, collaboration, and technical production quality in student videos

finding.finding_summary: The activity appears to have supported student engagement and participation, with students spending time preparing videos and using age-appropriate, playful formats in some cases. The paper does not provide standardized engagement measures, but it argues that the format increased interest, motivation, and active participation in learning physics.
finding.measure: Observed student participation and engagement during video production and discussion

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that student videos gave the teacher timely diagnostic information that would otherwise require long interviews or carefully designed questionnaires. The videos enabled the teacher to identify misconceptions, review instruction, and discuss learning activities before the term ended, suggesting improved assessment efficiency for classroom diagnosis.
finding.measure: Teacher diagnostic usefulness and timing of formative assessment process

paper_profiles.title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2020 ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of accessible computer science learning resources for Deaf and Hard of Hearing (D/HH) K-12 students, especially those who use American Sign Language (ASL) as a primary language. The authors argue that many existing coding resources rely heavily on English text or captions that may be inaccurate or linguistically inaccessible for D/HH learners, and that this creates barriers to participation in computing education.

The paper presents an early-stage design for an accessible block-based computer science curriculum and web application. The proposed system includes ASL video explanations of core programming concepts, captioned videos, visual feedback, ASL-based tooltips for blocks, and other accessibility supports intended for middle-school D/HH students. The work is framed around inclusive design principles and the HE4DWUX heuristics for deaf web user experience.

This is primarily a project/design paper rather than an empirical evaluation. The authors describe planned content, accessibility features, and future research directions, including a forthcoming study with middle-school deaf students to examine the impact of ASL videos on CS learning. No outcome data are reported in the paper, so it does not provide evidence about student achievement effects of formative assessment or other instructional practices.

paper_profiles.title: Consistent Bayesian meta-analysis on subgroup specific effects and interactions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical problem in subgroup meta-analysis: how to obtain consistent inferences about treatment effects within subgroups and treatment-by-subgroup interactions when trial subgroup prevalences differ across studies. The authors argue that conventional subgroup pooling can produce aggregation bias and mismatches between subgroup-specific estimates and interaction estimates, especially in meta-analyses with few studies or uneven subgroup composition.

To solve this, they propose Contribution-adjusted Meta-analysis by Subgroup (CAMS), a Bayesian model-based approach that adjusts for study-level subgroup contribution using the information fraction. CAMS is shown to recover the same interaction inference as standard within-trial interaction meta-analysis (BIM) while still providing interpretable subgroup-specific estimates. The paper is methodological and is demonstrated with an example from relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, comparing subgroup effects by age and disability (EDSS) across seven trials.

The main conclusion is that subgroup and interaction inference can be made coherent without relying on raw IPD, provided subgroup contribution is properly modeled. CAMS preserves within-trial interaction information, avoids ecological/aggregation bias from naive subgroup pooling, and allows subgroup estimates to be reported at a chosen prevalence or averaged over a prevalence distribution. The paper’s results are statistical and illustrative rather than about an educational intervention, so it does not provide K-12 achievement findings relevant to formative assessment.

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Student Learning Styles on the Learning Gains Achieved When Interactive Simulations Are Coupled with Real-Time Formative Assessment via Pen-Enabled Mobile Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether learning gains from a pedagogical model that combines interactive computer simulations with real-time formative assessment differ by student learning style. The authors ask whether the “Coupled Model” is especially effective for particular learners, using the Felder-Soloman Index of Learning Styles to test associations between learning-style dimensions and achievement gains.

The study was conducted in an undergraduate engineering physics laboratory course (“Advanced Physics Laboratory I”) with juniors in two course sections. Students used pen-enabled mobile devices (Tablet PCs) and InkSurvey to answer open-format formative assessment questions while interacting with simulations covering topics such as phasors in circuits, Fourier analysis, diffraction, standard deviation of the mean, and least squares.

Learning gains were measured using pre-tests and summative post-assessments scored with rubrics. Across five simulations, the class showed statistically significant gains (all p < 0.001), with average normalized gains ranging from 60% to 75%. However, correlations between gains and learning-style scores were near zero, indicating no statistically significant relationship between the effectiveness of the Coupled Model and student learning styles. The paper concludes that the model improves learning broadly, not selectively for any learning-style group.

finding.finding_summary: Students using interactive simulations coupled with real-time formative assessment showed significant learning gains on five physics/statistics topics. Average normalized gains ranged from 60% to 75% across the simulations (n=30 to n=41 per simulation), and all paired tests were significant at p < 0.001.
finding.measure: Pre-test to summative post-assessment scores on physics/statistics simulation-based conceptual questions (rubric-scored)
finding.study_size: n=30 to n=41 per simulation; total section enrollment n=41
finding.std_deviation: 0.12 (inter-rater reliability estimate SD for nine assessments)

finding.finding_summary: The paper specifically tested whether learning gains from the coupled simulation/formative-assessment model varied by learning style, using Pearson correlations with four learning-style dimensions. Correlations were near zero (e.g., ACT-REF r=0.02 to 0.25; SEN-INT r=-0.28 to 0.04; VIS-VRB r=-0.06 to 0.14; SEQ-GLO r=-0.15 to 0.06), suggesting no meaningful differential effect by learner preferences.
finding.measure: Correlation between normalized learning gains and Index of Learning Styles scores
finding.effect_size: r values near zero; not_reported as a standardized effect size
finding.confidence_interval: 95% confidence ranges reported for correlations, e.g., ACT-REF -0.28 to 0.32, SEN-INT -0.56 to 0.06, VIS-VRB -0.34 to 0.43, SEQ-GLO -0.47 to 0.39

paper_profiles.title: 3rd grade English language learners making sense of sound
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how 3rd grade English language learners (ELLs) use language to make sense of a physics topic: how string length and tension affect the sound produced by a string instrument. The authors are interested in how everyday language and academic/scientific language interact during students’ meaning-making, especially in an instructional setting that invites inquiry, discussion, and argumentation.

The study took place in a sheltered English immersion classroom in an urban K-8 public school. Thirteen third graders from diverse linguistic backgrounds participated; the class included students who were recent arrivals as well as students born in the United States, and nine first languages were represented. Data came from videotaped science lessons in a sound unit, with close analysis of one discussion episode in which students compared strings of different lengths and tensions on a teacher-built instrument.

The paper is qualitative and focuses on discourse analysis rather than measuring achievement gains. The authors conclude that the classroom created an emergent “Third Space” where students could draw on familiar, everyday terms and even invented onomatopoeic labels to communicate ideas about pitch, tension, and vibration. They argue that this supported students’ conceptual understanding and their use of academic vocabulary, but the paper does not report standardized outcome measures or causal effects relative to standard instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The discussion-based science activity supported students’ mechanistic reasoning about sound. In the analyzed lesson with 13 third graders (n=13), students used everyday language, invented labels, and emerging academic terms to explain how string length and tension affected pitch and loudness, indicating productive conceptual sense-making rather than a measured test-score gain.
finding.measure: Students’ discourse and mechanistic reasoning during a sound-unit discussion

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the inquiry setting helped ELLs practice and extend English language use while discussing science content. Students tried out academic terms such as “vibrate,” used peer-generated onomatopoeic labels, and were able to communicate their ideas despite limited English proficiency, suggesting support for oral language development in context (n=13).
finding.measure: Students’ oral discourse in English during science discussion

finding.finding_summary: The classroom interaction showed collaboration and shared meaning-making among peers. Students repeatedly rephrased one another’s ideas, checked interpretations, and co-constructed explanations about the string experiment, indicating collaborative reasoning and communication skills in the small-group discussion (n=13).
finding.measure: Peer-to-peer collaboration and co-construction of explanations in discussion

paper_profiles.title: Telework During the Pandemic: Patterns, Challenges, and Opportunities for People with Disabilities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how telework changed during the COVID-19 pandemic for U.S. workers with and without disabilities, and whether labor-market conditions affected the likelihood that disabled workers could obtain telework jobs. The authors argue that the pandemic both expanded employer acceptance of working from home and exposed structural limits, because workers with disabilities are disproportionately concentrated in occupations that are difficult to do remotely.

Using nationally representative U.S. data from the American Community Survey (2008-2020) and the Current Population Survey (May 2020-April 2022), the study compares pre-pandemic and pandemic telework patterns by disability status, disability type, occupation, industry, and demographic characteristics. It also estimates how declining state unemployment rates affected employment and telework during the pandemic. The analyses are regression-based and observational rather than experimental.

The main finding is that workers with disabilities were more likely than workers without disabilities to work from home before the pandemic, but during the pandemic they were less likely to do so overall because they were more concentrated in blue-collar and service jobs. After accounting for occupation and other characteristics, telework rates for some disability groups—especially people with cognitive/mental health and mobility impairments—were higher. Tight labor markets especially benefited people with disabilities, and a sizable share of their employment gains came through telework, with particularly strong effects for people with vision impairments and difficulty with self-care inside the home. The paper concludes that telework can be valuable for many disabled workers, but occupational segregation limits access, so broader labor-market and policy changes are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that telework expanded substantially during the pandemic, but workers with disabilities were less likely than those without disabilities to access pandemic-related telework once occupation and industry are considered. In linear probability models of CPS data (n=1,141,669), disability status was associated with a -0.027 gap in telework in the month-only model, which shrank to -0.003 with occupation controls and became +0.015 with full controls, indicating that occupational structure largely explains telework access rather than disability itself.
finding.measure: Pandemic-related telework / working from home; probability of teleworking

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that tighter labor markets improved employment opportunities for people with disabilities and increased the share of those gains coming from telework. A one-point decline in state unemployment was associated with a 0.0059 increase in any employment for adults with disabilities, and 51.8% of that increase came from telework employment (vs. 30.5% for people without disabilities), suggesting labor-market conditions can shape institutional hiring and accommodation practices.
finding.measure: Employment, telework employment, non-telework employment as functions of state unemployment rates

paper_profiles.title: Bayesian meta-analysis for evaluating treatment effectiveness in biomarker subgroups using trials of mixed patient populations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a meta-analytic problem in precision medicine: how to estimate treatment effects for a biomarker-positive subgroup when some trials report only mixed-population results, some report subgroup results, and some report both. The authors argue that standard meta-analysis either discards useful information from mixed-population trials or inflates heterogeneity when all studies are combined naïvely.

To solve this, they develop Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis models that progressively incorporate (1) biomarker-positive trials only, (2) biomarker-positive plus biomarker-negative subgroup results, and (3) biomarker-positive, biomarker-negative, and biomarker-mixed results. The mixed-population model uses the estimated systematic difference between biomarker groups and the proportion of biomarker-negative patients in each mixed trial to interpolate the biomarker-positive effect. The methods are illustrated with 13 randomized trials of anti-EGFR therapies in metastatic colorectal cancer (KRAS wild-type vs mutant) and evaluated in simulation.

In the colorectal cancer example, including mixed-population trials improved precision of the pooled treatment effect for KRAS wild-type patients without changing the point estimate materially; the reported precision gains were 19% for progression-free survival and 44% for overall survival in the main analysis. The simulation study found that the mixed-population model generally reduced uncertainty, but using unadjusted mixed-population effects could introduce bias when the treatment-effect difference between biomarker groups was large. Adjusting mixed-population effects for biomarker status reduced bias and improved robustness. Overall, the paper concludes that the proposed Bayesian framework can improve precision in subgroup meta-analysis when subgroup reporting is incomplete.

paper_profiles.title: P-VALUE EVALUATION, VARIABILITY INDEX AND BIOMARKER CATEGORIZATION FOR ADAPTIVELY WEIGHTED FISHER’S META-ANALYSIS METHOD IN OMICS APPLICATIONS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses statistical and computational problems in adaptively weighted Fisher’s meta-analysis (AW-Fisher), a p-value combination method used in omics studies to combine evidence across multiple independent studies. The authors focus on three issues: slow and imprecise p-value calculation, instability of the adaptive weight estimates, and the explosion of biomarker categories as the number of studies increases.

To address these issues, the paper proposes an importance-sampling-based p-value approximation with spline interpolation, a bootstrap-based variability index for AW weights, and a resampling-based co-membership matrix for clustering biomarkers into stable meta-pattern modules. The method is described in general and then demonstrated in simulations plus two transcriptomic applications: mouse metabolism microarray data and HIV transgenic rat brain RNA-seq data.

The results show that the proposed interpolation approach is much faster and more accurate than permutation-based p-value estimation, the variability index reflects instability in AW weight estimates, and the clustering procedure can recover biologically coherent gene modules with distinct study-specific or concordant differential-expression patterns. Overall, the paper is methodological and focused on improving transcriptomic meta-analysis rather than evaluating an educational intervention or student learning outcome.

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers can be supported to design and implement AI education that is integrated into existing core subjects, rather than taught only as standalone computer science content. The motivation is that many teachers lack AI experience and need curriculum designs that are accessible, relevant, and feasible in real classrooms.

The authors ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from a range of subjects and grade levels. Participants learned basic AI concepts and tools, discussed why AI matters for their students, and then worked in small groups with researchers to create draft integrated curricula. The workshop produced exemplar lesson plans for social studies, ESL, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and a physics example, with integration points centered on data, reflection, and ethics.

The study is qualitative and design-oriented rather than an outcomes study of student achievement. The main findings are that teachers value evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration when designing AI lessons, and they need scaffolding to teach ethics and connect AI to subject standards. The paper concludes that co-design with teachers can make AI curriculum more accessible and may help expand AI learning opportunities beyond computer science classrooms, but it does not test effects on student learning or compare against standard instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that co-designing integrated AI curriculum could support classroom implementation by clarifying lesson structure, resource choices, and ways to organize group work. The workshop produced first-draft implementable curricula, but this was based on teacher perceptions and design outputs rather than measured changes in efficiency.
finding.measure: teacher perceptions of lesson structure, resource use, and implementability during co-design; workshop deliverables

finding.finding_summary: The workshop emphasized student engagement as a central design concern, with teachers discussing anchoring activities in real-world issues, student-driven learning, competition, and gamification to motivate learners. These claims were qualitative and based on teacher design discussions, not on direct measurement of student motivation or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: teacher discussion of engagement strategies and perceived student interest

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly identified collaboration, reflection, and ethics discussion as key components of integrated AI lessons, indicating that the curricula were designed to support critical thinking, metacognition, and peer collaboration. The evidence is qualitative and comes from co-designed lesson drafts and workshop transcripts rather than student outcome data.
finding.measure: co-designed curricula and coded workshop discussions about reflection, collaboration, and ethics

paper_profiles.title: Surveying Turkish high school and university students’ attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates Turkish students’ attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving using a Turkish translation of the Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving (AAPS) survey. The authors’ main aim is not to test an instructional intervention, but to validate the translated instrument and examine how students’ responses vary by gender, grade level, school type, and comparison group.

The study adapted the AAPS survey from English to Turkish, reviewed it with bilingual experts and high school students, and then administered it to 528 students across six Turkish high schools and one university. Participants included 10th- and 11th-grade students from regular, science, and vocational high schools, plus first-year university science-education majors taking algebra-based physics. The study used descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, ANOVA, and exploratory factor analysis to analyze response patterns.

Overall, the Turkish version of the AAPS showed strong internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha about 0.82–0.90) and factor structure comparable to the original instrument. Students’ responses were mixed: there were no statistically significant differences in overall survey means by gender or grade level, but university students were somewhat more expert-like than vocational high school students overall, and some item-level differences favored different groups. In the cross-country comparison, U.S. university students in algebra-based physics were generally more expert-like than Turkish university students on the survey overall, though Turkish students were more favorable on a few metacognitive items such as reflecting on unreasonable answers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies physics problem-solving attitudes and approaches, including metacognition, reflection, and strategy use, all of which fall under durable skills. Across 528 Turkish high school and university students, overall means did not differ significantly by gender or grade level, but item-level responses showed mixed patterns: university students were more expert-like than vocational high school students on some items, while U.S. university students were more expert-like than Turkish university students on many items. No effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported for the item-level comparisons.
finding.measure: Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving (AAPS) survey responses; item-level favorable/unfavorable/neutral distributions and normalized scores
finding.study_size: n=528 (Turkish sample); n=43 Turkish university subset; n=397 U.S. comparison subset

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on physics problem-solving attitudes in a physics context rather than literacy, language, or mathematics achievement per se. The Turkish AAPS was validated for use with high school and university physics learners, and the results showed robust reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ranged from 0.817 to 0.897 across groups) with a 10-factor solution explaining 51.86% of variance. Because the paper measures attitudes rather than test scores, there is no direct achievement effect size.
finding.measure: AAPS survey reliability/validity metrics and item response patterns in physics problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines physics problem solving as a scientific reasoning domain, including understanding equations, identifying principles, and checking whether answers are reasonable. Results were mixed: university students were more expert-like than vocational high school students on overall favorable responses (50% vs 42%), but overall differences among grade levels and genders were mostly not significant, and Turkish university students were less expert-like than U.S. university students on the survey overall (+0.21 vs +0.38 normalized score).
finding.measure: AAPS survey scores and responses on physics/scientific problem-solving items
finding.study_size: n=528; university comparison n=43 Turkish vs n=397 U.S.

finding.finding_summary: Several AAPS items tap persistence, confidence, and willingness to continue solving difficult problems, which overlap with social-emotional skills. The findings were mixed: for example, many students endorsed giving up if they cannot solve a problem quickly, while other items showed expert-like persistence such as tracing back errors and spending time reflecting on unreasonable answers. The paper does not report a single aggregate effect size for persistence or engagement.
finding.measure: AAPS survey items related to persistence, confidence, and frustration tolerance in physics problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes institutional comparisons across school type, grade level, and country, and discusses how different educational settings relate to problem-solving attitudes. University students were more expert-like than vocational high school students on overall favorable responses, and U.S. university students were more expert-like than Turkish university students on many items, suggesting that schooling context and curriculum/instructional norms are associated with differences in problem-solving attitudes. However, the study is descriptive and does not test policy changes or institutional interventions.
finding.measure: School-type and cross-country comparisons of AAPS responses; reliability/validation of translated instrument

paper_profiles.title: Persepsi Siswa dalam Studi Pengaruh Daring Learning terhadap Minat Belajar IPA
paper_profiles.venue: SCAFFOLDING: Jurnal Pendidikan Islam dan Multikulturalisme
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether online learning (Daring Learning) affects sixth-grade students’ interest in learning science (IPA) at SD Negeri 03 Karanglo Tawangmangu. The authors frame the problem as low science achievement and low motivation under conventional, lecture-based instruction, and propose Daring Learning as a more engaging alternative that offers interaction, flexibility, and feedback.

The study used a quasi-experimental approach with 26 sixth-grade students split into an experimental class (n=13) and a control class (n=13), although the reported analysis focuses primarily on student questionnaire responses rather than achievement test scores. Students completed a response questionnaire about their experience with Daring Learning after science lessons. The results indicate generally positive perceptions: the average score was 2.78 with a reported percentage of 69.50, categorized as "setuju" (agree).

The paper concludes that Daring Learning made science learning more interesting, less boring, and more motivating for these elementary students, and that it may help create a learning community and improve flexibility of learning time and access to materials. However, the evidence presented is about student interest and perceptions, not academic achievement relative to standard instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Sixth-grade students reported more enthusiasm and interest in science learning under Daring Learning. Across 26 students, the questionnaire mean was 2.78 with a reported 69.50% agreement rate, indicating that students generally agreed the approach made science less boring and more motivating.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire responses about interest, enthusiasm, boredom, and motivation in science learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Daring Learning supported students’ ability to manage learning time and engage in collaborative learning, but these claims are based on perception data rather than direct skill measures. Students endorsed flexible, self-paced access to materials and interaction with peers/tutors, suggesting perceived gains in self-regulation and collaboration.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire responses and descriptive discussion of self-paced learning, interaction, and collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Teaching children to write: A meta-analysis of writing intervention research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical instructional question: which writing interventions most effectively improve the writing performance of students in the upper elementary grades? The authors note that many elementary students do not reach desired writing standards and that classroom writing instruction often receives limited time and support. To identify effective practices, they conducted a meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies focused on students in grades 4–6 in regular classroom settings.

The review synthesizes 32 studies yielding 55 effect sizes and compares ten intervention categories, including strategy instruction, text structure instruction, peer assistance, evaluation, goal setting, feedback, grammar instruction, revision, prewriting activities, and the process approach. Outcomes were based on posttest writing quality, typically holistic or analytical ratings of students’ texts. The overall average effect was positive and substantial (g = 0.72, 95% CI [0.49, 0.94]), but effects varied considerably by intervention type.

The strongest and statistically significant effects were found for goal setting (g = 2.03, though based on a single study with multiple conditions), strategy instruction (g = 0.96), text structure instruction (g = 0.76), feedback (g = 0.88), and peer assistance (g = 0.59). Grammar instruction (g = -0.37) and the process approach (g = -0.25) showed negative average effects, while evaluation, revision, and prewriting were positive but not statistically significant. Moderator analyses found that grade level mattered for strategy instruction, with larger effects in grade 6 than grades 4–5, and that analytical scoring reduced observed effects relative to holistic scoring in some cases. The paper concludes that targeted, explicit writing instruction is more effective than broad or isolated grammar-focused approaches for upper-elementary writers.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis synthesized 32 experimental and quasi-experimental studies (55 effect sizes) on upper-elementary writing instruction and found an overall positive effect on writing quality (g = 0.72, 95% CI [0.49, 0.94]). Effects varied by intervention: goal setting (g = 2.03), strategy instruction (g = 0.96), text structure instruction (g = 0.76), feedback (g = 0.88), and peer assistance (g = 0.59) were positive, while grammar instruction (g = -0.37) and the process approach (g = -0.25) were negative.
finding.measure: Posttest writing quality (holistic or analytical ratings of students' written texts)
finding.effect_size: g=0.72 overall; category effects ranged from g=-0.37 to g=2.03
finding.confidence_interval: overall 95% CI [0.49, 0.94]; category CIs reported in paper

finding.finding_summary: Several intervention categories included self-regulation- or feedback-related components, especially strategy instruction and goal setting, but the paper's central outcome was writing quality rather than motivation or self-regulation per se. The authors note that self-regulation strategies were part of many strategy-instruction studies, and that goal setting and feedback substantially improved writing performance, with the largest average effects in the review.
finding.measure: Writing-related self-regulation components embedded in interventions; not separately pooled as a standalone outcome

paper_profiles.title: Applications and Challenges of Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education: Integrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This integrative review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) has been used in medical education and what barriers hinder its implementation. The authors searched Medline, ERIC/Education Source, and Web of Science and screened peer-reviewed articles on AI applications in medical education, ultimately including 37 articles. Their review organized the literature into three main uses of AI: learning support, assessment of students’ learning, and curriculum review.

Most included studies focused on learning support, especially intelligent tutoring systems, virtual patients, and simulation-based tools that provide individualized guidance and feedback. A smaller set of studies examined automated assessment, such as machine scoring or prediction of student answers, and only one study addressed curriculum review. The paper concludes that AI is most commonly used to support learning because it can provide immediate, individualized feedback and guided pathways, but its wider adoption is constrained by difficulties in evaluating effectiveness, limited scalability, technical development challenges, data integrity concerns, and the need for multidisciplinary collaboration. The review emphasizes that stronger methodological designs and better evidence are needed before AI can be broadly adopted in medical education.

finding.finding_summary: Across 37 reviewed medical-education articles, AI was used mainly for learning support (n=32), assessment of learning (n=4), and curriculum review (n=1). The review reports that AI systems were valued for immediate feedback, guided learning pathways, and objective/quicker assessment, but also notes limited evidence on effectiveness and quality of feedback.
finding.measure: Counts and descriptive synthesis of AI use cases in medical education; reported advantages of AI applications

paper_profiles.title: Quantum Computing as a High School Module
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a one-week instructional module on quantum computing designed for motivated high school students ages 15–18. The module introduces core quantum concepts such as superposition, measurement, qubits, beam splitters, Stern-Gerlach experiments, quantum cryptography, quantum gates, entanglement, teleportation, and quantum algorithms, with problem sets and simulation-based labs used to reinforce ideas.

The paper is not an outcomes study of student learning; rather, it is a curriculum/practitioner resource that explains how the content is organized, the prerequisites assumed, and the learning objectives for each unit. The approach emphasizes accessible explanations, conceptual activities, and optional levels of mathematical complexity so the material can be adapted to students with different backgrounds. The main conclusion is that quantum computing concepts can be made approachable for high school learners through carefully scaffolded instructional materials and interactive simulations.

Because the paper is descriptive and pedagogical rather than empirical, it does not report measured effects on student achievement, engagement, or other implementation outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: What is essential is visible to the eye: Saliency in primary school ranking and its effect on academic achievements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ relative class rank in primary school affects later academic achievement, and whether the effect comes from the rank students can actually see versus an unobserved rank based on standardized test scores. The authors argue that rank salience matters: a rank computed from teacher-assigned grades is visible to students and may shape perceptions, motivation, and later performance, while a rank based on standardized tests is used as a placebo because students do not receive those scores.

Using a large administrative panel of Italian public school students, the study follows cohorts from grade 5 into grade 8 and grade 10, combining class grades, standardized test scores, class composition, and a student questionnaire. The identification strategy compares visible and invisible ranks and then adds increasingly flexible controls, including student fixed effects, to separate rank salience from underlying ability and peer composition. The paper also examines heterogeneity by gender, immigration status, SES, class size, peer ability, and individual ability.

The main conclusion is that visible rank has a sizable positive association with later academic achievement, while the invisible rank becomes small and statistically insignificant once the preferred controls are added. In the preferred specification, moving from bottom to top of the primary-school class rank predicts gains of about 8.5 percentile points in middle-school standardized tests and 7.7 percentile points in high-school tests. The paper finds little evidence that the rank effect differs by demographic group or class size, and it suggests the mechanism operates through students’ perceptions, self-esteem, and school engagement/aspirations. It also finds that class quality itself is much more important than rank, and that higher-achieving peer environments remain beneficial even after accounting for rank.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that higher visible primary-school class rank predicts better later academic performance in Italy. In the preferred specification with student fixed effects and flexible controls, ranking at the top versus the bottom of class in grade 5 is associated with gains of 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 standardized test scores and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10 standardized test scores (large-sample administrative panels).
finding.measure: National standardized test percentile scores in Italian and math in grades 8 and 10
finding.study_size: n=387,614 across two cohorts in the main sample (205,123 in 2018 cohort; 182,491 in 2019 cohort)

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that visible rank works partly through psychological channels. In the student questionnaire, higher visible rank is associated with better perceptions of school, higher self-esteem, stronger perceived peer recognition, and greater interest in studied subjects. Exact effect sizes are not reported in the excerpted text.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire items on self-esteem, perceived recognition by peers, school perceptions, and interest in subjects

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the choice of identification strategy matters for estimating rank effects, showing that standard approaches likely understate the effect because they do not fully remove ability peer effects and because the visible/invisible distinction matters. It also estimates class quality effects, finding that a one-standard-deviation increase in class quality is associated with gains of 13.0 percentile points in grade 8 and 13.3 percentile points in grade 10, roughly six times the effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in rank.
finding.measure: Estimated class quality (class value added) and comparison of rank-effect estimation methods
finding.effect_size: Class quality: +13.0 and +13.3 percentile points per 1 SD; rank: +2.2 and +1.9 percentile points per 1 SD
finding.std_deviation: 1 SD change in class quality; 1 SD change in rank

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret some mechanisms as involving motivation and self-perception, which are durable-skill-adjacent, but these are not the paper’s central outcomes. The main evidence is that higher visible rank increases students’ interest in the subjects studied and changes school-related perceptions, suggesting improved motivation and perhaps self-regulation, though no direct durable-skill measures are reported.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire items on interest in subjects and related attitudes

paper_profiles.title: Effects of Home Resources and School Environment on Eighth-Grade Mathematics Achievement in Taiwan
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how home resources and school environment relate to eighth-grade mathematics achievement in Taiwan. The author asks how much of the variation in math achievement is attributable to student-level factors, such as parents’ education and home educational possessions, and school-level factors, such as the economic composition of the school, neighborhood income level, and computer resources for math instruction.

The study uses TIMSS 2011 data from 4,605 eighth-grade students in 140 Taiwanese schools, along with school principal survey responses, and applies a two-level hierarchical linear model. Student-level predictors include mother’s education, father’s education, and home possessions; school-level predictors include the share of economically advantaged students, school location, and the number of computers available for math instructional purposes.

Results show that all measured student-level and school-level variables are positively associated with mathematics achievement. Higher parental education and more home possessions predict higher math scores, and schools with more advantaged students, in higher-income areas, and with more computers for math instruction also perform better, although the computer resource effect is small. The paper concludes that substantial achievement gaps exist across Taiwanese schools by socioeconomic context, but it does not evaluate an intervention or formative assessment practice; it is a correlational study of background and school-resource associations.

finding.finding_summary: This correlational multilevel study found that mathematics achievement was positively associated with all measured student- and school-level predictors. In the final model (n=4,605 students in 140 schools), mother’s education (γ=6.21, p<0.001), father’s education (γ=7.32, p<0.001), home possessions (γ=9.09, p<0.001), student economic background (γ=19.41, p=0.004), school location (γ=23.41, p=0.013), and school computer resources for math instruction (γ=0.20, p=0.016) were all significant positive predictors of eighth-grade math scores.
finding.measure: TIMSS 2011 mathematics achievement plausible values

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Activity-Based Method of Teaching Mathematics on Nigerian Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an activity-based teaching method improves secondary students’ mathematics achievement compared with the usual lecture method. The author frames the problem around persistent low performance in Nigerian secondary school mathematics and argues that more engaging, hands-on instructional approaches may improve learning outcomes.

The study used a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with intact classes from two government-owned senior secondary schools in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria. A sample of 96 Senior Secondary II students was split into an experimental group (activity-based teaching, n=48) and a control group (lecture method, n=48). Achievement was measured with a 20-item researcher-developed Mathematics Test (reliability alpha=0.86), focusing on circle geometry and construction. ANCOVA showed a statistically significant advantage for the activity-based group after controlling for pretest scores (F=114.461, p<0.001, partial eta squared=0.261), indicating substantially higher posttest achievement for students taught with the activity-based method.

finding.finding_summary: Students taught with the activity-based method outperformed those taught with the lecture method on a researcher-developed Mathematics Test covering circle geometry and construction. After controlling for pretest scores, the posttest difference was statistically significant (F=114.461, p<0.001), with the activity-based group explaining 26.1% of posttest variance (partial eta squared=0.261).
finding.measure: 20-item Mathematics Test (essay test) on circle geometry and construction; pretest and posttest scores
finding.std_deviation: Experimental posttest SD=8.84; Control posttest SD=6.22

paper_profiles.title: Areas of Strategic Visibility: Disability Bias in Biometrics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position statement responds to a request for information on biometrics and argues that biometric technologies can both help and harm disabled people. The authors focus on how accessibility barriers, biased training data, measurement error, and design choices can exclude disabled users or misclassify disability-related characteristics across recognition and inference systems.

The paper does not study a specific intervention or K-12 sample. Instead, it synthesizes examples from prior work and policy concerns to recommend accessibility-focused design, participatory stakeholder engagement, stronger governance, transparent data practices, and regulation. The central conclusion is that fairness alone is insufficient; biometric systems must be designed and governed through a disability justice lens to avoid reinforcing discrimination and creating new harms.

Because the paper is a policy/position statement rather than an empirical study, it does not report original outcome data or effect sizes. It is primarily aimed at technology developers, policymakers, and institutions considering biometric deployment in settings such as employment, education, healthcare, and public services.

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether elaborated, multimodal feedback is associated with better learning in high school physics, and whether students’ preferred ways of selecting feedback representations relate to performance. The authors focus on feedback that goes beyond simple verification (correct/incorrect) and can be opened in verbal, graphical, and mathematical forms within a computer-based practice platform.

The study used a prospective observational cohort design across 29 German high schools, with 661 students in grades 10–11 who completed pre- and post-tests and at least one platform exercise over 16–24 weeks. Students worked on kinematics exercises in the KI4SCool platform and could optionally open elaborated feedback in one or more representational formats. The researchers analyzed post-test scores using linear mixed-effects models and also clustered students by feedback-use patterns.

Results showed a small positive association between elaborated feedback use and post-test performance, independent of prior knowledge, platform score, and response confidence. In Cohort 1 the standardized association was β = 0.13 (95% CI [0.05, 0.22]); in Cohort 2 it was β = 0.08 (95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p = .054). Students tended to follow a few stable feedback-selection strategies, such as frequently opening all three representations or favoring verbal feedback, but there were no robust mean differences in post-test performance across these strategy clusters after adjustment. The paper concludes that multimodal elaborated feedback is promising for personalized instruction in physics, but because the design is observational, the findings cannot establish causality.

finding.finding_summary: Elaborated multirepresentational feedback was associated with higher post-test physics performance in a 16–24 week observational study of high school students (Cohort 1 n=351; Cohort 2 n=310). The association was small but positive and remained after controlling for pre-test score, platform score, exercises solved, and average confidence; standardized β = 0.13 (95% CI [0.05, 0.22]) in Cohort 1 and β = 0.08 (95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p = .054) in Cohort 2.
finding.measure: Post-test score on kinematics physics assessment
finding.study_size: n=661 total; Cohort 1 n=351; Cohort 2 n=310

finding.finding_summary: Average response confidence did not show a robust association with post-test achievement after adjustment, and feedback frequency was not correlated with confidence in either cohort (r=.00 to .10). The paper used response confidence as a learner characteristic relevant to feedback use, but it did not find evidence that confidence explained learning differences in the adjusted models.
finding.measure: Average response confidence and its association with post-test score / feedback use

paper_profiles.title: Distributed Readability Analysis of Turkish Elementary School Textbooks
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of International Conference on Information Technology and Computer Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of efficiently assessing the readability of large numbers of Turkish elementary school textbooks. The authors argue that traditional readability analysis methods are limited by small sample sizes and single-machine processing constraints, and therefore propose a distributed system for full-text readability analysis using Hadoop and MapReduce.

The system converts Ministry of National Education PDF textbooks into text, then preprocesses them through normalization, sentence segmentation, tokenization, and filtering of special characters, numbers, stop words, and author names. It analyzes textbooks from grades 4 through 8 using features aligned with Turkish readability formulas, especially average sentence length, average word length, and distinct word counts. The paper mainly reports system design and runtime performance, showing that the distributed approach is feasible and faster than a console-based single-machine implementation for larger numbers of textbooks.

The substantive educational context is Turkish elementary school textbooks, with the stated goal of helping educators and parents identify appropriate reading materials for students. The authors report that readability generally increases with grade level, although the 8th-grade textbooks show an unexpected drop in readability score relative to the 4th-7th grade materials. The paper does not test student learning outcomes or compare instructional interventions; its contribution is primarily a computational readability analysis tool and descriptive textbook profiling study.

finding.finding_summary: The distributed Hadoop/MapReduce system improved processing performance for readability analysis relative to a console application, especially as the number of textbooks increased. For 5 textbooks, the MapReduce version took 141.692 seconds versus a console application time of 10 seconds (as reported in the table), and the console application ran out of memory at 10 and 57 textbooks while the distributed system completed those tasks.
finding.measure: Execution time and system feasibility for textbook readability processing

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports descriptive readability analysis of Turkish elementary textbooks rather than student literacy outcomes. Readability scores and related text features generally increased with grade level from grades 4 to 7, but the 8th-grade textbooks showed a lower readability score (around 40) than the 4th-7th grades (roughly 60-80), indicating mixed patterns in textbook difficulty.
finding.measure: Readability scores, average sentence length, average word length, and distinct word counts
finding.study_size: n=5 grade-level textbook sets (grades 4-8); 1,994-2,482 sentences and 14,917-20,517 words per grade set

paper_profiles.title: Quadratic Forms and Automorphic Forms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a set of graduate-level lecture notes surveying the classical theory of quadratic forms over number fields, especially over Q and Z, and connecting that theory to modular and automorphic forms. It introduces foundational definitions and classification results for quadratic spaces and lattices, including orthogonal decomposition, local and global invariants, Hasse–Minkowski, Jordan decomposition, and neighboring lattices.

The notes then develop the theory of theta functions attached to positive definite quadratic forms and show how their transformation properties place them in the framework of modular forms. The main analytic conclusion is that modular-form methods can be used to study representation numbers r_Q(m), leading to results such as Tartakovsky’s theorem on local-global representability for sufficiently large m in at least five variables. This is expository mathematics rather than an empirical study, and it does not examine educational interventions, student populations, or K-12 outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: FEANEL: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Error Analysis in K-12 English Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces FEANEL, a benchmark for fine-grained error analysis in K-12 English writing. The authors argue that while large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in educational settings, their ability to identify, classify, and explain specific writing errors remains underexplored, especially for younger learners and second-language writing contexts.

To address this gap, the paper constructs a dataset of 1,000 anonymized essays written by K-12 students: 500 elementary and 500 secondary essays, with 8,676 annotated errors in total. Expert annotators rewrote essays, extracted edits, assigned each edit one of 29 error types, rated severity on a 1-5 scale, and provided explanations. The benchmark is then used to evaluate several state-of-the-art LLMs under zero-shot and one-shot prompting conditions across three subtasks: error classification, severity rating, and explanation generation.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs still struggle with fine-grained pedagogical feedback, especially on error classification and explanation quality, and perform substantially below human teachers.
