Performance improves when prompts include detailed definitions and examples, and larger or reasoning-oriented models generally do better on classification. The paper does not study formative assessment effects on student achievement directly; instead, it focuses on benchmarking models for writing-error analysis and feedback generation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate any literacy intervention on student writing achievement. Instead, it benchmarks LLMs on classifying, rating, and explaining K-12 English writing errors in a dataset of 1,000 essays (500 elementary, 500 secondary) with 8,676 annotated errors.
finding.measure: Error classification accuracy, macro-F1, severity MAE, and explanation quality (BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L) on K-12 English writing errors

paper_profiles.title: The Use of Fractional Blocks to Improve Mathematics for Second Grade Elementary School Students at South Bangka Indonesia
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This classroom action research examined whether using fractional block manipulatives could improve second-grade students’ motivation and mathematics learning outcomes in fractions. The paper was motivated by low achievement in fraction concepts when instruction relied mainly on pictures and teacher-centered explanation, which the authors argued did not match the concrete-operational development level of young learners.

The intervention used wooden fractional blocks as hands-on teaching aids during fraction lessons on 1/2, 1/3, and 1/4. The study involved 23 second-grade students at SD 9 Simpang Rimba in South Bangka, Indonesia, and used a one-group pretest-posttest style within two action-research cycles. Student motivation was observed with a Likert-scale instrument, and learning results were tracked through documentation and descriptive statistics.

The paper reports increases from before the action to the second cycle: motivation rose from a mean of 2.52 (low) to 3.91 (high), and average mathematics achievement rose from 65.0 to 80.2. Learning completeness increased from 39% to 100%, and the authors report N-gain values of 46.49% for motivation and 34.16% for learning outcomes. The conclusion is that fractional blocks helped make fraction concepts more concrete, increased student engagement, and improved fraction achievement in this small second-grade sample.

finding.finding_summary: In this classroom action research with 23 second-grade students, mathematics achievement in fractions improved after the fractional-block intervention. The mean score increased from 65.0 before the action to 73.7 in cycle 1 and 80.2 in cycle 2, with mastery increasing from 39% to 100%.
finding.measure: Fraction mathematics learning outcomes / test scores; learning completeness

finding.finding_summary: Student learning motivation increased substantially after use of the fractional blocks. The mean motivation score rose from 2.52 before the action (low) to 3.43 in cycle 1 and 3.91 in cycle 2 (high), with an N-gain of 46.49% reported for motivation. The paper also describes higher attention, interest, and enjoyment during learning.
finding.measure: Student learning motivation / engagement ratings (Likert-scale observation of enjoyment, attention, and interest)

paper_profiles.title: A review and evaluation of secondary school accountability in England: Statistical strengths, weaknesses, and challenges for ‘Progress 8’
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews England’s secondary school accountability metric, Progress 8, focusing on the statistical and policy choices behind how school performance is calculated, presented, and interpreted. Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention, it asks whether the current accountability model fairly measures schools’ contribution to student progress and how its design affects school comparisons, public reporting, and high-stakes judgments.

The article examines the Progress 8 system in state-funded secondary schools in England, which uses KS2 prior attainment and KS4 Attainment 8 outcomes to estimate school progress. The authors discuss strengths such as moving away from raw attainment measures and weaknesses such as measurement error in prior attainment, exclusion of some pupils, lack of adjustment for background characteristics, volatility over time, and limitations of the single-number school score and its confidence intervals.

The paper’s main conclusion is that Progress 8 is an improvement over earlier performance measures but remains an imperfect and sometimes misleading indicator of school effectiveness. The authors recommend changes such as better communication of uncertainty, consideration of contextual adjustments or similarity measures, greater use of multi-year averages, and more cautious interpretation of school rankings, especially after COVID-19 disruptions. The paper is primarily a policy/statistical critique of an accountability system, not an empirical study of student learning outcomes from an instructional intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Progress 8 has important institutional consequences for accountability, school comparison, and parental choice, but its statistical design can also misclassify schools and create incentives for gaming, teaching to the test, and exclusionary practices. It notes that unadjusted Progress 8 can shift school bandings substantially when background characteristics are added (e.g. about one-third of schools would change banding in the cited analysis), and that school rankings are unstable over time (e.g. correlation of 0.69 between 2016 and 2019 scores).
finding.measure: School accountability metrics, school bandings, school rankings, confidence intervals, and year-to-year stability of Progress 8

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review addresses how major self-regulated learning (SRL) models have developed and how they compare conceptually and empirically. Rather than testing a single instructional intervention, the paper synthesizes six influential SRL frameworks: Zimmerman, Boekaerts, Winne and Hadwin, Pintrich, Efklides, and Hadwin/Järvelä/Miller. It summarizes each model’s history, core phases or components, supporting empirical work, and measurement instruments.

The paper’s main purpose is to extract theoretical and practical implications for education from the accumulated SRL literature. It argues that SRL is an integrative framework for understanding cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, emotional, behavioral, and contextual aspects of learning, and that different models emphasize different parts of that process. The review also highlights evidence that SRL is beneficial for learning and that effects may differ by developmental stage or educational level.

The context is broad educational psychology, with evidence drawn from academic settings ranging from school-age learners to college students and collaborative/computer-supported learning environments. The paper does not focus on one K-12 intervention, but it repeatedly discusses instructional implications such as teaching students strategic learning, using learning diaries, and designing tasks or supports that foster monitoring, feedback, and reflection. Its conclusions are mainly conceptual: researchers and teachers should match SRL supports to students’ developmental level and the learning context, and future work should further examine emotion, motivation regulation, and socially shared regulation.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that SRL processes are associated with better learning and performance, including motivation, effort regulation, and self-reactions across phases of forethought, performance, and self-reflection. Across the cited studies, supports such as learning diaries enhanced SRL phases and improved students’ SRL and performance, and higher-achieving students showed greater use of SRL subprocesses (e.g., in science courses, n=51 high school seniors).
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning processes, motivation/effort regulation, self-reaction, and performance-related SRL behaviors

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion is that SRL can be taught and is linked to stronger metacognition, planning, monitoring, self-evaluation, and strategic learning. The review cites evidence that more SRL phases trained led to better basketball free-throw scores in college students (n=50), and that SRL skills predicted 90% of the variance in volleyball serving skills among college women, illustrating strong associations between SRL skills and performance.
finding.measure: SRL skills, planning/monitoring/self-evaluation processes, and task performance

finding.finding_summary: The review notes evidence from high school science courses showing that higher achievers used more of Zimmerman’s SRL subprocesses, suggesting a positive relation between SRL and science learning. However, this is based on correlational evidence rather than an intervention effect, so the conclusion is associative rather than causal.
finding.measure: Science course achievement and use of SRL subprocesses

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ use of classroom assessment techniques in primary mathematics education—an explorative study with six Chinese teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines how six Grade 3 mathematics teachers in Nanjing, China used a package of classroom assessment techniques (CATs) designed to reveal students’ understanding of division. The paper asks how teachers implement these CATs, what information they gain from them, and whether they view them as useful for future practice. The CATs were short assessment activities, some using whole-class red/green response cards and others using worksheets, all aligned to the Chinese Grade 3 textbook sequence on division.

The researchers collected data through teacher interviews, feedback forms, final reports, lesson observations, video recordings, and student work. The main implementation features explored were the degree to which CATs were embedded in lesson plans, how often they were used, whether teachers modified them, and whether teachers used the information to adapt instruction. Across teachers, CATs were generally feasible and liked, especially the red/green card format because it quickly revealed student understanding and increased engagement.

However, the study found a key limitation: although teachers gained new information about students’ correctness and sometimes their strategies, they rarely used that information to change subsequent instruction. Instead, they often integrated CATs as additional exercises within preplanned lessons, shortened them to save time, or gave immediate help during the activity. The authors conclude that CATs may support formative assessment practice in Chinese primary mathematics, but using assessment information to make informed instructional decisions remained difficult in this context.

finding.finding_summary: The CATs helped teachers elicit information about Grade 3 students’ understanding of division, especially place value, quotient length, and conceptual understanding beyond routine calculation. Teachers reported that most students could identify the watershed in CAT-1 correctly, and in CAT-2 many students solved problems correctly (e.g., 186/189 correct on 468 ÷ 2), but a substantial share appeared to rely on algorithm-like procedures despite being asked not to use the standard algorithm.
finding.measure: Students’ responses to division CATs, including correctness on card-based tasks and worksheet solutions without the division algorithm
finding.study_size: n=216 students (CAT-2 worksheet analysis reported on n=189 worksheets)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that the CATs, especially the red/green card format, engaged students and made them more interested in participating during lessons. Teachers said the activities helped students stay involved and made mathematics feel more interesting or mysterious, but these were qualitative perceptions rather than measured affective outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement and participation during CAT use

finding.finding_summary: Teachers found CATs feasible and efficient for quickly gathering whole-class information, particularly via red/green cards, but they also reported that CATs consumed precious lesson time and often had to be shortened or moved outside class. The study shows a tradeoff: CATs improved rapid information gathering, yet implementation was constrained by time pressure and limited use of results for later instructional adjustment.
finding.measure: Teacher reports on feasibility, time use, and implementation of CATs in lesson routines

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that CAT-1 helped students think systematically and recognize underlying rules, and teachers themselves noticed that the tasks revealed deeper understanding rather than just calculation skill. Some teachers explicitly framed the CATs as supporting insight into reasoning and conceptual understanding, though this was based on qualitative observations rather than direct measurement of metacognition or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Teacher observations/reports of conceptual understanding and systematic thinking

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education from 2007 to 2018. The authors ask how AI research in higher education has developed, how the field conceptualizes AI and its ethical implications, and what kinds of AI applications are being studied across the student life cycle. The review screened 2,656 records and included 146 journal articles for synthesis.

The review organizes the literature into four main application areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. Most studies were quantitative, came primarily from computer science and STEM, and focused on undergraduate settings. The authors conclude that the field is dominated by technical work, with very limited explicit definition of AI and very little critical reflection on ethics, privacy, or risks. They also note that most studies are short-term pilots or descriptive evaluations, with few longitudinal designs.

Across the reviewed studies, AI applications were generally reported as promising for assessment, feedback, prediction, and personalized support, often with high classification accuracy or positive pilot results. However, the review emphasizes that evidence on educational effectiveness is uneven, novelty effects are rarely addressed, and there is a weak connection to pedagogical theory. In the assessment and tutoring areas, the paper reports that automated grading and feedback can be efficient and sometimes comparable to human scoring, but feedback quality and appropriateness remain concerns, and some systems performed worse than control conditions. The paper is directly relevant for understanding implementation features such as feedback design, calibration/training needs, and teacher-facing support, although it is not a K-12 study.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI applications in higher education were frequently used to automate assessment, feedback, and administrative tasks, with strong evidence of efficiency gains in large classes. For example, automated essay scoring systems achieved high agreement with human raters (94.6%–98.2% in one study), and the authors note that such tools can reduce cost and time associated with multiple human assessors or routine staff work.
finding.measure: Agreement with human raters; administrative/assessment task efficiency; cost and time savings

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies used AI to monitor or predict engagement, motivation, and related learner states, usually through log data, clicks, or behavioral traces in virtual learning environments. The review reports mostly positive pilot results, but also one negative case in which a dialogue-based language-learning system underperformed on delayed post-tests, showing that learner support and engagement effects were not consistently positive.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and behavioral indicators in VLE/LMS data; delayed post-tests in language learning

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a small set of studies on collaboration support, metacognitive/self-regulatory support, and problem solving, especially in intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive systems. These studies generally reported positive preliminary results, such as adaptive hints, peer-dialogue systems, and self-regulation supports, but the evidence base was small and short-term, with one study reporting negative results for a more advanced learner group.
finding.measure: Collaboration quality, self-regulatory support, problem-solving performance

finding.finding_summary: The review identified automated essay scoring, automated writing feedback, and reading/writing tutoring systems as a substantial sub-area of AI in higher education. Systems often showed high scoring agreement or useful feedback functions, but the paper also notes persistent concerns about feedback quality, appropriateness for different genres and beginners, and cases where more detailed feedback led students to question their grades.
finding.measure: Essay scoring agreement; writing feedback quality; writing revision behavior

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics-related ITS and adaptive systems were included, but only as a minority of the literature. The review characterizes these systems as generally producing positive preliminary results for content learning and feedback, though the evidence is mostly short-term and not tied to a pooled effect estimate.
finding.measure: Performance in mathematics tutoring/content-learning systems

finding.finding_summary: Some reviewed intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning studies targeted STEM and science content, including medicine, physics, biology, and engineering. The authors summarize these studies as mostly showing positive or satisfactory preliminary results, although they caution that most are pilot implementations and do not establish long-term effectiveness.
finding.measure: Science/STEM learning outcomes in tutoring and adaptive systems

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the reviewed literature examined institutional and administrative uses of AI, such as admissions, retention, student services, policy support, and matching students to programs or careers. The review reports that machine-learning classifiers often achieved high prediction accuracy for these system-level tasks, suggesting potential value for institutional decision-making and targeting support.
finding.measure: Prediction accuracy for admissions, dropout/retention, course scheduling, and institutional decision support

paper_profiles.title: ISCED 2011: International Standard Classification of Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (cross-national education systems; not a learner sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is not an intervention study; it is the UNESCO Institute for Statistics’ reference classification manual for the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED 2011). Its purpose is to define internationally comparable categories for education programmes and educational attainment so that countries can report education statistics in a consistent way across systems and over time.

The paper explains the structure of ISCED 2011, including levels of education, programme orientation, completion and access-to-higher-level subcategories, and coding schemes for both programmes and attainment. It also clarifies the scope of formal and non-formal education, the treatment of modular and spanning programmes, and the statistical uses of ISCED for enrolment, entrants, graduates, attainment, and cross-national comparisons. The intended users are national and international education statisticians, policymakers, and agencies responsible for reporting education data.

The main conclusion is that ISCED 2011 provides a standardized framework to improve the reliability and comparability of education statistics worldwide. It does not evaluate student achievement or educational interventions, and it contains no empirical findings about formative assessment, feedback, or classroom data use.

finding.finding_summary: This is a classification and reporting framework, not an empirical impact study, so it does not test outcomes or estimate effects. Its contribution is systemic: it standardizes the reporting of education programmes, qualifications, enrolment, graduates, and attainment across countries to improve comparability and statistical consistency.
finding.measure: International education statistics classification and reporting framework

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, focusing on how scaffolding has been conceptualized, what it looks like in classroom practice, and whether it is effective. The authors argue that scaffolding is not just any teacher support, but a dynamic interaction characterized by contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility.

The paper synthesizes 66 English-language SSCI-listed articles published from 1998 to 2009, including theoretical, descriptive, effectiveness, and one meta-analytic study, across primary and secondary education. Most empirical studies were descriptive and focused on literacy, with fewer in math and science; a small number of quasi-experimental and correlational studies examined outcomes such as reasoning, conceptual understanding, transfer, and student involvement.

Across the reviewed effectiveness studies, scaffolding generally showed positive effects on students’ metacognitive and cognitive outcomes, though the evidence base was small and often relied on one-to-one tutoring or tightly controlled contexts. The authors emphasize that the main challenge in the field is measurement: many studies described scaffolding well but did not measure its key characteristics consistently or rigorously. They conclude that future work should better capture contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility, and should examine more naturalistic classroom settings.

finding.finding_summary: In Murphy and Messer (2000), 5- to 7-year-olds receiving contingent one-to-one scaffolding on a balance-scale task advanced more often in level of representation than children working in small groups or alone (N=122 total; scaffolding n=41, small group n=40, alone n=41). In Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998), fourth and fifth graders who received contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than students receiving partial, moderate, high, or no support, at immediate and delayed follow-up (n=40 total).
finding.measure: Balance-scale representation levels; long-division problem solving

finding.finding_summary: Mercer et al. (2004) found that teachers trained to use the 'Thinking Together' scaffolding program helped students improve reasoning talk and non-verbal reasoning in science lessons (experimental n=109, control n=121). Azevedo et al. (2005) also reported that adaptive human scaffolding was associated with greater shifts in mental models and greater knowledge gains in a hypermedia lesson on the circulatory system (adaptive n=38, fixed n=34, none n=37).
finding.measure: Reasoning talk coding, Raven Progressive Matrices, mental model shifts, circulatory system knowledge tasks

finding.finding_summary: Chiu et al. (2002) found that a cognitive apprenticeship condition that included scaffolding, coaching, and modeling improved 10th graders’ construction of mental models of chemical equilibrium compared with a non-CA control (n=20 vs n=10). Lajoie et al. (2001) and Chi et al. (2001) also reported better diagnostic or transfer-related performance when tutoring was more interactive or contingent, though the evidence for these studies was small or mixed.
finding.measure: Mental model construction of chemical equilibrium; diagnostic accuracy and transfer-related performance in tutoring contexts
finding.study_size: n=30 total in Chiu et al.; n=9 in Lajoie et al.; n=11 tutors/student pairs in Chi et al.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that scaffolding intended to support motivation, curiosity, and frustration control was associated with higher student involvement in mathematics classes. In Turner et al. (1998), whole-class classes with more intrinsic-support scaffolding and more transfer of responsibility had higher student involvement than lower-involvement classes (N=42 students across 34 lessons and 7 teachers); Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) found no enjoyment differences across contingent-support conditions, but the no-support control scored significantly lower on enjoyment than supported conditions.
finding.measure: Student involvement, enjoyment/affect questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the review is durable-skill outcomes such as metacognition, reasoning, self-regulation, and transfer. Across the effectiveness studies, contingent and interactive scaffolding was associated with better reasoning talk, more constructive participation, more accurate diagnosis of task demands, and higher performance on transfer questions; for example, Chi et al. (2001) found that more interactive tutoring elicited greater student responsibility and significantly higher transfer-question performance (n=11 students).
finding.measure: Metacognitive reasoning, self-regulated learning behaviors, transfer questions, diagnostic reasoning, constructive dialogue
finding.study_size: multiple small studies; key study n=11

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the value and practical implementation of formative assessment using an e-learning platform (BlackBoard) in a university setting. The authors argue that formative assessment can improve learning when it is frequent, paired with timely and detailed feedback, and embedded in an organized instructional structure.

The paper proposes weekly or fortnightly online tests in BlackBoard as a way to operationalize formative assessment. It describes a small implementation with 10-question online tests and reports student survey responses about continuous assessment, immediate feedback, and the convenience of online testing. Students generally favored the approach because it broke content into manageable pieces, provided immediate teacher feedback, and allowed them to monitor their understanding throughout the semester.

The study is primarily descriptive and survey-based rather than experimental, so it does not estimate causal effects on achievement. Its main conclusion is that formative assessment is perceived positively when it includes frequent low-stakes checks, immediate and specific feedback, and integration with online tools that make assessment more convenient and continuous. The authors also note concerns about stress and overemphasis on grades when assessments are too frequent.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent low-stakes assessments and immediate feedback helped them stay in touch with the subject, monitor their strengths and weaknesses, and feel more on track during the semester. However, some students also reported stress and pressure from too many tests, indicating that the perceived social-emotional effect was mixed but generally favorable toward formative assessment.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and stress/pressure from frequent assessments

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames formative assessment as supporting metacognition and self-monitoring, and students said the approach helped them identify mistakes, learn topics progressively, and understand whether they were on track. The evidence is based on survey responses and author interpretation rather than direct skill testing, so the finding is suggestive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Student perceptions related to metacognition, self-monitoring, and learning progression

paper_profiles.title: Metacognitive Training in Professional Development Can Improve and Sustain Student Achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a multi-year professional development system for secondary mathematics and science teachers can improve student achievement and sustain gains over time. The authors argue that high-quality professional development should not only transmit instructional strategies, but also build teachers’ metacognitive capacity to plan, evaluate, and adjust instruction in response to student data.

The intervention, the Mathematics and Science Teaching (MAST) System, combined workshops, instructional rounds, coaching, classroom observations, debriefings, co-planning, and action research over two years. A central feature was “Defense of Instruction,” in which teachers used student data and rubric-based feedback to justify instructional decisions and refine practice. Teachers in seven Alliance for College-Ready Public Schools secondary schools (45 teachers; over 11,000 students) participated.

The paper reports school-level improvements in California Standards Test mathematics performance during the intervention, with some schools showing large gains and reduced proportions of students below Basic. The authors compare these changes against district/state trends and ELA outcomes and argue the mathematics gains were associated with stronger implementation of adaptive-expert practices, as reflected in higher MAST rubric scores. They also report that gains persisted, and in some schools continued to improve, for two years after the formal intervention ended. The paper concludes that sustained, metacognitively rich professional development may be a pathway to stronger and more durable student achievement in secondary mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: The MAST System was associated with substantial gains in California Standards Test mathematics performance across seven secondary schools during the two-year intervention. For example, one school increased students at or above Proficient from 14% to 53% and reduced students below Basic from 58% to 25% (normalized change <c>=0.45 and -0.57, respectively); across the seven schools, the share at or above Proficient increased from 11% to 29% (<c>=0.20).
finding.measure: California Standards Test (CST) mathematics performance, including percentages at or above Proficient and below Basic; normalized change (<c>)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention explicitly aimed to improve student engagement, and teachers/students used reflection, goal-setting, self-assessment, and collaboration as part of the MAST curriculum. However, the paper does not report a standalone statistical test of social-emotional outcomes; instead, it describes improved engagement and achievement as part of the instructional process.
finding.measure: Student engagement, goal-setting, self-assessment, collaboration, and reflection as used within the MAST curriculum

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the program was developing teacher metacognition, self-regulation, reflective practice, and adaptive expertise. The paper argues these skills improved through repeated “Defense of Instruction,” data-driven reflection, and action research, and that stronger implementation of these practices was associated with larger student mathematics gains and sustained improvement after the intervention.
finding.measure: Teacher rubric scores for adaptive expert strategies and data-driven reflection; reflective practice and action research activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that schools with higher average MAST rubric scores, indicating stronger implementation of the PD model, had larger student gains, while low-implementation schools showed little or no change. It also reports that improvements persisted for two years after the intervention, suggesting changes in school culture and instructional practice beyond the immediate training period.
finding.measure: School-level implementation of research-based strategies and student mathematics achievement over time
finding.study_size: 7 schools in the main analysis; 5 schools followed for post-intervention persistence

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy built around classroom response systems (“clickers”), rich questions, whole-class discussion, and teacher adjustment based on student thinking. The central research problem is teacher change: how teachers develop comfort with TEFA, what tensions they experience, and what kinds of professional development help them adopt and adapt the approach.

The intervention combined classroom response technology with an intensive, multi-year professional development program. The project involved about 39 teachers across four sites in three western Massachusetts school systems, mostly middle- and high-school science and math teachers. The paper uses longitudinal mixed data sources (PD transcripts, journals, implementation logs, surveys, interviews, and classroom video), but the paper itself is primarily a narrative/case-based report of four teachers’ learning trajectories rather than an outcomes trial.

The main conclusion is that TEFA adoption is difficult but learnable, and that teachers typically move through a progression from mastering the technology, to improving question design, to rethinking classroom discussion and formative use of student responses. Teachers reported that TEFA helped them better understand student thinking and prompted lesson adjustments, but implementation was shaped by local context, teacher beliefs, prep time, classroom time, and student participation patterns. The paper argues that sustained, responsive professional development and iterative adaptation are essential, and that formative assessment becomes more consequential when teachers actually use the information to adjust instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on the implementation demands of TEFA for teachers. Teachers reported that using TEFA often required substantial preparation time to craft effective questions, while classroom time was also affected because whole-class discussion could be lengthy; at the same time, teachers became more efficient with practice and some used TEFA to manage class routines or streamline instruction. The study is descriptive (no effect size reported) but clearly shows both increased workload and some gains in instructional efficiency over time.
finding.measure: Teacher reports, monthly surveys, journals, implementation logs, and classroom video coding of TEFA use, discussion time, and implementation challenges

finding.finding_summary: Several participating math teachers changed their instruction in ways intended to improve students’ mathematical understanding and exam preparation, but the paper does not report standardized achievement gains. Kim and Gina both used TEFA to surface misconceptions, review for state math exams, and guide subsequent instruction, suggesting a positive instructional influence on mathematical learning processes rather than a measured score effect.
finding.measure: Mathematics classroom implementation, teacher-reported lesson changes, student response patterns, and perceived usefulness for math exam review

finding.finding_summary: The TEFA pedagogy was developed and studied primarily in science classrooms, with an explicit emphasis on question-driven instruction, dialogical discourse, and reasoning about concepts. Teachers reported that TEFA helped students articulate reasoning, compare ideas, and engage in deeper discussion, and several teachers revised lessons based on formative information about student thinking. No achievement test results are reported, so the evidence is qualitative and process-focused rather than outcome-based.
finding.measure: Science classroom discourse, teacher observations, video analysis, and reports of student reasoning and conceptual discussion

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports changes in student engagement, participation, confidence, and classroom atmosphere associated with TEFA use. For example, teachers noted increases in voluntary participation and more active discussion, and students often appeared more willing to share ideas once teachers adjusted implementation features such as withholding histograms or changing discussion format. These are qualitative observations rather than quantified effect estimates.
finding.measure: Student participation, engagement in discussion, willingness to speak, and classroom atmosphere as observed/reported by teachers

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that TEFA supported durable skills such as metacognition, collaboration, and reasoning. Teachers reported that students became more willing to explain thinking, compare ideas, and engage in self-moderation or peer discussion, while teachers themselves learned to use formative assessment to make agile instructional adjustments. The paper provides rich qualitative evidence but no quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Student discussion quality, student-to-student interaction, teacher-adjusted instruction, and metacognitive/meta-level conversations

finding.finding_summary: In addition to science and math learning, the paper describes TEFA being used to support broader curriculum goals, including lesson closure, homework motivation, and preparing students for standardized exams. These are ancillary academic uses rather than separately measured outcomes, and the paper does not report formal achievement data for them.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported curriculum support, homework motivation, lesson closure, and exam preparation

paper_profiles.title: New Curriculum, New Chance – Retrieval Augmented Generation for Lesson Planning in Ugandan Secondary Schools. Prototype Quality Evaluation.
paper_profiles.venue: Ndejje University Second Annual Research Dissemination Symposium 2024
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper examines whether a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) prototype can produce lesson plans of sufficient technical quality for use in Ugandan secondary schools. The motivation is that many teachers in Uganda face limited time, insufficient materials, and incomplete training for lesson planning, and the rollout of a new competency-based curriculum has made older lesson plans obsolete.

The authors built the NDU Lesson Plan Generator (NLPG), which uses a Cohere large language model, sentence embeddings, and LangChain to generate lesson plans from government-approved secondary-level textbooks in ICT, Mathematics, and History. The study generated 24 lesson plans and had three independent raters assess them with an adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) that is designed for East African competency-based curricula. The lesson plans averaged about 75-80% on the LPAP, with none below 65%, suggesting they were generally very good and technically fit for classroom implementation.

The paper concludes that the prototype can create lesson plans that meet minimum technical standards and, in some cases, outperform human-created plans reported in a comparable Rwandan study. However, the authors emphasize that the system can hallucinate when textbook coverage is thin, as illustrated by one plan that substituted an incorrect topic, and they recommend future teacher review, broader subject coverage, and direct teacher evaluation of content quality. The paper is primarily a prototype quality evaluation and does not measure student learning outcomes directly.

finding.finding_summary: The NLPG prototype substantially improved the technical quality and likely speed/feasibility of lesson planning by generating 24 usable lesson plans from government-approved textbooks. Across three raters, the average LPAP score was about 75-80%, and none of the plans scored below 65%, indicating that the tool can produce lesson plans that are directly usable with little or no adaptation, though teacher review is still recommended.
finding.measure: Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) quality score; technical quality of generated lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that RAG-based lesson plan generation could support implementation of Uganda's new competency-based curriculum by helping teachers update obsolete lesson plans and by providing context-aligned materials at scale. The conclusion is that the tool may help the government deploy the new curriculum more quickly and efficiently, although this is a prototype evaluation rather than a policy-impact study.
finding.measure: Policy/implementation relevance of the prototype for curriculum alignment and deployment

paper_profiles.title: The TalkMoves Dataset: K-12 Mathematics Lesson Transcripts Annotated for Teacher and Student Discursive Moves
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the TalkMoves dataset, a curated corpus of 567 K-12 mathematics lesson transcripts annotated at the sentence level for teacher and student discursive moves grounded in accountable talk theory. The authors motivate the work by arguing that sustained classroom discourse is central to rich and equitable learning, but that research on classroom talk is constrained by the scarcity of accessible, well-annotated K-12 data.

The paper’s main contribution is a dataset and accompanying coding protocol, not an intervention trial. The transcripts come from classroom videos and existing public resources, are annotated for six teacher talk moves and four student talk moves, and are additionally labeled with dialogue acts. The dataset is presented as a resource for NLP, educational data mining, and teacher-facing analytics, including the TalkMoves application, which provides automated, immediate feedback on mathematics classroom discourse.

Although the paper does not test student achievement outcomes directly, it reports descriptive corpus statistics and benchmark model performance for classifying talk moves. It also summarizes prior/adjacent evidence suggesting that personalized automated feedback on classroom discourse is perceived as useful by teachers and may increase their use of talk moves over time. Overall, the paper argues that accountable talk and related feedback tools have promise for supporting instructional improvement in K-12 math classrooms, but the article itself is primarily a data/resource paper rather than an effectiveness study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate student math achievement or numeracy outcomes. Its empirical results are limited to dataset description and benchmark classification performance for identifying teacher/student talk moves in K-12 mathematics lessons (teacher macro-F1 up to 76.32; student macro-F1 up to 73.12 on the test set, n=567 transcripts), not learner achievement.
finding.measure: Talk move classification performance in mathematics lesson transcripts

finding.finding_summary: The study analyzes teacher and student discourse in mathematics classrooms, but it does not measure student language fluency outcomes such as speaking proficiency or listening comprehension. The quantitative results concern annotation reliability and model performance on utterance-level discourse labels, not learner language gains.
finding.measure: Discourse move annotations and dialogue-act classification

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that automated talk-move detection can scale feedback that would otherwise require highly trained classroom observers and be time-consuming and expensive to provide. In benchmark tests, transformer models achieved macro-F1 scores of 76.32 for teacher talk moves and 73.12 for student talk moves, suggesting the system can automate discourse analysis with usable accuracy.
finding.measure: Model performance for automated identification of teacher/student talk moves

paper_profiles.title: Interdisciplinary Teams for Teacher Professional Development
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers (preservice and inservice STEM teachers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and iterative refinement of the San Antonio Teacher Training Astronomy Academy (SATTAA), a summer professional development program for secondary STEM teachers. The central problem is that many teachers who are expected to teach astronomy lack sufficient content background and pedagogical support, which can limit confidence and classroom implementation. The authors argue that interdisciplinary collaboration among astronomers, STEM educators, and informal education partners can produce stronger teacher learning experiences than content-only training.

The program was run across three cohorts (2018–2020) and evolved from a mostly face-to-face pilot to a hybrid format and then a fully online format during COVID-19. Across iterations, the team changed the balance of content, pedagogy, logistics, and field experiences based on participant feedback: reducing lecture-like sessions, increasing hands-on inquiry, adding more time for lesson planning and curricular connections, shortening overly demanding field trips, and creating a post-program alumni network. The paper reports descriptive participant feedback and a small pre/post content knowledge snapshot, showing improved astronomy knowledge and positive self-reported changes in interest and understanding.

Overall, the paper concludes that interdisciplinary team-based professional development can support stronger astronomy teacher preparation when content expertise is explicitly integrated with pedagogy, technology, and collaborative planning. The strongest practical lessons emphasized in the paper are the value of iterative redesign, hands-on inquiry, curricular alignment, and sustained networking after the workshop. However, the paper is primarily a program description and reflective case study rather than a rigorous causal evaluation of student achievement effects.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher participants showed improved astronomy content knowledge after the program, with pre/post scores rising from M=6.83 (SD=3.167) to M=8.72 (SD=2.845) on 15 moderately difficult questions. In the reported paired-samples test, the gain was statistically significant (t=5.24, n=18, p=0.000) with a large effect size (1.24).
finding.measure: Pre/post astronomy content knowledge quiz (15 moderately difficult questions)

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently reported increased interest in astronomy and better understanding of the content across all iterations, suggesting gains in motivation and confidence to teach astronomy. Survey data on a 5-point scale showed positive pre/post change for every group, with interest increases ranging from +0.2 to +1.1 and understanding increases ranging from +0.7 to +2.0.
finding.measure: Pre/post self-reported interest and understanding of astronomy content (5-point Likert scale)
finding.study_size: 2018 n=7; 2019 preservice n=6, inservice n=5; 2020 preservice n=4, inservice n=15

finding.finding_summary: The program emphasized collaborative lesson planning, peer exchange, and community-of-practice formation, and participants reported that these features were beneficial. Inservice teachers specifically said they wanted time to exchange classroom tips and co-plan lessons, indicating that the program fostered collaboration and professional network building even though no formal skill test was reported.
finding.measure: Participant feedback on collaboration, lesson co-planning, and networking

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the program expanded participation across cohorts, formed an alumni network, and created a sustained community of practice with weekly touchpoints. It also notes that fully online delivery improved reach, including access for teachers who could not have attended in person, and helped diversify participation.
finding.measure: Program participation/reach, alumni network formation, and qualitative reports of accessibility and continuity
finding.study_size: 3 cohorts (2018–2020); participant totals n=7, n=11, n=19

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (examples include Grade 12 and other classroom contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide on how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in educational settings. The authors organize their discussion around established formative-assessment frameworks: clarifying learning goals, identifying where learners are, and helping learners move forward, while also emphasizing feedback at the task, process, and self-regulation levels.

Rather than testing a single intervention empirically, the paper synthesizes prior research and provides classroom-facing prompt examples, illustrative outputs, and implementation guidance. It argues that LLMs may help teachers scale activities such as rewriting learning objectives in student-friendly language, co-constructing success criteria, generating exemplars and sample work, creating questions for short-cycle checks of understanding, and drafting feedback. The paper also cautions that quality depends heavily on prompt design, teacher expertise, and careful contextual adaptation.

The review is especially focused on practical implementation features that could strengthen formative assessment use: clear and specific prompts, alignment with lesson goals, iterative teacher review, and use of LLMs to support rather than replace pedagogy. It notes limitations in current evaluation metrics and warns against overreliance on AI-generated responses, recommending that educators use LLMs to support deeper learning, transferable skills, and classroom discussion. Because the paper is conceptual and not an empirical evaluation, it does not report effect sizes or direct achievement outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or streamlining formative-assessment tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating exemplars, drafting questions, and producing feedback. No empirical effect size is reported, but the review repeatedly frames these uses as time-saving and scalable, especially in large classrooms and resource-constrained settings.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time saved in preparing formative-assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that LLM-supported formative assessment can promote metacognition, self-regulation, and critical thinking when used to generate student-friendly goals, exemplars, and process-level feedback. The paper does not test these claims experimentally, but it consistently argues that well-designed prompts and reflective tasks can help learners internalize criteria and evaluate their own work.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, critical thinking, reflection

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses LLM support for writing-related formative tasks, including simplifying learning objectives, generating sample essays/methods sections, and providing feedback on student writing. Evidence cited is illustrative rather than direct; the paper presents examples and prior studies showing that GPT-3.5/ChatGPT can generate text that is judged reasonably well in simplification tasks, but no achievement effect is estimated for K-12 students.
finding.measure: Writing quality / quality of generated exemplars and learning objectives

finding.finding_summary: Several examples are drawn from biology and fMRI/science contexts to show how LLMs might help clarify scientific learning goals, generate domain-specific questions, and support methods-section writing. The paper suggests these uses could improve scientific understanding and reasoning, but it provides no direct causal evidence or achievement data.
finding.measure: Scientific understanding, method-section writing, domain-specific questioning

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers in Korea envisioned using ChatGPT in science lesson planning. The paper addresses a timely implementation question: how teachers integrate a generative AI tool into curriculum goals, instructional strategies, and formative assessment, and what benefits and risks they anticipate.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary teachers enrolled in a science education course. After a short instructional sequence introducing ChatGPT, participants wrote 45-minute elementary science lesson plans that had to include at least one instructional strategy and at least one interaction with ChatGPT, along with simulated chat transcripts. The authors evaluated the lesson plans with a modified TPACK-based rubric and analyzed open-ended survey responses using constant comparative coding.

Results show that participants imagined a wide range of ChatGPT uses across science domains and methods, especially cooperative learning, POE, the learning cycle, analogy generation, and concept mapping. Lesson plans scored relatively well overall (M=3.29/4), but teachers were less adept at selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with curriculum goals and instructional strategies. Pre-service teachers saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative assessment, but they also worried about inaccuracy, hallucinations, and student over-dependence. The paper concludes that science teacher preparation should include AI literacy, critical evaluation of model outputs, and structured classroom routines to support, rather than replace, teacher-led instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student achievement directly; instead, it analyzes pre-service teachers' lesson plans and perceptions about how ChatGPT could support science learning. Teachers expected ChatGPT to aid prediction, explanation, inquiry, and concept understanding in elementary science, but they also identified inappropriate uses (e.g., using it for visual phenomena or experiment design) and warned about hallucinations that could mislead scientific understanding.
finding.measure: Lesson plan analysis and open-ended survey responses about ChatGPT use in science instruction

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers frequently anticipated that ChatGPT would increase students' motivation, interest, active participation, and self-directed learning. These perceptions were based on ChatGPT's perceived ability to provide instant, context-aware responses and individualized support, but the study did not test these outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about anticipated effects on motivation, interest, and self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: The study centrally examines durable-skills-related uses of ChatGPT, especially critical thinking, questioning, collaboration, and self-directed learning. Teachers believed repeated questioning with ChatGPT could deepen critical thinking and support collaborative learning routines, but they also worried that students might over-rely on ChatGPT and weaken their practical inquiry skills if use was not structured carefully.
finding.measure: Lesson plan rubric scores and open-ended survey responses about anticipated classroom use

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that ChatGPT may improve planning and classroom efficiency by supplying supplementary information, summarizing long student-generated scenarios, supporting role-play organization, and giving prompt feedback. The paper reports that teachers viewed ChatGPT as helpful for managing tasks within a 45-minute lesson, although no direct workload or time-savings outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Lesson plan analysis and survey responses about instructional planning and classroom management uses

finding.finding_summary: The paper is mainly about teacher preparation rather than institutional outcomes, but it argues that teacher education should include professional development, AI/digital literacy, and guidance on how to integrate ChatGPT safely and appropriately. The authors frame these needs as preparation for future classroom and schooling systems where AI tools are more common.
finding.measure: Author discussion and implications drawn from lesson plan analysis and survey data

paper_profiles.title: NiCE Teacher Workshop: Engaging K-12 Teachers in the Development of Curricular Materials That Utilize Complex Networks Concepts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design, implementation, and outcomes of the Networks in Classroom Education (NiCE) teacher workshop, which was created to help K-12 teachers learn network science and develop classroom-ready curricular materials using network concepts. The authors argue that network science can serve both as a content area and as a cross-cutting lens that supports standards-aligned teaching, particularly under the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS).

The workshop brought together 21 teachers from a wide range of grade levels and subject areas for a four-day professional learning experience at West Point. The program combined short pre-workshop videos, presentations, hands-on activities, group brainstorming, lesson-planning sessions, and repeated feedback cycles with network scientists and peers. Participants produced 13 resources, including 10 lesson plans and 3 education projects, all made publicly available online.

The paper reports largely descriptive outcomes from pre/post self-ratings, workshop observations, and the final products created by participants. Teachers reported increased knowledge of network concepts and increased likelihood of using them in their classrooms, and the authors characterize the workshop as highly motivating and productive. The main conclusion is that collaborative, teacher-centered professional development can successfully build capacity for integrating network science into K-12 instruction and can generate usable curricular materials.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop was designed to make network science easier to integrate into teaching by providing lesson-plan structures, standards mapping, and collaborative development time. The paper reports that the workshop produced 13 usable resources (10 lesson plans and 3 projects) and that participants felt the materials could help them create cross-curricular lessons and ease workload, but no formal productivity or workload effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Number of curricular resources produced; participant perceptions of usefulness for lesson planning and workload

finding.finding_summary: The workshop aimed to build teachers' ability to think with network concepts, collaborate, and develop lesson ideas across disciplines. Self-ratings showed large pre/post increases in knowledge of network-related concepts and in likelihood of using them in lessons, indicating gains in conceptual understanding and transfer-oriented planning, though no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-rated knowledge of network concepts and likelihood of using them in the classroom (pre/post survey)

finding.finding_summary: A central goal was to create publicly available, standards-aligned curricular materials and foster broader adoption of network science in K-12 education. The workshop yielded 13 resources for the teaching community and the authors argue that this collaborative model supports future dissemination and integration into schools, but the paper does not report institutional-level effect sizes or adoption outcomes beyond participant intentions.
finding.measure: Creation of publicly available lesson plans and education projects; participant intention to bring materials back to home institutions

finding.finding_summary: Participants described the workshop experience in overwhelmingly positive terms, using words such as 'informative,' 'inspiring,' 'relevant,' and 'connected.' The paper also notes that the workshop fostered motivation, creativity, and ownership of the initiative, suggesting positive effects on engagement and professional confidence, but these were measured descriptively rather than with standardized instruments.
finding.measure: Open-ended three-word experience responses and qualitative workshop observations

paper_profiles.title: Analysis of Brownian Motion by Elementary School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a remote, inquiry-oriented science workshop for motivated elementary school students in Japan. The workshop used video analysis of Brownian motion, a dice-based 2D random-walk activity, and discussion of protein dynamics to help students experience a simplified research process: asking a question, analyzing data, forming a hypothesis, and testing it with a model.

The intervention was implemented online during the COVID-19 pandemic with 27 students in grades 4–6. Students used Tracker software to trace particle motion and a spreadsheet to share data, then completed a hands-on dice simulation to model random molecular collisions. The authors also used pre- and post-workshop questionnaires to gauge prior knowledge, perceived difficulty, and interest.

The main conclusion is that even though many students found the workshop difficult, they also found it very interesting, suggesting that carefully structured, beginner-friendly but challenging scientific inquiry can stimulate curiosity among motivated elementary students. The paper emphasizes design features such as simplified software setup, small-group support by teaching assistants, gamified elements, and explicit scaffolding of abstract concepts. It does not report achievement test outcomes; instead, it reports participant perceptions and feasibility observations.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop was designed to engage elementary students in a simplified scientific research process: setting a question, analyzing observed motion quantitatively, building a hypothesis about Brownian motion, and verifying that hypothesis with a dice-based model. The study does not report test-score gains, but it concludes that students could participate in this inquiry process and that the structured activities helped them understand the mechanism of Brownian motion at a basic level.
finding.measure: Workshop participation in inquiry/scientific reasoning activities; post-workshop questionnaire and task completion
finding.study_size: n=27 (27 students initially; n=26 post-workshop survey responses)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high interest despite perceived difficulty: all respondents rated the workshop as interesting or very interesting, while more than half rated it as difficult or very difficult. This pattern suggests strong engagement and curiosity for motivated elementary students, even when the content exceeded typical grade-level knowledge.
finding.measure: Post-workshop interest and difficulty questionnaire (5-point ratings)

finding.finding_summary: The workshop required students to perform video analysis, share results in a spreadsheet, and work in small groups with remote teaching-assistant support, which directly exercised collaboration and basic data-handling/problem-solving skills. The paper reports that more than half of students found both the video analysis and the random-walk experiment easy or very easy, indicating the activities were feasible for this age group with scaffolding.
finding.measure: Feasibility/ease-of-use questionnaire; completion of analysis and simulation tasks

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that preparatory implementation features reduced friction: they precompiled the Tracker analysis file, sent files to parents in advance, verified installation, and used small-group online support to simplify student participation. They report that students could do video analysis without much stress when the initial analysis file was prepared properly, indicating improved task efficiency and lower procedural burden.
finding.measure: Observed workshop implementation; post-workshop ease-of-analysis questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: Teacher-to-classroom assignment and student achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student achievement can be improved by changing which teachers are assigned to which classrooms, without changing the teacher workforce itself. The authors focus on whether teacher-to-classroom reallocation can produce meaningful gains when assignments are based on observable teacher practice, student baseline achievement, and classroom peer composition.

The study uses data from the Measures of Effective Teaching (MET) project in six large urban U.S. districts. Teachers were randomly assigned within schools to classrooms in the experiment, but the realized data include non-compliance and student movement, so the authors estimate a semiparametric instrumental-variables model and then simulate counterfactual teacher reassignments across existing classrooms. Their key finding is that better matching of existing teachers to classrooms could raise average achievement by about 0.02 standard deviations relative to the status quo, and as much as 0.04 standard deviations under the best versus worst feasible assignment. The gains are largest when teacher classroom assignment is made more assortative with respect to teacher FFT ratings and student baseline achievement, suggesting that assignment policy can matter even when classroom composition is held fixed. The paper is about teacher assignment rather than formative assessment, feedback interventions, or classroom data use, but it provides adjacent evidence that observational teaching-practice measures can be used to improve allocation decisions.

finding.finding_summary: Counterfactual teacher-to-classroom reassignments are estimated to raise average student achievement in elementary and middle schools. Using MET data and a semiparametric IV approach, the authors estimate that the status quo assignment versus the optimal assignment would increase average test scores by about 0.02 standard deviations, with a best-versus-worst assignment gap of about 0.04 standard deviations.
finding.measure: End-of-year standardized state test scores in mathematics and English language arts (ELA), reported as district-standardized z-scores
finding.study_size: about n=8,500 students and 614 teachers in math; about n=9,600 students and 649 teachers in ELA

paper_profiles.title: Automating RT Planning at Scale: High Quality Data For AI Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a data bottleneck in AI for radiotherapy (RT) planning: high-quality, standardized treatment-plan datasets are scarce, heterogeneous, and expensive to produce manually. The authors argue that these limitations hinder progress in dose prediction and other RT planning tasks, and they propose an automated iterative radiotherapy planning (AIRTP) pipeline to generate large volumes of curated, clinically aligned plans.

The AIRTP system integrates AI-based organ-at-risk auto-contouring, helper-structure generation, scripted planning through Varian Eclipse/ESAPI, RapidPlan-based or scorecard-derived objective initialization, optimization and dose calculation, and an iterative refinement loop guided by plan-quality evaluation. The pipeline is applied to head-and-neck and lung cancer cases from public TCIA datasets and collaborators, producing 3,730 plans across 1,622 patients for the released HMM-RT dataset, substantially larger than prior public RT planning datasets.

The paper reports that the automated plans are generally comparable in quality to manually created clinical plans and that the pipeline can reduce planning time from roughly 3–6 hours to about 0.1–1 hour per plan. It also demonstrates a method for reproducing deliverable plans from predicted 3D dose distributions, supporting downstream benchmarking of dose-prediction models. Overall, the contribution is primarily infrastructural and methodological: it is about scalable data generation, not clinical outcome testing, and the paper does not present causal evidence on patient health outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The AIRTP pipeline substantially reduces planning time compared with manual radiotherapy planning, which the paper states typically takes 3–6 hours per plan. Automated planning is reported to take about 0.1–1 hour per plan, while producing plan quality comparable to manual plans; no formal statistical test or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Planning time per radiotherapy treatment plan; workflow automation of contouring, optimization, and dose calculation

paper_profiles.title: Implementation of SPN21 Curriculum in Brunei Darussalam: A Review of Selected Implications on School Assessment Reforms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Brunei Darussalam’s SPN21 curriculum reforms interact with school assessment reform, especially at the secondary level. The author argues that curriculum change alone is unlikely to improve student learning unless examinations, continuous assessment, and teacher preparation are also redesigned to better support mastery, practical skills, affective development, and fairer selection decisions.

The paper is a qualitative policy review based on content analysis of Ministry of Education documents and related literature, not an empirical intervention study. It discusses several assessment-related implementation issues: the over-emphasis on examinations, inclusion of affective and vocational/technical skills, use of informal and authentic assessments, moderation of borderline marks, the relationship between formative and summative assessments, and the need to strengthen pre-service and in-service teacher education in assessment. The author also recommends nationalizing and localizing senior secondary examinations over time.

The context is Brunei’s inclusive education and SPN21 reform environment, with attention to how assessment practices affect regular, disabled, and gifted/talented students. The main conclusion is that assessment reform must accompany curriculum reform if the system is to better measure desired competencies, support learning, and reduce the distortions created by high-stakes public examinations. Because the paper is a conceptual review rather than an outcome study, it offers recommendations rather than direct effect estimates.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that SPN21 implementation requires concurrent reform of school assessments, teacher education, and examination governance to avoid continued over-reliance on high-stakes norm-referenced exams. It does not report outcome data, but qualitatively concludes that curriculum reform without assessment reform is unlikely to succeed and may continue exam-dominant practices.
finding.measure: Policy and assessment reform themes identified through document/content analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on assessment of non-core subjects such as vocational, technical, practical, and affective domains. It argues these areas are currently underemphasized in examinations and that raising their status and including them in public exams would encourage teaching and learning of these skills, but no empirical effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Presence and status of vocational/technical, practical, and affective skills in examinations and curriculum

finding.finding_summary: The author contends that informal assessment, peer assessment, self-assessment, and portfolio assessment can support motivation, self-confidence, self-esteem, and reduced anxiety/stress, especially for disabled and gifted learners. These are presented as plausible benefits drawn from prior literature and policy reasoning rather than direct findings from the Brunei case.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-confidence, self-esteem, anxiety/stress, self-discipline

finding.finding_summary: The paper recommends and conceptually supports assessment approaches that develop self-reflection, peer interaction, critical observation, and constructive appraisal. It also argues that formative and informal assessments can help students master concepts and skills, but this is a qualitative argument without direct measurement of achievement or skill gains.
finding.measure: Self-assessment, peer assessment, critical observation, self-reflection, concept mastery

paper_profiles.title: The effects of self-monitoring and self-reflection in A1 adult learners in an English blended learning environment
paper_profiles.venue: Universidad de La Sabana master's thesis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This master’s thesis examines whether self-monitoring and self-reflection strategies can improve the learning experience of A1 adult learners in an English blended-learning course. The study is framed around formative self-assessment in a context where participants previously experienced more traditional assessment practices with limited feedback and little opportunity for ongoing reflection. The researcher asks whether these strategies help learners become more aware of their progress, identify strengths and weaknesses, and take more responsibility for their own learning.

The intervention was implemented with a group of adult distance tutors at Universidad Nacional Abierta y a Distancia (UNAD) in Bucaramanga, Colombia, enrolled in an elementary English blended course. Data were collected through checklists, surveys, students’ journals, and a teacher journal, and analyzed qualitatively through coding and categorization. The paper argues that the blended format created opportunities for both face-to-face and online engagement, while self-assessment activities supported learner autonomy and metacognitive development.

The main conclusions are that self-monitoring and self-reflection were perceived positively and appeared to increase learners’ awareness of the language-learning process, their involvement in learning, and their ability to set goals and monitor progress. Participants also responded positively to scaffolded instruction and to the blended-learning modality itself. The thesis emphasizes that self-assessment should be guided and supported by teachers, especially in contexts where learners are not accustomed to reflective practices.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported more awareness of their learning process, increased involvement in their individual learning, and more positive attitudes toward self-assessment and the blended course. The qualitative evidence indicates that self-monitoring and self-reflection helped learners identify areas for improvement, monitor progress, and set goals, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student journals, surveys, checklists, and course reflections on learning awareness, involvement, and self-assessment
finding.study_size: n=group of adult learners; exact number not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly emphasizes metacognitive development: learners learned to identify strengths and weaknesses, monitor their progress, and plan learning goals. These outcomes are presented as improvements in self-regulation and reflective capacity rather than as tested achievement gains, and the study reports no quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Metacognitive reflections, self-monitoring checklists, and journals documenting goal setting and progress monitoring
finding.study_size: n=group of adult learners; exact number not reported

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (theoretical review; no single study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews six major models of self-regulated learning (SRL)—Zimmerman, Boekaerts, Winne and Hadwin, Pintrich, Efklides, and Hadwin/Järvelä/Miller—and compares how each conceptualizes cognition, motivation, emotion, context, and phases of regulation. The author’s main purpose is to synthesize the theoretical development of SRL and to extract implications for education from the accumulated empirical literature and prior meta-analyses.

The review is not an intervention study; instead, it surveys model histories, empirical support, and measurement tools associated with each framework. Across the models, the paper emphasizes that SRL is multi-component and that different models foreground different processes: Zimmerman emphasizes cyclical phases, Boekaerts emphasizes goal pathways and emotion, Winne and Hadwin emphasize metacognitive monitoring and feedback, Pintrich includes cognition, motivation, behavior, and context, Efklides distinguishes person-level and task×person-level regulation, and Hadwin/Järvelä/Miller extend SRL into collaborative settings.

The paper’s main conclusion is that the SRL models together form an integrative framework useful for teaching students to become more strategic and successful learners, but that different models may fit different developmental stages or educational levels. It also argues that future research should better integrate motivation regulation, emotion, trace data, and social/shared regulation, and that educators should apply differential SRL approaches depending on learners’ needs and contexts.

finding.finding_summary: This review centrally focuses on self-regulation, metacognition, and collaboration as durable skills. Across the six SRL models, the paper concludes that students can be taught to be more strategic and successful, and that empirical work shows differential effects of SRL approaches depending on developmental stage or educational level. The review does not report one pooled effect size because it is a narrative synthesis rather than a quantitative meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, metacognitive monitoring, strategic learning, collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) Using R: A Workbook
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is an introductory workbook on partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) implemented in R via the SEMinR package. It is designed to teach readers the core concepts, model-building logic, and analysis workflow for PLS-SEM, including reflective and formative measurement models, structural model evaluation, mediation, and moderation.

The text is methodological rather than an empirical study of a substantive domain.
