It explains when to use PLS-SEM versus covariance-based SEM, emphasizing PLS-SEM’s prediction-oriented, composite-based approach, its suitability for complex models and small samples, and practical guidance for evaluating measurement and structural models. The examples and case study are drawn from business research, not K-12 education.

Because the paper is a methods workbook and not a study of educational interventions or assessment practices, it does not provide empirical evidence about formative assessment, feedback interventions, or classroom data use in K-12 settings. Its relevance to the retrieval question is only indirect, as background on how one might analyze such interventions statistically, not evidence on which implementation features improve achievement.

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction in primary and secondary education. The authors focus on three central issues: how scaffolding is conceptualized, what forms it takes in classroom practice, and whether it appears to improve learning and engagement outcomes.

Across 66 included articles, the review synthesizes theoretical, descriptive, and effectiveness studies. It argues that scaffolding is best understood as contingent support that is gradually faded while responsibility is transferred to the learner. The review also proposes an analytic framework distinguishing scaffolding means (e.g., feedback, hints, instructing, explaining, modeling, questioning) from scaffolding intentions (e.g., metacognitive, cognitive, affective support).

The evidence base was dominated by small descriptive studies, especially in literacy, with fewer studies in math and science and very few rigorous effectiveness studies. The review concludes that scaffolding appears effective for metacognitive and cognitive outcomes, with mixed but generally positive evidence for student affect, but it emphasizes that the field is limited by measurement problems, inconsistent definitions, and a lack of strong experimental evidence in naturalistic classroom settings.

finding.finding_summary: Literacy was the most developed domain in the review, but evidence was largely descriptive rather than experimental. The review notes that scaffolding in literacy classrooms commonly involved modeling, questioning, clarifying, and gradual release of responsibility, and that existing studies generally portrayed scaffolding as supportive of text comprehension and literacy learning; however, few direct effect estimates were available.
finding.measure: Literacy-related classroom discourse, reading/text comprehension practices, and literacy strategy use

finding.finding_summary: Several included effectiveness studies in math found beneficial effects of contingent scaffolding. For example, fourth- and fifth-grade students who received fully contingent support on long-division problems solved significantly more problems than peers in other conditions at immediate and follow-up testing, and the review also notes supportive patterns in elementary math classrooms.
finding.measure: Math problem solving and transfer on long-division tasks; classroom scaffolding patterns

finding.finding_summary: Science-focused studies showed that scaffolding can improve students’ reasoning and conceptual understanding. In one study of 7th and 10th grade students working on the circulatory system, adaptive human scaffolding led to significantly more shifts in mental models and greater knowledge gains than fixed or no scaffolding (N=38, 34, 37). Other studies in science and conceptual change also reported better model construction under scaffolded conditions.
finding.measure: Mental model shifts, knowledge gains, and scientific reasoning during science learning tasks
finding.study_size: n=38, n=34, n=37 (Azevedo et al.); additional studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review found some evidence that scaffolding can support student affect, engagement, and involvement. In a correlational study of 42 fifth- and sixth-grade students across 34 mathematics lessons, classes with more whole-class scaffolding aimed at motivation/curiosity and frustration control showed higher student involvement, and a quasi-experimental study found students without support reported lower enjoyment than students receiving scaffolding.
finding.measure: Student involvement, motivation/affect, and enjoyment questionnaires
finding.study_size: n=42 for correlational study; enjoyment study sample size not fully reported in excerpt

finding.finding_summary: This review centrally addresses durable skills such as metacognition, self-regulation, collaboration, and transfer of responsibility. Across effectiveness studies, contingent scaffolding improved students’ reasoning together, self-regulating behaviors, constructive participation, and transfer performance; for example, adaptive scaffolding in hypermedia learning was associated with more self-regulated learning shifts, and interactive tutoring led to more constructive student behavior and higher transfer-question performance.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning behaviors, collaborative reasoning/talk, constructive participation, transfer performance, and mental model change
finding.study_size: N=109 vs 121 (Thinking Together); N=38, 34, 37 (Azevedo et al.); N=11 tutors with N=11 students (Chi et al.); additional studies not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Primary Teacher Training through Academic Portfolios in Advanced Mathematics Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether academic portfolios can improve mathematics teacher preparation by bridging the gap between advanced disciplinary mathematics and the practical needs of primary classroom teaching. The central problem is that preservice primary teachers often experience advanced mathematics courses as abstract and disconnected from their future instructional work, which can undermine engagement, motivation, and perceived relevance.

The intervention studied is the integration of academic portfolios into two undergraduate courses in algebra and number systems for primary teacher candidates at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. The portfolio model included a negotiated learning contract, explicit rubrics, reflective prompts, draft-and-feedback cycles, personalized support, and final presentations/discussion tables. Data came from course records, self-assessments, peer evaluations, reflective writing, and instructor observations across four cohorts (n=37 total), making this a mixed-methods implementation study rather than a causal experiment.

The paper reports consistently positive associations between portfolio use and several outcomes: attendance above 70%, frequent access to course materials, improved course grades across semesters, and strong student perceptions that the portfolio supported self-study, time organization, conceptual understanding, and reduced mathematics anxiety. However, the author explicitly notes that multiple confounds could explain the observed changes, and that stronger causal claims would require larger samples, longer follow-up, and more rigorous controls. Overall, the study presents portfolios as a promising assessment and instructional structure for preservice teacher education, especially when embedded in a well-supported learning environment with feedback and reflection.

finding.finding_summary: Portfolio implementation was associated with higher course grades in both advanced mathematics courses for preservice primary teachers. In MAT2920, the average grade increased from 4.43 in the prior semester to 5.89 when portfolios were introduced, then to 5.71 and 6.44 in later semesters; in MAT2925, grades increased from 5.52 to 5.80 and then 6.44. The paper treats these as promising associations rather than causal effects because cohort and instructional differences may also explain the improvement.
finding.measure: Course grades in Algebra and Number Systems I and II (Chilean scale 1.0-7.0)

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio approach was associated with stronger engagement, intrinsic motivation, and lower mathematics anxiety. Attendance remained above 70% with no absences for assessed activities, and 11 of 12 respondents (91.7%) said alternative assessment methods like portfolios helped reduce math anxiety. Students also reported that the gradual, revision-based process and emphasis on personal growth made the course less stressful.
finding.measure: Attendance, self-assessment survey responses, and reported mathematics anxiety
finding.study_size: n=12 for anxiety survey; n=37 overall course implementation

finding.finding_summary: The study found positive associations with self-regulation-related and metacognitive skills, including self-study, time organization, reflection, and deeper conceptual processing. In the self-assessment survey, 85.7% reported improved self-study and 100% reported improved time organization; qualitative reflections also described better connections between abstract concepts and teaching applications. Peer reviews additionally suggested that students could identify strengths and weaknesses in portfolio work, indicating growth in evaluative and critical thinking skills.
finding.measure: Self-assessment survey, peer evaluation, reflective paragraphs, and portfolio quality indicators
finding.study_size: n=12 for self-assessment survey; n=7 for peer-evaluated portfolios in one cohort

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio structure appears to have increased time-on-task and active use of course materials. Students reported substantial weekly time investment in portfolio development, with 42.9% spending more than eight hours per week, and digital platform usage averaged 185 page views per week. These indicators suggest greater sustained engagement with coursework, though the study does not measure instructor workload or efficiency directly.
finding.measure: Reported weekly time spent on portfolios and CANVAS page views
finding.study_size: n=12 for survey responses; n=37 overall implementation

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers in Korea envisioned using ChatGPT in lesson plans and what they believed its educational benefits and risks would be. The paper is motivated by the lack of empirical evidence on how generative AI can be integrated into actual science teaching and learning, especially at the K-12 level, where most prior writing has been speculative rather than classroom-based.

The authors asked 29 pre-service elementary teachers to attend four instructional sessions on ChatGPT and science pedagogy, then draft a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan that incorporated ChatGPT and a simulated chat exchange. The lesson plans were analyzed with a modified TPACK-based rubric and open-ended survey responses were coded qualitatively. The sample spans multiple science domains and instructional approaches, including cooperative learning, POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, experimentation, and concept mapping.

Overall, the lesson plans showed moderately strong integration quality (mean TPACK-based rubric score M = 3.29/4, SD = .91). Participants were strongest at aligning ChatGPT with curriculum goals and instructional strategies, but weaker at choosing the most appropriate ChatGPT functions for a given lesson. Qualitatively, they expected ChatGPT to support questioning, self-directed and individualized learning, and formative assessment, but they also worried about inaccurate responses and over-reliance by students. The paper concludes that pre-service teachers can imagine many productive uses of ChatGPT, but targeted professional development is needed to improve function selection, critical evaluation of AI output, and classroom structuring to prevent dependence and misinformation.

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to support science learning by prompting questioning, explanation, prediction, and inquiry-oriented activity, especially in POE and learning-cycle lessons. However, this paper does not test student achievement directly; it reports pre-service teachers' lesson-plan design quality and perceptions, with a mean rubric score of M = 3.29/4 (SD = .91) across 29 plans.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan integration of ChatGPT into science instructional strategies and inquiry-oriented activities; modified TPACK-based rubric

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed ChatGPT could increase motivation, interest, and active participation by enabling self-directed and individualized learning. These are anticipated benefits reported in survey responses rather than measured student outcomes, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Pre-service teacher survey responses about anticipated motivation, interest, and self-directed learning benefits

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT may support critical thinking, continuous questioning, collaboration, and reflection, but also warns that poor use could reduce students' practical inquiry skills or encourage over-dependence. This conclusion is based on qualitative analysis of 29 lesson plans and survey responses, not student performance data.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of lesson plans and survey responses about critical thinking, collaboration, and over-reliance risks

finding.finding_summary: A major anticipated use of ChatGPT was to make lesson planning and classroom activity design more efficient, including generating role-play scripts, summarizing lengthy student scenarios, and supplying quick responses to consecutive questions. The paper reports an average rubric score of M = 3.48/4 (SD = .99) for 'instructional strategies & ChatGPT,' suggesting relatively strong perceived fit for instructional workflow support.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan integration quality and qualitative claims about support for planning, summarization, and feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-integrated science instruction will require professional development, AI/digital literacy, and classroom structures that mitigate hallucinations and over-dependence. It does not evaluate policy or institutional change directly, but it clearly frames teacher training and implementation support as necessary conditions for broader adoption.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of teacher preparation needs and implementation constraints

paper_profiles.title: AI and Machine Learning for Next Generation Science Assessments
paper_profiles.venue: Machine learning, natural language processing and psychometrics
paper_profiles.population: K-12 (middle and high school examples; broader K-12 science assessment context)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter reviews how artificial intelligence and machine learning are being used to support the next generation of science assessments, especially in K-12 settings aligned to the Framework for K-12 Science Education and the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). The central problem is that conventional assessments, especially multiple-choice items, do not adequately capture three-dimensional science learning, scientific practices, or knowledge-in-use. The chapter argues that performance-based tasks such as written explanations, argumentation, and drawn models are better aligned to these goals but are difficult and time-consuming for teachers to score manually.

The chapter surveys the evolution of machine learning-based automatic scoring for science assessments, including supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, pre-trained, zero-shot, and fine-tuned large language model approaches. It uses K-12 science assessment examples, including middle school performance tasks, to illustrate how automated scoring can provide timely feedback and reduce teacher workload. The chapter also presents a framework for understanding factors that influence machine-human score agreement, such as response length, rubric clarity, construct complexity, examinee characteristics, training/validation approach, and algorithm/feature design.

Overall, the chapter concludes that ML-based scoring can improve the practicality of authentic science assessment by making complex tasks more feasible for classroom use and by supporting faster feedback and instructional adjustment. However, it also emphasizes important limitations: scoring accuracy varies by task and design choices, evidence is uneven across methods, and fairness, generalizability, and validity remain major concerns. The paper is primarily a conceptual and synthesis-oriented chapter rather than an empirical impact study of student achievement.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that machine learning-based assessments are well suited to science reasoning tasks such as explanation, argumentation, investigation, and model-based performance in K-12 science. It does not report a single causal achievement effect; instead, it synthesizes evidence that automated scoring can handle these complex constructs with varying accuracy depending on task design, with examples such as supervised scoring of scientific argumentation, explanations, and investigations achieving satisfactory agreement, while other approaches show weaker performance.
finding.measure: Machine-human score agreement on science explanation, argumentation, investigation, and model-based assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: A major conclusion is that automated scoring can substantially reduce teacher workload by scoring written and drawn responses more quickly than manual grading. The chapter gives a classroom example in which scoring one middle school science assessment task for 100 students could take about 100 minutes manually, while ML systems can provide timely and objective feedback that alleviates this burden.
finding.measure: Teacher scoring time / workload for performance-based assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The chapter positions ML-based science assessment as a field-level shift toward assessments aligned with NGSS and the Framework for K-12 Science Education. It argues that these tools can change classroom assessment practice by enabling more authentic performance tasks at scale, but it also notes unresolved institutional issues around validity, fairness, generalizability, privacy, and implementation guidance.
finding.measure: Adoption/readiness of ML-based assessment systems for NGSS-aligned science education

paper_profiles.title: ASK•IT / A2L: Assessing Student Knowledge with Instructional Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This technical report describes the ASK•IT / Assessing-to-Learn (A2L) approach, a classroom model for integrating formative assessment, collaborative learning, and instructional technology in physics instruction. The authors argue that traditional assessment practices—especially periodic cumulative exams—push students toward short-term, answer-focused behaviors and provide little information that teachers can use to adjust instruction.

The paper proposes a formative-assessment-centered classroom structure organized around a "question cycle": present an item, let students work individually or in groups, collect answers, show a histogram of responses, discuss as a class, and wrap up. The approach is intended to increase student participation, promote explanation and reasoning, and give teachers real-time information about student thinking. The report also lays out "habits of mind," cognitive goals, collaborative-learning practices, and technology functions (e.g., collecting and displaying responses) that are meant to support deeper conceptual understanding and concept-based problem solving.

The context is physics education at the high school and college levels, not a controlled intervention study. The document is largely a conceptual/design report grounded in the authors' experience with teaching and cognitive research, rather than an empirical evaluation of achievement effects. Its main conclusion is that formative assessment is most powerful when it is frequent, low-stakes, integrated into lesson flow, supported by peer discussion, and paired with technology that makes whole-class feedback visible and actionable.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report empirical test-score gains, but it presents a theory of how formative assessment and concept-based items should improve students' physics understanding, reasoning, and problem solving. The central claim is conceptual: by using frequent items, peer discussion, and histogram feedback, students should better confront misconceptions and develop scientific reasoning, but no effect sizes or sample-based results are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding, reasoning, and problem-solving in physics

finding.finding_summary: The report substantively targets durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, communication, and collaboration, describing them as intended learning outcomes of the ASK•IT/A2L classroom. It argues that students will improve these skills through habits of mind, group work, and meta-communication, but it provides no empirical estimates, sample size, or measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, communication, collaboration

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is operational efficiency in classroom assessment: technology is described as making it easier to collect, sort, display, and store student responses, and to manage transitions within lessons. The report claims that classroom communication systems reduce time and effort for teachers and make group work and feedback more efficient, but these are asserted benefits rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Time and effort required to collect, compile, display, and store student responses; classroom transition efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment can increase engagement, participation, confidence, and willingness to explain thinking, especially when students see the class distribution and work in collaborative groups. It frames the approach as low-stakes and low-stress, but again does not report empirical data on engagement or motivation outcomes.
finding.measure: Engagement, confidence, willingness to participate, low-stakes/low-stress classroom experience

paper_profiles.title: New Curriculum, New Chance – Retrieval Augmented Generation for Lesson Planning in Ugandan Secondary Schools. Prototype Quality Evaluation.
paper_profiles.venue: Ndejje University Second Annual Research Dissemination Symposium 2024
paper_profiles.population: Secondary School (Ugandan secondary schools; Secondary 1 level)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper asks whether a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system can produce lesson plans that meet technical quality standards for use in Ugandan secondary classrooms. The authors frame the problem as one of poor lesson planning quality, limited teacher time, and weak support for implementing a new competency-based curriculum, especially in rural schools.

The intervention studied is a prototype lesson plan generator built with Cohere LLM, sentence embeddings, and LangChain, which retrieves content from government-accredited textbooks and generates lesson plans in the Ugandan format. The prototype was trained on three Secondary 1 textbooks (ICT, Mathematics, and History/Political Education), and 24 lesson plans were generated and rated by three independent raters using an adapted Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP). The evaluation focused on technical/format quality rather than classroom impact or student learning outcomes.

Results show that the generated lesson plans averaged about 75–80% on the LPAP, which the authors interpret as “very good,” and none scored below 65%. They conclude the generated plans meet the technical standards needed for direct classroom implementation and outperform human-made lesson plans discussed in a comparable Rwandan study, though they caution that content hallucinations can occur when source material is sparse. The paper’s main contribution is evidence about lesson-plan quality and implementation feasibility, not achievement effects.

finding.finding_summary: The RAG-based lesson plan generator improved the technical quality and efficiency of lesson planning. Across 24 generated lesson plans rated by three independent raters, the average LPAP score was about 75–80%, and none scored below 65%, suggesting the tool can produce classroom-ready plans with reduced teacher preparation burden. No direct effect size on student outcomes was reported.
finding.measure: Lesson Plan Analysis Protocol (LPAP) technical quality scores; lesson plan completeness/format adherence

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the tool could support implementation of Uganda’s new competency-based curriculum by producing lesson plans aligned with government-approved textbooks and the official lesson-plan format. The authors argue this may help teachers, schools, publishers, and the government deploy the curriculum more efficiently, but these are projected institutional benefits rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Alignment of generated lesson plans with government-approved textbooks and Ugandan lesson-plan format

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping high school teachers learn to facilitate collaborative argumentation in classroom discussions. The authors developed Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that uses NLP to automatically classify student talk along three dimensions: argument moves, specificity, and collaboration. DT then presents visual analytics such as pie charts, annotated transcripts, collaboration maps, strengths/weaknesses, and instructional planning supports.

The study evaluated DT in real classrooms with 18 high school English Language Arts teachers from 4 schools. Teachers used a desktop version of DT after their discussions were transcribed and manually coded, and then completed surveys and cognitive interviews about usability and usefulness. The evaluation focused on teacher perceptions of the system and on the performance of the underlying classifiers, rather than student learning outcomes.

Teachers reported that DT was helpful for understanding students’ discussion strengths and weaknesses, generating instructional goals, and supporting reflection on facilitation. The usability ratings were generally high, with most items receiving agree/strongly agree responses. The NLP classifiers achieved moderate to substantial agreement with human coders for argument moves and specificity, and moderate performance for collaboration, though some collaboration labels were harder to predict. Overall, the paper concludes that discussion analytics can support teacher learning about collaborative argumentation, but it does not provide evidence of effects on student achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Discussion Tracker was helpful for analyzing classroom discussions and supporting reflection, goal-setting, and instructional planning. In surveys from the usability study (n=18 teachers), the overall helpfulness item averaged 4.72/5, and items on the overview, annotated transcript, strengths/weaknesses, and goal-setting all scored highly (means 4.56-4.89).
finding.measure: Teacher usability/helpfulness survey ratings of DT features and workflow support

paper_profiles.title: The TalkMoves Dataset: K-12 Mathematics Lesson Transcripts Annotated for Teacher and Student Discursive Moves
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the TalkMoves dataset, a curated corpus of 567 human-annotated K-12 mathematics lesson transcripts drawn from classroom video recordings and other public or confidential sources. The central problem is the lack of accessible, research-ready classroom discourse data for studying teaching practices and for training NLP models that can detect instructional talk moves. The dataset annotates teacher and student utterances at the sentence level using a theory-driven accountable talk framework, and it also includes dialogue-act labels to support computational analysis of classroom discourse.

The paper is primarily a dataset and methods paper rather than an intervention study. It describes how transcripts were collected, standardized, and annotated; reports high inter-rater reliability for the talk-move coding; and presents benchmark transformer models for automatic talk-move classification. In addition, it describes the TalkMoves application, which gives teachers immediate feedback on their classroom discourse, and it notes that initial evidence suggests teachers find the feedback valuable and may increase their use of talk moves over time. However, the paper does not present a controlled evaluation of achievement impacts or causal effects on student outcomes.

The population is K-12 mathematics classrooms, with the dataset skewed toward U.S. middle school lessons and whole-class discussion/small-group work. The intended users are educators and researchers, especially those interested in classroom discourse, teacher feedback, and AI-supported professional learning. Overall, the paper’s main contribution is infrastructural: it provides a theoretically grounded dataset and an application pipeline for analyzing and giving feedback on teacher-student discourse, laying groundwork for later studies on whether and how such feedback influences instruction and learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the TalkMoves application automates a process that otherwise requires highly trained classroom observers, making feedback on classroom discourse more scalable and less time-consuming for teachers and researchers. It benchmarked transformer models for talk-move detection, with test-set macro-F1 scores around 75.38%-76.32% for teacher models and 71.28%-73.12% for student models, supporting practical feasibility, but it did not evaluate downstream productivity at scale.
finding.measure: Automatic classification performance for teacher and student talk-move detection; workflow scalability for feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that sustained classroom discourse supported by accountable talk can promote equitable participation, student engagement, and active listening in mathematics classrooms. This claim is grounded in the dataset’s theoretical framing and descriptive analysis of talk moves, but the paper does not provide a causal estimate of changes in student engagement or motivation from the TalkMoves application.
finding.measure: Classroom discourse patterns; talk-move frequencies; teacher feedback utility (descriptive/initial evidence)

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on accountable talk moves that support reasoning, explanation, reacting to peers, and building on classmates’ ideas, which are core collaboration and metacognitive/discursive skills. In the dataset, teacher pressing for reasoning was present in 1.17% of teacher utterances and student providing evidence/reasoning in 13.353% of student utterances, but the paper does not test whether these moves improve durable skills outcomes.
finding.measure: Frequency of accountable talk moves in classroom transcripts; annotated discourse actions

finding.finding_summary: The paper is explicitly situated in K-12 mathematics instruction and presents accountable talk as a discourse framework intended to support mathematical understanding and rigorous thinking. However, it does not report student math achievement scores, effect sizes, or a causal evaluation of whether the TalkMoves application or specific implementation features improve numeracy.
finding.measure: Mathematics classroom discourse annotations; benchmark model performance on math lesson transcripts

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: ICPE 2013 – International Conference on Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines whether student-produced videos can serve as a formative assessment tool in high school physics. The authors argue that video production may reveal students’ misconceptions, reasoning, and understanding in ways that standard tests do not, while also capturing transferable skills such as planning, collaboration, and persistence.

The activity was implemented in a Brazilian high school (Colégio Pedro II, Rio de Janeiro) with students aged roughly 14–17 across grades 1–3 of high school. After a term of instruction, 232 students working in self-selected groups produced 55 short videos on physics topics; each group also submitted a short written explanation. Teachers reviewed the videos, provided comments, and held a class discussion session in which the products were analyzed for physical correctness, clarity, coherence, and technical quality.

The paper reports descriptive and correlational evidence rather than a controlled impact study. Most videos were at least partially correct, and the authors observed a strong correlation between technical quality and conceptual/content quality: among technically very well done videos, 90% were entirely conceptually correct. The authors conclude that student video production can be a useful and reliable formative assessment resource because it exposes learning difficulties, supports classroom discussion, and encourages careful planning and cooperative work. However, the study does not isolate causal effects on achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Student-produced videos provided evidence of physics understanding, but performance was uneven: 35% of the videos were fully correct and 45% were partially correct, while 15% were incorrect (n=55 videos, n=232 students). The paper also reports that 47% of videos presented the physics clearly, 75% had a satisfactory connection between proposal and product, and 87% had a logical sequence, suggesting that the activity revealed both correct reasoning and persistent misconceptions.
finding.measure: Correctness, clarity, logical sequence, and connection between proposal and product in student-produced physics videos

finding.finding_summary: The authors explicitly identify planning, replanning, collaboration, and metacognitive reflection as central features of the video task. They report that students usually chose production forms requiring careful planning and implementation, and that the activity supported cooperative work and active participation, though no standardized skill measures were used.
finding.measure: Observed planning, collaboration, and quality of production choices in student video work

finding.finding_summary: The activity is described as engaging and motivating: students were said to spend time preparing videos, interact with peers, and use familiar media formats, which the authors interpret as supporting active participation in learning. Evidence is descriptive only and based on teacher observation of the class process and video products.
finding.measure: Observed engagement/participation during video production and classroom discussion

finding.finding_summary: Although the focus is physics, the paper also treats the video assignment as a broader academic task requiring students to communicate content in an audiovisual product. The authors report that technical quality and content quality were strongly correlated, indicating that students’ ability to present subject matter effectively was related to the overall quality of the assigned work.
finding.measure: Technical quality and content quality of student-produced videos

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators (elementary, middle, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 educators prefer lesson plans written by human curriculum designers or generated by two GenAI systems: a prompt-engineered GPT-4 model and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model. The motivation is practical: lesson planning is time-consuming, and the authors want to understand where AI-generated plans may be acceptable or even preferable, and where human-authored plans still outperform them.

The study used a controlled pairwise preference design with 16 experienced K-12 mathematics educators (originally 20 recruited, 4 withdrew) who evaluated 529 lesson-plan pairs across four dimensions: warm-up, main tasks (explain/reinforce), cool-down, and overall quality. The lesson plans were aligned to grade level and Common Core math standards. Educators were blinded to author source and provided binary preferences plus optional comments; the authors analyzed the data quantitatively and with thematic analysis/topic modeling.

Results showed that human-authored lesson plans were generally preferred for warm-up activities, main instructional tasks, overall quality, student discourse, group work, and inclusive supports. GenAI plans, especially the customized GPT-4 version, were more competitive for cool-down activities and structured lesson wrap-ups, and the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model became more competitive in middle/high school contexts. The paper concludes that GenAI is best viewed as a collaborative planning aid rather than a replacement for educator expertise, with human review still needed for pedagogical nuance and classroom adaptation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI can reduce educator workload by assisting with lesson planning, and educators saw AI-generated plans as potentially useful planning aids. However, this was a preference study rather than a student outcome study, so the evidence is about perceived planning efficiency and usability rather than measured time savings or productivity gains.
finding.measure: Educator preferences/comments about lesson-plan usefulness, structure, and potential as an assistive planning tool

finding.finding_summary: The study argues for a human-AI collaborative model for lesson planning and suggests that domain-specific fine-tuning and educator feedback loops are important for responsible AI integration in K-12 settings. It does not test policy or institutional outcomes directly, but it does provide evidence relevant to adoption decisions and implementation design.
finding.measure: Educator evaluations of GenAI vs. human-authored lesson plans across grade levels and instructional components

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.population: K-12 (primarily K-12 mathematics teachers; pilot teachers serving grades 3-12)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of providing K-12 mathematics teachers with timely, scalable, and individualized feedback on classroom discourse practices, specifically the use of “talk moves” that are associated with productive mathematical discussion. The authors motivate the work as a response to the difficulty and expense of human observation and coding of classroom transcripts, and they aim to automate this feedback using natural language processing and speech recognition.

The core intervention is the TalkMoves application, which processes classroom audio/video recordings, transcribes speech, classifies teacher utterances into six accountable-talk categories, and generates dashboards showing talk-move frequency, teacher/student talk balance, wait time, and other discourse analytics. The modeling work compares BiLSTM, attention, and transformer-based architectures on 501 K-12 math lesson transcripts (176,757 sentences), with RoBERTa-Large achieving the best test performance (F1=79.33%, MCC=0.7779), though a smaller DistilRoBERTa model was deployed for efficiency.

The system was piloted with 21 teachers across two Midwestern U.S. school districts during the 2019–2020 academic year, with teachers recording 3–15 lessons each and providing survey/interview feedback. The paper’s main conclusion is that transformer-based NLP can approximate expert coding well enough to support automated feedback on classroom discourse, but it remains a technical/implementation paper rather than an outcomes study. The authors also note important limitations, including noisy classroom speech, especially under-detection of young students’ speech by ASR, and they suggest that broader context windows may improve classification of some talk moves.

finding.finding_summary: The system substantially automates what would otherwise require highly trained human observers to hand-code classroom transcripts, indicating potential gains in efficiency and scalability for instructional feedback workflows. On the modeling side, transformer-based classifiers improved talk-move detection from a prior F1 of 65% to 79.33% (RoBERTa-Large; MCC=0.7779), which the authors frame as making automated feedback more practical for deployment.
finding.measure: Model classification performance and system automation of discourse coding/feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student achievement or math test outcomes, so it does not provide direct evidence that TalkMoves improved mathematical numeracy. Instead, it argues theoretically that accountable talk and productive classroom discourse are linked to mathematics learning and engagement, and the system is designed to support those practices.
finding.measure: No direct student math achievement measure reported
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers in pilot use; 3-15 lessons each

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly evaluate student engagement, motivation, or self-regulation outcomes, although it cites prior research claiming that talk moves can positively affect student engagement. The reported study itself focuses on discourse classification and teacher feedback rather than measuring learner affective or behavioral outcomes.
finding.measure: No direct engagement or social-emotional outcome measure reported
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers in pilot use; 3-15 lessons each

paper_profiles.title: Communication of Prospective Teachers with Students in Mathematics Learning at Senior High School (SMA)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how prospective mathematics teachers communicate with students during senior high school mathematics lessons. The authors are interested in the role of teacher communication in helping students understand mathematical symbols, procedures, strategies, and problem-solving processes, especially in calculus topics involving limits and derivatives.

The study was conducted at SMAN 1 Madura with a preservice teacher from a mathematics education program. Using interviews, field notes, documentation, and video recordings, the researchers qualitatively describe classroom communication practices such as oral explanation, board work, guidance during problem solving, discussion facilitation, and question-and-answer exchanges. The paper argues that effective communication helps students understand mathematics better, participate in discussions, and apply procedures in new contexts.

The main conclusion is descriptive rather than causal: prospective teachers should master communication skills, use language suited to students' level, and direct discussion and Q&A effectively to support mathematics learning. The paper does not test an intervention or estimate achievement effects, but it emphasizes communication as an important teaching practice for facilitating understanding and student engagement in mathematics classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes that prospective teachers communicated mathematical procedures, formulas, rules, and methods clearly while teaching limits and derivatives in calculus. The authors report that this communication helped students understand symbols, procedures, and strategies and supported problem solving on the board, but no achievement test or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Classroom communication about mathematical procedures, problem solving, and teacher explanation quality
finding.study_size: n=1 prospective teacher classroom case study; student count not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teacher communication stimulated students to be active in discussion and supported question-and-answer activity, indicating improved engagement in mathematics learning. These conclusions are based on qualitative observation rather than quantified engagement or motivation measures.
finding.measure: Observed student participation in discussion and question-and-answer activities
finding.study_size: n=1 prospective teacher classroom case study; student count not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The authors emphasize that the communication process helped students understand mathematical strategies and apply procedures in newly encountered contexts, which is framed as developing higher-order mathematical communication and reasoning. This is a qualitative claim grounded in classroom observation, not a measured assessment of metacognition or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Observed use of mathematical communication, discussion, and application of procedures in new contexts
finding.study_size: n=1 prospective teacher classroom case study; student count not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Deep Neural Networks for the Assessment of Surgical Skills: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews the literature on deep neural networks (DNNs) for automated surgical skill assessment, using PRISMA methods to screen 530 papers and retain 25 studies published through June 2020. The central problem is that traditional surgical skill assessment in training and certification is subjective, time-consuming, and limited by poor inter-rater reliability, motivating objective, data-driven alternatives.

The review synthesizes studies using kinematic and video-based data from simulators, robotic systems, and a smaller number of laparoscopic and other surgical contexts. It compares common model families (CNNs, RNNs, and hybrid CNN-RNN/FCN approaches), data processing pipelines, and validation strategies such as LOSO and k-fold cross-validation. The authors conclude that DNNs can achieve strong accuracy for classifying surgical expertise and that CNN-based approaches often perform best, with some models also providing interpretable visual feedback via class activation maps.

The review also highlights major limitations in the field: small and imbalanced datasets, limited public benchmarks, weak standardization of ground-truth scoring, and a lack of rigorous regression studies. Although the paper is focused on surgical training rather than K-12 education, it is relevant as adjacent evidence on AI-enabled assessment and feedback systems because it identifies implementation features associated with stronger automated assessment performance, including end-to-end modeling, visual feedback, and the use of larger public datasets.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that DNN-based assessment can reduce the subjectivity and time burden of surgical skill evaluation by automating scoring from kinematic and video data. Across 25 studies, these methods were described as enabling objective assessment and real-time or near-real-time feedback, although no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Automation of surgical skill assessment; assessment speed/time burden; objective scoring capability

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that some DNN systems, especially CNNs with class activation maps, can provide interpretable visual feedback to trainees by highlighting portions of performance that contributed to the score. This was discussed as supporting learner improvement and personalized training, but the review did not report a quantitative effect on trainee metacognition or self-regulation.
finding.measure: Interpretability / visual feedback for trainees

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how a constructionist tinkering practice can be integrated into primary school classrooms, and what helps or hinders that integration. The authors propose a model called TIDE (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration) to connect open-ended tinkering workshops with curriculum-linked follow-up activities, especially in physics/light-related learning. The central implementation question is not whether tinkering is engaging, but how teachers can make use of it in formal schooling without stripping away its exploratory character.

The project was implemented in four primary schools in Bologna and involved 13 classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students. Teachers participated in professional development, used a resource library, and documented classroom activity through written notes, photos, videos, and a fishbowl reflection protocol; the final teacher feedback survey was completed by 20 teachers. The evidence is mainly qualitative and descriptive, supplemented by simple frequency counts from teacher questionnaires and coded reflections.

Findings suggest that tinkering strongly increased student engagement, participation, and collaboration, especially for students who were typically less successful or less engaged in conventional school activities. At the same time, some high-achieving or highly school-oriented students experienced frustration when tasks were open-ended and did not yield immediate success. A major implementation barrier was teacher discomfort with disciplinary science: teachers often felt unprepared to answer students’ questions or to turn emerging questions into sustained scientific inquiry. Even though a science-oriented resource library was provided, many teachers preferred to connect tinkering to language, storytelling, and expressive work rather than physics. The authors conclude that successful integration requires more disciplinary support, stronger documentation/relaunch cycles, and careful preservation of tinkering’s open-ended nature.

finding.finding_summary: Tinkering generated authentic scientific questions and inquiry opportunities, especially around light phenomena, but teachers often could not sustain or answer those questions because they felt underprepared in physics. The study is descriptive rather than inferential; it reports that many research questions emerged during workshops and that teachers recognized their own inadequacy in relaunching them, indicating both promise and an implementation bottleneck.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire responses, fishbowl documentation protocol, classroom observation/reflection notes
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers (questionnaire); 13 classrooms; approximately n=300 students

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported unexpectedly high engagement, participation, motivation, and collaboration during tinkering, particularly among students who struggled in conventional schooling. Seventy percent of teachers said tinkering revealed unexpected or partially expected behavior, and the qualitative responses consistently emphasized enthusiasm, sustained attention, and willingness to participate in pairs or groups.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire on student behavior and engagement during tinkering workshops

finding.finding_summary: The paper links tinkering to collaboration, self-reflection, hypothesis generation, problem solving, and the ability to manage frustration when immediate success is not possible. Teachers noted that students learned to work together, exchange ideas, and focus on process and reasoning, suggesting gains in collaboration and persistence rather than in tested academic performance.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire narratives and coded fishbowl reflections

finding.finding_summary: Implementation was feasible but constrained: the planned eight-month project was compressed into four months because of pandemic conditions, and the documentation protocol was reduced from an intended ongoing relaunch tool to a one-time end-of-project reflection. The paper suggests that teacher capacity improved through training and co-design, but also that lack of disciplinary preparation and limited time made deeper integration into lesson planning difficult.
finding.measure: Project implementation records, teacher feedback, documentation protocol use

paper_profiles.title: The Hands-Up Problem and How to Deal With It: Secondary School Teachers’ Experiences of Debugging in the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines secondary school computing teachers’ experiences of teaching and supporting debugging in text-based programming classrooms. The authors ask how teachers describe student debugging behavior, what barriers make debugging difficult, and what classroom practices teachers use to help students work through errors.

The study is based on nine semi-structured interviews with lower-secondary teachers in England and two teachers from other countries, all teaching Python and sometimes other text-based programming languages. Using thematic analysis, the authors identify a recurring pattern they call the “hands-up problem”: many students raise their hands as soon as they encounter an error, creating a classroom situation where the teacher is unable to support everyone quickly enough. Teachers described several contributing factors, including limited lesson time, syntax-heavy text-based languages, unclear error messages, low student resilience, and negative emotions around errors.

Teachers also described ways to counter the problem, including requiring students to try independently before asking for help, using peer support, modeling debugging strategies, teaching students how to interpret programming error messages, encouraging incremental testing, and creating a positive error culture where mistakes are normalized and even celebrated. The paper concludes that debugging-specific pedagogical content knowledge and professional development are especially important for less confident teachers, but the evidence base remains small and largely qualitative.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that debugging often provoked frustration, disappointment, anxiety, and disengagement among students, especially when errors were frequent or emotionally costly because students were invested in their own code. At the same time, some students experienced strong positive emotion and increased resilience when they eventually solved errors, suggesting debugging can also build persistence when classroom support and culture are favorable.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports of observed student emotions, motivation, resilience, and disengagement during debugging

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described instructional approaches that supported metacognition and independent problem-solving, such as asking students to explain what they expected, what the program did, and what they had tried; modeling debugging; and teaching students to externalize their thinking. These practices were reported to improve students’ debugging behaviors over time, including greater ability to spot common syntax errors and more independent troubleshooting.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student debugging behaviors, independence, and reflective problem-solving during classroom practice

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central finding is that debugging problems create a major classroom management and workload issue for teachers, which the authors label the “hands-up problem.” Teachers reported that many students raise their hands at once, making it unrealistic to support everyone in classes of roughly 25-30 students and causing lessons to become busy, chaotic, and time-pressured.
finding.measure: Teacher interview reports of classroom workflow, number of students requesting help, and perceived burden of providing debugging support

finding.finding_summary: The study concerns the teaching and learning of debugging in secondary computing, a programming skill central to students’ success in text-based coding tasks. Teachers reported that strategies such as incremental testing, modeling, and interpreting error messages helped students become better debuggers, but the paper does not report direct achievement test outcomes or quantitative learning gains.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of students’ debugging ability and classroom programming performance

paper_profiles.title: Human-Centered Design for AI-based Automatically Generated Assessment Reports: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the design and implementation of AI-based automatically generated assessment reports (AutoRs) for formative assessment in K-12 STEM classrooms. The authors focus on how these reports can support teachers’ instructional decision-making by synthesizing assessment data into interpretable and actionable feedback, while reducing cognitive load through human-centered design.

Using a conceptual framework grounded in cognitive load theory, the review examines 29 publicly available, real-world AutoR systems drawn from websites, professional associations, and literature. The paper codes each system along dimensions such as content, information synthesis, depth of data mining, user functionality, presentation format, and AI integration, then uses latent class analysis to identify patterns in design and functionality.

The main conclusion is that most current AutoRs provide basic tabular, filterable, class- and individual-level data, but underuse design elements that could reduce teacher cognitive demands, such as text-based summaries, visual aids, and advanced interactive features. The paper argues that better alignment between report content, presentation, and AI functions could make formative assessment data more usable for teachers and more actionable for students, but it does not evaluate student achievement effects directly.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AutoRs are primarily designed to reduce teachers’ cognitive and administrative workload by automating assessment reporting, filtering, synthesis, and live feedback. Across 29 systems, common features included filtering (93%), tabular display (93%), class-level synthesis (79%), and live functionality (62%), but the authors conclude that many systems still impose high initial cognitive demands because text, plots, and special visual aids are underused.
finding.measure: Design features of automatically generated assessment reports; latent class patterns of usability, live interaction, filtering, and visualization

paper_profiles.title: Effects of Hints on Debugging Scratch Programs: An Empirical Study with Primary School Teachers in Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether automatically generated hints about bug patterns help primary school teachers in training debug Scratch programs more effectively and efficiently, and whether those hint-based learning experiences transfer to later debugging without hints. The motivation is that primary teachers are increasingly expected to support programming instruction, yet many lack deep subject knowledge for identifying and repairing bugs in student code.

The study embedded a short Scratch self-study module in a university course for 163 primary school teachers in training. Participants were assigned to a control group or a treatment group that received LitterBox-generated static-analysis hints for the first seven buggy Scratch tasks; both groups then completed seven additional tasks without hints. The paper measures task correctness and completion time, and also collects participants’ ratings and comments on the hints.

Results show that hints substantially improved immediate debugging performance: across Tasks 1-7, the treatment group produced 34% more correct solutions (82% vs. 48%) and finished faster on average (5.24 vs. 8.66 minutes). The benefits were not uniform across tasks; one hint slightly harmed performance for experienced participants, especially when the hint pointed to a different script than where the fix had to be made. In the no-hint transfer phase (Tasks 8-14), there were no significant differences between groups, suggesting limited evidence that a single exposure to hinted debugging transfers robustly to later independent debugging. The paper concludes that bug-pattern hints can support teacher debugging practice, but their design should better localize bugs, clarify when multiple fixes are possible, and provide clear guidance for use in teacher education.

finding.finding_summary: Automatically generated bug-pattern hints improved debugging efficiency for primary school teachers in training. Across Tasks 1-7, the treatment group needed 5.24 minutes on average versus 8.66 minutes for controls, a reduction of 3.41 minutes; the reported average effect size was ÂA12=.70, indicating medium effects in favor of hints.
finding.measure: Time to submit a corrected Scratch program for debugging tasks

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved immediate debugging effectiveness, a problem-solving skill relevant to durable skills. Across Tasks 1-7, the treatment group produced 34% more correct solutions than the control group (82% vs. 48%); the average odds ratio was 13.05 over the first seven tasks, with task-level odds ratios ranging from 2.20 to 44.38.
finding.measure: Correct completion of buggy Scratch debugging tasks

finding.finding_summary: In the transfer phase without hints (Tasks 8-14), the treatment and control groups did not differ significantly in efficiency. The treatment group averaged 7.00 minutes per task versus 7.69 minutes for controls, with an average effect size of ÂA12=.55, but the authors summarize the phase as showing no significant differences overall.
finding.measure: Time to submit a corrected Scratch program on transfer tasks without hints

finding.finding_summary: There was no significant evidence that learning to debug with hints versus without hints produced better transfer to later debugging without hints. In Tasks 8-14, the treatment group was only slightly better overall (54% correct vs. 47%), and the authors conclude that the transfer effects were not statistically significant overall, despite one significant task (Task 14).
finding.measure: Correct completion of transfer debugging tasks without hints

paper_profiles.title: Teacher-Driven Professional Development and the Pursuit of a Sophisticated Understanding of Inquiry
paper_profiles.venue: American Journal of Physics (conference proceedings/APA-style article context not fully specified in text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how a teacher-driven professional development program can strengthen secondary science teachers’ understanding of inquiry-oriented instruction. The authors focus on a small cohort of four middle and high school physical science teachers working in high-needs urban schools, asking how their conceptions of inquiry evolve over time through collaborative reflection, lesson sharing, and discussion.

The intervention was Streamline to Mastery, an NSF-funded, learner-centered professional development program in which teachers chose their own growth goals, shared lessons, planned classroom research, and engaged in periodic reflective discourse with researchers. Data came from lesson-sharing reflections, repeated inquiry survey prompts, and video of professional development meetings, analyzed through the five essential features of inquiry from the NRC framework.

Findings suggest that teachers’ understanding of inquiry became more expert-like over the year. Early reflections were often ambiguous and mixed with terms like constructivism, hands-on, and real-world; later reflections increasingly referenced evidence-based inquiry features, and the group eventually developed its own shared definition of inquiry as socially constructing evidence-based meaning through intentionally sequenced events. The paper argues that teacher learning may be strengthened when professional development is grounded in teachers’ own classroom experience, collaborative sensemaking, and teacher-driven agendas rather than externally delivered expertise.

finding.finding_summary: Across a year of teacher-driven professional development, the participating teachers developed a more sophisticated understanding of scientific inquiry, as reflected in increasing use of the NRC inquiry features in lesson reflections and survey responses. For example, references to communicating and explaining increased approximately five-fold from the first to second inquiry survey administration, and by the fifth lesson four of the five essential inquiry features were referenced. The study does not report an effect size, but the direction of change was clearly positive for teachers’ inquiry-oriented conceptual understanding.
finding.measure: Teacher conceptions of inquiry / references to the five essential features of inquiry in lesson reflections and survey responses

paper_profiles.title: The effect of a formative assessment practice on student achievement in mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a professional development programme (PDP) focused on formative assessment changed classroom practice in ways that improved student achievement in year-7 mathematics. The authors argue that formative assessment is often conceptualized broadly, so they carefully describe the enacted practices after the PDP and test whether those changes were associated with higher post-test mathematics scores.

The intervention was not a student-facing program per se, but a teacher PD experience centered on the Wiliam and Thompson (2008) formative assessment framework (the ‘big idea’ plus five key strategies). Teachers were encouraged to use evidence of student learning to adjust instruction, clarify learning goals, provide feedback, activate peer and self-assessment, and support student ownership. The comparison group was the remaining year-7 mathematics teachers in the same Swedish municipality who did not receive the PDP or in-service formative assessment training.

The study used pre- and post-tests for all year-7 students in the municipality and compared post-test achievement between students taught by the PD teachers (n=291) and control teachers (n=275), controlling for pre-test scores. The authors report no statistically significant difference on the post-test between groups and no significant correlation between the number of formative assessment activities implemented and post-test achievement. In practical terms, the study suggests that this particular, teacher-centered implementation of formative assessment did not isolate a measurable achievement benefit under the conditions studied.

finding.finding_summary: In an ANCOVA controlling for pre-test scores, there was no significant difference in mathematics post-test achievement between students whose teachers participated in the formative assessment PDP and those in the control group. The study used municipality-developed mathematics pre/post tests; sample size was 291 intervention students and 275 control students (14 vs. 15 teachers), but the paper excerpt does not report the exact F, p, or standardized effect size.
finding.measure: Mathematics pre-test and post-test scores

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of CATs on Mathematical Thinking and Logical Thinking Among Fourth-Class Scientific Students
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether classroom assessment techniques (CATs), used as a formative assessment approach, improve fourth-grade scientific students’ mathematical thinking and logical thinking in mathematics. The authors frame CATs as an assessment-for-learning approach that combines instruction, questioning, feedback, peer/self-evaluation, and other classroom activities intended to help teachers adjust teaching while students learn.

The study used a two-group quasi-experimental design with 44 female students from Al-Istiqlal Secondary School for Girls in Baghdad, Iraq (22 experimental, 22 control). The experimental group was taught with CATs through a teacher’s guide and classroom techniques such as feedback sessions, deep questions, concept maps, and group-work evaluation, while the control group received traditional/usual instruction. Posttests measured mathematical reasoning/thinking and logical reasoning/thinking. The paper reports statistically significant advantages for the CATs group on both outcomes, with large effect sizes (reported as eta squared values and d values), leading the authors to conclude that CATs positively affect both mathematical and logical thinking in this context.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group taught with classroom assessment techniques (CATs) outperformed the control group taught in the usual/traditional way on the mathematical reasoning/thinking posttest. The paper reports a statistically significant difference (p=0.04) with large effects; the reported effect sizes include η²=0.95 and η²=0.64 in the paper's effect-size table, indicating a very large positive impact.
finding.measure: Mathematical reasoning / mathematical thinking test (20 multiple-choice items covering modeling, generalization, symbolic expression, abstraction, and solution finding)

finding.finding_summary: CATs also improved logical thinking/logical reasoning relative to traditional instruction. The posttest difference was statistically significant (p=0.03), and the paper reports a very large effect size (d=1.089; η²=0.192), suggesting substantial gains in students' logical reasoning skills under the CATs condition.
finding.measure: Logical reasoning / logical thinking test (25 items measuring classification, induction, inference, and deduction)

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment as a Tool to Enhance the Development of Inquiry Skills in Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether using formative assessment classroom techniques (FACTs) improves upper secondary students’ inquiry skills in science compared with teaching without FACTs. The authors frame formative assessment as a set of regular, interactive teacher-student techniques that provide feedback and guide next steps, and they focus on whether such techniques can strengthen inquiry-related competencies even in largely teacher-centered classrooms.

The study used a pre-test/post-test two-group design in three Slovak upper secondary schools. The experimental group (n=73; ages 15–16) received science instruction across biology, chemistry, physics, mathematics, and informatics with FACTs such as true/false statements, K-W-L charts, Frayer models, self-assessment cards, exit cards, concept maps, checklists, and task cards; the control group (n=48) received comparable teacher-centered instruction without FACTs and no external intervention. Both groups were taught by the same teachers, with similar content and duration, over a five-month period.

Students were assessed with a 16-item inquiry skills test before and after the intervention. The experimental group improved significantly more than the control group on overall inquiry skill scores, and the paired pre/post gain was significant for the experimental group but not the control group. Among subskills, only “designing experiments” showed a statistically significant gain; other inquiry subskills did not. The authors conclude that FACTs can improve inquiry skills, especially for lower-performing students, but the intervention was not a clean isolation of formative assessment from adjacent practices because it involved classroom feedback and multiple assessment-like techniques rather than a single standardized FA treatment.

finding.finding_summary: Upper secondary students who experienced teaching with formative assessment classroom techniques (FACTs) scored significantly higher on the post-test inquiry skills measure than controls taught without FACTs. The experimental group (n=73) improved from x̄=.273 to .327, while the control group (n=48) changed only from x̄=.228 to .239; the post-test between-group difference was statistically significant (p=.001).
finding.measure: 16-item inquiry skills test covering hypothesis formulation, designing experiments, transforming data, relating variables from tables/graphs, and identifying sources of error
finding.std_deviation: Pre-test SDs: experimental .138, control .102; post-test SDs: experimental .162, control .126

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core outcome is inquiry skill development, which overlaps with durable skills such as critical thinking and problem solving. Overall inquiry skill development increased significantly in the experimental group (paired t-test p=.004; mean gain .054) but not in the control group (p=.613; mean gain .011), indicating that FACTs improved students’ ability to reason through inquiry tasks.
finding.measure: Overall inquiry skills test score and subskill scores
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI for experimental mean gain: .018 to .090
finding.std_deviation: Experimental paired difference SD=.156; control paired difference SD=.152

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the Efficacy of a Professional Development Program in Formative Classroom Assessment in Middle School English Language Arts and Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether a state-developed professional development program in formative classroom assessment improved middle school teachers’ assessment knowledge and their students’ achievement in English language arts (ELA) and mathematics. The program was designed to help teachers create higher-quality classroom assessments, align items with standards, develop rubrics and performance tasks, and use assessment information formatively and summatively.

Year 1 used a cluster randomized trial in low-performing South Carolina middle schools, with schools assigned to treatment or no professional development. Years 2 and 3 used a quasi-experimental comparison of two treatment levels (trained assessment coach vs. relatively untrained facilitator) and matched control schools. Teacher assessment knowledge improved in all treatment conditions, but student achievement on the state PACT exam did not improve; instead, adjusted ELA scores were significantly lower in treatment schools in all three years (about -0.08 to -0.26 SD), and mathematics scores were lower only in Year 3 (-0.33 SD). The authors conclude that stronger teacher assessment knowledge did not translate into higher student achievement, and that formative assessment professional development may not improve student learning unless teachers can use assessment evidence to change instruction effectively.

finding.finding_summary: In English language arts, students in professional development schools scored lower than matched control students on adjusted PACT scores in all three years. The adjusted treatment effects were -2.39 points in 2005–06, -1.15 points in 2006–07, and -3.46 points in 2007–08, corresponding to standardized effects of -0.16, -0.08, and -0.26, respectively (all statistically significant).
finding.measure: PACT English Language Arts scale scores
finding.study_size: Year 1 n=2066; Year 2 n=3203; Year 3 n=1403

finding.finding_summary: In mathematics, there were no significant treatment effects in Years 1 and 2, but Year 3 showed significantly lower adjusted achievement for the professional development schools. The Year 3 treatment coefficient was -3.76 PACT points with a standardized effect size of -0.33 (p=0.01).
finding.measure: PACT Mathematics scale scores
finding.study_size: Year 1 n=2708; Year 2 n=2745; Year 3 n=1297

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved teacher assessment knowledge, as measured by pretest-posttest multiple-choice assessment knowledge tests and split-plot ANOVA comparisons. Treatment groups improved more than controls in Year 1 (treatment +8.51 vs. control +1.85 points), and both treatment levels improved substantially in Years 2 and 3; the reported effect sizes for time were large (ω²=0.60 in Year 2 and ω²=0.56 in Year 3).
finding.measure: Teacher assessment knowledge test scores (multiple-choice pre/post tests)
finding.study_size: Year 1 n=151; Year 2 n=146; Year 3 n=71
finding.std_deviation: Year 1 pretest SD 6.84 control / 7.19 treatment; Year 1 posttest SD 8.25 control / 11.47 treatment

finding.finding_summary: The professional development program increased teachers’ formative assessment knowledge regardless of whether it was delivered by a trained coach or an untrained facilitator, suggesting the curriculum was implementable at scale with some fidelity loss. However, the institutional effect on student outcomes was adverse, raising concerns about translating teacher assessment training into classroom practice and student gains.
finding.measure: Professional development implementation and teacher assessment knowledge; school-level student achievement effects
finding.study_size: Year 1 n=38 schools ELA, 44 schools mathematics; Years 2–3 matched school comparisons

paper_profiles.title: The effect of a formative assessment practice on student achievement in mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether a professional development programme (PDP) focused on formative assessment led secondary school mathematics teachers to change classroom practice in ways that improved student achievement. The paper is motivated by prior evidence that formative assessment can help learning, but that effects vary widely depending on implementation, subject, and context.

The intervention involved 14 randomly selected year-7 mathematics teachers in a Swedish municipality who participated in a term-long PDP based on Wiliam and Thompson’s formative assessment framework. After the PDP, classroom observations and interviews showed that teachers adopted new formative assessment activities, especially frequent elicitation of evidence of learning (e.g., exit tickets, mini-whiteboards), clearer learning goals, and more consciously planned feedback. However, teachers made relatively few changes to peer assessment and collaborative formative practices, and much of the responsibility for the process remained teacher-centered.

Achievement was measured with municipality-developed pre-tests and post-tests in mathematics for year-7 students, comparing students taught by PDP teachers with students taught by non-participating teachers and controlling for pre-test scores. The main result was null: there were no significant post-test differences between intervention and control groups, and no significant correlation between the number of formative assessment activities implemented and post-test achievement.
