The study concludes that the specific implementation examined did not improve mathematics achievement, suggesting that both the quality and completeness of formative assessment enactment may matter, and that more experimental work is needed.

finding.finding_summary: Students taught by teachers who participated in the formative assessment PDP did not score significantly higher on the mathematics post-test than students in the control group after controlling for pre-test scores. The paper also found no significant partial correlation between the number of new formative assessment activities implemented and post-test achievement.
finding.measure: Mathematics pre-test and post-test scores (municipality-developed curriculum-aligned tests)

paper_profiles.title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a conceptual theory of formative assessment rather than testing an intervention empirically. Black and Wiliam revisit their earlier work and argue for a unifying framework that explains formative assessment as classroom practice in which evidence about student learning is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or peers to decide next instructional steps. The paper’s main purpose is to clarify the logic of formative interaction, not to estimate achievement effects.

The authors organize formative assessment around five strategies: clarifying learning intentions and success criteria, engineering tasks and discussions that elicit evidence, providing feedback that moves learning forward, activating peers as instructional resources, and activating learners as owners of their own learning. They connect these strategies to broader theories including self-regulated learning, cognitive acceleration, dynamic assessment, and classroom discourse, with examples drawn from mathematics, science, and other subjects. These examples are illustrative and theoretical, not presented as new outcome data.

The conclusion is that formative assessment is best understood as contingent interaction embedded in pedagogy, with the teacher making rapid diagnostic and prognostic decisions based on evidence of student thinking. The paper argues that effective feedback depends on how teachers interpret learner responses and on the larger instructional aims guiding their actions. It offers a framework for future research and improvement of practice, but it does not provide subject- or grade-specific achievement estimates for K-12 students.

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, focusing on how scaffolding has been conceptualized, how it appears in classroom practice, and what is known about its effectiveness. The authors argue that the field lacks a consistent definition, but they identify three core characteristics of scaffolding: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility.

The paper synthesizes 66 English-language SSCI-listed articles published from 1998 to 2009, including theoretical, descriptive, effectiveness, and one meta-analytic study, across primary and secondary education. Most studies were descriptive and concentrated in literacy, followed by math and science; the small number of effectiveness studies were mostly one-to-one or small-group tutoring studies. Across the reviewed evidence, scaffolding is generally described as effective for students’ cognitive and metacognitive outcomes, with mixed or limited evidence for affective outcomes. The authors conclude that the main challenge is measurement: studies often operationalize scaffolding inconsistently and rarely capture contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility together.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that scaffolding research is most developed in literacy, with many descriptive studies and several theoretical frameworks centered on reading comprehension and related literacy practices. However, the review does not report a pooled effect size for literacy achievement, and the evidence is largely descriptive rather than directly comparable across studies.
finding.measure: Literacy-related classroom practices and, in some effectiveness studies, comprehension/reading outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies mathematics as one of the main domains where scaffolding has been studied and includes a small number of effectiveness studies. In the cited math tutoring study (Pratt & Savoy-Levine, 1998), fourth and fifth grade students receiving contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than peers in other conditions at immediate and follow-up measurement, but the review does not provide an effect size.
finding.measure: Long-division problem solving

finding.finding_summary: Science is another central domain in the review, with both descriptive and effectiveness studies. In the strongest cited science-related effectiveness studies, seventh- and tenth-grade students receiving adaptive scaffolding showed greater shifts in mental models and more knowledge gains about the human circulatory system than students receiving fixed or no scaffolding, and ninth-grade students in cognitive apprenticeship conditions built better mental models of chemical equilibrium; however, the review reports no pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Mental models, knowledge gains, and reasoning in science learning tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a small body of evidence on affect, motivation, and engagement. In one correlational study of fifth- and sixth-grade mathematics lessons, whole-class scaffolding strategies aimed at motivation and frustration control were more common in high-involvement classrooms, while in a quasi-experiment on contingent tutoring, students’ enjoyment did not differ meaningfully across support conditions except that the no-support group scored lower than the others.
finding.measure: Student involvement/enjoyment in mathematics and classroom affect
finding.study_size: n=42 for the correlational study; n=40 in the quasi-experimental comparison reported for enjoyment (plus other conditions in the same study)

finding.finding_summary: A major conclusion of the review is that scaffolding supports durable skills such as metacognition, reasoning, collaboration, and transfer of responsibility. In the reviewed effectiveness studies, students in scaffolding or adaptive tutoring conditions showed better use of talk for reasoning, more self-regulating behaviors, greater responsibility for learning, and stronger transfer performance, but the review does not aggregate these into a single effect size.
finding.measure: Reasoning talk, self-regulated learning, diagnostic accuracy, transfer questions, and collaborative learning behaviors
finding.study_size: n=109 vs 121; n=38, 34, 37; n=9; n=11; n=42; plus smaller tutoring samples

finding.finding_summary: The review briefly notes scaffolding work outside core subject achievement, including identity formation and other classroom processes, but these are not central. Because the paper primarily synthesizes instructional interaction rather than subject achievement outside literacy, math, and science, evidence for this category is indirect and thin.
finding.measure: Identity formation and other non-core classroom outcomes mentioned in descriptive studies

paper_profiles.title: The effects of self-monitoring and self-reflection in A1 adult learners in an English blended learning environment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This master’s thesis examines whether self-monitoring and self-reflection strategies affect the learning experience of A1 adult learners in an English blended-learning course. The study is framed around self-assessment and self-regulated learning, asking whether guided reflection and monitoring can help learners become more aware of their progress, identify strengths and weaknesses, and set learning goals.

The intervention was implemented with a group of adult distance tutors at Universidad Nacional Abierta y a Distancia (UNAD) in Bucaramanga, Colombia, enrolled in an elementary English blended course offered to staff. Data sources included checklists, surveys, students’ journals, and the teacher’s journal, and the analysis was qualitative/action-research in nature. The findings indicate that participants responded positively to the self-assessment strategies: they reported greater awareness of the language-learning process, more active involvement in their own learning, and appreciation for the blended format and scaffolded instruction.

The paper is not an achievement study in the K-12 sense and does not report standardized test effects, control-group comparisons, or subject/grade-band estimates. Its contribution is primarily descriptive and pedagogical, showing that self-monitoring and self-reflection may support learner autonomy, metacognitive awareness, and engagement in adult English instruction. Evidence on academic achievement is indirect and not directly comparable to K-12 formative-assessment trials or meta-analyses.

finding.finding_summary: Participants responded positively to the self-assessment strategies, reporting greater awareness of their language-learning process and increased involvement in their individual learning. The thesis describes improved ability to identify areas for improvement, monitor progress, and set learning goals, but it does not report standardized effect sizes or pre/post scores.
finding.measure: Student journals, surveys, checklists, and qualitative reflections on learning experience

finding.finding_summary: The study’s main reported benefits were metacognitive: learners became better able to monitor their learning, reflect on progress, and plan goals. These changes were identified through qualitative analysis of checklists, journals, and surveys rather than quantitative achievement measures.
finding.measure: Self-monitoring, self-reflection, goal-setting, and awareness of learning progress

finding.finding_summary: The intervention took place in an English course and participants reported more awareness of their language-learning process and progress in English, along with positive reactions to scaffolded instruction. However, the paper does not provide direct measures of speaking, listening, or other language-proficiency gains.
finding.measure: Perceptions of English learning process in a blended course

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper discussing elementary through professional education contexts; no primary sample studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential opportunities and risks of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, the authors synthesize early research and argue that LLMs could support learning and teaching across levels by generating questions, explanations, summaries, feedback, and instructional materials.

The paper discusses use cases for elementary, secondary, higher education, and professional training, with examples spanning reading and writing support, language learning, math problem generation, scientific argument feedback, assessment support, and teacher workflow automation. It also emphasizes major challenges such as bias, privacy, plagiarism, overreliance, and the need for human oversight, critical thinking, and curricular integration. The article concludes that LLMs may be useful educational tools, but only if implemented responsibly and with strong governance, teacher expertise, and verification practices.

Because this is a conceptual position paper, it does not report primary empirical effects on student achievement. Its references include several early studies on question generation, curiosity prompting, feedback, peer assessment, and automated evaluation, but those are cited as background rather than systematically reviewed or meta-analyzed here. Evidence on differences by subject area or grade band is therefore indirect and not directly comparable within this paper.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses potential uses of LLMs to support reading comprehension and writing, such as generating summaries, explanations, quizzes, and grammar/style feedback, but it does not present empirical achievement evidence for literacy outcomes. No sample, effect size, or measured literacy outcome is reported in this position paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics is mentioned only as a domain where LLMs might generate practice problems or support problem solving, but the paper does not test mathematics achievement or report any math-specific results. No empirical effects by grade band are provided.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper references a high school climate activity and the use of feedback to help students revise scientific arguments, but this is cited from prior work rather than newly evaluated here. No direct evidence on scientific reasoning achievement, sample size, or effect size is reported in this article.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or accelerating tasks such as quiz generation, feedback writing, assessment support, and grading. The paper cites prior work suggesting substantial efficiency gains (e.g., grading effort reduced by up to 85% in one referenced study), but this position paper itself does not empirically test those gains.
finding.measure: teacher workload / grading and content-creation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM-based tools may improve student engagement, interaction, curiosity, and willingness to communicate, and it cites prior studies on curiosity-prompting and language anxiety support. However, the article does not provide original empirical estimates for these outcomes, and reported effects are indirect from referenced studies.
finding.measure: student engagement, curiosity, language anxiety, willingness to communicate

finding.finding_summary: Critical thinking, problem solving, fact checking, and collaboration are treated as major intended benefits and risks of LLM use. The paper argues LLMs may support these durable skills through prompts, explanations, and discussion scaffolds, but also warns they may weaken critical thinking through overreliance; no primary effect sizes or student outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem solving, fact checking, collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s strongest substantive focus is on institutional implications: policy, governance, privacy, fairness, accessibility, and responsible integration of LLMs in schools and universities. It recommends oversight, transparency, bias mitigation, and curricular guidance, but reports no empirical institutional outcome data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: policy, governance, privacy, fairness, access, responsible adoption

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Teachers Practices of Classroom Assessment in Secondary Science Classes in Bangladesh
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary school science teachers in Bangladesh conduct classroom assessment and feedback, with a particular interest in whether their practices support formative assessment. The study is motivated by concerns that classroom assessment in Bangladesh is dominated by traditional, summative-oriented questioning rather than assessment for learning.

Using observations of 30 science lessons taught by 30 teachers across six secondary schools in Dhaka, plus pre- and post-observation interviews, the author documents what teachers actually do during lessons. The assessment approach was overwhelmingly oral questioning, largely closed and recall-based, with little use of self-assessment, peer assessment, written feedback, or tasks that required higher-order thinking.

The study concludes that classroom assessment practices in these secondary science classrooms are weak and mainly serve summative, right/wrong checking rather than formative support for learning. Feedback was typically oral and evaluative, not descriptive, and students had limited opportunities to ask questions, explain ideas, or engage in problem solving. The paper argues for more formative, student-centered assessment strategies and professional development for teachers.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers' assessment practices did not support higher-order scientific reasoning. In 30 observed secondary science lessons (n=30 teachers), higher-order learning was rarely assessed (M=1.47, SD=0.776), and classroom tasks were mostly textbook-based, closed, and recall-oriented rather than investigative or analytical.
finding.measure: Classroom observation ratings of assessment of higher-order learning in secondary science lessons

finding.finding_summary: The observed classroom climate offered limited support for engagement and student agency in assessment. In 30 lessons, students were seldom encouraged to ask questions (M=2.20, SD=0.805), share ideas, or participate actively, and teachers rarely used assessment practices that would promote self-regulation such as self-assessment (M=1.00, SD=0) or peer assessment (M=1.60, SD=1.003).
finding.measure: Observation ratings of student participation, questioning, self-assessment, and peer assessment

finding.finding_summary: The study found little evidence that classroom assessment fostered durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, or collaboration. Teachers rarely used open questions, problem solving/investigation work (M=1.40, SD=0.770), group work (M=1.67, SD=1.155), or self-assessment, and most questions were closed and focused on simple recall.
finding.measure: Observation ratings of open questioning, problem solving/investigation work, group work, and self-assessment

finding.finding_summary: Assessment practice was reported as inefficient and narrow in classroom implementation, with teachers relying mainly on oral questioning and having difficulty assessing all students. The paper attributes this partly to large class size and short class periods (35-40 minutes), which limited the use of varied assessment strategies and broader coverage of students.
finding.measure: Observed assessment practices and teacher interview reports about feasibility and class constraints

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is not an achievement-outcome study, it directly documents assessment practices in secondary science classes rather than changes in test scores. The classroom assessment observed was largely oral, teacher-controlled, and focused on lower-order knowledge, suggesting limited support for science learning beyond recall-based performance.
finding.measure: Observation of classroom assessment practices in secondary science

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of artificial intelligence tools in educational measurement and assessment
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines how artificial intelligence tools, especially large language models, can be used across the educational measurement and assessment cycle. The paper discusses AI applications in test purpose determination, blueprinting, item generation, test instruction writing, item assembly, administration, scoring, interpretation, analysis, and reporting, as well as broader uses such as formative assessment, automated essay scoring, learning analytics, and predictive analytics.

The article is not an empirical study of student outcomes; instead, it is a conceptual review and advocacy piece focused on potential use cases, benefits, and limitations of AI in assessment. It argues that AI can improve efficiency, personalization, feedback, and test administration while also raising concerns about bias, transparency, privacy, limited human interaction, and implementation cost. The paper emphasizes that teachers remain essential for designing assessments, interpreting results, and ensuring ethical and valid use of AI tools.

For the retrieval sub-question on differential formative assessment effects, this paper provides no direct evidence. It mentions that AI-based tools may help identify students at risk, support individualized instruction, and accommodate students with disabilities, but it does not report achievement outcomes, prespecified moderator analyses, subgroup analyses, or any design that would allow estimation of differential effects for English learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, or students with different prior achievement levels. Any such claims would be too indirect to support from this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Promising Evidence on Personalized Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This RAND report examines whether personalized learning schools funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation produced better student achievement than matched comparison students in similar schools. The study focuses on 62 public charter and district schools using a variety of personalized learning models, and analyzes two years of NWEA MAP mathematics and reading growth for about 11,000 students, with an additional longer-term analysis for a subset of 21 schools.

The main achievement analysis uses a matched comparison group (NWEA virtual comparison group) rather than random assignment, making this a quasi-experimental design. The report finds positive effects on both mathematics and reading, with two-year effect sizes of d=0.27 in math and d=0.19 in reading; results were generally stronger in elementary grades and over longer exposure to personalized learning. The report also finds that lower-performing students tended to gain more than higher-performing students, especially in mathematics, but it does not provide direct moderator analyses for English learners, students with disabilities, or low-income students.

Beyond achievement, the report describes how schools implemented personalized learning strategies such as learner profiles, personal learning paths, competency-based progression, flexible learning environments, and college/career readiness supports. Implementation varied widely across schools, with more common use of data-driven supports and individualized assistance and less common use of fully competency-based progression or highly flexible student choice. Overall, the report concludes that personalized learning showed promising achievement gains, but the evidence is limited by nonrandomized matching and school-level heterogeneity.

finding.finding_summary: Students in personalized learning schools made greater gains in reading than matched comparison students over two years. The report estimates an overall reading effect size of d=0.19 for about n=11,000 students across 61 schools; results were positive but not statistically significant in high school grades.
finding.measure: NWEA MAP reading assessment growth

finding.finding_summary: Students in personalized learning schools made greater gains in mathematics than matched comparison students over two years. The report estimates an overall math effect size of d=0.27 for about n=11,000 students across 62 schools, with stronger gains in elementary grades and positive accumulation over longer exposure.
finding.measure: NWEA MAP mathematics assessment growth

finding.finding_summary: The report includes survey and implementation evidence suggesting that personalized learning schools provided supports for student motivation, self-direction, and engagement, but these are not tied to causal achievement impacts and are not analyzed as an outcome effect. Evidence is therefore descriptive and indirect rather than a strong outcome estimate.
finding.measure: Student and teacher survey reports on study habits, attitudes toward learning, and support structures
finding.study_size: n=7,023 student spring survey respondents; n=181 teachers with logs (fall) and n=153 (spring)

paper_profiles.title: Online eLearning for undergraduates in health professions: A systematic review of the impact on knowledge, skills, attitudes and satisfaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether online eLearning improves educational outcomes for undergraduate health professions students compared with traditional learning or with other eLearning formats. The review was motivated by the growing use of online learning in health workforce training and the need for evidence on whether it is effective.

The authors systematically searched major databases for randomized controlled trials published from 2000 to August 2013 and included 59 articles (60 trials) involving 6,750 students in medicine, nursing, dentistry, pharmacy, physical therapy, and one undefined university sample. The interventions included fully online eLearning, blended learning, spaced education, video conferencing, and other web-based formats. Outcomes were knowledge, skills, attitudes, satisfaction, and secondary outcomes such as cost and adverse effects.

Across studies, online eLearning was generally equivalent to traditional learning and sometimes superior for knowledge and skills, while attitudes and satisfaction were usually similar between groups. The evidence was heterogeneous and often at high risk of bias, so the authors caution against strong universal claims. They also found no usable evidence on cost-effectiveness or adverse effects, and no meta-analysis was possible because of the wide variation in interventions and outcome measures.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review synthesized 60 randomized trials (n=6,750) of online eLearning in undergraduate health professions education. Knowledge outcomes were mixed overall: 12 studies reported significantly higher knowledge gains for online eLearning, 24 found no significant difference, 3 showed mixed results, 1 did not test significance, and 3 favored traditional learning.
finding.measure: Knowledge tests, including MCQs, test questions, written case analyses, numeracy tests, exams, and other knowledge assessments
finding.study_size: n=6750 across 60 trials; knowledge reported in 43 RCTs and 7 cRCTs

finding.finding_summary: Skill outcomes were also mixed. Of the studies that measured skills (15 studies total), 6 found significantly greater skill acquisition for online eLearning, 3 found no significant difference, 1 showed mixed results, and 1 favored traditional learning. Reported sample sizes for the skill studies ranged from 44 to 303 participants.
finding.measure: Clinical skills assessments, OSCE-style ratings/checklists, search skills tests, written case analyses, open questions on standardized tasks, self-assessment reports, and time to complete exercises
finding.study_size: n=44 to 303 per study; 15 studies total

finding.finding_summary: Attitudes toward eLearning were usually unchanged. In 12 studies assessing attitudes, 8 found no statistically significant difference between groups or mixed results, 3 did not test significance, and none favored online eLearning; one study favored traditional learning. This suggests little consistent impact on student attitudes toward the learning mode.
finding.measure: Attitude questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: Student satisfaction was mostly similar between online eLearning and traditional learning. Across 29 studies, 4 reported significantly higher satisfaction for online eLearning, 20 found no significant difference, 4 measured satisfaction without testing significance, and 1 favored traditional learning. Overall, satisfaction effects were small or inconsistent.
finding.measure: Satisfaction questionnaires or surveys, including Likert-scale instruments

paper_profiles.title: Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether computer-based scaffolding improves student learning in problem-based learning (PBL) STEM settings, and whether the effects vary by scaffold type, customization, strategy, intended higher-order skill, and discipline. The authors use a Bayesian meta-analysis of 21 studies (47 outcomes) published from 1990 to 2015, focusing on cognitive learning outcomes in STEM PBL contexts.

The interventions include conceptual, metacognitive, and strategic scaffolding; scaffolding customization such as fading, adding, and fading/adding; customization methods including performance-adapted, self-selected, and fixed-time approaches; and scaffolding strategies such as feedback, question prompts, hints, expert modeling, and multiple-strategy systems. The analysis found an overall positive effect of computer-based scaffolding on cognitive outcomes (g = 0.385, 95% CrI = 0.022 to 0.802), with larger effects for metacognitive and strategic scaffolds than conceptual scaffolds.

The paper also reports heterogeneity by design features: self-selected customization outperformed performance-adapted and fixed-time methods; analysis-level outcomes showed larger effects than synthesis or evaluation; and effects were larger in engineering, technology, and mathematics than in science or integrated STEM. However, this study does not provide direct evidence about formative assessment effects varying for English learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, or prior-achievement subgroups. The only adjacent evidence is a moderator analysis for scaffolding customization methods, including performance-adaptation and self-selection, which is too indirect to support strong claims about differential effects for student subgroups.

finding.finding_summary: Computer-based scaffolding in STEM problem-based learning produced a positive overall effect on cognitive learning outcomes, with g = 0.385 and a 95% credible interval of 0.022 to 0.802 across 21 studies and 47 outcomes. Although the paper frames outcomes broadly as cognitive and higher-order learning, many included tasks were in STEM problem-solving and analysis, making scientific reasoning a central outcome area.
finding.measure: Cognitive learning outcomes / higher-order thinking outcomes in STEM problem-based learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies higher-order thinking skills as its central outcome, including analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. Overall scaffolding improved higher-order outcomes (g = 0.385), with the largest effect for analysis (g = 0.537, 95% CrI = 0.038 to 0.981), smaller effects for synthesis (g = 0.156, 95% CrI = 0.004 to 0.329), and evaluation (g = 0.147, 95% CrI = 0.003 to 0.288).
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking skills (analysis, synthesis, evaluation)
finding.effect_size: g=0.385 overall; analysis g=0.537; synthesis g=0.156; evaluation g=0.147
finding.confidence_interval: overall 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802; analysis 0.038 to 0.981; synthesis 0.004 to 0.329; evaluation 0.003 to 0.288

paper_profiles.title: School Climate, Developmental Assets, and Academic Success in KIPP Hispanic Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines whether school climate is related to Hispanic students’ developmental assets and academic success in a KIPP charter school context. The study is motivated by concerns about high dropout rates and low achievement among Hispanic and other at-risk students, especially in Texas, and by the possibility that KIPP’s school culture may help explain stronger student outcomes.

The author uses a quantitative cross-sectional design with self-report surveys from students and staff at two KIPP schools in San Antonio, Texas (Aspire and Camino), along with academic records. School climate is measured with the Search Institute’s Creating a Great Place to Learn survey, developmental assets are measured with the Developmental Assets Profile, and academic success is operationalized using GPA, Texas state assessment results, and attendance. Multiple regression and moderation analyses are used to test whether school climate moderates the link between developmental assets and achievement, and whether those relationships differ by gender.

The main reported finding is that school climate moderates the association between several developmental assets and GPA among Hispanic middle school students. Specifically, the organizational-attributes dimension of school climate shows significant interaction effects with developmental assets such as empowerment, boundaries and expectations, constructive use of time, positive values, and social competencies. The relationships dimension also significantly moderates academic success and social competencies. The study is focused on Hispanic students in one KIPP setting and does not provide direct evidence about differential formative assessment effects for English learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, or prior-achievement subgroups; any such implications would be indirect at best.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that school climate is significantly associated with academic success, operationalized primarily as GPA, among 78 Hispanic students in grades 6-8. In particular, the organizational-attributes dimension of school climate significantly moderated the relationship between multiple developmental assets (including empowerment, boundaries and expectations, constructive use of time, positive values, and social competencies) and GPA.
finding.measure: Overall GPA in core subject classes

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that developmental assets related to social-emotional functioning are positively related to academic success in this sample of Hispanic middle school students. School climate, especially the relationships dimension and organizational attributes, significantly moderated the association between academic success and social competencies, indicating that more supportive climates were linked with stronger academic-related benefits of these assets.
finding.measure: Search Institute Developmental Assets Profile (e.g., social competencies, empowerment, positive values)

paper_profiles.title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical account of formative assessment and situates it within broader theories of pedagogy, self-regulated learning, classroom discourse, cognitive acceleration, and dynamic assessment. Rather than reporting a new intervention study, Black and Wiliam synthesize prior research and conceptual frameworks to explain what makes formative assessment effective and how teachers can interpret learner responses and adjust instruction in real time.

The paper organizes formative assessment around five strategies: clarifying learning intentions, engineering classroom discussion to elicit evidence, providing feedback that moves learning forward, activating students as instructional resources, and activating students as owners of their own learning. It argues that formative assessment is contingent on teachers’ interpretations of student responses, the instructional goals at stake, and the tactical choices teachers make in feedback and follow-up. The paper emphasizes that effective formative work is not just about collecting evidence but about using evidence to make better-founded decisions about next steps.

The discussion is grounded mainly in K-12 classroom contexts, especially elementary and secondary settings, and draws on examples from mathematics, science, and general classroom discourse. It highlights implementation features that matter theoretically—such as specificity and timeliness of feedback, teacher judgment, and whether teachers respond to evidence by adapting instruction—but it does not present original student-achievement data. Instead, it makes a conceptual case that formative assessment can be powerful when embedded in coherent pedagogical systems and supported by teacher training, explicit task design, and dialogic classroom interaction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses mathematics classrooms extensively, especially the use of formative assessment in problem solving, equivalent fractions, and the Japanese lesson design example. However, it provides no original achievement data for mathematics; the claims are conceptual and illustrative rather than empirical.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Science is used as a recurring example, including a classroom illustration about plant growth and photosynthesis and references to cognitive acceleration and science education programs. The paper does not report new science achievement outcomes; instead, it argues that formative assessment can support deeper scientific reasoning through better feedback and teacher adaptation.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines metacognition, self-regulated learning, and learner autonomy as theoretical outcomes of formative assessment. It argues that practices such as self-assessment, peer assessment, and feedback that prompts revision can strengthen students’ monitoring and control of their own learning, but it does not present direct effect estimates.
finding.measure: metacognition/self-regulated learning/learner autonomy (conceptual and illustrative discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper links formative assessment to motivation, engagement, persistence, and volitional control through its discussion of growth versus well-being tracks in self-regulated learning. The argument is theoretical: supportive feedback and cognitively challenging dialogue are presented as ways to sustain engagement and reduce withdrawal, but no student outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: motivation/engagement/persistence (conceptual discussion)

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines how scaffolding has been conceptualized, described, and evaluated in teacher–student interaction research over roughly a decade (1998–2009), with a focus on primary and secondary education. The authors argue that scaffolding is best understood as an interactive, contingent process involving three key characteristics: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility. They also synthesize the many descriptive classifications of scaffolding strategies into a framework that distinguishes scaffolding means (e.g., feedback, hints, instructing, explaining, modeling, questioning) from scaffolding intentions (e.g., metacognitive, cognitive, affective support).

The paper reviews 66 articles, including theoretical, descriptive, effectiveness, editorial, and one meta-analytic study. Most empirical studies are descriptive and concentrated in literacy, with smaller bodies of work in math and science; a smaller set of effectiveness studies examines outcomes such as reasoning, conceptual understanding, transfer, and student involvement. Across these studies, the review concludes that scaffolding is generally effective, but the evidence base is limited by small samples, inconsistent definitions, and weak measurement approaches. The authors emphasize that future work should more rigorously measure scaffolding, especially by capturing contingency, fading, transfer of responsibility, and actual student responses in interaction.

Because this is a review of varied research rather than a single intervention study, its main contribution is conceptual and methodological: it clarifies what counts as scaffolding and argues that stronger evidence depends on better operationalization and fidelity measurement. The review also notes that teacher training and adaptive/contingent delivery appear important in the limited effectiveness studies, but most studies do not yet provide strong causal evidence about which implementation features drive stronger achievement effects.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that literacy is the most developed domain in scaffolding research, with many descriptive studies and several effectiveness studies drawing on reading and writing-related tasks. However, the paper does not aggregate a single effect size for literacy achievement; instead, it concludes that scaffolding generally appears effective in literacy contexts but evidence is heterogeneous and often descriptive rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Literacy outcomes across descriptive and effectiveness studies (e.g., text comprehension, literacy tasks, classroom discourse)

finding.finding_summary: Several effectiveness studies in the review concern mathematics, including balance-scale reasoning and long-division performance. For example, Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) found that fourth and fifth graders receiving contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than peers in other support conditions at immediate and follow-up testing (n=40 across five conditions), and Murphy and Messer (2000) found more children in the scaffolding condition advanced in level of representation on a balance-scale task (N=41 scaffolding, 40 small-group, 41 alone).
finding.measure: Math problem solving and transfer on long-division and balance-scale tasks
finding.study_size: n=40 (Pratt and Savoy-Levine, 1998); n=122 total (Murphy and Messer, 2000)

finding.finding_summary: The review includes science-focused effectiveness studies showing positive learning effects from scaffolding. Mercer et al. (2004) reported better use of talk for reasoning and greater gains on non-verbal reasoning measures in the trained/scaffolded condition (N=109) than in the control condition (N=121), and Azevedo et al. (2005) found that adaptive human scaffolding produced more shifts in mental models and greater knowledge gains than fixed or no scaffolding in a hypermedia biology environment (N=38, 34, and 37).
finding.measure: Scientific reasoning, conceptual understanding, and reasoning talk in science tasks
finding.study_size: n=109 vs n=121 (Mercer et al., 2004); n=38/34/37 (Azevedo et al., 2005)

finding.finding_summary: The review also includes domain-general academic outcomes in simulation-based learning and conceptual change contexts, such as diagnostic accuracy and construction of mental models in biology/medical problem solving. Chiu et al. (2002) found that students in the cognitive apprenticeship/scaffolding condition outperformed controls on mental models of chemical equilibrium (N=20 vs N=10), although the authors note scaffolding was only one component of the approach, so the effect cannot be attributed to scaffolding alone.
finding.measure: Conceptual change / mental models / diagnostic performance in domain-general academic tasks
finding.study_size: n=20 vs n=10 (Chiu et al., 2002); n=9 total (Lajoie et al., 2001, no differences)

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies a small set of studies on affect, motivation, and involvement. Turner et al. (1998) found that classes with more whole-class scaffolding aimed at motivation/emotion had higher student involvement in mathematics, and Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) found no differences in enjoyment across contingent-support conditions but lower enjoyment in the no-support control group. Overall, the evidence suggests a generally positive association between scaffolding-related support and student affect/involvement, but effects are modest and inconsistent.
finding.measure: Student involvement and enjoyment/self-report affect measures
finding.study_size: N=42 across 34 mathematics lessons (Turner et al., 1998); n=40 total across 5 conditions (Pratt and Savoy-Levine, 1998)

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the review is that scaffolding supports durable skills such as metacognition, self-regulation, and collaboration. The review highlights studies where students in scaffolding conditions showed better reasoning talk, more self-regulating behavior, greater responsibility for learning, and improved transfer performance, especially when teachers adapted support contingently and faded responsibility over time.
finding.measure: Reasoning talk, self-regulated learning behaviors, transfer questions, and responsibility-taking

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency is not a main focus, but the review notes that scaffolding can reduce cognitive load and sometimes reorganize teacher–student interaction more efficiently. However, it provides no direct quantitative evidence on productivity, task time, or teacher workload, so any efficiency implication remains theoretical rather than empirically established in this paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper revisits the question of how effective feedback is for student learning by meta-analyzing primary studies from prior meta-analyses in the education literature. The authors were motivated by the large impact estimates reported in the Visible Learning synthesis and asked whether those estimates hold up when primary studies are integrated directly and weighted appropriately.

The analysis includes 435 studies with 994 effect sizes and more than 61,000 participants, spanning educational contexts from kindergarten through university. The paper examines overall effects of feedback and moderating features such as research design, publication type, outcome type, feedback type, feedback channel, and feedback direction. The core intervention studied is feedback broadly defined, including corrective, reinforcement/punishment, and high-information feedback, rather than a specific formative assessment program.

Overall, feedback had a medium positive effect on learning outcomes after removing extreme outliers (d = 0.48, 95% CI 0.44–0.51), but effects were highly heterogeneous. The strongest effects were found for high-information feedback (d = 0.99) and student-to-student feedback (d = 0.85), while reinforcement/punishment was much weaker (d = 0.24). The paper concludes that feedback is not a single uniform treatment; its effectiveness depends strongly on the amount of information it conveys and on how it is delivered.

finding.finding_summary: Across 435 studies (994 effect sizes; N > 61,000), feedback had a positive overall effect on educational learning outcomes. Using a random-effects model and excluding extreme outliers, the weighted mean effect was d = 0.48 (95% CI 0.44–0.51), indicating a medium positive impact on student achievement/learning measures.
finding.measure: Student learning / achievement outcomes (cognitive test performance, retention, and related learning measures)

finding.finding_summary: Feedback effects on motivational outcomes were smaller than on cognitive outcomes. For motivational measures such as intrinsic motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, and persistence, the pooled effect was d = 0.33 (95% CI 0.23–0.42), and 21% of the motivational effect sizes were negative, especially for uninformative rewards/punishments.
finding.measure: Motivation-related outcomes (intrinsic motivation, locus of control, self-efficacy, persistence)

finding.finding_summary: The review found feedback to be more effective when it supported learning processes and self-regulation rather than simply signaling correctness. High-information feedback, which includes task, process, and sometimes self-regulation information, showed the largest effects (d = 0.99, 95% CI 0.82–1.15), suggesting benefits for metacognitive/strategic learning processes.
finding.measure: High-information feedback effects on learning outcomes that reflect process/self-regulation support

paper_profiles.title: Classroom assessment and pedagogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that formative and summative assessment should be understood within a broader theory of pedagogy, rather than treated as separate or secondary domains. Black and Wiliam review key literature on curriculum, instruction, classroom dialogue, feedback, and assessment to propose a model in which teachers use evidence from student work and interaction to shape instruction and, when needed, to support summative judgments.

The paper does not report a new empirical intervention study or student outcome analysis. Instead, it synthesizes prior research and illustrates how assessment can be integrated into teaching through responsive dialogue, elicitation of evidence, feedback that moves learning forward, peer/self-assessment, and the use of summative tests for formative purposes. The authors also discuss the challenges of teacher-made summative assessment, including moderation, reliability, training, and workload, using examples such as the King’s-Oxfordshire Summative Assessment Project.

Its main conclusion is that assessment is central to effective pedagogy and that good classroom assessment requires teachers to gather evidence from all students, interpret it well, and adapt instruction accordingly. The paper also argues that accountability systems can undermine learning when they overemphasize external tests, but that formative and summative purposes can be made mutually supportive when assessment is designed and used carefully.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that teacher-developed summative assessment systems can improve rigour, consistency, and confidence, but it also notes that moderation and standardization add complexity and workload. In the KOSAP example, teachers reported that moderation was valuable, while the authors acknowledge the approach can be burdensome and requires training and support.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, moderation/standardization processes, assessment system feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that assessment systems shape pedagogy and that high-stakes accountability can distort classroom practice by encouraging teaching to the test and narrowing learning. It also contends that teacher contribution to summative assessment can be valuable if systems include uniformity, moderation, training, and comparability, as illustrated by the KOSAP discussion.
finding.measure: Assessment system design, moderation, reliability, accountability effects on schooling

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents dialogue, peer assessment, self-assessment, and responsive teaching as supporting metacognition, collaboration, and learners' ability to regulate their own work. However, this is a conceptual synthesis rather than a new outcome study, so no numeric effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Metacognition, collaboration, self-regulation, dialogue quality

paper_profiles.title: Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines the validity and reliability of Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills (DIBELS) as a formative assessment for special education students. The central question is whether scores from DIBELS correlate with scores from the Woodcock-Johnson III (WJ III), and whether repeated administration and double-rating produce reliable results. The paper also reviews formative assessment literature emphasizing timely feedback, teacher use of assessment data, and instructional adjustment, but those ideas are presented primarily as background rather than as tested implementation features in this study.

The empirical study used 30 special education students in grades 3-6 at one elementary school in Fresno Unified School District. Students were assessed on four DIBELS subtests—Initial Sound Fluency, Letter Naming Fluency, Phoneme Segmentation Fluency, and Nonsense Word Fluency—and on two WJ III reading subtests—Letter-Word Identification and Word Attack. Two trained raters administered and scored the DIBELS measures to estimate inter-rater reliability. The design is correlational and validity-focused rather than an intervention study.

Findings indicate strong inter-rater reliability for DIBELS and mixed validity evidence against the WJ III. Letter Naming Fluency, Phoneme Segmentation Fluency, and Nonsense Word Fluency showed significant positive correlations with WJ III reading measures, while Initial Sound Fluency showed weak or nonsignificant relationships. The study concludes that DIBELS is a reliable and generally valid formative assessment for special education students, though the Initial Sound Fluency subtest appears weaker than the others.

finding.finding_summary: In a sample of 30 special education students in grades 3-6, three DIBELS subtests showed significant positive correlations with WJ III reading measures, while Initial Sound Fluency did not. Specifically, Letter Naming Fluency correlated with WJ III Letter-Word Identification (r=.331, p=.074) and Word Attack (r=.455, p=.011), Phoneme Segmentation Fluency correlated with Letter-Word Identification (r=.341, p=.065) and Word Attack (r=.482, p=.007), and Nonsense Word Fluency correlated with Word Attack (r=.328, p=.077) but not Letter-Word Identification (r=-.074, p=.698).
finding.measure: DIBELS Initial Sound Fluency, Letter Naming Fluency, Phoneme Segmentation Fluency, and Nonsense Word Fluency; WJ III Letter-Word Identification and Word Attack
finding.effect_size: r=.331 to .482 (significant positive correlations for several subtests)
finding.std_deviation: DIBELS SDs: ISF 16.55, LNF 24.88, PSF 16.11, NWF 13.50; WJ III SDs: Letter-Word 17.77, Word Attack 17.87

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that DIBELS is brief and easy to administer, score, and graph for progress monitoring, but this is framed as practice implication rather than a tested outcome. The only directly measured efficiency-related evidence is that two trained raters produced highly similar DIBELS scores, suggesting the tool can be administered consistently by different personnel.
finding.measure: Inter-rater reliability for DIBELS administration/scoring

paper_profiles.title: Theory and Practice of Online Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This edited volume surveys the theory and practice of online learning in higher education and distance education contexts. The book is organized as a collection of chapters on learning theory, infrastructure, course design, and delivery/support, with emphasis on how online environments can be designed to improve teaching and learning.

The retrieved text is the book front matter, table of contents, introduction, and the beginning of Chapter 1. It is primarily conceptual and descriptive rather than an empirical study of a specific intervention. The chapter excerpt argues that learning outcomes depend more on instructional design than on the delivery medium, and it outlines behaviorist, cognitivist, constructivist, and connectivist implications for online instruction, including feedback, sequencing, and support. No direct student-achievement evaluation of formative assessment implementation features in K-12 classrooms is reported in the provided text.

paper_profiles.title: A comparative analysis of international frameworks for 21st century competences: Implications for national curriculum policies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how eight international frameworks define 21st century competences and what they recommend for curriculum implementation and assessment. The authors analyze documents from frameworks such as P21, EnGauge, ATCS, NETS/ISTE, NAEP technological literacy, OECD DeSeCo/New Millennium Learners, the EU key competences framework, and UNESCO ICT competency standards for teachers. They also review three international studies on how countries and schools have taken up these competences in policy and practice.

The study is not an intervention study and does not test student outcomes; instead, it compares policy and framework documents to assess horizontal consistency (agreement on what competences matter) and vertical consistency (alignment between intentions, implementation, and assessment). The analysis finds strong agreement across frameworks on collaboration, communication, ICT literacy, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and social/cultural competence, but much weaker alignment between policy intentions and classroom practice.

For implementation, the paper argues that 21st century competences are usually intended to be integrated across the curriculum, supported by pedagogies such as problem-based learning, cooperative learning, experiential learning, and formative assessment. It also emphasizes the importance of teacher professional development, stakeholder involvement, and assessment systems that are authentic, performance-based, and formative. The paper concludes that national policy frameworks often articulate ambitious goals, but actual classroom practices and assessment systems lag behind, creating a gap between policy and practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds strong horizontal consistency across international frameworks on the importance of 21st century competences, but weak vertical consistency between intended policy, implementation, and assessment. In the reviewed country-level studies, many systems had adopted these competences in policy, yet classroom practices and assessment remained much less aligned, indicating a substantial implementation gap.
finding.measure: Document analysis of 8 international frameworks and 3 international comparative studies of policy and practice

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Peer Assessment on Academic Performance: A Meta-analysis of Control Group Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines whether peer assessment improves student academic performance and which implementation features are associated with stronger or weaker effects. The authors note that prior literature on peer assessment has relied heavily on narrative reviews and correlational evidence, and they therefore synthesize only control-group experimental and quasi-experimental studies.

The review includes 55 studies (143 effect sizes) across primary, secondary, and tertiary settings and multiple subjects, with outcomes ranging from writing quality and science performance to statistics and other academic tasks. The overall effect of peer assessment on academic performance was positive and small-to-moderate (g = 0.31, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.44), with benefits relative to no assessment (g = 0.31) and teacher assessment (g = 0.28), and no significant difference relative to self-assessment (g = 0.23, ns).

The meta-regressions tested several implementation features relevant to formative assessment, including frequency, online versus offline delivery, anonymity, freeform versus structured rubrics, written versus dialogic versus grading components, and task transfer. Most moderators were not statistically significant, suggesting the effect was fairly robust across contexts. One notable exception was grading: peer grading appeared beneficial for tertiary students (g = 0.55) but not for primary or secondary students, indicating that the value of adding grades may depend on student age and educational level.

finding.finding_summary: Across studies focused on writing and reading-related tasks, peer assessment improved literacy outcomes relative to control conditions. The meta-analysis reports positive effects for literacy-related academic performance overall (e.g., writing outcomes g = 0.30 to 0.35 in subgroup analyses), with the strongest evidence coming from writing tasks, which comprised the largest share of included effects.
finding.measure: Writing quality, essay performance, and reading-related academic performance
finding.study_size: n=55 studies; k=143 effect sizes (literacy-related subsample not separately reported)
finding.effect_size: g=0.31 overall; writing subgroup g=0.30 to 0.35
finding.confidence_interval: overall 95% CI 0.18 to 0.44; writing subgroup not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment also improved science-related academic performance. The review included multiple science studies across primary and tertiary settings, and subgroup estimates for science-related/other academic tasks were positive overall, contributing to the overall positive meta-analytic effect.
finding.measure: Science achievement tasks and course assessments
finding.study_size: n=55 studies; science-related subsample not separately reported
finding.confidence_interval: overall 95% CI 0.18 to 0.44; science-related subgroup not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes statistics-related and numeracy-adjacent academic outcomes, with positive peer-assessment effects contributing to the overall synthesis. However, the paper does not isolate a separate numeracy-only effect size in the text provided, so the evidence is indirect and based on included statistics achievement studies.
finding.measure: Statistics achievement and related numeracy course performance
finding.study_size: n=55 studies; statistics-related subsample not separately reported
finding.confidence_interval: overall 95% CI 0.18 to 0.44; numeracy-related subgroup not_reported

finding.finding_summary: For academic outcomes outside literacy, science, and numeracy, peer assessment still showed a positive overall effect. The meta-analysis found a small-to-moderate benefit across diverse subjects such as accounting, IT, medicine, politics, psychology, performing arts, and education, with no evidence that subject area substantially moderated the effect.
finding.measure: Course grades, exams, and subject-specific academic performance across non-literacy/non-science/non-numeracy domains

paper_profiles.title: The effect of a formative assessment practice on student achievement in mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a professional development programme (PDP) focused on formative assessment in mathematics led teachers to implement classroom practices that improved student achievement, and whether doing more formative assessment activities was associated with larger achievement gains. The authors situate the work in a broader literature showing mixed effects of formative assessment and argue that stronger evidence is needed from studies that carefully describe what teachers actually do in classrooms, not just what an intervention intends teachers to do.

The study followed a stratified random sample of 14 Swedish year-7 mathematics teachers who participated in a year-long PDP centered on Wiliam and Thompson’s formative assessment framework (the ‘big idea’ plus five key strategies). The PDP included weekly 4-hour meetings across one term plus additional planning and reading time. Researchers observed classrooms before and after the PDP, interviewed teachers, and coded the new formative assessment activities teachers actually adopted. Most teachers increased the frequency of eliciting evidence of learning (for example, exit tickets and mini-whiteboards), gave more adjusted feedback, and somewhat increased goal sharing and self-regulation supports, but made few changes to peer-assessment practices.

Student achievement was measured with municipality-administered pre- and post-tests in mathematics for all year-7 classes in the municipality, comparing students taught by intervention teachers (n=291) with students in the control group (n=275) while controlling for pre-test scores. The main quantitative result was null: there were no significant post-test differences between intervention and control groups, and no significant correlation between the number of formative assessment activities implemented and post-test achievement. The paper concludes that simply increasing the number of formative assessment activities was not enough in this context, and suggests that the quality and specific nature of implementation may be more important than dosage alone.

finding.finding_summary: In an ANCOVA controlling for pre-test scores, students taught by teachers who had completed the formative assessment PDP did not significantly outperform the control group on the post-test. The intervention group included 291 students and the control group 275 students; the paper also reports no significant correlation between the number of formative assessment activities implemented and post-test scores.
finding.measure: Municipality mathematics pre-test and post-test scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports descriptive evidence that some implementation features increased student engagement and thinking, especially the use of mini-whiteboards and randomly distributed questions during whole-class sessions. However, these are not tested as separate outcomes with inferential statistics, and the paper does not report an overall quantitative effect on engagement or self-regulation.
finding.measure: Classroom-observed engagement and teacher-reported student engagement/thinking

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the Efficacy of a Professional Development Program in Formative Classroom Assessment in Middle School English Language Arts and Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether a state professional development program in formative classroom assessment improved middle school teachers’ assessment knowledge and their students’ achievement in English language arts (ELA) and mathematics. The study responds to a broader concern in the formative assessment literature: teacher learning in assessment practices does not always translate into higher student achievement, and evidence on that connection had been limited and methodologically weak.

The intervention was a one-year, three-hour recertification course developed by the South Carolina Department of Education and delivered in low-performing middle schools from 2005 to 2008. In Year 1, schools were randomly assigned to treatment or control, with treatment delivered by a trained assessment coach. In Years 2 and 3, the researchers compared delivery by a trained coach versus a relatively untrained facilitator, alongside matched control schools. The program emphasized aligning assessments to standards, creating performance tasks, rubrics, checklists, multiple-choice items, portfolios, and using assessment results formatively and summatively. Fidelity was imperfect: coaches/facilitators implemented only about 68%–73% of curriculum activities, and teachers completed 47%–63% of required hours.

The main conclusion is mixed but important for implementation questions. Teacher assessment knowledge improved in every year and did so similarly whether the PD was delivered by a trained coach or an untrained facilitator. However, student achievement results were negative: students in PD schools tended to score lower than matched controls on state ELA and mathematics tests, with statistically significant negative effects in ELA across all three years (e.g., d-like effects of -0.16, -0.08, and -0.26) and in mathematics in Year 3 (d-like effect -0.33). The authors suggest that teachers may have learned assessment terminology and construction skills without sufficiently changing instruction based on student evidence, and they explicitly raise concerns about whether teachers could diagnose misconceptions and select effective reteaching actions.

finding.finding_summary: Across all three replication years, students in professional development schools scored lower on adjusted English language arts PACT scores than matched control students. The adjusted differences were -2.39 points (Year 1), -1.15 points (Year 2), and -3.46 points (Year 3), with standardized effect sizes of -0.16, -0.08, and -0.26, respectively; all were statistically significant at p<.05.
finding.measure: State English Language Arts scale scores on the Palmetto Achievement Challenge Test (PACT), adjusted via multilevel modeling
finding.study_size: Year 1 n=2,066 students; Year 2 n=3,203 students; Year 3 n=1,403 students

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics outcomes were not significantly different in Years 1 and 2, but Year 3 showed a significant negative treatment effect for students in PD schools. The adjusted Year 3 mathematics PACT score was 3.76 points lower for treatment schools, with a standardized effect size of -0.33 (p=.01); Year 1 and Year 2 effects were near zero (-0.01 and 0.03 reported).
finding.measure: State mathematics scale scores on the Palmetto Achievement Challenge Test (PACT), adjusted via multilevel modeling
finding.study_size: Year 1 n=2,708 students; Year 2 n=2,745 students; Year 3 n=1,297 students

finding.finding_summary: The professional development increased teachers’ assessment knowledge, including skills tied to analyzing cognitive levels, aligning items to standards, and developing assessment tasks. In Year 1 the treatment group improved by 8.51 points from pretest to posttest versus 1.85 points for controls, and in Years 2 and 3 both treatment conditions improved significantly from pretest to posttest with large within-group effects (ω²=.60 and .56).
finding.measure: Teacher assessment knowledge / assessment practices test scores (multiple-choice pretest-posttest)
finding.study_size: Year 1 n=151 teachers; Year 2 n=146 teachers; Year 3 n=71 teachers
finding.std_deviation: Pretest and posttest SDs reported in tables but not as a single study-level value

finding.finding_summary: The study directly compared delivery models for the professional development program: implementation by a trained assessment coach versus a relatively untrained facilitator. Teacher knowledge gains did not differ by delivery model, and the authors report no significant differences in student achievement by level of treatment in Years 2 and 3, suggesting that the added coaching support did not produce measurable achievement advantages.
finding.measure: Comparative effects of professional development delivery model (coach vs untrained facilitator) on teacher assessment knowledge and student PACT outcomes
finding.study_size: Year 2 n=146 teachers; Year 3 n=71 teachers; student samples as above

paper_profiles.title: Toward Reducing Anxiety and Increasing Performance in Physics Education: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether frequent formative assessment using clicker technology can improve physics outcomes and reduce anxiety among secondary students. The authors focus on a practical implementation of formative assessment in which students answer multiple-choice questions at the end of each physics lesson, receive immediate feedback, and remain anonymous while responding.

The study was conducted over 17 weeks in one Dutch secondary school with 139 physics students across six classes taught by three teachers. Students were randomly assigned at the class level to either a treatment condition with clicker-based questioning three times per week for 10–15 minutes per lesson or to a control condition with traditional teaching and homework-based feedback. The intervention was designed to isolate formative assessment itself, without reward systems or attendance incentives.

Results from multilevel regressions showed that the treatment group had significantly lower physics anxiety and higher physics exam performance than the control group. The estimated effects were moderate in size: anxiety decreased by about 0.28 SD and academic performance increased by about 0.34 SD after covariate adjustment. A mediation analysis suggested that reduced anxiety partially explains the achievement gain. The paper concludes that repeated, anonymous formative assessments with immediate teacher feedback can be a feasible way to improve both affective and academic outcomes in secondary physics, though the study cannot disentangle the separate contributions of testing and feedback.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized experiment with 139 secondary physics students (n=139), repeated clicker-based formative assessments improved post-test physics performance relative to traditional teaching. In adjusted multilevel models, the intervention effect was 0.34 SD (p<0.025), indicating a medium positive effect on a final physics exam scored on standardized z-scores.
finding.measure: Final physics exam score (standardized z-score; open-ended Dutch national physics exam questions)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention significantly reduced students’ anxiety in physics. In adjusted multilevel models, the post-test anxiety score was 0.28 SD lower for the treatment group than for the control group (p<0.025), based on a 6-item physics anxiety scale administered before and after the 17-week intervention.
finding.measure: Physics anxiety scale (adapted Mathematics Anxiety Scale; post-test z-score)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the intervention may improve metacognitive monitoring and confidence indirectly through repeated formative assessment and immediate feedback, but it does not directly measure durable skills as a primary outcome. The authors discuss improved self-monitoring and understanding of course material as plausible mechanisms, yet the empirical evidence in this paper centers on anxiety and achievement rather than a direct metacognition measure.
finding.measure: Discussion of metacognitive monitoring / self-confidence as mechanism, not a direct outcome measure

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.venue: arXiv / Technology in Practice Strand (WIPTTE-related conference paper)
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (K-12, undergraduate, graduate, and adult learners across diverse educational settings)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for real-time formative assessment using pen-enabled mobile devices. The authors ask whether collecting open-format student responses during instruction can improve learning, engagement, and instructional responsiveness across a range of educational settings and subjects.

The paper is a multi-vignette report drawing on classroom experiences from seven instructors in the United States and Mexico, spanning K-12, community college, undergraduate engineering, graduate courses, and food science. Students respond to open-ended prompts with digital ink, and instructors use the immediate feedback to identify misconceptions, tailor subsequent instruction, and promote more active participation.

The evidence presented is largely descriptive and observational, with a few informal comparisons to prior cohorts or parallel sections. Reported outcomes include reduced persistence of misconceptions on later exams, improved standards-based algebra performance in a high school setting, increased participation and problem-solving activity, and stronger performance on summative quizzes after formative assessment cycles. The paper concludes that InkSurvey appears promising for supporting timely instructional adjustment and student learning, but it does not provide a single controlled evaluation across the settings described.

finding.finding_summary: In a high school Algebra I context, students receiving regular and repeated individual and whole-group feedback through InkSurvey reportedly showed stronger gains on standards-based assessments than students not exposed to the intervention. The paper does not provide the exact test statistics in this article, but it explicitly states that female students showed especially large gains relative to the control group.
finding.measure: standards-based assessments in Algebra I

finding.finding_summary: Several examples suggest improved conceptual understanding in STEM/engineering contexts when InkSurvey was used for real-time formative assessment. One comparison reported that after a calculus III lesson using InkSurvey, only 1 of 87 students still made a particular triple-integral misconception error on follow-up exam items, versus 12 of 103 students in a comparable section without InkSurvey. Another engineering physics vignette reported steady improvement in problem-solving skills over the semester, and a chemical engineering vignette reported average conceptual competence increasing from about 1.8 to 3.1 on a 4-point scale after instructor-guided, scaffolded use of simulations plus InkSurvey.
finding.measure: summative exam items, problem-solving skill ratings, and 4-point conceptual competence ratings
finding.study_size: n=87 vs n=103; other vignettes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Student feedback suggests InkSurvey increased engagement, motivation, and perceived ownership of learning. In one survey of 63 advanced laboratory physics students, 54 (86%) agreed that InkSurvey gave the instructor a better understanding of what they did and did not understand, and 48 (76%) said creating InkSurvey responses helped them better understand the material or realize what they did not know.
finding.measure: anonymous student survey on perceived understanding, engagement, and metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that InkSurvey can support metacognition and problem-solving. Students reported that constructing responses helped them identify gaps in understanding, and one upper-level engineering physics vignette reported steady semester-long improvement in problem-solving skill scores as students repeatedly responded to structured formative prompts. The paper also describes students revising their thinking based on immediate feedback, suggesting gains in self-monitoring and reflective thinking.
finding.measure: survey responses about metacognition; problem-solving skill scores
finding.study_size: n=63 for the survey; other study sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that InkSurvey improves instructional efficiency by giving instructors immediate visibility into student thinking and allowing them to adjust instruction in real time. Students described the tool as enabling the teacher to quickly see whether the class understood, slow down when needed, revisit misconceptions, and spend less time on material the class already understood; these are qualitative reports rather than quantified workload measures.
finding.measure: student and instructor reports of immediate feedback and instructional adjustment

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment I. Applications in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for collecting real-time formative assessment responses from students using pen-enabled mobile devices. The authors argue that open-ended, handwritten responses allow instructors to probe student thinking more deeply than multiple-choice clicker questions and to respond to misconceptions more quickly and flexibly.

The paper presents seven descriptive vignettes from diverse settings, including K-12 algebra and biology classrooms, community college, and university STEM courses in the United States and Mexico. In each vignette, instructors use InkSurvey to ask open-format questions, review student work immediately, and adjust instruction during class. The central claim is that the tool supports active learning, reveals student misconceptions, and enables timely instructional adaptation, but the paper does not report a controlled comparison or quantitative achievement analysis in this article itself; it explicitly notes that a companion paper contains data and evidence of effectiveness.
