Because the article is primarily a technology-in-practice and implementation description, it is best characterized as qualitative/descriptive rather than an outcome study. It provides concrete examples of how formative assessment can be delivered with mobile devices, including near-daily use, sequential questioning, and immediate class discussion, but it does not provide student achievement effect sizes or experimental estimates in this paper.

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes a K-12 Algebra I vignette in which InkSurvey was used nearly daily to collect students' written solutions and allow the teacher to address misconceptions before students practiced independently. However, no quantitative achievement results, effect sizes, or pre/post comparisons are reported in this article.
finding.measure: Student algebra problem-solving responses and classroom misconceptions
finding.study_size: n=25 (Algebra I class, described in vignette)

finding.finding_summary: Several STEM vignettes in physics, biology, and food chemistry describe using InkSurvey to probe student understanding of scientific concepts, reveal misconceptions, and support immediate instructional adjustment. The article does not report student achievement data, so any impact on scientific reasoning is descriptive rather than empirically estimated here.
finding.measure: Open-ended formative assessment responses on physics, biology, food chemistry, and chemical engineering concepts

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests that open-format InkSurvey prompts may support metacognition, independent thinking, and collaborative idea generation, especially in the creativity-in-physics vignette. These claims are illustrated through classroom routines rather than measured outcomes, and no formal data on critical thinking, collaboration, or metacognitive gains are reported.
finding.measure: Classroom idea generation, questioning, and critical-comment activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that InkSurvey increased engagement and participation by making students actively respond in class and by reducing barriers to sharing ideas anonymously. These are descriptive observations from implementation vignettes; the paper does not include survey data or other quantitative evidence of motivation or engagement gains.
finding.measure: Observed participation and engagement during formative assessment activities

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, individualized formative assessment for complex, open-ended geometry tasks in K-12 mathematics. The authors developed an automated grading and feedback system using a large language model (GPT-4) integrated into the Algeomath online geometry platform, aiming to support constructive geometry tasks that require students to make multistep constructions, explain reasoning, and revise work across multiple attempts.

The system was designed to grade three types of tasks: closed-ended items via rule-based matching, open-ended explanations via few-shot LLM prompts, and dynamic geometry construction tasks via programmatic object checking. Teacher-authored exemplars were used both for grading open responses and generating feedback that varied by attempt number, with earlier attempts receiving hints and later attempts receiving more explicit guidance. The study piloted the system with 79 middle-school students in four classes in South Korea during November 2024.

Results showed high agreement with teacher judgments for closed-ended and construction tasks, and substantial but imperfect agreement for open-ended explanations (overall Cohen’s kappa = 0.737, agreement = 0.866 on 878 responses). Feedback was judged moderately useful overall (pooled mean 3.98/5, n=754), but quality varied by item and was weakened by answer leakage, imprecise terminology, and overly generic or overly revealing prompts. In terms of student learning, 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next attempt (260/708), with stronger post-feedback conversion for closed-ended questions (55.1%) than for CGT (35.6%) or open-ended questions (33.9%). However, analyses of transfer to later questions found no statistically significant effect, suggesting that the system supported rapid within-item correction more clearly than durable transfer across tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The system was used to support and evaluate student performance on constructive geometry tasks and open-ended geometry explanations. Across 79 middle-school students, 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next attempt (260/708), with higher post-feedback conversion for closed-ended items (55.1%) than CGT items (35.6%) or open-ended explanation items (33.9%). However, analyses of later-question transfer found no statistically significant effects, so the evidence is strongest for short-term within-item correction rather than broader achievement gains.
finding.measure: Attempt-level correctness on geometry tasks; post-feedback correctness conversion rate; teacher-aligned scoring of open-ended geometry explanations
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 708 feedback-supported incorrect attempts; 878 open-ended response records

finding.finding_summary: The feedback design appeared to support persistence and revision behavior by encouraging students to retry and improve their answers. Students corrected many errors after feedback, and the platform’s staged prompting was intended to sustain engagement across up to three retries per item; however, the paper did not report a causal test of motivation or engagement outcomes, only descriptive evidence from student revision behavior and survey responses.
finding.measure: Revision behavior across attempts; learner survey ratings of the activity

finding.finding_summary: The study provides qualitative evidence that feedback supported iterative refinement of mathematical explanations, shifting student responses from vague statements toward more precise, conceptually grounded reasoning. In a documented example, a student’s answer progressed from 'Equal' to a correct explanation of equidistance after successive feedback, suggesting support for metacognitive revision and conceptual reasoning, though no formal effect size or causal transfer test was reported.
finding.measure: Quality and specificity of iterative answer refinement; rubric-based expert judgments of explanation quality
finding.study_size: n=79 students; qualitative case evidence from individual response sequences

paper_profiles.title: Fostering Student Engagement in a Mobile Formative Assessment System for High-School Economics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a mobile self-assessment tool can support high-school students’ learning and engagement in Microeconomics. The authors are interested in formative assessment in a mobile environment, especially whether an adaptable quiz system can help students check their knowledge, identify misconceptions, and become more engaged in studying economics concepts such as demand and price elasticity.

The intervention is a mobile application that lets learners select questions by difficulty, topic, and educational level, then receive topic-level results after completing quizzes. The study was conducted in a Greek senior high school with 10 teachers and 83 students, focusing on students aged about 16-17 who were studying compulsory Microeconomics content tied to university admission exams. Teachers first evaluated usability and suitability, and then students used the app in a 7-day period and were compared with a pen-and-paper quiz group.

Findings suggest the tool was highly usable (SUS 83.25 from teachers; student SUS also above 80), improved engagement, and was associated with better achievement on a class test. The app group completed the quiz more often and scored higher on the summative assessment than the comparison group (16.73 vs. 13.86, p=0.046568). The paper concludes that the mobile formative self-assessment approach appears acceptable and potentially beneficial for motivating students and helping them understand microeconomics concepts, while also noting that feedback features and adaptation options could be strengthened in future versions.

finding.finding_summary: High-school students using the mobile self-assessment app scored higher on the subsequent class test than students using the pen-and-paper version. The app group’s average score was 16.73 versus 13.86 for the comparison group, and the difference was statistically significant (2-tailed t-test, p=0.046568).
finding.measure: Summative class test scores on Microeconomics concepts

finding.finding_summary: The study reports stronger student engagement, motivation, and participation when students used the mobile formative assessment tool. In the app group, 100% used the quiz at least once and there were 33 additional reruns during the 7-day period; students also reported the tool motivated them and helped them realize their knowledge gaps.
finding.measure: Quiz usage/reruns, reported motivation, participation, and engagement
finding.study_size: n=30 in the experimental comparison; n=15 app group for usage data

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests gains in students’ self-regulation/metacognitive awareness, because the tool presented topic-level results and errors, prompting students to revisit textbook sections. Students agreed or strongly agreed that the application helped them realize their true knowledge and misconceptions.
finding.measure: Student self-reports of recognizing knowledge/misconceptions and revisiting learning materials
finding.study_size: n=15 app group for student feedback

paper_profiles.title: Learning Progression-Guided AI Evaluation of Scientific Models To Support Diverse Multi-Modal Understanding in NGSS Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper asks how a validated learning progression (LP) can guide machine-learning-based evaluation of students’ science models and written explanations so that feedback can be personalized and aligned to multiple modes of expressing understanding. The authors focus on the challenge of scoring open-ended student responses in a way that captures qualitatively different levels of reasoning and can support timely formative feedback.

The study develops analytic rubrics for an electroscope item aligned to an NGSS-based LP on electrical interactions. Using posttest responses from 9th-grade students in a physical science curriculum study, the authors trained a CNN/ResNet-18 model to score drawing-based scientific models and a BERT model to score short written explanations. The paper reports high human-machine agreement for most rubric categories (generally above 90% accuracy on test data) and argues that LP-guided rubric design can help AI produce more meaningful, construct-aligned feedback.

The paper’s main contribution is methodological rather than evaluative: it demonstrates how LP structure can be used to define rubric categories and train scoring models, and provides examples of feedback that could be generated from the scores. It does not test whether the AI feedback improves student learning or achievement; the paper states that the feedback is planned for future piloting. As a result, the paper is best understood as an AI assessment development and validation study in a high school science context.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether AI models can score high school students’ scientific model drawings and written explanations aligned to a learning progression for electrical interactions. It reports strong human-machine agreement on test data (generally >90% accuracy across most rubric categories), but it does not measure student achievement gains, so there is no direct evidence of an effect on scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: Human-machine agreement on scoring categories for scientific models and written explanations aligned to an NGSS learning progression
finding.study_size: n=1211 scored responses from 9th-grade students (models and explanations); 884 model responses used for training and 327 for testing; 1060 explanation responses used for training/testing

paper_profiles.title: Effects of Technology-integrated Formative Assessment on Students’ Retention of Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge in Chemical Equilibrium Concepts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether technology-integrated formative assessment (TIFA) improves secondary school students’ retention of chemical equilibrium knowledge, with attention to both conceptual and procedural understanding. The authors note that formative assessment can be time-consuming for teachers and propose technology as a way to make feedback and assessment more efficient and workable in classrooms.

The study used a quasi-experimental non-equivalent pretest-posttest-follow-up design with three groups: a technology-integrated formative assessment group, a formative-assessment-only group, and a conventional instruction group. The sample included 132 grade 11 students from government secondary schools in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Students completed conceptual and procedural chemical equilibrium tests at pretest, posttest, and a follow-up posttest two months later.

Results from mixed-model ANOVAs showed significant group, time, and interaction effects for both conceptual and procedural scores. All groups improved from pretest to posttest, but the TIFA group had the strongest gains and the highest follow-up scores, indicating better retention over time than the other groups. The posttest scores were higher than follow-up scores, but the experimental conditions still maintained more learning than the conventional group. The paper concludes that technology-integrated formative assessment can strengthen both conceptual and procedural chemistry learning and support retention beyond immediate post-intervention achievement. It also argues, at a general level, that technology may reduce practical constraints of formative assessment such as time burden in class, though no direct workload outcome was measured.

finding.finding_summary: Technology-integrated formative assessment produced significantly higher conceptual chemistry scores than formative assessment alone and conventional instruction, with a large main effect of group (F(2,129)=16.73, p<0.001, ηp²=0.21) and a large time effect (F(2,258)=419.04, p<0.001, ηp²=0.77). Mean conceptual scores increased from 7.70 at pretest to 16.89 at posttest and remained elevated at follow-up (14.88) after 2 months, indicating retention beyond immediate post-intervention achievement (n=132).
finding.measure: Chemical equilibrium conceptual knowledge test scores
finding.std_deviation: pretest SD=2.78; posttest SD=3.97; follow-up SD=3.60

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also significantly improved procedural chemistry knowledge, with large main effects for time (F(1.30,167.97)=773.19, p<0.001, ηp²=0.86) and group (F(2,129)=24.03, p<0.001, ηp²=0.27), plus a significant time-by-group interaction (F(2.60,167.92)=9.18, p<0.001, ηp²=0.13). Mean procedural scores rose from 3.78 at pretest to 10.39 at posttest and then declined to 9.23 at the 2-month follow-up, showing some decay but sustained advantage over baseline and stronger retention in the TIFA group (n=132).
finding.measure: Chemical equilibrium procedural knowledge test scores
finding.std_deviation: pretest SD=2.07; posttest SD=1.68; follow-up SD=1.86

paper_profiles.title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical account of formative assessment rather than reporting a new empirical intervention study. Black and Wiliam revisit their earlier work to clarify what counts as formative assessment and to connect the concept to broader theories of pedagogy, self-regulated learning, classroom discourse, cognitive acceleration, and dynamic assessment.

The paper argues that formative assessment is best understood as classroom practice in which evidence about student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or peers to make better-informed decisions about next instructional steps. It organizes formative assessment into five strategies: clarifying learning intentions, engineering discussions/tasks that elicit evidence, providing feedback that moves learning forward, activating peers as instructional resources, and activating students as owners of their own learning.

The discussion is largely conceptual and synthesizes prior literature on classroom interaction, metacognition, and feedback. It uses examples from K-12 classrooms and mentions that some related programs, such as cognitive acceleration and dynamic assessment, have stronger long-term effects, but this paper itself does not present original outcome data. Its main conclusion is that formative assessment should be theorized as contingent, interactive pedagogy aimed at regulating learning, and that stronger theoretical models are needed to guide feedback and implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally theorizes formative assessment as a process that supports metacognition, self-regulation, learner autonomy, and students' ability to interpret and act on feedback. It does not report original effect sizes or direct student-outcome data, but it argues from prior literature that these durable skills are core mechanisms through which formative assessment may improve learning.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, learner autonomy, and strategic response to feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses motivational and affective dimensions of classroom feedback, including the risk that students shift from growth-oriented to well-being-oriented regulation when feedback threatens competence or belonging. It highlights possible negative effects such as avoidance, helplessness, and reduced effort, but provides no new empirical estimates in this article.
finding.measure: Motivation, well-being, effort, avoidance, helplessness

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that formative assessment requires teachers to make rapid diagnostic and prognostic decisions, often within seconds, and that implementation can be challenging in large classes. However, it does not report direct measures of teacher workload, class time costs, or testing burden in this article.
finding.measure: Teacher decision-making demands and instructional responsiveness

paper_profiles.title: Consolidating understanding of variation as part of STEM: experimenting with plant growth
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Year 6 students developed understanding of statistical variation while participating in an integrated STEM plant-growth investigation. The authors were interested in whether students could use TinkerPlots representations and classroom discussion to identify variation within and between treatments, describe change over time, and interpret experimental outcomes in a science context.

The study took place across three school terms in an Australian independent Catholic school with 64 Year 6 students in three classes. In the activity, students designed and ran small-group experiments on plant growth using different seeds, soils, and treatments, then entered their results into TinkerPlots and answered workbook questions focused on variation. The paper uses qualitative analysis of workbook responses as formative evidence and a later end-of-year questionnaire as summative evidence of longer-term learning.

Findings suggest that many students could identify multiple features of variation in the plots, compare treatments, and describe how plant growth changed over time. End-of-year responses showed that most students retained an appreciation of control-versus-treatment comparisons, missing data, and growth trends, though many responses remained at a basic or intermediate SOLO level. The authors conclude that plant-growth investigations within STEM can support developing statistical understanding of variation in primary school, especially when digital representations and repeated opportunities for analysis are used.

finding.finding_summary: The plant-growth STEM activity supported students' understanding of experimental comparison, variation, and interpreting plotted data. In formative workbook responses, many students identified variation across height, treatment, and time; at end-of-year, 85% gave substantively correct reasons for using a control and three treatments, 80% correctly explained gaps as missing measurement days, and 88% could compare the control with other treatments.
finding.measure: Workbook responses and end-of-year questionnaire items about interpreting experiment plots, controls, gaps in data, and treatment comparisons

finding.finding_summary: Students showed developing understanding of statistical variation and data representation in a STEM context. In the workbook, students described variation within and between treatments and across days; on the end-of-year questionnaire, 81% described how the data changed and 88% compared the control with other treatments, with responses ranging from ikonic to relational SOLO levels.
finding.measure: TinkerPlots-based plot interpretation, workbook questions on variation, and SOLO-coded end-of-year responses

finding.finding_summary: The task required students to reason across multiple aspects of an investigation and to connect measurements, plots, and conclusions, which the authors treated as evidence of increasingly integrated understanding. Some end-of-year responses reached relational SOLO level, indicating linked reasoning about how treatments affected growth and how data varied over time, though the paper did not report a separate durable-skills measure.
finding.measure: SOLO-coded complexity of open-ended responses on the end-of-year questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not provide evidence that the intervention improved teacher workload or classroom efficiency; instead, it describes a complex, highly structured activity requiring explicit instructions, workbook prompts, and later coding of open-ended responses. No quantitative measure of workload, time cost, or efficiency was reported, so there is no direct evidence of operational benefit or burden beyond narrative description.
finding.measure: Narrative description of implementation and coding process; no direct workload measure

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper discusses formative assessment and argues for its use to improve learning, especially through an e-learning platform (BlackBoard). The authors frame the problem as how assessment can be used diagnostically, with frequent low-stakes tests and immediate feedback helping students identify errors, stay engaged with the subject, and improve performance on later summative exams.

The implementation described is a proposed set of weekly or fortnightly online tests in BlackBoard, including multiple-choice, true/false, matching, ordering, fill-in-the-blank, and essay items, with detailed immediate feedback after submission. The study context is a Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) course environment, and the paper reports a student survey on perceptions of continuous assessment and the BlackBoard test option rather than an experimental comparison of learning outcomes.

Students generally supported frequent online formative assessments because they break content into manageable chunks, provide convenience and immediate feedback, and help them monitor whether they are on track. However, some students reported concerns that too many tests could create stress/pressure and that learning might be overemphasized relative to grades. Overall, the paper is mainly a descriptive/survey-based discussion of perceived benefits and drawbacks, with no direct causal evidence of achievement gains, retention, transfer, or longer-term attainment.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent online formative assessments were helpful for keeping them on track, checking strengths and weaknesses, and learning topics progressively, suggesting positive effects on motivation and self-monitoring. At the same time, some students said that too many tests would create stress/pressure to perform, indicating a negative affective tradeoff. No objective outcome measure or effect size was reported; findings come from survey responses and open-ended comments.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of motivation, stress/pressure, and self-monitoring under frequent online formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition by giving students feedback on errors and helping them understand how to improve, and students reported that the approach helped them check whether they were on track and learn progressively. This is based on perceptions and theoretical rationale rather than a direct skill assessment. No effect size, sample size, or statistical outcome for metacognition/critical thinking was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived metacognitive monitoring and reflective learning from feedback

finding.finding_summary: The BlackBoard implementation was described as a more convenient way to deliver frequent assessments because it offered immediate automated feedback and flexibility compared with classroom tests. Students favored the BB test option largely for convenience and immediate feedback, but the paper did not measure teacher workload, time savings, or administrative efficiency directly. No effect size or quantitative workload outcome was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived convenience/flexibility of online assessment delivery and feedback

paper_profiles.title: Providing Authentic Long-term Archival Access to Complex Relational Data
paper_profiles.venue: European Space Agency Symposium “Ensuring Long-Term Preservation and Adding Value to Scientific and Technical Data”
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how archives can preserve and later provide authentic access to complex relational databases over long time periods. The authors argue that conventional backup- or export-based approaches are insufficient because database content is tightly coupled to proprietary RDBMS software, non-standard SQL dialects, implementation-specific character encodings, and undocumented metadata that are often essential for understanding the data years later.

To address this, the paper presents SIARD (Software-Invariant Archiving of Relational Databases), a workflow and Java application suite for extracting databases from operational RDBMSs, normalizing data and database logic into standard SQL:1999, and packaging table data, large objects, and XML reference metadata into a long-term archival information package. The workflow includes three stages: automated analysis and extraction (A0), metadata completion and description (A1), and reload/access (A2). The system is designed for use by archives, database administrators, records managers, and other non-technical staff working with government and scientific databases.

The paper is primarily a technical proposal and system description, supported by tests on databases ranging from tens of tables to 250 tables and 250,000 rows across commercial and open-source RDBMS products. The authors conclude that SIARD can preserve relational databases with reasonable authenticity while maintaining future usability, but note continuing challenges from proprietary SQL extensions, character set issues, and metadata extraction. The paper does not study K-12 education or formative assessment outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that SIARD reduces the manual labor involved in long-term database archiving by automating analysis, extraction, normalization to standard SQL, and packaging of data and metadata. The system is intended to replace highly manual archival workflows for complex relational databases, and the authors report successful tests on databases up to 250 tables and 250,000 rows, though no controlled performance metrics or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: archival workflow automation / database extraction and preservation process

finding.finding_summary: The central claim is that SIARD enables national archives and science data archives to preserve relational databases independently of proprietary software and hardware, thereby improving long-term institutional preservation capacity and access. The paper reports successful application across multiple commercial and open-source RDBMS products, but provides no quantitative institutional outcome measures or effect sizes.
finding.measure: long-term archival preservation capability and access to relational databases

paper_profiles.title: GPT Chatbots for Alleviating Anxiety and Depression: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial with Afghan Women
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study tests whether a GPT-4-based chatbot can reduce anxiety and depression among Afghan women facing severe social constraints, including Taliban restrictions, domestic violence, stigma around help-seeking, and limited access to mental health care. The authors compare two chatbot conditions: a standard GPT-4 chatbot and a customized "supportive listener" version that was explicitly instructed to use empathetic, nonjudgmental, culturally sensitive language and avoid invasive or traumatic prompts, plus a waiting-list control.

Sixty Afghan women were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions and completed the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) before the intervention and one week later. The supportive listener condition showed significant reductions in overall HADS scores (mean pre-post difference = 2.60, 95% CI [0.14, 5.06], Cohen’s d = 0.47), while the standard GPT-4 condition showed a significant increase in HADS (mean difference = -3.15, 95% CI [-5.61, -0.69], d = -0.57); the waiting-list group did not change significantly. Linguistic analyses suggested the supportive listener produced more positive tone, more positive emotion, and higher language style matching, and higher LSM correlated with greater reductions in HADS (r = -0.35). The paper concludes that carefully designed AI chatbots may provide accessible mental health support, but it also emphasizes the short duration, small sample, and the need for longer follow-up and human clinical oversight.

finding.finding_summary: The supportive listener chatbot significantly reduced anxiety/depression symptoms relative to baseline and to the other groups, as measured by HADS. In the supportive listener group (n=20), overall HADS decreased by 2.60 points from pre- to post-intervention (95% CI [0.14, 5.06], Cohen’s d=0.47), while the standard GPT-4 group increased by 3.15 points (95% CI [-5.61, -0.69], d=-0.57) and the waiting-list group showed no significant change.
finding.measure: Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS; overall score, plus HADS-A and HADS-D subscales)

finding.finding_summary: The study found that language style matching (LSM), a measure of conversational alignment, was higher in the supportive listener condition and was negatively correlated with changes in HADS, suggesting that greater linguistic alignment was associated with better short-term mental health outcomes. Supportive listener dyads had higher LSM than GPT-4 dyads (0.75 vs 0.69; t(38)=-2.258, p=0.030, Cohen’s d=-0.714), and LSM correlated with reductions in HADS (r=-0.35, p=0.026).
finding.measure: Language Style Matching (LSM) in chatbot-user dialogue; correlation with HADS change
finding.study_size: n=40 chatbot participants for LSM comparison; n=60 for HADS change correlation
finding.effect_size: d=-0.714 for LSM group difference; r=-0.35 for LSM-HADS change correlation

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed as a one-hour chatbot session with real-time monitoring and a minimum chat duration of 50 minutes, but the paper does not report formal measures of teacher workload, class time, or implementation burden. The only operationally relevant evidence is indirect: the authors note that the system had limitations for simultaneous access and required batching participants into groups of 10, indicating some infrastructure constraints rather than educational productivity gains.
finding.measure: Implementation logistics / simultaneous access constraints; no direct workload metric reported

paper_profiles.title: Correct power for cluster-randomized difference-in-difference trials with loss to follow-up
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical design problem for cluster-randomized trials with baseline and follow-up measurements: how to correctly calculate the variance, power, and sample size for difference-in-differences (DID) analyses when there is loss to follow-up (LTF), with or without replacement of lost participants. The authors derive general and special-case formulas for mixture designs in which some individuals are observed at both time points, some are observed only at baseline, and replacements are observed only at follow-up.

The paper is methodological rather than an evaluation of an educational intervention. It uses a dating-violence prevention trial as a worked example to illustrate the sample-size implications of different follow-up and replacement scenarios, but it does not report a new K-12 outcome study. The main conclusion is that LTF with replacement often has only mild variance inflation relative to a no-LTF cohort design, while LTF with no replacement can be more or less efficient than a reduced cohort design depending largely on subject autocorrelation and follow-up rates.

For K-12 researchers, the relevance is indirect: the paper offers guidance for planning cluster-randomized pre/post studies and choosing between cohort, reduced cohort, and replacement-based mixture designs when attrition is expected. It also highlights that missing-data handling and follow-up design choices can materially affect required sample sizes and statistical efficiency, but it does not examine student learning, retention, anxiety, workload, or other education outcomes empirically.

paper_profiles.title: A complex meta-regression model to identify effective features of interventions from multi-arm, multi-follow-up trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper develops a new Bayesian meta-regression framework for synthesizing evidence from complex interventions when trials are multi-arm, include multiple follow-up times, and cannot easily be decomposed into standard intervention components. The authors are motivated by a large systematic review of nearly 250 randomized controlled trials of childhood obesity prevention interventions, and they use that evidence base to illustrate the model.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is not an educational intervention study and does not report academic outcomes. It focuses on obesity prevention trials in children and uses change in standardized BMI (zBMI) as the outcome for method demonstration, so no direct evidence is provided for academic outcomes.
finding.measure: zBMI (standardized body mass index)

finding.finding_summary: No direct social-emotional outcomes such as motivation or anxiety are measured. The paper does report that follow-up time patterns and intervention intensity were examined, but these are modeled as obesity outcomes rather than student psychosocial outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses a methodological model and does not empirically evaluate implementation burden, teacher workload, or class-time costs. No outcome data on operational efficiency are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article has no policy, governance, or institutional implementation outcomes. Its contribution is methodological, proposing a meta-regression approach for complex intervention synthesis and demonstrating it on obesity prevention data.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Long-Term Feature Banks for Detailed Video Understanding
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a computer vision problem: how to improve video understanding by giving models access to longer-range context than the usual 2–5 second clip. The authors argue that many actions in videos are ambiguous without temporal memory, so they propose a long-term feature bank (LFB) that stores time-indexed features over an entire video and lets a short-term 3D CNN attend to or pool from this longer context.

The method is evaluated on three standard video benchmarks: AVA spatio-temporal action localization, EPIC-Kitchens verb/noun/action recognition, and Charades video-level action recognition. In each setting, the long-term feature bank is plugged into a 3D CNN backbone and compared against short-term baselines and alternative long-context designs. Across datasets, the LFB improves performance, with gains especially strong for tasks requiring longer context or object-level reasoning.

The paper is not an educational study and does not investigate K-12 formative assessment, student learning, retention, transfer, teacher workload, or similar education outcomes. It instead reports benchmark accuracy improvements in video recognition, showing that long-term context can materially boost model performance on complex temporal tasks.

paper_profiles.title: A Chain-of-Thought Prompting Approach with LLMs for Evaluating Students’ Formative Assessment Responses in Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of efficiently scoring and explaining open-ended formative assessment responses in K-12 science, where teacher grading is time-consuming and can be inconsistent. The authors explore whether GPT-4 can be prompted to score short-answer responses and generate rubric-aligned explanations for middle school Earth science formative assessments.

The approach combines few-shot in-context learning, chain-of-thought prompting, and a small active-learning loop. Using assessment data from two Vanderbilt-approved SPICE studies at a Southeastern U.S. public middle school (270 students), the authors compare zero-shot, few-shot, few-shot with CoT, and CoT plus active learning against human consensus scores. The model often achieved strong agreement with human raters, and in some cases almost perfect agreement, especially for simpler concept items.

The paper’s main conclusion is that LLMs, when paired with human-in-the-loop prompt design, can support automated scoring and generate useful explanations for formative assessment in middle school science. However, the authors also show important limitations: chain-of-thought prompting and active learning can overfit, especially on ambiguous items, and the method sometimes worsened performance on particular reasoning subscores. The paper does not evaluate student learning outcomes, retention, delayed transfer, or classroom workload empirically; those benefits and costs are discussed only as potential future implications.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that GPT-4 with few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, and active learning can score middle school formative assessment responses with strong agreement to human raters, suggesting potential efficiency gains in grading and feedback generation. However, the study does not quantify teacher time savings or workload reduction directly; the evidence is limited to automated scoring performance (e.g., QWK up to 1.00 on some subscores) rather than measured operational outcomes.
finding.measure: Automated short-answer scoring agreement with human consensus; accuracy, Macro F1, and Cohen’s quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)

paper_profiles.title: Long-term Compliance Habits: What Early Data Tells Us
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2018 ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether early compliance with wearable-device use can predict longer-term adherence in an ongoing college cohort study. The motivating problem is attrition in longitudinal health-monitoring research: when participants stop wearing devices like Fitbits, researchers lose data and may struggle to sustain valid long-term studies.

The authors analyze data from 392 first-year university students in the NetHealth study at the University of Notre Dame, who were asked to wear a Fitbit Charge HR as much as possible over roughly two and a half years. They define “early compliance” using the first month of device-wearing data and compare it to later dropout and long-term compliance, including a 1-nearest-neighbor classification analysis and quartile-based group comparisons.

Results show that low first-month compliance is strongly associated with later dropout (Fisher’s Exact, p < .001) and that students with high first-month compliance maintain significantly higher compliance over the next 27 months (t-tests, p < .001). The paper concludes that compliance habits can be detected very early and may help researchers identify participants at risk of attrition or poor long-term adherence, supporting targeted monitoring or interventions to reduce data loss. The paper is about participant compliance in a longitudinal wearable study rather than K-12 learning or formative assessment.

finding.finding_summary: Early compliance data predicted long-term retention and adherence in the study, which could improve research efficiency by helping investigators identify likely dropouts and participants needing closer monitoring. Among 392 students, low first-month compliance was associated with dropout (Fisher’s Exact, p < .001), and among the 226 who remained, high first-month compliers maintained higher monthly compliance over 27 months (t-tests, p < .001).
finding.measure: Wearable-device compliance over time and study dropout

paper_profiles.title: Cost-Aware Logging: Measuring the Financial Impact of Excessive Log Retention in Small-Scale Cloud Deployments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether default, long log-retention settings in small cloud deployments create unnecessary financial and operational costs. The author asks how much value is lost, and how much cost can be saved, by shortening log-retention windows in early-stage or resource-constrained engineering environments.

The study uses a simulation-based approach with synthetic log data representing 90 days of cloud logging activity. Four retention policies are compared: 7, 14, 30, and 90 days. The analysis evaluates storage cost, the ratio of operationally useful logs, and cost per useful log, with usefulness defined by whether logs needed for simulated debugging and incident-analysis queries remain available.

Results indicate that reducing retention substantially lowers storage costs while preserving most operational value. In particular, moving from 90 days to 14 days reduces storage cost by about 84% while maintaining about 97% of useful queries, and even 7-day retention preserves 95% of query satisfaction. The paper concludes that shorter retention windows can be a low-risk cost-optimization strategy for small engineering teams, though it does not study K-12 education outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Shorter log-retention windows substantially improved cost efficiency in the simulation. Reducing retention from 90 days to 14 days lowered storage costs by about 84% while preserving approximately 97% of operationally useful logs (based on 10,000 synthetic queries), and the normalized cost per useful log fell to 0.17 from 1.00 at the 90-day baseline.
finding.measure: Storage cost, useful log ratio (query satisfaction), and cost per useful log under simulated debugging/incident-analysis queries
finding.study_size: n=10000 synthetic queries; synthetic log stream over 90 days (approximately 10-20 million log entries)

paper_profiles.title: Sustainability of Developed Self-Regulation by Means of Formative Assessment Among Young Adolescents: A Longitudinal Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This longitudinal study asked whether gains from a formative assessment intervention in upper primary school would persist after students transitioned to secondary education. The authors were especially interested in whether self-regulation skills, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy developed through formative assessment would remain stable over an 8-week summer break and into the start of secondary school.

The intervention was implemented with 695 Dutch sixth graders from 17 primary schools. Schools were randomly assigned to a self-assessment condition, a peer-assessment condition, or a control condition. In the intervention conditions, students completed writing assignments supported by criteria clarification, checklists/rubrics, evaluation, revision opportunities, and teacher feedback; the control group completed ordinary writing instruction without the formative assessment training.

Using a pretest-posttest-follow-up design with multilevel analyses, the study found that self-regulation improvements from the formative assessment intervention were maintained at follow-up, with no decline after the transition to secondary education. Intrinsic motivation also remained higher in the intervention groups, while extrinsic motivation increased across all groups after the transition. Self-efficacy did not show a clear sustained intervention effect at follow-up. The paper concludes that formative assessment can help develop self-regulation in primary school and that these gains may carry over into the first months of secondary education.

finding.finding_summary: The formative assessment intervention improved students’ self-regulation and these gains were sustained after the transition to secondary education. In a longitudinal sample of 695 Dutch sixth graders, multilevel analyses showed significant intervention effects on self-regulation at posttest and no decline at the 10-week follow-up after summer break.
finding.measure: Self-regulation scale from the Inventory Learning Style Questionnaire (ILS)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was associated with higher intrinsic motivation, and this pattern persisted through follow-up rather than declining after the transition to secondary education. The reported analyses found significant condition-by-time effects for intrinsic motivation, with the intervention groups outperforming the control group at posttest and no significant drop by follow-up.
finding.measure: Intrinsic motivation scale from the Inventory Learning Style Questionnaire (ILS)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention did not produce a differential effect on external regulation. Multilevel analyses found no significant condition effects or condition-by-time interactions, suggesting that students’ dependence on external regulation did not change as a result of the formative assessment approach.
finding.measure: External regulation scale from the Inventory Learning Style Questionnaire (ILS)

finding.finding_summary: Extrinsic motivation increased from posttest to follow-up across all conditions, but this change was not attributable to the formative assessment intervention. The study reported significant time effects but no condition or interaction effects, indicating a transition-related increase rather than an intervention effect.
finding.measure: Extrinsic motivation scale from the Inventory Learning Style Questionnaire (ILS)

finding.finding_summary: The formative assessment intervention did not show a sustained differential effect on self-efficacy after transition to secondary education. Although some condition-specific main effects were reported at individual time points, there were no significant condition-by-time interactions, and the follow-up results did not indicate a stable intervention advantage.
finding.measure: Self-Efficacy for Task Performance Questionnaire (STPQ)

paper_profiles.title: The effect of a formative assessment practice on student achievement in mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a formative assessment professional development programme changed year-7 mathematics teachers’ classroom practices in ways that improved student achievement. The authors focus on a specific conception of formative assessment: the “big idea” of using evidence of student learning to adjust instruction, together with the five strategies of Wiliam and Thompson (2008), including clarifying goals, eliciting evidence, giving feedback, using peers, and promoting self-regulation.

The intervention was a year-long professional development programme for a stratified random sample of 14 secondary school mathematics teachers in one Swedish municipality. After the programme, the intervention teachers implemented new formative assessment activities such as exit passes, mini-whiteboards, clearer learning goals, improved feedback, and some self-assessment and peer-support activities. These teachers taught 291 students; 15 comparison teachers taught 275 students. Student achievement was measured with municipality-developed pre- and post-tests in mathematics, and the authors compared post-test scores between groups controlling for pre-test performance.

The main finding was null: there were no significant differences in adjusted post-test mathematics achievement between students taught by teachers in the intervention group and those in the control group. The authors also found no significant correlation between the number of new formative assessment activities a teacher implemented and students’ post-test scores after controlling for pre-test scores. The paper concludes that simply increasing the quantity of formative assessment activities was not enough to improve achievement, and suggests that the quality and implementation of the practice may be critical.

finding.finding_summary: Students taught by teachers who participated in the formative assessment PDP did not significantly outperform control students on the mathematics post-test after controlling for pre-test scores. The study reports no significant post-test difference between groups in a sample of 291 intervention students and 275 control students, and no significant correlation between the number of formative assessment activities implemented and post-test achievement.
finding.measure: Mathematics pre-test and post-test scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses student engagement, thinking, and self-regulated learning as part of the formative assessment practices, but these were not directly measured with a separate validated instrument. Because the study's only empirical outcomes are achievement test scores, there is no direct empirical evidence of an effect on social-emotional skills in the results.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The effect of formative assessment on high school students' mathematics achievement and attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study asks whether formative assessment practices improve 10th-grade students’ mathematics achievement and attitudes toward mathematics, and how students perceive those practices. The authors situate the study in the context of low mathematics achievement in Turkey and the need for instructional approaches that make learning goals, feedback, and student participation more explicit during instruction.

The quantitative part used a 12-week quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design in a Turkish high school. Fifty-one 10th graders were assigned to an experimental group (n=26) receiving mathematics instruction based on formative assessment strategies and a control group (n=25) taught with the regular curriculum. The intervention incorporated Wiliam and Thompson’s five strategies, including clarifying learning intentions, eliciting evidence of understanding, providing feedback, activating self/peer assessment, and reflective prompts.

Results showed statistically significant advantages for the formative-assessment group on both mathematics achievement and attitudes toward mathematics. Achievement increased more in the experimental group than in the control group, with a moderate group effect (η2=.092) and a significant group-by-time interaction (η2=.113); attitude scores also favored the experimental group, with a moderate group effect (η2=.099) and a strong interaction effect (η2=.286). Qualitative interviews supported these results: most students reported that the practices made learning clearer, increased participation, helped them notice gaps in understanding, and made mathematics lessons more engaging and comfortable.

finding.finding_summary: Formative assessment practices significantly improved 10th-grade students’ mathematics achievement on the Functions Achievement Test. The experimental group (n=26) outperformed the control group (n=25) on the post/retention trajectory, with a significant group effect (F=4.962, p=.031, η2=.092) and a significant group × measurement interaction (F=6.260, p=.003, η2=.113).
finding.measure: Functions Achievement Test (FAT) pre-test, post-test, and retention test
finding.std_deviation: pre-test SDs: 6.52 (experimental), 5.61 (control); post-test SDs: 19.10 (experimental), 18.54 (control); retention SDs: 21.34 (experimental), 18.32 (control)

finding.finding_summary: Formative assessment practices also improved students’ attitudes toward mathematics. The experimental group (n=26) scored higher than the control group (n=25) on the mathematics attitude scale, with a significant group effect (F=5.379, p=.025, η2=.099) and a strong group × measurement interaction (F=19.671, p=.000, η2=.286).
finding.measure: Mathematics Attitudes Scale (MAS) pre-test and post-test

finding.finding_summary: Students’ interview responses indicated that formative assessment helped them identify what they understood and did not understand, supported self-assessment, and encouraged reflection on learning. Most students described the reflective prompts as beneficial (90.48%, 19/21? as reported in the table; the table shows 19 positive and 2 negative responses in the interview sample of 15 students, so counts are reported as given in the paper).
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on reflective prompts, self-assessment, and peer interaction

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Formative Assessment Practices on Student Motivation for Learning the English Language
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Education and Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether formative assessment practices are associated with students’ motivation for learning English in Albanian secondary schools. The authors focus on four classroom assessment practices: student portfolios, self-assessment, peer assessment, and teachers’ strategic questioning.

The study used a questionnaire with students from three high schools in Durres, Albania. Although the paper frames the practices as important for learning, its design is non-experimental and correlational, so it estimates associations rather than causal effects. The sample used for analysis was 278 students (from an initial 300), and the authors used factor analysis and multiple linear regression to examine relationships between assessment practices and motivation.

Results indicated that all four formative assessment practices were positively associated with motivation for learning English. Teachers’ strategic questions showed the largest regression coefficient, followed by self-assessment, peer assessment, and student portfolios. The model explained 25.8% of the variance in motivation. The study concludes that formative assessment practices may support student autonomy, confidence, critical thinking, and engagement in English learning, but the evidence is based on student perceptions and correlational analysis rather than an intervention trial.

finding.finding_summary: Formative assessment practices were positively associated with student motivation for learning English. In a multiple regression model, the combined set of practices explained 25.8% of the variance in motivation (R2=0.262; adjusted R2=0.258), with all coefficients positive and statistically significant (p<=0.001).
finding.measure: Student motivation for learning English, measured by questionnaire-based subscales including goal orientation, interest, sense of self as a learner, effort, self-esteem, self-regulation, self-efficacy, and locus of control

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that formative assessment practices were linked to durable-learning competencies such as critical thinking, reflection, autonomy, and self-analysis. Students’ portfolio, self-assessment, peer assessment, and strategic questioning were each described as helping learners understand strengths and weaknesses and improve their work.
finding.measure: Questionnaire items on self-assessment, peer assessment, portfolio use, and teacher strategic questioning; perceived autonomy, reflection, and self-analysis

paper_profiles.title: ISCED 2011
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document presents the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED) 2011, a global statistical framework for classifying education programmes and educational attainment across countries. Its purpose is to improve comparability of education statistics by providing shared definitions, coding schemes, and rules for mapping national systems onto international categories.

The document is not an intervention study; it is a standards and classification reference produced by UNESCO Institute for Statistics. It explains how education programmes should be categorized by level, orientation, completion status, and access to higher levels, and it describes the scope of formal, non-formal, and informal learning in statistical reporting. It also details how ISCED should be used for enrolment, graduates, attainment, and cross-national data collection.

The intended users are education statisticians, ministries, researchers, and policymakers who need comparable administrative and survey data. The main conclusion is that ISCED 2011 offers an updated, internationally agreed framework for organizing education data, but it does not evaluate any educational intervention, learning outcome, or school practice.

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, with an emphasis on how scaffolding is conceptualized, how it appears in classroom practice, and whether it is effective. The authors argue that the literature lacks consensus on definition, and they synthesize scaffolding around three key characteristics: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility.

The paper reviews 66 articles published from 1998 to 2009 across primary and secondary education, including theoretical, descriptive, effectiveness, and one meta-analytic study. Most empirical work was descriptive and concentrated in literacy, with smaller amounts in math and science; the effectiveness studies were mostly small-scale tutoring or classroom interventions. The authors conclude that scaffolding appears effective for students’ metacognitive and cognitive activities, and that evidence for affective outcomes is mixed, but they stress that the field is limited by major measurement problems.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the article organizes the field with a framework that distinguishes scaffolding means (e.g., modeling, questioning, feedback) from intentions (e.g., cognitive structuring, direction maintenance, recruitment). It highlights that many studies label generic teacher support as scaffolding without adequately measuring contingency, fading, or transfer of responsibility. The main contribution is a conceptual and methodological synthesis intended to support future research, including more rigorous measurement and stronger experimental designs.

finding.finding_summary: Across the review’s included math-related effectiveness studies, scaffolding was generally associated with better performance, but effects varied by design and outcome. In Murphy and Messer (2000; n=122), children aged 5-7 in one-to-one scaffolding advanced more in representation level than children working alone or in small groups, with the significant difference specifically between the scaffolding and small-group conditions. In Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998; n=40), students receiving fully contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than all other support conditions on immediate and follow-up tests, but in the correlational study by Turner et al. (1998) the evidence was about motivation rather than achievement.
finding.measure: Balance scale test; long-division problem solving; math lesson performance/contextual learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive effects of scaffolding in science learning and reasoning across several studies. In Mercer et al. (2004; n=230), students in the Thinking Together science program were better able to use talk for reasoning and made greater gains on Raven Progressive Matrices than controls. In Azevedo et al. (2005; n=109/34/37 across conditions), adaptive human scaffolding in a hypermedia circulatory-system environment was associated with more self-regulated learning behaviors, greater shifts in mental models, and higher knowledge gains than no-scaffolding controls; Chiu et al. (2002; n=30) also found better construction of mental models of chemical equilibrium under cognitive apprenticeship/scaffolding support.
finding.measure: Talk-for-reasoning coding; Raven Progressive Matrices; self-regulated learning coded from think-alouds; knowledge tests on human circulatory system; mental models of chemical equilibrium

finding.finding_summary: The review includes one correlational study and one quasi-experimental study on affective outcomes, both suggesting at least some positive association between scaffolding and student engagement/enjoyment. Turner et al. (1998; n=42 students, 34 math lessons) found that whole-class scaffolding strategies intended to promote motivation and emotion were more prevalent in high-involvement classes than in low-involvement classes. In Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998; n=40), students in the no-support condition reported significantly lower enjoyment than students in the contingent, moderate, high, and partly contingent support conditions, although differences among the experimental support conditions were not significant.
finding.measure: Student involvement self-report scale; enjoyment questionnaire (6 items, 5-point scale)

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the review centers on durable skills such as metacognition, collaborative reasoning, and transfer of responsibility. Mercer et al. (2004; n=230) found that scaffolding through exploratory talk improved students’ reasoning together in small groups, and Chi et al. (2001; n=11 tutors, eighth grade students) found that more interactive, contingent tutoring led students to be more constructive, take greater responsibility for learning, and perform significantly better on transfer questions. The authors conclude that the available effectiveness evidence largely points in the same direction: scaffolding supports metacognitive and collaborative learning processes.
finding.measure: Coding of group-work transcripts; transfer questions; interactive vs. non-interactive tutoring codes; student responsibility/constructiveness

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Teachers Practices of Classroom Assessment in Secondary Science Classes in Bangladesh
paper_profiles.population: Secondary (secondary school science teachers and classrooms)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how secondary science teachers in Dhaka, Bangladesh assess students’ learning in classroom settings and how they provide feedback during those assessments. The paper is motivated by concerns that classroom assessment in Bangladeshi secondary schools remains dominated by traditional, summative practices rather than formative assessment approaches that support learning.

The study used a descriptive mixed-methods approach with random sampling of 30 science teachers from six secondary schools. Data came from classroom observations using a Likert-scale protocol, field notes, and pre- and post-observation interviews. The focus was not on implementing an intervention but on documenting current practices such as questioning, use of self/peer assessment, feedback types, and attention to higher-order learning.

Findings show that teachers relied heavily on oral, closed questioning, mostly assessed lower-order recall, rarely used self- or peer-assessment, and provided mainly evaluative rather than descriptive feedback. Students were given limited opportunity to ask questions, share ideas, or engage in higher-order thinking. The paper concludes that classroom assessment practices in these secondary science classrooms are weakly formative and need professional development, richer assessment strategies, and more emphasis on assessment for learning.

finding.finding_summary: Secondary science teachers in 6 Dhaka schools relied mainly on oral questioning and textbook-based, closed questions rather than tasks that probe scientific understanding or inquiry. Teachers rarely assessed higher-order learning or misconceptions, suggesting weak support for scientific reasoning; no effect size was reported because this was an observational study of practice (n=30 teachers/classrooms).
finding.measure: Classroom observation ratings of assessment practices related to science learning, including higher-order learning, problem solving/investigation work, and exploration of misconceptions

finding.finding_summary: The observed classrooms provided limited opportunities for student participation, questioning, idea sharing, and time to think before answering, which likely constrained engagement and active participation. Teachers seldom encouraged students to ask questions or share ideas, and students were mostly passive responders during oral questioning (n=30 classrooms).
finding.measure: Observation ratings of student participation, opportunity to ask questions, and time allowed for responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper found minimal use of practices that support collaboration, metacognition, and self-regulation, such as self-assessment, peer assessment, group work, and descriptive feedback. These formative practices were largely absent in the 30 observed secondary science classrooms, indicating limited support for durable skills development.
finding.measure: Observation checklist items on self-assessment, peer assessment, group work, and feedback practices

finding.finding_summary: The study concludes that classroom assessment culture in Bangladeshi secondary science education is dominated by summative, traditional practices and is not aligned with the government’s push toward formative assessment. The findings suggest a systemic need for teacher training and policy-supported change in assessment practice, but no causal effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Descriptive assessment-practice patterns across secondary schools and teacher interviews

paper_profiles.title: Scaling Up Intervention Studies to Investigate Real-Life Foreign Language Learning in School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of scaling instructional research in second-language learning from controlled laboratory settings to authentic K-12 classrooms. The authors argue that large, ecologically valid field trials are needed to understand whether effects observed in more controlled studies generalize to real school contexts, especially for foreign language learning in secondary schools.

To do this, they developed FeedBook, a web-based workbook / intelligent tutoring system integrated into regular seventh-grade English classes in German Gymnasien. The system provides immediate scaffolded feedback on form, meaning, and orthography for workbook exercises, and the paper reports the first results from an ongoing year-long within-class randomized controlled trial. Students were randomly assigned within classes to receive specific scaffolded grammar feedback or a control version with that specific feedback disabled, while still receiving other forms of feedback and the same general homework platform.

The empirical study focused on Theme 2 of the curriculum, targeting conditionals, comparatives, and relative clauses. Across 205 analyzed students in 10 classes, the intervention group improved more than the control group on a 40-item pre/post grammar test. The authors conclude that immediate scaffolded feedback can improve L2 grammar learning in a real classroom setting, and that the platform is promising for future large-scale research on feedback, individual differences, and other ISLA questions in school contexts.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-class RCT on seventh-grade English homework, students receiving specific scaffolded grammar feedback improved more than controls on a grammar pre/posttest covering Theme 2 constructions (conditionals, comparatives, relative clauses). On the change score, the intervention group gained M=7.82 (SD=5.4) versus M=4.81 (SD=5.24) for controls, t(203)=4.04, p<0.0001, with Cohen’s d=0.56 (medium).
finding.measure: 40-item grammar test (pretest/posttest change score; true/false and fill-in-the-blank items on conditionals, comparatives, and relative clauses)
finding.std_deviation: SD=5.4 (intervention change score); SD=5.24 (control change score)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students’ questionnaire data included expectancy/self-concept, intrinsic value, attainment value, utility value, effort, and emotional cost, but these were collected as background or future individual-difference variables rather than as primary outcomes of the RCT. As a result, the study does not provide an empirical causal finding on social-emotional outcomes from the intervention itself.
finding.measure: Questionnaire scales on expectancy (academic self-concept), intrinsic value, attainment value, utility value, effort, and emotional cost

paper_profiles.title: Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews gradient-based machine learning methods for document and handwriting recognition, with a focus on how backpropagation, convolutional neural networks, and globally trainable graph transformer networks can improve recognition accuracy. The central question is how to build recognition systems that learn directly from data, rather than relying on hand-engineered features and manually tuned modules.

The paper presents LeNet-5, a convolutional neural network for isolated handwritten character and digit recognition, and then extends the discussion to multi-module document recognition systems that can be trained end-to-end. Experiments are reported on the modified NIST handwritten digit dataset (MNIST), which was built from NIST digit images including samples written by high-school students. On MNIST, LeNet-5 achieved 0.95% test error without artificial distortions and 0.8% with distorted-data augmentation, outperforming several baseline classifiers such as linear models and nearest-neighbor methods.

The paper is not an education intervention study and does not examine formative assessment, teaching practices, or student learning outcomes in schools. Its empirical contribution is in machine learning for OCR and handwriting recognition, not K-12 educational outcomes. The strongest evidence presented concerns pattern recognition accuracy on benchmark image classification tasks.

finding.finding_summary: On the modified NIST handwritten digit benchmark, LeNet-5 achieved a 0.95% test error rate after training on 60,000 examples, and 0.8% test error when trained with 540,000 additional distorted training patterns. The paper reports that this convolutional network outperformed the linear classifier (12% error on regular data; 8.4% on deslanted images) and nearest-neighbor baselines on digit recognition.
finding.measure: Handwritten digit recognition test error on MNIST / modified NIST dataset

paper_profiles.title: High School Summer Camps Help Democratize Coding, Data Science, and Deep Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper documents a series of summer camps for high school students designed to introduce coding, data science, and deep learning through an on-campus, immersive university experience. The camps were organized in three progressive levels: introductory coding in Snap!, data science in Python, and deep learning in Keras. The authors describe the program structure, mentorship model, and lessons learned from running the camps in 2024.

The study uses interviews with a small number of randomly selected Level 3 participants and pre-/post-camp survey data to understand student experiences and perceived outcomes. The paper emphasizes personalized feedback, structured collaboration, diverse mentorship, and the value of in-person exposure to a university environment. It reports that many students increased their confidence in coding and that 68.6% expressed interest in AI and data science careers by the end of Level 3.

Overall, the paper concludes that summer camps can help broaden participation in computing and data science, especially for underrepresented minority students. However, the evidence presented is descriptive and based on self-reports rather than a controlled comparison, so the paper functions more as a program description and exploratory mixed-methods report than a causal evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported increased confidence in coding after the camp, and interview excerpts described the experience as transformative for students with limited prior coding background. The paper does not report a standardized pre/post scale or an effect size; the evidence is based on self-reported survey and interview data from Level 3 campers.
finding.measure: Self-reported coding confidence; interview themes about confidence and enjoyment of coding

finding.finding_summary: The camps emphasized collaboration, and students described coding as a collaborative activity that helped them solve difficult problems. The paper presents qualitative evidence that structured group work and peer support improved collaboration and problem-solving, but no quantitative effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Interview themes about collaboration and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: The program is presented as a mechanism for widening access to computing and data science for high school students, especially underrepresented minorities, by providing an on-campus university experience and mentorship. The evidence is descriptive rather than causal, and no institutional effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Participation and self-reported interest in AI/data science careers; program access for underrepresented students

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback generation for open-ended middle-school mathematics responses. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned open-source LLM (GOAT, based on Mistral 7B with LoRA), an established similarity-based method (SBERT-Canberra), and GPT-4 used zero-shot with a rubric prompt. The task is not to test a classroom intervention on student learning, but to benchmark model outputs against teacher scores and teacher judgments of feedback quality.

The study uses historical data from an online learning platform containing 50 open-response math problems, each with 100 student answers, teacher scores, and teacher-written feedback. Models are trained on 4,000 responses and tested on 1,000 responses; two teachers also manually rate feedback quality on 100 sampled test entries. For scoring, GOAT performs best (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422), outperforming SBERT and GPT-4. For feedback quality, GPT-4 is preferred by human evaluators and scores highest on accuracy (86% consensus), relevance (91% consensus), and preference (77.5% selected), while GOAT is generally intermediate and SBERT lowest. The paper concludes that fine-tuned LLMs can improve automated scoring, but GPT-4 still produces the most preferred feedback in this dataset.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates automated scoring of middle-school open-ended math responses, not student learning outcomes. GOAT achieved the best scoring performance against teacher labels (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422; n=1,000 test responses), outperforming SBERT-Canberra (AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, Kappa=0.362) and GPT-4 (AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.160, Kappa=0.266). This indicates the fine-tuned model was the closest to teacher scoring on the tested math responses.
finding.measure: Automated prediction of teacher-assigned scores for open-ended middle-school math responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies whether automated systems can reduce teacher grading and feedback workload for open-ended math responses. Human raters judged feedback quality for 100 sampled responses, and the authors argue that LLM-based scoring/feedback can serve as a helpful starting point for teachers. However, GPT-4 was preferred most often (77.5%), suggesting the strongest potential for usable teacher support, while GOAT improved over SBERT but still lagged GPT-4 on feedback quality.
finding.measure: Teacher judgments of feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, and preference; automated scoring performance as a support tool
finding.study_size: n=100 feedback-rated responses; n=1000 scored test responses

paper_profiles.title: From Computing to Quantum Mechanics: Accessible and Hands-On Quantum Computing Education for High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a high school quantum computing course designed for students with limited prior background in advanced mathematics and physics. The authors argue that traditional introductions to quantum mechanics can be too abstract for secondary students, so they reverse the usual sequence: the course begins with classical computing concepts and gradually builds toward quantum computing and then quantum mechanics.

The intervention is an eight-week curriculum organized into four two-week modules: introductory computing, matrices for quantum computing, the quantum circuit model, and how to build a quantum computer. The course includes hands-on activities using portable NMR quantum computers from the Gemini/Triangulum series, as well as lecture notes, exercises, and experiments on quantum gates and algorithms such as Deutsch’s algorithm and Grover’s algorithm.

The paper is primarily a pedagogical/course design article rather than an outcomes study. Its main evidence is descriptive and based on implementation in a Hong Kong Education Bureau gifted-student program in 2022, which reportedly served 40 high school students and received favorable feedback.
