The authors conclude that the accessible, hands-on structure appears promising for engaging high school students and could be adapted for broader secondary-school use, but they do not report controlled quantitative learning-effect estimates.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that a high school quantum computing curriculum, implemented with 40 gifted students in a Hong Kong Education Bureau program, received encouraging/favorable feedback and was viewed as effective for introducing quantum computing and quantum mechanics. However, the paper does not report pre/post test scores, effect sizes, or other controlled learning outcomes; the evidence is descriptive rather than inferential.
finding.measure: Student/program feedback on the quantum computing course; qualitative indicators of engagement and perceived effectiveness

finding.finding_summary: The authors emphasize student engagement, curiosity, and enthusiasm as central goals, and state that the initial gifted-program implementation received favorable reviews and substantial engagement. No survey instrument, numeric engagement score, or comparative estimate is reported, so the finding is qualitative only.
finding.measure: Observed/elicited student engagement and enthusiasm; program feedback

finding.finding_summary: The course is designed to teach quantum computing content beyond standard school subjects, including binary logic, matrices, quantum circuits, Grover’s algorithm, and quantum hardware concepts. The paper claims the approach improved accessibility and comprehension for high school learners, but it provides no direct quantitative evidence of content mastery.
finding.measure: Course-based understanding of quantum computing concepts

paper_profiles.title: Which Feedback Works for Whom? Differential Effects of LLM-Generated Feedback Elements Across Learner Profiles
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines which design elements of large-language-model-generated feedback are most helpful for high school students answering multiple-choice biology questions, and how learners’ subjective reactions differ by personality profile. The authors focus on six feedback elements—Baseline, Keywords, Actionability, Novelty, Coverage, and Positivity—derived from prior pedagogical work on feedback generation. Using GPT-5, they generate response-specific feedback for biology items and study how students revise their answers after receiving different feedback versions.

The experiment involved 321 first-year high school students in Japan working on seven basic-biology multiple-choice questions selected from a national admissions dataset and filtered for curriculum fit. Students answered questions, received pre-generated feedback tied to their chosen option, rated that feedback on six subjective criteria, and revised answers until correct if needed. The analysis compares first-revision accuracy, an overall effectiveness metric based on attempts-to-correct, correlation among rating dimensions, and personality-cluster differences in feedback evaluation.

The main finding is that feedback elements that clearly identify what to fix and provide sufficient coverage of relevant points perform best for learning outcomes: Baseline, Coverage, and Keywords are the strongest for answer revision, while Positivity is weakest. Subjectively, Keywords, Baseline, and Actionability receive the highest ratings, but preferences vary across Big Five-based clusters. The paper concludes that effective LLM feedback should be personalized not only by task content but also by learner characteristics such as personality traits.

finding.finding_summary: In a learning experiment with 321 first-year high school students on basic biology multiple-choice questions, the feedback elements most supportive of answer revision were Baseline, Coverage, and Keywords. First-revision accuracy ranged from 46.63% to 65.66%, and the overall effectiveness ranking was consistent with Baseline highest, followed by Coverage and Keywords, indicating that clearer diagnostic guidance and more complete conceptual coverage improved students’ ability to move toward correct answers.
finding.measure: First revised attempt accuracy; overall answer-revision effectiveness based on attempts required to reach the correct answer
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI shown in figure for accuracy bars, but numerical CI not reported

paper_profiles.title: AI-Fuzzy Markup Language with Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on the 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning, an outreach and educational event intended to introduce high-school and some elementary-school students to the basics of computational intelligence (CI). The school covered fuzzy logic, neural networks, evolutionary computation, and an AIoT workshop using AI-FML tools and robots such as Kebbi Air and related platforms.

The paper is primarily descriptive, outlining the summer school structure, participant demographics, lecture topics, and workshop activities. Students worked in small groups, explored fuzzy-system parameters, used AI-FML learning tools, and interacted with robot-based AIoT devices. The reported evidence comes from short reports and feedback surveys rather than a controlled evaluation.

The authors conclude that participants generally understood CI concepts to a higher degree and that the event was effective as an outreach activity for high-school students and other pre-university learners. However, the paper does not present a formal experimental design, comparison group, or inferential effect estimates, so its findings should be interpreted as qualitative feedback from an educational program rather than causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The summer school aimed to help students understand core computational intelligence concepts, including fuzzy logic, neural networks, and evolutionary computation. Based on submitted short reports and feedback surveys from 80 reports and 77 surveys, the authors state that participants understood these principles to a higher degree than in previously organized schools, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported understanding of computational intelligence concepts (fuzzy logic, neural networks, evolutionary computation) from short reports and feedback surveys
finding.study_size: n=77 survey responses; n=80 short reports

finding.finding_summary: The workshop asked student teams to examine parameter effects, design robot expressions based on system outputs, and present short reports on what they learned, which indicates emphasis on collaboration, problem solving, and applied reasoning. The paper reports that participants gained experience co-learning with machines and successfully engaged in these tasks, but no formal measures or effect sizes were provided.
finding.measure: Workshop task completion, group participation, and short report/presentation activities
finding.study_size: 8 high school teams and 2 elementary school teams; total attended at least two-thirds of sessions n=78

finding.finding_summary: The event was designed to stimulate student interest in computational intelligence and motivate participation in future research adventures, according to participant and teacher feedback quoted in the paper. The authors also report that the workshop attracted attention and engagement from students during the AIoT activities, but the evidence is qualitative and no standardized engagement or motivation measure was reported.
finding.measure: Participant and teacher feedback; engagement during lectures and AIoT workshop
finding.study_size: n=77 survey responses; n=80 short reports

paper_profiles.title: A self-evolving multi-role collaborative framework with fine-grained difficulty guidance for innovative mathematical problem generation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic mathematical problem generation for high-school education, with a focus on producing problems that are not only correct but also innovative and appropriately difficult. The authors argue that existing large language model (LLM) approaches to math problem generation tend to be coarse-grained in difficulty control and often suffer from a tradeoff between correctness and innovation.

To address this, the paper proposes a self-evolving multi-role collaborative framework built around a single fine-tuned LLM that plays generator and evaluator roles, supported by a sampler, state machine, and memory module. The system introduces a fine-grained 16-bit difficulty encoding scheme and a data-driven association-guided path sampling (DAPS) algorithm to generate structured difficulty requirements. It also uses a multi-stage post-training pipeline with continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, group relative policy optimization, and knowledge distillation from an expert model to improve generation and evaluation capabilities.

The empirical context is Chinese high-school mathematics, especially the chapters on derivatives, sequences, and probability. The paper builds and uses the HSM3K-CN dataset (3,160 raw high-school math problems; derived generation/evaluation subsets totaling 6,320 samples) and evaluates the system on a 90-item simulated requirement set (SIMU-90). The authors report that their method improves average judged quality, innovation, discrimination, and difficulty accuracy relative to baseline open-source and closed-source LLMs, while maintaining high correctness. However, the paper is an engineering/modeling study rather than a causal intervention study in schools, so it does not provide student-learning impact estimates.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies automated generation of high-school mathematics problems and reports that the proposed framework significantly improves the innovation of generated problems while maintaining high correctness rates compared with baseline models. On the SIMU-90 benchmark, the system achieved an overall average score of 8.56 in expert mode and 6.80 in apprentice mode, outperforming the listed baselines on the judge-based evaluation, but the paper does not report a single classroom-learning effect size such as d or g.
finding.measure: LLM-judged math-problem quality across nine dimensions, including correctness, innovation, discrimination, and difficulty accuracy on SIMU-90
finding.study_size: n=90 problem-design requirements (SIMU-90); plus HSM3K-CN with n=3,160 raw problems

paper_profiles.title: Évaluation entre pairs en mathématiques : activité d’étudiant·es lors d’évaluations de preuves
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines peer assessment in mathematics in a post-secondary setting, focusing on what students actually do when they evaluate peers’ proof-based work. The authors situate the study in research on formative assessment and peer assessment, and ask how the evaluator role changes student activity compared with ordinary problem solving, what elements students attend to, what corrections they make, what resources they use, and how the evaluator role may contribute to learning.

The study was carried out in a first-year French preparatory class (CPGE MPSI) with 42 students. Students solved two math exercises, then evaluated anonymized peer copies; the researchers collected 44 original copies, 64 take-home peer evaluations from 30 students, 6 videotaped think-aloud pair interviews, and a questionnaire completed by 38 students. The main analytic focus was the first exercise on sets and bounds, where students’ evaluation activity was coded using an a priori framework that distinguished reading, understanding, validating/invalidation, correcting, and commenting on proof structure and syntax.

Findings show that peer assessment changed students’ activity in several ways: they spent substantial effort reading and trying to understand proofs, often validating or invalidating by checking hypotheses, producing counterexamples, recalling course results, or referring to their own solution and provided correction sheet. The authors report seven characteristic activity axes, including proof comprehension, validity judgments, attention to result versus method, corrections, syntax/redaction concerns, and value judgments. Rather than reporting an intervention effect size, the paper argues qualitatively that peer assessment has potential to promote mathematical learning at the undergraduate level, especially through proof analysis, correction, and metacognitive awareness.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines students’ mathematical proof-solving and proof-evaluation activity in a peer-assessment setting, but it does not test achievement gains with a comparison group. In the analyzed exercise on bounds and sets, 34 of 42 students used a growth-based strategy; however, the paper reports that none of the students who relied on informal shortcuts produced a valid proof that the supremum was 1, and many peer evaluations involved identifying or correcting mathematical errors rather than improving performance on a measured outcome.
finding.measure: Resolution and evaluation of proof-based mathematics exercises (bounds and sets; peer-annotated copies and coded interview activity)
finding.study_size: n=42 (class); 44 original copies; 64 evaluated copies; 6 interviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that peer assessment elicited metacognitive and critical-thinking activities, including proof comprehension, checking validity, generating counterexamples, and reflecting on what counts as sufficient justification. Students also discussed how to reorganize arguments and what information is necessary in a correct proof, indicating gains in metacognitive awareness and evaluative judgment, though these were not quantified with effect sizes.
finding.measure: Observed and verbalized evaluator activity; questionnaire responses about perceived activity
finding.study_size: n=42 in class; questionnaire n=38; think-aloud pairs n≈10

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Feedback Generation for Short Answer Questions Using Answer Diagnostic Graphs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing individualized formative feedback on short-answer reading comprehension questions, which is typically burdensome for teachers and often reduced to simple scoring without explanation. The authors propose an automatic feedback generation system based on an Answer Diagnostic Graph (ADG), a graph representation of the logical structure of a prompt text and its model answer, linked to feedback templates.

The system is designed to map student responses to nodes in the ADG using an automatic short-answer scoring model and justification cues, then generate feedback tailored to the inferred misunderstanding. The study evaluates this approach in a user experiment with Japanese high school students answering two critical-essay prompts in 70–80 words. One condition received only official answer explanations, while the other received those explanations plus oracle-generated feedback from the proposed system.

The empirical study focuses on re-answering performance, student perceptions, and motivation. Results showed no significant difference in score improvement after re-answering between the feedback and explanation conditions, but questionnaire results and free-text comments suggest the feedback helped students recognize errors, better understand key points in the text, and feel more motivated. The authors conclude that the feedback design is promising for supporting revision and motivation, but that the current templates are still too vague and need refinement to better convey the logical structure of texts.

finding.finding_summary: In a user study with Japanese high school students (n=39), the feedback system was evaluated on short-answer reading comprehension prompts. Re-answering scores did not improve significantly relative to the answer-explanation condition (Table 5 reports ns for both prompts), but questionnaire and comment data suggest students better understood their mistakes and the main points of the prompt text.
finding.measure: Short-answer reading comprehension re-answering scores; questionnaire items about understanding the logical relationship of the prompt text and comprehension of main points
finding.std_deviation: Table 1 S.D. values reported per item: 0.7-1.4; Table 5 S.D. for score gains: prompt 1 feedback 4.28 vs explanation 4.47; prompt 2 feedback 4.22 vs explanation 3.04

finding.finding_summary: The feedback condition was rated more favorably on motivation-related questionnaire items than the answer-explanation condition. For example, 'I was more motivated to re-answer' had higher mean ratings under feedback (5.2, S.D. 0.7) than under explanations (4.2, S.D. 1.4), with a significant difference (p<0.01). Participants also reported greater satisfaction and willingness to use the feedback again.
finding.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire on motivation, satisfaction, confidence, and usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The study also examined whether the feedback helped students understand the logical structure of the text and revise their answers, which aligns with metacognitive and comprehension-monitoring skills. Type 3 responses showed significant positive perceptions for 'Learning Progression' and 'Relevance,' and many free-text comments indicated the feedback highlighted insufficient elements in responses and supported revision, although some students still found the instructions vague.
finding.measure: Questionnaire items on learning progression, relevance, and understanding how to revise responses; free-text comments about revising answers

paper_profiles.title: Power-Optimal Feedback-Based Random Spectrum Access for an Energy Harvesting Cognitive User
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (wireless cognitive radio systems; no human participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a wireless cognitive radio system in which a secondary user (SU) with energy-harvesting capability shares spectrum with a primary user (PU). The main question is how the SU should use imperfectly overheard primary feedback, probabilistic spectrum sensing, and adaptive transmit power levels to maximize its own throughput while preserving primary-user quality-of-service constraints.

The authors develop a queueing-theoretic model with interacting PU and SU queues, imperfect feedback decoding, and Rayleigh fading with multi-packet reception. They derive steady-state queue probabilities, closed-form average primary packet delay, and lower/upper bounds on SU throughput under different energy-arrival and feedback-reliability assumptions. The paper then formulates and numerically solves a constrained optimization problem over sensing, access, and power-allocation parameters.

Results are presented through analytical bounds and numerical optimization, showing that higher energy-arrival rates and more reliable overheard primary feedback improve secondary throughput, while also reducing primary delay. The paper also shows that optimizing transmit power yields better SU throughput than always transmitting at maximum power. This is a communications/networking theory paper and does not study K-12 educational interventions or outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Optimal Random Access and Random Spectrum Sensing for an Energy Harvesting Cognitive Radio with and without Primary Feedback Leveraging
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (wireless communication systems; no human K-12 population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a cognitive radio networking problem, not an education intervention. The authors analyze how a secondary wireless transmitter with energy-harvesting capability should allocate its sensing and channel-access decisions when sharing spectrum with a primary user, under queue stability and delay constraints.

The proposed schemes combine random spectrum sensing, random access after sensing, direct access without sensing, and optionally leveraging overheard primary ARQ feedback. The model incorporates sensing errors, multipacket reception at receivers, and an energy queue for the secondary transmitter. Using queueing-theoretic analysis and dominant-system arguments, the paper derives stability regions and optimal access/sensing probabilities that maximize secondary throughput while preserving primary queue stability and, in a second formulation, bounding primary queueing delay.

The paper reports numerical results showing that feedback leveraging can enlarge the stability region and increase secondary throughput, especially when the primary queue is often active and receiver interference tolerance is strong. Because the paper is entirely about wireless communications and contains no K-12 educational population, intervention, or learning outcome, it does not map onto any of the education outcome categories.

paper_profiles.title: How Students Use AI Feedback Matters: Experimental Evidence on Physics Achievement and Autonomy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the way students use generative AI feedback changes its effects on learning and autonomy. The authors argue that prior AI-in-education work has focused too much on what feedback content is provided and too little on usage patterns, especially in secondary STEM settings.

The study reports two sequential randomized controlled trials conducted in a Chinese high school physics context. In Experiment 1, students were assigned to personalized recommendations with GAI-generated heuristic hints, recommendations with workbook answers/explanations, or no recommendations; in Experiment 2, students received either fully learner-controlled on-demand help, shared-control on-demand help, or no intervention. Across both five-week experiments, outcomes included standardized physics exam scores and self-regulated learning/learner autonomy questionnaires.

Results showed heterogeneous effects by baseline achievement. In Experiment 1, low-achieving students improved on physics achievement when receiving AI-generated hints (d=0.673), while medium-achieving students declined with workbook-based recommendations (d=-0.539), and high-achieving students showed a decline in self-regulated learning without achievement gains (d=-0.477). In Experiment 2, fully learner-controlled AI help improved achievement for high-achieving students (d=0.378) without harming autonomy, whereas lower achievers experienced reduced autonomy under on-demand AI help (d=-0.383). The main conclusion is that AI feedback in K-12 STEM can be beneficial or harmful depending on how it is structured and who uses it, so usage pattern and learner level matter substantially.

finding.finding_summary: The paper measured high school physics exam performance across two randomized experiments. In Experiment 1 (n=121 analyzed), low-achieving students in the AI-hint condition improved by d=0.673 (p<0.05), while medium-achieving students receiving workbook answers/explanations declined by d=-0.539 (p<0.05) and high-achieving students showed no significant achievement gain. In Experiment 2 (n=266 analyzed), fully learner-controlled on-demand AI help improved achievement for high-achieving students by d=0.378 (p<0.05), with no significant negative effect on autonomy.
finding.measure: Standardized physics exam scores (pre/post z-scores)

finding.finding_summary: The study directly assessed self-regulated learning/learner autonomy using questionnaires. In Experiment 1, high-achieving students in the AI-recommendation condition experienced a significant decline in self-regulated learning (d=-0.477, p<0.05) without achievement gains. In Experiment 2, lower achievers exposed to on-demand AI help showed reduced autonomy overall (d=-0.383, p<0.05), with a particularly strong decline in the technical-psychological dimension (d=-0.549, p<0.05).
finding.measure: SRL questionnaire / learner autonomy questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: Fostering Student Engagement in a Mobile Formative Assessment System for High-School Economics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a mobile self-assessment system can support formative assessment in high-school Microeconomics. The authors are interested in three main issues: usability of the tool, suitability for school Microeconomics, and whether the tool improves student engagement and knowledge.

The intervention is a domain-independent mobile assessment application that lets learners select questions by topic, difficulty, knowledge level, and educational level. It supports multiple item types (e.g., multiple choice, matching, true/false, drag-and-drop, hotspot) and provides end-of-test statistics by topic and subtopic. The study was conducted in a Greek senior high school with 10 teachers and 83 students, focusing on introductory Microeconomics content such as demand, price elasticity of demand, factors affecting demand, and income elasticity of demand.

The evaluation combined teacher usability/suitability judgments, System Usability Scale (SUS) scores, and a student comparison between an app group and a pen-and-pencil group. Teachers rated usability highly (SUS = 83.25) and judged the tool appropriate for formative assessment in Microeconomics. In the student phase, the app group showed higher average class-test performance than the pen-and-pencil group (16.73 vs. 13.86; two-tailed t-test p = 0.046568), and the authors report stronger engagement and improved understanding among app users. Overall, the paper concludes that the mobile formative assessment tool was usable, motivating, and educationally promising, but it is an early-stage evaluation with limited sample size and no randomized causal design claimed.

finding.finding_summary: The study targeted high-school Microeconomics learning and reports higher class-test performance for the app group than the pen-and-pencil group. On a 20-point summative test with similar questions, the app group averaged 16.73 compared with 13.86 for the comparison group; the difference was statistically significant (two-tailed t-test, p=0.046568).
finding.measure: Class test scores in Microeconomics (summative assessment)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central claim is that the mobile self-assessment tool improved student motivation, participation, and engagement. All students in the app group used the quiz at least once, with 33 additional re-runs across the week, and the authors state that the tool significantly improved motivation and participation in the learning process.
finding.measure: Engagement/participation with the mobile quiz; teacher and student reports of motivation
finding.study_size: n=15 app group; n=15 comparison group; teacher usability sample n=10

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports improved student understanding of concepts and awareness of misconceptions, which it frames as a learning advantage of self-assessment. Students in the app group reported that the tool helped them realize what they knew and revisit textbook sections tied to erroneous answers; the authors characterize this as improved understanding rather than a separately quantified cognitive test.
finding.measure: Self-reported understanding of Microeconomics concepts and misconceptions

paper_profiles.title: GPT-4 as a Homework Tutor can Improve Student Engagement and Learning Outcomes
paper_profiles.venue: Arxiv Preprint / Under Review at ACM
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether GPT-4 can serve as an interactive homework tutor in a real high-school classroom setting, and whether replacing traditional homework with GPT-4-supported homework improves learning and student experience. The authors argue that homework is often weakly supported by feedback, and that an LLM-based tutor could provide scalable, individualized corrective support without requiring major teacher workload.

The intervention was deployed in an Italian technical institute across four English classes (third- and fifth-year students, roughly ages 16 and 18). Students in the treatment group completed weekly homework through a GPT-4 chat interface that was prompted with the exercise purpose, description, and example, while control students completed standard homework. The study used stratified random assignment within class, pre/post tests on course content, and repeated questionnaires measuring engagement, perceived usefulness, and self-efficacy.

Main findings suggest that GPT-4 homework produced positive but uneven effects. Overall learning gains were modest and not statistically significant when pooling all students (d=0.251, p=0.314), but the third-year cohort showed a larger, marginally significant gain (d=0.603, p=0.087) while the fifth-year cohort showed essentially no difference (d=-0.004, p=0.991). Treatment students also rated homework as more interesting and felt they had more resources/support, and most wanted to keep using the tutor. The paper reports very low rates of apparent hallucination/errors and no evidence of novelty effects over the intervention period.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention targeted English homework, with learning measured by pre-test/post-test performance on English-content multiple-choice questions and homework tasks. Overall learning gains favored GPT-4 tutoring but were modest and not statistically significant when all students were pooled (Cohen’s d=0.251, p=0.314; n=75 across 4 classes), while the 3rd-year subgroup showed a larger, marginally significant gain (d=0.603, p=0.087) and the 5th-year subgroup showed no difference (d=-0.004, p=0.991).
finding.measure: English pre-test/post-test scores on teacher-designed multiple-choice questions; homework performance
finding.effect_size: d=0.251 overall; d=0.603 (3rd year); d=-0.004 (5th year)

finding.finding_summary: Students in the GPT-4 group reported better engagement and experience with homework during the intervention. Weekly ratings were higher on interestingness (d=0.593, p=0.011) and level of resources/support (d=0.586, p=0.015), and treatment students also showed higher overall positive responses on several homework-related survey items. The authors additionally report that 32/35 treatment respondents wanted to continue using the tutor.
finding.measure: Weekly Likert-scale questionnaires on interestingness, usefulness, comprehensiveness, and perceived resources/support; final survey satisfaction/continuation responses
finding.study_size: n=75 total; survey responses vary by week (not_reported exact n per measure)
finding.effect_size: d=0.593 interestingness; d=0.586 level_of_resources; d=0.356 usefulness; d=0.281 comprehensiveness

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was explicitly designed to reduce the burden of homework feedback and provide a scalable alternative to tutoring. The paper reports that teachers needed only to supply a homework purpose, description, and example, and that the teacher later said the system would reduce workload somewhat in the long term; however, this was not measured with a formal efficiency metric, so the evidence is qualitative/self-reported rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload / preparation effort for homework setup

paper_profiles.title: Spike Up Prime Interest in Science and Technology Through Constructionist Games
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper describes the design and early classroom/club use of educational robotics games built with LEGO Spike Prime and related robotics sets. The authors position the work within Constructionism and game-based learning, arguing that hands-on, modifiable, real-world games can increase motivation and support learning in physics, mathematics, science, programming, and related subjects.

The paper presents several project sets: Word Blocks games created with children in a robotics club, Python-based games created for secondary school use, projects created by undergraduate students in a practical robotics seminar, and tasks used in the Robot League competition. The central intervention is not a single treatment but a collection of tangible, constructionist game activities with building instructions, 3D models, lesson plans, and supporting materials.

Evidence reported in the paper is mostly descriptive and qualitative. The authors report positive student feedback from a small evaluation in a Bratislava gymnasium class (12 students aged 15-17) and anecdotal feedback from robot club participants and Robot League teams, but they do not provide controlled comparisons or effect estimates. Their conclusion is that the game-based robotics projects were enjoyable, motivating, and feasible, and that they plan more controlled studies in future work.

finding.finding_summary: In a small classroom evaluation of the Python projects, 12 students aged 15-17 reported that they enjoyed the lesson, found it fun and interesting, and liked learning how different parts worked together. The paper reports positive qualitative feedback and no quantitative effect estimate.
finding.measure: Student feedback / enjoyment responses and qualitative comments

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims the activities supported programming, creativity, and problem solving through modifying game rules, debugging, and working with legacy code. However, this is based on descriptive observations and student feedback rather than a controlled measure, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Observed/claimed programming and problem-solving skill development; student feedback

finding.finding_summary: The projects were intended to support learning in computer programming and robotics-related content, especially Python and Scratch-like Word Blocks work with LEGO Spike Prime. The paper reports that students and competition teams successfully built and used the games, but it provides no quantitative achievement measure or controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Programming task completion / project implementation
finding.study_size: n=12 plus additional club and competition participants; exact total not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Common Problems and Effects of Feedback on Fun When Programming Ozobots in Primary School
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 17th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education (WiPSCE ’22)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what kinds of problems primary school children encounter while programming Ozobot Evo robots and how different forms of corrective feedback relate to the fun children report during the activities. The authors are especially interested in whether feedback that is needed to solve a problem, and the tutoring style used (e.g., explanations, direct instruction, hints, stickers, guiding questions), changes children’s enjoyment of the activity.

The study was conducted in seven workshops with 116 third- and fourth-grade students (age 8–10) working in pairs or small groups. Across seven Ozobot activities, supervisors noted common problems and the feedback they gave, while children completed the Fun Toolkit after each activity using the Smileyometer and the Again Again table. The paper uses thematic analysis for the qualitative problem/feedback data and correlational comparisons between problem/feedback categories and fun ratings.

The main findings are that task-understanding issues, color-code mistakes, Ozobot-specific sensor/actuator issues, directionality, U-turns, app use, and other technical problems were common. Fun ratings were generally high, but some problems were associated with lower likeability, especially when the feedback was urgently needed or when the child had to wait to proceed. Direct instruction was associated with worse Smileyometer ratings, while hints were associated with better ratings; explanations and guiding questions were generally neutral. The authors conclude that encouraging, autonomy-supportive feedback is preferable and that many recurring problems can be anticipated with preparatory materials, stickers, and spare robots.

finding.finding_summary: Fun and enjoyment were generally very high across the 116 third- and fourth-grade students, with mean scores of 1.9/2 on the Again Again table and 3.72/4 on the Smileyometer. However, receiving corrective feedback sometimes reduced enjoyment, especially when the problem was urgent or could affect self-efficacy; the Smileyometer was significantly lower when feedback had been received overall (p=0.029, r=0.11).
finding.measure: Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again table) and correlations between fun ratings and problem/feedback categories
finding.effect_size: rpb=0.11 (overall feedback vs. Smileyometer); other category correlations ranged roughly from -0.17 to 0.18

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively addresses problem-solving and debugging-related thinking in programming activities, especially understanding task constraints, interpreting directions, and fixing color-code or app-related issues. While not a direct test of learning gains, the study reports that hints and guiding questions supported children in working through problems, whereas direct instruction was less supportive of enjoyment.
finding.measure: Observed problem categories and tutoring feedback categories during Ozobot programming tasks

paper_profiles.title: Diagnosing Failures in Large Language Models’ Answers: Integrating Error Attribution into Evaluation Framework
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a problem in evaluating large language models (LLMs): standard judge models can assign scores and provide feedback, but they do not reliably identify why an answer is wrong. The authors argue that error attribution is important for diagnosing failure modes and improving model quality, especially in large-scale real-world LLM deployments.

To address this, they propose a Misattribution Framework with 6 primary and 15 secondary error categories, and construct AttriData, a manually annotated dataset of 21,702 question-answer instances with score, feedback, and error labels. They then fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B to create MisAttributionLLM, which generates a score, feedback, and the most relevant misattribution category. The paper evaluates the model against several open- and closed-source LLM judges using correlation with human scores, error-detection and multi-classification metrics, and pairwise human preference judgments for feedback quality.

The study is conducted in an adult NLP/LLM evaluation context rather than a K-12 education setting. Its main conclusion is that incorporating misattribution labels substantially improves judge-model performance: MisAttributionLLM achieves stronger alignment with human scorers and better error attribution than baseline LLM judges, including GPT-4 on several metrics. The work is methodological and primarily about automated evaluation for LLMs, not an educational intervention.

paper_profiles.title: A Soft Sensing-Based Cognitive Access Scheme Exploiting Primary Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a cognitive radio spectrum-access problem, not an education intervention. The authors ask how secondary users can improve access to licensed spectrum by combining soft sensing with overheard primary-user feedback (ACK/NACK), while preserving primary-user queue stability.

The proposed method is a hybrid access scheme: secondary users compute access probabilities from an energy-detection statistic, and they completely back off for one slot after hearing a NACK so that the primary retransmission can proceed without collision. The analysis is queueing-theoretic and derives closed-form expressions for secondary throughput and primary packet delay under both the baseline soft-sensing scheme and the proposed feedback-based extension.

The paper compares the proposed method against conventional soft sensing, hard-decision sensing, and a genie-aided perfect-sensing upper bound. Using analytical results and illustrative performance plots for a four-primary-user/two-secondary-user setting, the authors conclude that the feedback-based soft-sensing scheme improves secondary throughput and reduces primary delay, often approaching the perfect-sensing benchmark. No K-12 educational outcomes are studied.

paper_profiles.title: Differentiated Instruction in Secondary Education: A Systematic Review of Research Evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the empirical evidence on within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education. The authors ask what forms of differentiated instruction have been studied, how these approaches are operationalized, what effects they have on student academic achievement, and what contextual or personal factors may shape those effects.

Using a best-evidence synthesis, the review screened studies published from 2006 to 2016 and retained 12 unique empirical studies (14 papers) meeting strict inclusion criteria. The included interventions covered several forms of differentiation, including generic adaptive-teaching trainings, ability grouping/tiering, individualized reading instruction, mastery-oriented approaches, heterogeneous grouping, and remediation in a flipped classroom. Most studies were quasi-experimental and focused on mathematics, reading, science, or prevention content in secondary settings.

Overall, the review concludes that differentiated instruction shows generally small to moderate positive associations with achievement, but the evidence base is limited, heterogeneous, and often methodologically weak. Summarized effects across studies ranged roughly from d = +0.509 to +0.741 when an outlier was omitted, though several individual studies showed null or inconsistent findings. The authors emphasize that more rigorous research is needed, especially to determine which forms of differentiation work best and for which students.

finding.finding_summary: Across the included secondary-math studies, effects ranged from large positive to null depending on the intervention and subgroup. Examples include a very large effect for a project-based differentiated mathematics intervention in Turkey (combined d = +4.504, reported from researcher-made achievement tests) and a positive effect for ability-grouped problem-based learning in Bosnia and Herzegovina (overall d = +0.539, 95% CI [0.228, 0.851]), but a flipped-classroom/remediation study in Taiwan produced only a small, nonsignificant overall effect (d = +0.376, 95% CI [-0.064, 0.815]).
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement tests (researcher-made algebra/math tests; achievement in algebra, trigonometry, and project-based math units)
finding.effect_size: d=+0.539 overall; individual studies ranged from d=+0.376 to d=+4.504
finding.confidence_interval: overall 95% CI [0.228, 0.851] for one study; other study CIs reported in text

finding.finding_summary: The individualized reading intervention study in U.S. middle schools found negligible effects on reading outcomes. For the multi-site SEM-R study, the combined effect on reading comprehension was essentially null in two sites (East MS d = +0.030; North MS d = +0.007) and small positive in two others (South MS d = +0.266; West MS d = +0.135), indicating mixed but generally weak evidence for literacy gains.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension and reading fluency tests
finding.effect_size: Combined site effects ranged from d=+0.007 to d=+0.266

finding.finding_summary: The science-focused differentiated/adaptive instruction studies reported positive achievement effects. In the U.S. tiered collaborative science intervention for 8th grade students (including students with disabilities), the combined science achievement effect was d = +0.386 (95% CI [0.115, 0.657]), with positive effects on both a unit test (d = +0.466) and a high-stakes end-of-year test (d = +0.306). The review also reports a small nonsignificant positive effect in the adaptive-teaching science study (d = +0.133) when primary and secondary results were combined.
finding.measure: Science achievement tests (unit test, end-of-year standardized/high-stakes science test)
finding.study_size: n=213 for the science tiered collaborative learning study; n=623 in the adaptive-teaching project (combined primary+secondary sample)
finding.effect_size: d=+0.386; component effects d=+0.466 and d=+0.306; adaptive-teaching combined d=+0.133
finding.confidence_interval: [0.115, 0.657] for combined science effect; [0.194, 0.738] unit test; [0.036, 0.576] end-of-year test; adaptive-teaching CI not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review also includes an alcohol/tobacco/other drug prevention study, where differentiation was implemented through learning-style adaptations and teacher support. The intervention produced a large positive effect on the ATOD survey outcome (d = +1.374, 95% CI [1.209, 1.538]) relative to traditional prevention instruction, indicating substantially better prevention knowledge/attitudes or related survey performance.
finding.measure: Alcohol, tobacco and other drug prevention survey
finding.study_size: n=1,170? not_reported exact total in extracted text; intervention classes n=978 and control n=192 across grades 6–8

paper_profiles.title: Designing and enacting instruction that enhances language for mathematics learning: a review of the state of development and research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This survey paper reviews four decades of research on the role of language in mathematics learning and organizes the literature around six design principles for instruction that enhances language for mathematics learning. The authors focus on how instruction can support rich mathematical discourse, language routines, connections between language varieties and representations, multilingual resources, macro-scaffolding across lessons, and comparison-based language awareness.

The paper is not a primary intervention study but a structured review of both qualitative and quantitative studies from mathematics education, linguistics, and language education. It synthesizes research on the design of learning environments as well as enacted teaching practices, especially teacher moves and classroom norms, to explain what conditions make language-responsive mathematics instruction productive. The review emphasizes that successful designs usually combine multiple principles rather than relying on a single feature.

The paper concludes that there is a substantial but still limited empirical base for language-enhancing mathematics instruction. It finds that topic-specific interventions and carefully orchestrated discourse practices often show strong effects, while topic-independent approaches are less consistently effective. The authors also highlight major research gaps, especially around whole-class enactment, ecological validity, and the need for more quantitative studies that can test moderator effects and transfer across contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed quantitative studies, topic-specific language-related interventions in mathematics often showed positive effects on mathematics learning, with several reported large effects such as d=1.22 for fractions (n=72), d=0.60 for percentages (n=108), d=0.99 for fractions (n=128), d=0.87 for word problems (n=167), and d=0.78 for metacognitive discourse/problem solving (n=824). However, not all approaches were effective: a sheltered instruction approach showed no significant mathematics effect, and a general reading-strategy intervention showed no advantage for math modeling (d=0.2, p>0.05).
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement, problem solving, fractions, percentages, word problems, math modeling, number operations/decimals
finding.study_size: multiple studies; individual samples ranged from n=22 to n=824
finding.effect_size: mixed; examples include d=1.22, d=0.99, d=0.87, d=0.78, d=0.60, d=0.20

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that many instructional approaches improved students' mathematical language use, explanation quality, and participation in discourse. Evidence cited includes studies where teacher supports increased the frequency of student explanations and engagement with others' ideas, and where language routines, revoicing, paraphrasing, and multilingual resources supported richer language production and meaning-making.
finding.measure: Student explanations, discourse participation, language production, classroom discussion quality
finding.study_size: multiple studies; n=71 in one quantitative study on participation, plus qualitative studies

finding.finding_summary: Several studies synthesized in the review link language-responsive instruction to durable skills such as argumentation, reasoning, and metacognitive discourse. For example, one randomized study found that metacognitive self-question prompts improved the depth of discourse and transferred to mathematical problem solving (d=0.78, n=824), and another study found that participation in explaining ideas and building on others' ideas predicted achievement.
finding.measure: Metacognitive discourse, reasoning, explaining, building on others' ideas, problem solving
finding.study_size: multiple studies; n=824 in one quantitative study; n=71 in another
finding.effect_size: d=0.78 for metacognitive discourse transfer; other effects not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that some teacher moves and classroom norms supported student participation, confidence, and willingness to contribute in mathematics discussions. In particular, supportive follow-up questions, positive handling of mistakes, and classroom norms that valued student ideas were associated with greater participation and perceived attentiveness from teachers.
finding.measure: Student participation, perceptions of being listened to, classroom engagement
finding.study_size: multiple studies; one quantitative study n=71 and others qualitative

paper_profiles.title: Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education STEM learners (mixed populations across included studies)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether computer-based scaffolding improves student learning in problem-based learning (PBL) settings for STEM education, and whether effects differ by scaffolding type, customization, strategy, higher-order skill target, and discipline. The authors use Bayesian meta-analysis to synthesize 21 studies with 47 outcomes published between 1990 and 2015, focusing on cognitive learning outcomes and higher-order thinking.

The study examines several kinds of computer-based scaffolding, including conceptual, metacognitive, strategic, and motivational scaffolds; customization approaches such as fading, adding, and fading/adding; and delivery methods such as performance-adapted, self-selected, and fixed interval scaffolding. It also analyzes higher-order thinking outcomes (analysis, synthesis, evaluation) and disciplinary contexts (science, technology, engineering, mathematics, integrated STEM).

Overall, the meta-analysis finds a positive but moderate effect of computer-based scaffolding on cognitive outcomes in PBL (g = 0.385, 95% credible interval [0.022, 0.802]). Effects vary substantially across moderators: metacognitive and strategic scaffolding outperform conceptual scaffolding; self-selected customization is stronger than performance-adapted or fixed timing; and scaffolds are more effective for analysis than for synthesis or evaluation. By discipline, effects are larger in engineering, mathematics, and technology than in science, with comparatively smaller effects in integrated STEM.

The paper concludes that computer-based scaffolding can support STEM learning in PBL, but its effectiveness depends on the design of the scaffold and the target skill level. It also argues that current systems are better suited to supporting analysis-level thinking than more advanced synthesis or evaluation tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Computer-based scaffolding had a positive overall effect on cognitive learning outcomes in PBL STEM settings, with g = 0.385 (95% CrI = 0.022 to 0.802). Across moderator analyses, effects were strongest for analysis-level outcomes (g = 0.537), indicating improved higher-order thinking performance overall, especially for identifying components of information and relations among them.
finding.measure: Cognitive learning outcomes / higher-order thinking outcomes in problem-based learning

finding.finding_summary: The review directly studied STEM learning in problem-based learning and found that computer-based scaffolding improved cognitive outcomes tied to scientific and problem-solving processes. For the science discipline subgroup, the effect was positive but smaller than in engineering, mathematics, and technology (g = 0.146, 95% CrI = 0.003 to 0.295).
finding.measure: Cognitive outcomes in STEM/PBL, including science-related problem solving and higher-order thinking
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CrI = 0.003 to 0.295 (science subgroup); overall 95% CrI = 0.022 to 0.802

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the free, web-based InkSurvey system is an effective way to collect real-time formative assessment data across a range of educational settings. The authors frame the need as a practical classroom problem: instructors need an efficient way to elicit open-ended student thinking during instruction and then use those responses to adapt teaching before misconceptions become entrenched.

InkSurvey is a pen-enabled mobile-device platform that lets instructors pose open-format questions and receive students’ digital-ink responses instantly. The paper synthesizes seven vignettes spanning K-12, university, and graduate settings in the United States and Mexico, across subjects including physics, mathematics, engineering, food chemistry, and biology. Evidence includes teacher observations, student surveys, and comparisons of summative performance before and after use of InkSurvey or against non-InkSurvey comparison groups.

The main conclusion is that InkSurvey appears to support learning gains, improved student metacognition and engagement, and more responsive instruction, but the evidence is largely descriptive and drawn from heterogeneous case examples rather than a single rigorous study. Reported effects include reduced persistence of a calculus misconception, improved Algebra I standards-based performance in a high school context, stronger quiz performance in redesigned undergraduate and graduate courses, and steady gains in problem-solving skill in an upper-level engineering physics course. The paper also reports that students generally value the instant feedback and that instructors find the tool useful for diagnosing understanding and differentiating instruction.

finding.finding_summary: In the K-12 Algebra I vignette, high school students using InkSurvey showed greater gains on standards-based assessments than students not exposed to the intervention. The paper does not report an effect size, but it states that female students in the mixed-gender classes demonstrated particularly strong learning gains relative to the control group; the K-12 comparison is described qualitatively rather than with full statistics.
finding.measure: Standards-based assessments in Algebra I

finding.finding_summary: Across physics and engineering examples, InkSurvey was associated with improved conceptual understanding and problem-solving. One calculus III vignette reported that only 1 of 87 students still showed a target misconception two weeks after the lesson, compared with 12 of 103 students in a comparison section without InkSurvey; another upper-level engineering physics class showed steady improvement over the semester in problem-solving skill, and chemical engineering students’ average competence rose from about 1.8 to about 3.1 on a 4-point scale after instructor-guided use of simulations plus InkSurvey.
finding.measure: Summative exam questions, problem-solving strategy scores, and concept-competence ratings
finding.study_size: n=87 and n=103 for the calculus comparison; other vignettes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported favorable attitudes toward InkSurvey, including increased engagement, motivation, and awareness of what they understood. In one survey of 63 junior-level physics students, 54 (86%) said InkSurvey gave the instructor a better understanding of what they did and did not understand, and 48 (76%) said creating responses helped them better understand the material or realize what they did not understand.
finding.measure: Student survey agreement about feedback, understanding, and metacognitive benefit

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes metacognitive and problem-solving benefits from open-format, real-time formative assessment. Students reported that InkSurvey helped them think through problems, recognize misunderstandings, and stay actively involved in class, while the upper-level engineering physics vignette found steady improvement in problem-solving skills over the semester.
finding.measure: Metacognitive self-report, problem-solving strategy analysis, and class participation observations
finding.study_size: n=63 for survey data; other vignette sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Instructors reported that InkSurvey provided immediate diagnostic information that let them tailor instruction in real time, identify common difficulties, and adjust pacing or launch follow-up questions. The paper presents this mainly as practitioner testimony and classroom observation rather than as quantified efficiency data.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported ability to diagnose misconceptions and adapt instruction

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment. I. Applications in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (mixed; includes high school, undergraduate, graduate, and community college)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes InkSurvey, a free web-based tool that lets instructors pose open-ended questions and collect students’ handwritten responses in real time on pen-enabled devices. The central problem addressed is how to make formative assessment more immediate, informative, and usable during instruction, especially when traditional assessment methods are too slow or limited to multiple choice.

The paper presents seven descriptive vignettes across diverse settings: a university honors calculus class, a high school Algebra I class, college biology, physics, food chemistry, chemical engineering, and creativity-in-physics courses in the United States and Mexico. In each case, instructors used InkSurvey to surface misconceptions, scaffold thinking, and adjust instruction on the spot. The paper is primarily an implementation and rationale piece; it argues that open-format, real-time formative assessment can improve engagement and give instructors richer insight into student understanding, but it does not report a controlled study or quantitative achievement analysis in this manuscript.

Across the vignettes, the authors emphasize practical classroom use rather than measured causal effects. Reported examples include students revising misconceptions in calculus after class discussion of responses, near-daily feedback use in high school algebra, and improved scaffolding/feedback in biology and other STEM courses. The conclusion is that InkSurvey is broadly applicable across subjects, devices, and educational levels, and that it can support timely instructional adjustment and active learning.

finding.finding_summary: In the honors calculus vignette, InkSurvey was used to diagnose misconceptions about setting up triple integrals and regions of integration. Students improved immediately after discussion: on question Q4, 32 of 83 responses showed the constant-bound misconception, but on a follow-up question after instructor feedback, none of the students provided all constant bounds and only 4 still showed the misconception in one dimension.
finding.measure: Student written responses to open-ended calculus questions about inequalities defining triple-integral regions
finding.study_size: n=87 (87 students enrolled; 83 responses on Q4)

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly uses InkSurvey to probe students’ conceptual understanding in STEM settings, including physics, biology, chemistry, and chemical engineering. In the physics vignette, students had to justify answers to conceptual questions in writing; instructors reported that this exposed faulty reasoning even when students reached a correct answer, enabling immediate correction during class.
finding.measure: Open-ended conceptual explanations and sketches in physics/biology/chemistry/engineering classes

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that InkSurvey increased student engagement and participation across settings by making all students respond and by creating a more interactive classroom climate. In the biology vignette, the sequence of questions was described as engaging students in their learning and motivating participation in discussion; in the creativity vignette, anonymity was said to reduce evaluation apprehension and encourage participation regardless of gender, race, etc.
finding.measure: Observed classroom participation, student engagement, and reported receptiveness to discussion

finding.finding_summary: A major substantive focus of the paper is the use of InkSurvey to support metacognition, sensemaking, and reasoning. The authors argue that open-ended questions force students to articulate what they do and do not understand, and that real-time instructor feedback helps students repair misconceptions and connect ideas across prior knowledge and new content.
finding.measure: Student reasoning quality, metacognitive prompting, and problem-solving explanations

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes InkSurvey as a way to make formative assessment less cumbersome and to reduce delays in instructor response to misconceptions. Instructors could rapidly scan all responses, compare alternate solutions, and quickly adjust instruction in class, suggesting improved feedback efficiency and broader coverage than calling on a few students at the board.
finding.measure: Instructor review of student work and speed/timeliness of instructional feedback

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper discusses the educational rationale for formative assessment and explores how it can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System. The authors argue that frequent, low-stakes assessments paired with immediate, detailed feedback can support learning more effectively than relying only on end-of-term summative exams.

The practical implementation described is a series of weekly or fortnightly online tests created in Blackboard, with question types such as multiple choice and true/false, automatic score display, and explanatory feedback after submission. The paper also reports a student survey of perceptions toward continuous assessment and Blackboard-based testing. Students generally supported the approach, especially because it broke content into smaller topic assessments, provided immediate teacher feedback, and allowed flexible, convenient assessment.

The study was conducted with university students at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus), and it compared perceptions across Business, Engineering, and IT streams. The main reported finding was that Engineering students were more favorable toward open-book continuous assessment and the Blackboard testing option than Business and IT students, with statistically significant differences across streams. The paper is primarily descriptive and perception-based; it does not report achievement gains from the intervention, but it concludes that formative assessment and rapid feedback may help students improve learning and potentially perform better on later summative assessments.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported supportive attitudes toward frequent internal assessments and Blackboard-based testing, mainly because these features provided immediate feedback, flexibility, and a sense of keeping up with the subject. The paper describes these perceptions as helping motivation and reducing the feeling that learning is delayed until final exams, but it does not report achievement effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard test option

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment with detailed feedback supports metacognition and helps students identify strengths, weaknesses, and how to close the gap between current and desired performance. Evidence is based on student survey responses and author interpretation rather than a direct measured skill outcome, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Survey items on perceived value of feedback for checking strengths/weaknesses and staying on track

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students favored splitting course work into 10-12 smaller Blackboard assessments and believed this would help them learn individual topics progressively and support performance on the summative semester examination. The evidence is perception-based and descriptive; no direct achievement measure or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and expected effects on semester examination learning

paper_profiles.title: Modernizing use of regression models in physics education research: A review of hierarchical linear modeling
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a methodological review of regression modeling in physics education research, focused on when hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) is more appropriate than single-level methods such as multiple linear regression (MLR) for nested educational data. The authors argue that student outcomes in multi-course or multi-institution physics datasets are typically clustered within courses, and that ignoring this structure can bias estimates, standard errors, and statistical significance.

To illustrate the issue, the paper first explains disaggregation, aggregation, and HLM using a toy example of student SAT verbal scores and Force Concept Inventory (FCI) post-test scores nested within courses. It then reanalyzes a real large-scale physics dataset from 5,959 students in 112 introductory physics courses at 17 institutions, comparing MLR and HLM models predicting learning gains from pretest scores and course instructional context (lecture, collaborative learning without learning assistants, collaborative learning with learning assistants). The main conclusion is that MLR can overstate effects and underestimate uncertainty when course-level clustering is present, while HLM produces more reliable estimates; in this dataset, MLR found collaborative learning without learning assistants to be the strongest condition, whereas HLM showed that this difference was not statistically significant and that one should not draw the same substantive conclusion from the two methods.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central empirical result is that analysis method changes estimated physics learning outcomes on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI). In the reanalysis of n=5,959 students in 112 courses, MLR and HLM produced different coefficients and significance tests for instructional conditions: collaborative learning without learning assistants was strongly positive in MLR (coef.=12.99, p<0.001) but much smaller and not significant in HLM (coef.=3.26, p=0.283), while learning-assistant-supported courses were positive in both models (MLR coef.=7.27; HLM coef.=5.94).
finding.measure: Force Concept Inventory (FCI) post-test / gain scores; model coefficients for instructional condition

paper_profiles.title: Inquiry-Based Mathematics Education: a call for reform in tertiary education seems unjustified
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical scoping review of the inquiry-based mathematics education (IBME) literature, focused on whether tertiary mathematics should be reformed toward minimally guided, discovery-oriented instruction. The authors synthesize evidence from cognitive science, educational psychology, and prior meta-analyses to evaluate three common claims made by IBME advocates: that students learn better when not explicitly taught, that inquiry improves conceptual understanding and transfer, and that inquiry is better for equity.

The review argues that these claims are not supported by the evidence. Drawing on prior controlled studies and meta-analytic findings, the paper concludes that unassisted discovery/inquiry is less effective than explicit instruction for novices, especially when learning novel or high-element-interactivity content. It also argues that the purported equity benefits of inquiry-based approaches are not established. The paper’s main recommendation is that instruction in tertiary mathematics should begin with explicit teaching and worked examples, with problem-solving and inquiry used after learners have acquired sufficient prior schemas.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that unassisted inquiry/discovery learning is less effective than explicit instruction for mathematics learning, especially for novice learners. It cites a meta-analysis of 108 studies (580 comparisons) showing explicit teaching outperformed unassisted discovery with a mean effect of d = -0.38, 95% CI [-0.50, -0.25].
finding.measure: Learning outcomes and conceptual understanding in mathematics instruction; transfer/application tests in cited studies
finding.study_size: n=varies across included studies; meta-analysis of 108 studies / 580 comparisons

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses a randomized study of elementary students learning the control-of-variables strategy (CVS), a foundational scientific-reasoning skill. Direct instruction produced far more masters than discovery learning (77% vs 23%; in the low-performing subgroup, 69% vs 15%), and transfer performance among masters was comparable across conditions.
finding.measure: Mastery of control-of-variables strategy and transfer task performance (science-fair poster evaluation)

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that inquiry/discovery places high demands on working memory and metacognitive control, which can undermine effective learning for novices. It frames the relevant durable-skill outcome as self-regulation/metacognitive monitoring during problem solving, but reports no new primary effect estimate beyond synthesizing prior evidence that minimal guidance is inferior.
finding.measure: Metacognitive control / self-monitoring during learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses claims that inquiry may increase motivation, engagement, and ownership, but does not present new empirical results showing such benefits in K-12 settings. Its overall conclusion is that any presumed motivational advantages do not outweigh the learning disadvantages documented for novices, and it treats these benefits as unsubstantiated in the reviewed evidence.
finding.measure: Motivation/engagement/ownership claims in inquiry-based learning literature

paper_profiles.title: Tackling CS education in K-12: Implementing a Google CS4HS Grant Program in a Rural Underserved Area
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers in rural underserved Nebraska districts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the implementation of a Google CS4HS-funded professional development program, Computer Science Principles on the Prairie (CSPoP), designed to help rural Nebraska teachers develop the knowledge and materials needed to teach computer science and computational thinking in K-12 schools. The paper addresses a practical access problem: many rural districts lacked qualified CS teachers and CS graduation requirements, limiting students’ exposure to CS pathways.

The program combined a face-to-face workshop, a seven-week graduate-level online course (IT Teaching Methods), and an online community of practice. Participants were certified teachers from rural and some urban Nebraska districts who wanted to add CS/IT to their instruction; the course emphasized App Inventor, Scratch, computational thinking, and CS curricular design. The paper mainly reports implementation details, participation counts, and participant feedback rather than a controlled evaluation.

The main conclusions are that the program was feasible and well received, and that several teachers reported implementing the curriculum they developed in their classrooms. The author concludes that hands-on face-to-face PD and sustained in-person support during the school year are important for maintaining engagement, especially for isolated rural teachers who may be the only CS-integration teacher in their district.

finding.finding_summary: The program increased the local capacity to offer CS/IT instruction by preparing teachers to develop and implement CS curriculum, with 15 teachers completing the online course and several reporting that they used the curriculum in their classes. The paper also reports that the effort supported a broader rural-school initiative to expand CS opportunities and build a community of practice, but it does not provide causal outcome data on school- or district-level change.
finding.measure: Teacher participation/completion, reported curriculum implementation, and community-of-practice participation
finding.study_size: n=15 course completers; n=15 workshop participants; 25 teachers in the Google Community

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the PD helped teachers efficiently generate usable curricular materials for their own classrooms, reducing the burden of creating CS lessons from scratch. This is supported by teacher comments and reports that the projects and curricular units developed in the course were implemented, but no formal workload or time-use metrics were collected.
finding.measure: Self-reported use of course materials and curriculum developed during the course

finding.finding_summary: The program explicitly targeted computational thinking, problem solving, creativity, and curriculum design as teacher learning goals. Evidence is limited to course structure and participant reflections; the paper does not report pre/post assessments of these skills, so the finding is based on qualitative reports rather than measured gains.
finding.measure: Participation in computational-thinking and CS curriculum-development activities; participant reflections

finding.finding_summary: Participant comments indicate high satisfaction, motivation, and interest in continuing CS learning, including desires to become highly qualified in computer science and to use the materials in class. The paper also notes that the community of practice was intended to reduce isolation among rural teachers, though engagement was lower than hoped and no formal social-emotional measures were administered.
finding.measure: Teacher feedback/comments on satisfaction, motivation, and willingness to continue CS learning

paper_profiles.title: Complexity in Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual/theoretical chapter; no empirical sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This encyclopedia chapter surveys the role of complexity theory in mathematics education and organizes the discussion around four uses of the term: epistemological, historical, disciplinary, and pragmatic. Rather than presenting a single study or intervention, it argues that mathematics learning and teaching are best understood as involving nested, adaptive, emergent systems that connect individual cognition, classroom interaction, institutional structures, and broader cultural/ecological contexts.

The chapter reviews how complexity-informed ideas align with theories of learning such as constructivist, sociocultural, embodied, and critical approaches, and how they can reframe mathematics as historically evolving rather than fixed. It also argues that new computational tools make complex phenomena accessible to K–12 learners through curriculum that includes modeling, simulation, and agent-based approaches.

Its main conclusion is that complexity sensibilities can support more productive classroom organization, interdisciplinary modeling, and transdisciplinary pedagogies, shifting school mathematics away from linear, individualistic conceptions toward collaborative, emergent, and context-sensitive forms of knowing. The piece is conceptual and theoretical; it does not report an empirical study, intervention effects, or subgroup analyses.

paper_profiles.title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the accessibility gap in K-12 computer science instruction for deaf and hard-of-hearing (D/HH) students, especially middle school students who may not have access to ASL-fluent teachers or appropriate STEM vocabulary in sign language. The authors argue that conventional captioned videos and text-heavy instruction are often insufficient because many D/HH learners use ASL as a first language and may have lower English literacy.

The paper proposes an accessible block-based computer science learning environment that integrates ASL video tutorials, captions, and visual feedback. The curriculum covers core programming concepts such as algorithms, loops, variables, functions, debugging, and object-oriented programming, and the environment is designed to support both instructional content and robot-based programming activities. Accessibility features are guided by Deaf web usability heuristics, including sign-language tooltips, caption control, and visually rich feedback.

This is primarily a design and position/prototype paper rather than an evaluation study. It does not report learner outcomes, subgroup analyses, or achievement effects; instead, it outlines the planned system and future study to test the impact of ASL videos on CS learning with middle-school deaf students. The main conclusion is that ASL-based, visually oriented, block-programming instruction is a promising approach for improving access and inclusion in K-12 computing education for D/HH learners.

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical conceptual review of the ethical challenges and opportunities associated with integrating artificial intelligence into K-12 STEM education. It focuses on issues such as algorithmic bias, privacy, surveillance, equity gaps, and the need for teacher and student AI literacy rather than testing a specific intervention with new empirical data.
