The authors synthesize recent literature on intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, predictive analytics, and AI surveillance technologies to argue that AI can support personalized learning, feedback, and operational efficiency but can also intensify inequities for marginalized students if deployed without safeguards. The paper proposes a three-phased implementation roadmap and a four-phase professional development model grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy. It emphasizes low-resource adaptations, culturally responsive design, bias audits, and governance structures to support responsible AI adoption in K-12 STEM settings.

Because the article is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, it does not report original sample sizes, effect sizes, or moderator analyses. Its main contribution is a framework for equitable AI integration and a summary of ethical risks and implementation considerations for educators and school systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-powered tools such as automated assessments and intelligent tutoring systems can reduce teacher workload by automating scoring, delivering immediate feedback, and supporting scalable diagnostics. However, these claims are presented as a synthesis of prior literature rather than as original empirical findings, so no new effect size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload; assessment/scoring efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional and policy-level implications of AI adoption in K-12 STEM, including governance, equity audits, data privacy, professional development, and alignment with UNESCO/OECD guidance. It concludes that AI can support system-wide improvement only if schools adopt bias audits, low-resource adaptations, and stronger data governance; otherwise, it may widen inequities and surveillance risks.
finding.measure: policy alignment, governance practices, equity audits, professional development models

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI-supported tools and ethics activities can increase student engagement, critical engagement, and agency, including through project-based learning and role-play activities. These are presented as literature-based assertions and illustrative examples, not as directly measured outcomes in a new study.
finding.measure: student engagement; critical engagement; agency

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the paper focuses on AI ethics literacy and critical algorithmic literacy, arguing that students should learn to interrogate AI systems, identify bias, and reason about societal impacts. The paper cites prior work suggesting project-based AI ethics instruction can produce gains in critical thinking, but it does not report original effect sizes or samples.
finding.measure: critical thinking; AI ethics literacy; algorithmic literacy

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI integration in STEM contexts, including simulations, dataset bias analysis, and science-focused examples such as facial recognition ethics and biology classification. It suggests these approaches can support scientific inquiry and content learning, but no original achievement data or moderator effects are reported.
finding.measure: scientific inquiry; STEM learning; science content understanding

paper_profiles.title: Emerging technologies in physics education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews three emerging technologies in physics education—Physlets, the Andes Intelligent Tutoring System, and Microcomputer-Based Laboratory (MBL) tools—and evaluates them from the perspective of cognitive science and physics education research. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the paper synthesizes prior research and argues that these tools can support conceptual change, expert-like problem solving, and more meaningful laboratory experiences.

The discussion is framed around how each technology fits established learning principles. Physlets are presented as interactive simulations that can promote conceptual understanding through prediction, exploration, and problem solving; Andes is described as an intelligent tutoring system that coaches students through structured physics problem solving with immediate feedback and hints; and MBL tools are discussed as laboratory technologies that make data collection and analysis more efficient and help students connect physical phenomena with graphical representations.

The paper’s population focus is primarily introductory university physics students, though it notes that MBL tools can be used across levels from elementary school to university. Its conclusions are largely interpretive: the author argues that these technologies are most effective when embedded in structured, collaborative curricula and that they can help address longstanding shortcomings of traditional lecture, homework, and laboratory instruction in physics education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Physlets, Andes, and MBL tools can strengthen conceptual change and physics understanding, but it does not present original empirical achievement results. It synthesizes prior studies suggesting improved conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance in related interventions, while also noting limitations such as weak support for metacognition in Andes and incomplete error-analysis support in MBL labs.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding, physics problem solving, and laboratory-based reasoning as reported in prior studies and discussed by the author

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the paper is that these technologies support expert-like problem solving, scaffolding, and collaboration. The author particularly emphasizes that Physlets and Andes can provide guided practice, hints, and structured problem-solving sequences, while also noting that Andes does not explicitly train planning, monitoring, or evaluation and therefore only partly supports metacognition.
finding.measure: Problem-solving strategies, scaffolding, collaboration, and metacognitive activity

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents MBL tools as improving laboratory efficiency by reducing time spent on data collection and graphing and by allowing real-time display and analysis of results. This is described as freeing class time for discussion, prediction, and experimentation, although the paper also notes that error analysis receives less attention in current implementations.
finding.measure: Laboratory time use, data collection and display efficiency, and time available for analysis/discussion

paper_profiles.title: EDUKG: a Heterogeneous Sustainable K-12 Educational Knowledge Graph
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of insufficient, coarse-grained, and unsustainable educational knowledge graphs for K-12 education, especially in Chinese high-school settings. The authors argue that prior systems are limited in interdisciplinary coverage, resource richness, and the ability to grow with new curriculum content and online materials.

To address this, they introduce EDUKG, a heterogeneous and sustainable K-12 educational knowledge graph built with a fine-grained ontology spanning knowledge topics, educational resources, and external heterogeneous data. The system combines textbook parsing, named entity recognition, entity linking, open information extraction, and human annotation to extract concepts, relations, rhetorical roles, and exercises from 46 textbooks and 302 exam papers, while also indexing data from 32 external sources such as news, statistics, lexical databases, and domain KGs.

The paper is primarily a system/construction and descriptive evaluation study rather than an intervention study with student outcome measurement. Its main conclusions are that EDUKG is much larger and more heterogeneous than prior educational KGs, and that its ontology-guided, hot-swappable construction plus entity-linking-based maintenance can support future educational applications, including tutoring systems, question answering, and educational data mining.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that EDUKG's construction and maintenance pipeline can process textbooks, exam papers, and heterogeneous web data into a large-scale K-12 knowledge graph, indicating substantial gains in indexing and organization efficiency. The system converts data from 32 sources into more than 250 million entities and supports incremental, hot-swappable maintenance, but it does not report a controlled efficiency comparison with baseline systems.
finding.measure: Scale of indexed resources and described system maintenance capability

paper_profiles.title: Development of astronomy research and education in Africa and Ethiopia
paper_profiles.venue: Education and Heritage in the Era of Big Data in Astronomy. Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 367
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a descriptive overview of the rapid development of astronomy research, education, and institutional capacity-building in Africa, with a particular focus on Ethiopia. It argues that astronomy can support broader development goals by contributing to science education, human capacity development, technological innovation, and socio-economic growth.

The paper surveys major astronomy initiatives across African countries, including radio-astronomy collaborations such as SKA, AVN, HIRAX, and related observatories, as well as optical and gamma-ray facilities. It also highlights human-capacity efforts such as postgraduate programs, teacher-training initiatives, outreach, and international collaborations.

A substantial portion of the paper focuses on Ethiopia, describing the creation of the Ethiopian Space Science Society, Entoto Observatory, and the Ethiopian Space Science and Technology Institute, along with postgraduate programs, staff development, policy work, school outreach, and STEM-for-girls activities. The main conclusion is that international collaboration, infrastructure development, and educational programs are key to sustaining astronomy growth in Africa and leveraging it for societal benefit, but the paper does not present a formal evaluation study or quantitative impact assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes substantial institutional growth in astronomy across Africa and Ethiopia, including new observatories, national and regional collaborations, postgraduate programs, professional societies, and policy development. These developments are presented as strengthening research capacity, human-capacity development, and international visibility, but no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional development indicators described qualitatively (e.g., observatories established, postgraduate programs launched, collaborations, policies/roadmaps developed)

paper_profiles.title: Short-Term Efficacy of an Innovative Mobile Phone Technology-Based Intervention for Weight Management for Overweight and Obese Adolescents: Pilot Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examined whether a mobile phone–based weight-management program could improve health behaviors and weight-related outcomes for overweight and obese adolescents receiving care in primary care clinics. The authors were interested both in short-term efficacy and in whether the intervention was feasible and acceptable in routine clinical settings.

The intervention combined a Fitbit Flex activity monitor, a 3-month online educational program (iStart Smart for Teens), and 3 months of biweekly text-message support during maintenance. Participants were 40 adolescents ages 13 to 18, predominantly Chinese American and from low-income families, recruited from two community clinics in northern California. The control group received a pedometer, a food-and-activity diary, and an online general-adolescent-health program.

At 6 months, the intervention group showed significantly better outcomes than the control group on BMI, BMI-z, diastolic blood pressure, physical activity days per week, TV/computer time, fruit and vegetable intake, soda/sweetened drink intake, and physical activity and dietary self-efficacy. Reported effect sizes were medium to large for several outcomes, suggesting the program had promising short-term benefits. The paper concludes that mobile technologies may be a practical adjunct to weight management for adolescents in primary care, especially in culturally tailored, underserved settings.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved adolescents' self-efficacy related to both physical activity and diet at 6 months compared with the control group. In multilevel regression models, the time×group effect was significant for dietary self-efficacy (z=5.05, P<.001; effect size 0.74) and physical activity self-efficacy (z=2.75, P=.01; effect size 0.96).
finding.measure: Physical activity self-efficacy; dietary self-efficacy questionnaires
finding.confidence_interval: 90% CI not_reported for self-efficacy models in the text

finding.finding_summary: The intervention reduced TV and computer time, which is a proxy for sedentary behavior but also reflects improved self-management of daily routines. At 6 months the intervention group had significantly better outcomes than control (z=-3.34, P=.001), with a large effect size reported (0.93 in the table).
finding.measure: TV and computer time (hours/day)

paper_profiles.title: On the Development of a Computer-Based Tool for Formative Student Assessment: Epistemological, Methodological, and Practical Issues
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual and practical discussion of computer-based formative assessment systems in schools, with a focus on how such systems should be designed, calibrated, and used to support learning. The paper addresses a broad question: how can formative assessment be made more valid, scalable, and useful through computer-based tools, especially when the goal is to provide teachers and students with actionable feedback.

The authors develop an interpretive argument for formative assessment using the framework of scoring, generalization, extrapolation, and implication. They argue that computer-based systems can improve objectivity, scoring consistency, item calibration, and the comparability of results across time and grades, especially when paired with item response theory, adaptive testing, and calibrated item banks.

The paper describes a large-scale assessment system developed for German-speaking parts of Switzerland covering German, English, French, and mathematics across grades 3–9. The system is presented as a case example to illustrate item development, vertical scaling, online calibration, item banking, assessment literacy, and ethical/data-protection issues. The authors conclude that computer-based formative assessment can strengthen classroom decision-making and long-term learning progress, but they do not report an evaluation study of student achievement effects in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Collaboration in Designing a Pedagogical Approach in Information Literacy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter addresses how information literacy (IL) teaching should be designed in response to contemporary learning environments and changing student needs. It reviews earlier research on information literacy, especially European work, and argues that IL is best understood as a broader competence involving critical evaluation, ethical use, communication, and problem-solving rather than only search skills.

The chapter’s main empirical basis comes from the authors’ own experiences and small-scale surveys/interviews with university students in Norway and Romania, alongside examples from collaboration and development projects in Moldova and the Western Balkans. These observations are used to illustrate how student preferences, existing library services, and institutional context shape IL training design, such as timing, relevance, use of authentic tasks, and emphasis on evaluation of online information.

The book chapter also synthesizes pedagogical literature on contemporary teaching, didactic design, and student-centered learning. Its conclusion is that effective IL instruction requires flexible, context-sensitive, collaborative teaching that connects library services with academic programs and adapts to learner characteristics and institutional realities. The chapter is largely conceptual and practice-oriented rather than a controlled evaluation of a single intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that information literacy instruction improves students’ ability to find, evaluate, and use information in academic contexts, but the evidence presented is descriptive rather than causal. In the authors’ surveys and interviews, students reported that IL courses were useful and relevant, and they valued practical tools for databases and journals, as well as search and evaluation skills; no standardized achievement effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of course usefulness/relevance and reported learning of information literacy skills
finding.study_size: n=93 (Bergen) and n=100 (Brasov) for the 2007-2008 survey; n=105 (Brasov) and n=12 (Bergen) for the 2016 study

paper_profiles.title: Promotion of mental health in young adults via mobile phone app: study protocol of the ECoWeB (emotional competence for well-being in Young adults) cohort multiple randomised trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a study protocol for the ECoWeB project, which aims to test whether a mobile phone app can improve mental well-being and prevent poor mental health in young people. The study is motivated by the need for scalable, evidence-based mental health promotion and prevention approaches that do not require substantial professional time and can be delivered broadly at population scale.

The intervention uses a cohort multiple randomized controlled trial design with two parallel trials embedded in one longitudinal cohort: ECoWeB-PROMOTE for participants without elevated emotional-competence risk and ECoWeB-PREVENT for those with elevated risk based on baseline emotional competence profiles. Participants aged 16-22 from the UK, Germany, Spain, and Belgium are randomized to one of three arms: usual-practice self-monitoring control, generic CBT self-help in the app, or personalized emotional-competence self-help tailored to their baseline profile.

The app targets emotional competence domains including achievement appraisal, social appraisal, rumination/worry, and emotion knowledge/perception, and it will be evaluated using repeated assessments at baseline, 1, 3, and 12 months. Because this is a protocol, the paper reports planned methods, outcomes, and sample sizes rather than results. The main conclusion is that the trial is designed to provide causal evidence on whether personalized app-based emotional competence training can improve well-being or reduce depressive symptoms in young adults, and whether personalization adds benefit over generic digital CBT self-help.

finding.finding_summary: This is a study protocol and reports no empirical results. It specifies planned measurement of emotional competence, including emotion regulation, emotion knowledge/perception, and emotion production/appraisal, but no effect estimates are available yet. The trial will assess these constructs repeatedly in a planned sample of 2142 young people aged 16-22.
finding.measure: Emotional Competence measures including the brooding subscale of the Ruminative Response Scale, Penn State Worry Questionnaire-Abbreviated, Components of Emotional Understanding Task (CEUT), Geneva Emotion Recognition Test (GERT-S), Rejection Sensitivity Questionnaire, Control Belief Scale, Perceived Academic Control, Growth Mindset Scale, Academic Value scales, and Achievement Emotions Questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: The protocol includes planned assessment of growth mindset, perceived control, and academic value, which are related to metacognitive and self-regulatory skills. However, no results are reported because the paper describes a trial that has not yet been conducted.
finding.measure: Growth Mindset Scale, Control Belief Scale, Perceived Academic Control, Academic Value scales, Achievement Emotions Questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: Twelve Years of Education and Public Outreach with the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper reviews twelve years of the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope Education and Public Outreach (E/PO) program. Rather than testing a single instructional intervention, it describes a portfolio of outreach, curriculum, professional development, and informal learning products intended to increase understanding of high-energy astrophysics, broaden participation in STEM, and support teachers and students across K-14 settings.

The program includes classroom curricula, educator ambassador workshops, online courses, student research experiences, interactive simulations, webcomics, planetarium and television media, and amateur-astronomy activities. The paper reports participation and dissemination counts, along with selected external evaluation notes from WestEd and brief anecdotal feedback, such as GTN interns reporting increased interest in astronomy and science careers and teachers benefiting from the NASA’s Multiwavelength Universe course.

Because the article is primarily descriptive and programmatic, it does not present a controlled impact study or subgroup analysis of achievement outcomes. Its main conclusion is that the Fermi E/PO infrastructure has reached large audiences, supported teacher professional development, and produced widely used standards-aligned materials, with evaluation used to refine and sustain the program.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the Global Telescope Network and related authentic research experiences are intended to help students develop scientific inquiry skills, and a WestEd interview of four female high school interns found that their interest in astronomy, science, and the scientific method had grown considerably over the summer. No controlled effect size or pre/post achievement metric is reported.
finding.measure: Interest in astronomy, science, and the scientific method; scientific inquiry skills (interview/evaluation feedback)
finding.study_size: n=4 interviewees for the GTN intern feedback; broader participation over 200 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes inquiry-based and research-based activities as supporting scientific inquiry skills, problem solving, and application of scientific methods. Evidence is descriptive rather than experimental, and no quantitative skill gains are reported.
finding.measure: Scientific inquiry skills and problem-solving from research experiences and curriculum activities

finding.finding_summary: Several program components are described as increasing student interest, engagement, and motivation in science, including GTN internships and after-school/club activities. The only extractable participant feedback is qualitative: four female GTN interns reported that their interest in astronomy, science, and the scientific method had grown considerably over the summer, but no validated survey scores or effect sizes are given.
finding.measure: Interest in astronomy/science; career interest; engagement feedback
finding.study_size: n=4 interviewees for the specific internship feedback; other program counts reported descriptively

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames online curricula, downloadable materials, and teacher workshops as efficiency-enhancing supports for broad dissemination and implementation. However, it does not measure workload reduction, time savings, or productivity with a formal metric.
finding.measure: Program dissemination and implementation supports (online curriculum, downloadable materials, workshops)

paper_profiles.title: Use of Analogies in Science Education, A Systematic Mapping Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic mapping study of the literature on analogies as a didactic strategy in science education. Its goal was not to test a single intervention, but to identify, classify, and synthesize how analogies have been used in science teaching, what instructional models have been proposed, what research methodologies have been used, what classroom resources support analogy use, and how learning outcomes have been evaluated.

The authors searched five databases for English-language publications from the prior 20 years and retained 28 studies, with a strong representation of primary and secondary school contexts. The review reports that analogies are commonly used to help students understand abstract scientific concepts, often through verbal explanation, images, illustrations, and videos. It also identifies multiple instructional models for analogy use (e.g., teacher-generated, student-generated, explicit mapping, FAR-type approaches) and notes that studies typically assess learning with multiple-choice tests, interviews, written pre/post measures, delayed posttests, and student-created analogies.

The paper concludes that analogies are a widely used and potentially valuable tool for science learning, especially when teachers make the mapping explicit and note where the analogy breaks down. However, because this is a mapping study rather than an effect study, it does not provide a pooled effect size or subgroup moderator evidence. It mainly offers an organized overview of the field and practical implications for how analogies can be selected, presented, and assessed in science classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The mapping study concludes that the reviewed literature generally supports analogies as a way to improve science understanding and conceptual learning, with many studies using pre/post tests, multiple-choice tests, and analogy-generation tasks to assess gains. Across the 28 included studies, the paper reports that analogies are used to facilitate learning of scientific concepts, but it does not synthesize a pooled effect size or provide moderator estimates.
finding.measure: Science learning / conceptual understanding measured through multiple-choice tests, oral tests, pretest-posttest assessments, delayed posttests, interviews, and student-generated analogies
finding.study_size: n=28 studies (systematic map); individual study samples not consistently reported

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that several analogy-based approaches were studied in relation to student interest, motivation, and self-efficacy, including self-generated analogies and elaborate analogies in science texts. The paper does not pool results, but it indicates that these affective outcomes were commonly measured alongside achievement in some studies.
finding.measure: Interest, motivation, self-efficacy, and attitudes toward learning

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for collecting open-ended, real-time formative assessment responses on pen-enabled mobile devices, appears effective across a variety of educational settings. The motivation is practical: instructors need an efficient way to gather immediate evidence of student thinking during instruction and then respond quickly to misconceptions.

The paper is a multi-vignette report drawing on experiences from seven instructional contexts across the United States and Mexico, including K-12 algebra, undergraduate and graduate physics and engineering, chemistry, and food science. Students used tablet PCs, iPads, and Android devices to draw, sketch, write, or graph responses to open questions, and instructors used those responses to adjust instruction in real time.

Evidence is mostly descriptive and comparative rather than experimental. Reported results include reduced persistence of a triple-integrals misconception in one calculus section compared with a non-InkSurvey section, improved Algebra I mastery in a high school setting, gains in quiz performance in undergraduate and graduate courses, improved problem-solving skills in an upper-level engineering physics course, and strong positive student attitudes. The paper concludes that InkSurvey has broad potential for supporting formative assessment and learning across diverse environments, while also noting that some claims warrant further investigation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved mathematics learning in a high school Algebra I setting using InkSurvey for regular individual and whole-group feedback. It states that students gained traction on mastery of fundamental concepts on standards-based assessments compared with students not exposed to the InkSurvey intervention, and notes that female students in particular showed greater learning gains than the control group, although no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Standards-based assessments in Algebra I; exam questions on triple integrals in Calculus III

finding.finding_summary: Across physics and engineering contexts, InkSurvey was associated with improved understanding and problem-solving performance. In one Calculus III example, only 1 of 87 students still showed a triple-integrals misconception on a summative assessment two weeks later, compared with 12 of 103 in a similar lecture section without InkSurvey; the paper also reports steady semester-long improvement in upper-level engineering physics problem-solving skills and increased competence from about 1.8 to about 3.1 on a 4-point scale in chemical engineering courses when InkSurvey-guided simulation work was added.
finding.measure: Summative exam items, problem-solving skill scores, and 4-point competence ratings on concept understanding
finding.study_size: n=87; n=103; study size not_reported for other vignette data

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that InkSurvey increased engagement, motivation, and perceived usefulness of feedback. In a survey of 63 junior-level physics students, 54 (86%) said their InkSurvey responses gave the instructor a better understanding of what they do and do not understand, and 48 (76%) said creating responses helped them better understand the material or realize what they did and did not understand.
finding.measure: Student survey responses on feedback usefulness, metacognitive awareness, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests InkSurvey supports metacognition and problem-solving as students analyze their own thinking and revise understanding in real time. Students reported that the tool helped them identify misconceptions and think through solutions more carefully, and instructors observed improved problem-solving skills and deeper conceptual understanding; however, no standardized durable-skills effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student self-reports of metacognition; instructor/analyzed problem-solving skill scores
finding.study_size: n=63 for survey data; not_reported for problem-solving study

finding.finding_summary: In undergraduate and graduate non-math science/engineering courses, InkSurvey was associated with improved performance on summative quizzes and course tasks. The paper reports mean improvements of 0.6 points in an undergraduate course and 0.5 points in a graduate course on 10-point quizzes after incorporating frequent formative assessment with Tablet PCs and InkSurvey, compared with student performance in the same courses four years earlier.
finding.measure: Summative quiz scores out of 10

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that InkSurvey helps instructors identify misconceptions quickly and tailor instruction in real time, reducing the delay between assessment and response. Reported benefits include immediate feedback, quicker identification of common difficulties, and more efficient adjustment of teaching pace and follow-up explanations, but these are described qualitatively rather than with workload metrics.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported ability to identify difficulties and provide immediate feedback

paper_profiles.title: Contributions from Cognitive Research to Mathematics and Science Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Workshop on Research in Science and Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This invited workshop talk argues that cognitive research can inform mathematics and science education by clarifying how knowledge is constructed, organized, accessed, and used. Rather than presenting a single intervention study, the paper synthesizes cognitive-science ideas—especially constructivism, expert–novice differences, misconceptions, metacognition, and problem-solving models—to motivate instructional practices that go beyond information transmission.

The paper is aimed at educators and researchers working in mathematics and science education, with examples drawn largely from introductory physics and general science/mathematics contexts. It reviews evidence on misconceptions, chunking, hierarchical knowledge structures, and novice means–ends problem solving, then proposes pedagogy such as using multiple representations, building interconnections among concepts, extending context, comparing and contrasting cases, and revisiting content in multiple passes. The central conclusion is that effective teaching requires modeling the learner’s knowledge state and engaging in interactive, communication-based instruction that helps students construct more expert-like knowledge structures.

Because this is a conceptual/invited talk rather than an empirical evaluation of a specific educational intervention, it does not provide extractable subgroup or moderator effects, and it offers no K-12 achievement effect sizes. Its main contribution is theoretical and practice-oriented: to translate cognitive research into general instructional principles for science and mathematics classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reviews cognitive research relevant to mathematics learning, but it does not report original achievement data. It argues that prior conceptual frameworks can impede mathematics learning less than science learning in some cases, and that novices benefit from instruction that promotes concept-based reasoning, multiple representations, and hierarchical knowledge organization.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes research on misconceptions, novice–expert differences, and problem solving in physics and related sciences. It reports that experts outperform novices in recalling realistic circuits and classifying problems by deep structure, while novices focus on surface features and means–ends analysis; however, these are literature summaries, not new empirical results from this paper.
finding.measure: problem categorization, circuit recall, qualitative problem-solving performance

finding.finding_summary: The talk emphasizes motivation, self-confidence, perseverance, and self-motivation as important components of successful learning and expertise development. It cites prior work suggesting that confidence-building, success-oriented task sequencing, and reducing cognitive overload can support student persistence, but it does not provide original quantitative effects.
finding.measure: observed student persistence, self-confidence, self-motivation (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is metacognition, reflection, and expert-like problem solving. The author argues that students should learn to perform qualitative analysis, recognize patterns, and reflect on solutions before and after execution; the cited studies suggest that training novices to classify by principle can shift problem categorization in the expert-like direction, but no effect size is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: qualitative analysis before problem solving; problem categorization by principle vs surface feature; reflection/evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that communication-based, constructivist teaching and the use of multiple representations, cumulative exams, and repeated passes over content can make learning more efficient. These claims are argued theoretically rather than demonstrated with original productivity or workload data.
finding.measure: instructional efficiency / communication effectiveness (conceptual)

paper_profiles.title: Work from Home and Job Satisfaction: Differences by Disability Status among Healthcare Workers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether working from home is associated with better job satisfaction and workplace experiences, and whether that association differs by disability status. The central question is whether remote work can reduce disability-related gaps in job satisfaction and related perceptions such as organizational commitment, perceived support, inclusion, and relationships with managers and coworkers.

The study uses a novel survey of healthcare workers from a large state-wide university-affiliated health system. The analytic sample includes 993 employees, of whom 228 reported a disability or health impairment. The authors estimate multivariable regressions with disability-by-work-from-home interaction terms, comparing employees who do not work from home, work from home less than three days per week, or work from home three or more days per week.

The results show that workers with disabilities report substantially less favorable workplace experiences than workers without disabilities on most measures, even after covariate adjustment, although they do not differ significantly on the single direct job-satisfaction item. Work from home is positively associated with job satisfaction and many work-experience measures for the full sample, but the positive association is generally smaller for employees with disabilities and does not close the disability gap. The strongest exception is that remote work appears to be especially weak or even negative for supervisor and coworker relations among employees with disabilities, suggesting social isolation may be a key mechanism.

finding.finding_summary: Working from home was associated with improved work experiences that likely support productivity and task functioning, including job autonomy and perceived organizational support, across the full sample of healthcare workers (n=993). For example, compared with no work from home, working from home 3+ days/week was associated with higher job autonomy (b=0.294) and perceived organizational support (b=0.253), while 1-2 days/week was also positive (b=0.226 and b=0.188, respectively).
finding.measure: Job autonomy; perceived organizational support; related workplace experience indices

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that working from home is generally associated with more favorable job satisfaction-related experiences, but the benefits are smaller for workers with disabilities and do not eliminate gaps. Job satisfaction itself did not differ significantly by disability status (0.592 vs 0.648), but workers with disabilities reported higher turnover intentions (0.420 vs 0.323), lower organizational commitment (0.459 vs 0.530), lower perceived support (0.309 vs 0.403), and weaker inclusion/climate measures; remote work improved many of these outcomes overall, though less so for the disability group.
finding.measure: Job satisfaction, turnover intentions, organizational commitment, perceived organizational support, openness/inclusion indices

paper_profiles.title: Modernizing use of regression models in physics education research: A review of hierarchical linear modeling
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) for physics education research and argues that many commonly used single-level regression analyses are inappropriate for hierarchical educational data, such as students nested within courses. The paper contrasts disaggregation, aggregation, and HLM using a toy example and then reanalyzes a real multi-institution dataset to show how ignoring nesting can bias coefficients, standard errors, and statistical significance.

The empirical application uses pretest and post-test concept inventory data from the Learning About STEM Student Outcomes (LASSO) platform: 5,959 undergraduate students in 112 introductory physics courses at 17 institutions. The authors compare multiple linear regression (MLR) and HLM models predicting gain scores from student pretest scores and course instructional context (lecture, collaborative learning without learning assistants, and collaborative learning with learning assistants). They find that MLR overweights large collaborative-learning classes and produces inflated standard errors and stronger apparent effects than HLM. In the preferred HLM model, both learning-assistant use and collaborative learning without learning assistants are positive predictors of gains, but the collaborative-without-LA coefficient is no longer statistically significant (Coef.=3.26, SE=3.02, p=0.283) after accounting for nesting. The paper’s main conclusion is methodological: educational researchers should use multilevel methods when data are hierarchical because single-level regression can yield misleading findings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies student gains on physics concept inventories, using Force Concept Inventory (FCI) and Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation (FMCE) post-test gains as the outcome. In the preferred HLM model, the intraclass correlation was 13%, showing meaningful course-level variation; model 3 estimated a negative association between pretest and gain (Coef.=-0.44, SE=0.02, p<0.001), and course context coefficients differed notably by modeling approach (e.g., collaborative learning without LAs: MLR Coef.=12.99 vs HLM Coef.=3.26, p=0.283 in HLM).
finding.measure: Physics concept inventory gain scores (post-test minus pretest) on FCI and FMCE

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CHI workshop / ACM conference paper)
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers and instructors (working with K-12 classrooms)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 teachers can be supported to integrate AI education into core subject classrooms, especially for non-computing subjects and diverse learner needs. The authors note that most AI curricula are standalone or computer-science oriented, which can limit accessibility for teachers and students outside CS pathways.

To address this, they ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from multiple countries and subject areas. Participants learned basic AI concepts and tools, then worked in small groups to co-create integrated AI lesson plans for social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The paper analyzes workshop audio, questionnaires, and participant deliverables to identify teacher priorities and design considerations.

The main conclusions are that teachers want AI curriculum that supports evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration, and that AI can be meaningfully embedded into core subjects through three main integration points: data, reflection, and ethics. The study is primarily design-oriented and qualitative, with no student outcome evaluation; its contribution is an exemplar of how to co-design accessible AI curriculum with educators and how AI can be integrated into non-CS K-12 contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the co-designed AI curricula should support student engagement, collaboration, and reflection, and that these features were important for making AI learning accessible and motivating in K-12 classrooms. The workshop did not measure student outcomes directly; the evidence comes from educator discussion and the resulting lesson-plan drafts from 15 participants.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions and co-designed lesson-plan features related to engagement, collaboration, and reflection

finding.finding_summary: The study centrally focuses on durable skills such as collaboration, critical reflection, and metacognition as design priorities in integrated AI curriculum. Teachers repeatedly emphasized group work, student reflection on AI outputs and ethics, and using frameworks to help students reason about data and model behavior, but no student-level achievement effect was measured.
finding.measure: Teacher-generated curriculum design features and discussion themes on collaboration, reflection, and critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: One co-designed curriculum targeted literacy for students with learning disabilities, using vocabulary words and image classification to integrate AI into English literacy instruction. The paper describes the lesson design and teacher discussion, but does not report literacy achievement outcomes or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum content and alignment to English literacy standards

finding.finding_summary: An ESL-focused curriculum was co-designed around building an AI-powered pronunciation application, explicitly linking AI to speaking/pronunciation practice. The paper reports the lesson concept and teacher reasoning about using pronunciation data, but it does not provide student fluency outcomes or any quantitative effect estimates.
finding.measure: Co-designed ESL pronunciation curriculum and teacher discussion of pronunciation practice

finding.finding_summary: The paper documents an integrated social studies curriculum centered on data, government policy, and the CROWN Act, showing that teachers could embed AI into non-CS core subjects such as social studies, history, and economics. This is evidence of curriculum design feasibility rather than an achievement effect; no learner outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Co-designed social studies curriculum integrating AI concepts with government policy and social justice content

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that involving teachers in co-design revealed practical needs for AI curriculum adoption, including scaffolding, tool usability, logistics, and teacher confidence. The remote workshop produced three implementable curriculum drafts and suggests a pathway for broader institutional adoption of integrated AI education, but no policy-level outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Teacher confidence, workshop outputs, and feasibility of integrated AI curriculum adoption

paper_profiles.title: “Medium-n studies" in computing education conferences
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conference guidelines / research methods paper; no student population studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how computing education conference guidelines handle empirical studies with small, medium, and large sample sizes, with a focus on when authors should compute p-values and when statistical testing is inappropriate because a study is underpowered. The author frames the issue as a tension between replicability, statistical rigor, and the practical realities of common class-sized datasets in computing education research.

Rather than evaluating an intervention or instructional practice, the paper surveys author and reviewer guidelines from several computing education conferences, including ICER, SIGCSE TS, ITiCSE, EAAI, CompEd, and Koli Calling. The paper summarizes how these venues discuss statistical analysis, case studies, and qualitative work, and notes that guidance varies substantially across conferences.

The main conclusion is normative: the author argues that conference venues should more explicitly require either rich qualitative analysis or appropriate statistical tests, because papers with medium-sized datasets can otherwise be ambiguous and potentially misleading. The paper does not report student outcome effects, but instead offers preliminary recommendations for conference policy and research reporting practices.

paper_profiles.title: Income, education, and other poverty-related variables: a journey through Bayesian hierarchical models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Bayesian hierarchical models can be used to explain poverty-related variables in Thailand using household-level administrative survey data. The authors compare extreme modeling choices—complete pooling and no pooling—to hierarchical models that partially pool information across regions, and they evaluate model fit using WAIC. Although the central motivating problem is poverty and policy modeling rather than education research, the paper focuses heavily on household income as a function of regional context, education level, and years of formal education.

The data come from Thai government agencies and include nearly 13 million households nationwide. The paper first models monthly household income by region, then extends the analysis to a two-cluster model using both region and education level, and finally fits Bayesian hierarchical regressions relating income to years of education. Across these models, higher education is consistently associated with higher household income, while regional differences shrink substantially after accounting for education. In the regression models, the best-performing specification is a robust hierarchical model with varying intercepts and slopes, indicating that additional years of education are associated with higher income in every region and that the income–education relationship is broadly similar across regions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that Bayesian hierarchical models fit Thai household poverty-related data better than complete pooling or no pooling alternatives, based on WAIC comparisons. For monthly income, the preferred model was a hierarchical specification with fixed ν (WAIC=1378.58), outperforming complete pooling (WAIC=1410.13) and no pooling (WAIC=1382.01) on a nationwide household dataset (n≈12.98 million, minus 569 zero-income households).
finding.measure: Model fit and explanatory performance using WAIC on household income and poverty-related variables

finding.finding_summary: Education is strongly associated with higher household income in Thailand, and the relationship is consistent across regions. The paper reports that each additional year of education increases monthly household income by about 1,880 THB nationally, with regional estimates ranging from 1,278 THB in Western Thailand to 2,545 THB in Eastern Thailand; households with high education earn 8,325 THB more per month than mid-education households and 14,844 THB more than low-education households.
finding.measure: Monthly household income by education level and years of formal education
finding.confidence_interval: National yearly-education effect: (1322, 2443) THB; regional intervals reported in Table 5

paper_profiles.title: Dynamic Models of Learning and Education Measurement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a probabilistic measurement model of learning based on pretest-posttest scores and normalized gain. The central question is why normalized gain is often weakly correlated with pretest score across classes and populations, and what that pattern implies about learning processes and student ability.

The author proposes a dynamic score-based model with three types of transitions: alpha processes (instruction acting on students’ incorrect or missing knowledge), beta processes (instruction acting on already-correct knowledge), and gamma processes (associative interactions between correct and incorrect knowledge). Under simplifying assumptions, the model derives the normalized-gain formula and shows why gain can be independent of pretest score when learning is dominated by alpha processes, while positive gain-pretest correlations emerge when gamma processes or non-constant alpha are present.

The paper applies the framework to physics education data, especially force concept inventory (FCI) and other concept inventories in calculus-based mechanics and related courses. It uses previously published class and student data to illustrate how pre/post change patterns differ across populations such as average university students versus honor/elite students, and how these differences may reflect varying mixtures of alpha and gamma processes. The main conclusion is that normalized gain is not a pure measure of instruction alone; it reflects both instructional effectiveness and student learning ability, and its relationship with pretest score depends on population composition, prior training, and possible measurement noise.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a theoretical/analytic treatment of scientific-reasoning-related assessment in physics education, using normalized gain on concept inventories and Lawson test scores as the main examples. It reports prior empirical findings that FCI normalized gains correlate positively with scientific reasoning ability, including r=0.51 with Lawson test scores (N=65), and interprets this as evidence that higher general reasoning ability is associated with higher learning gains.
finding.measure: Force Concept Inventory (FCI) normalized gain; Lawson Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning scores

paper_profiles.title: Researching Effective Pedagogy in the Early Years
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines what constitutes effective pedagogy in the Early Years/Foundations Stage and how practitioner practices relate to children’s developmental progress. It was written in response to evidence from the larger EPPE longitudinal study and asks which pedagogical strategies are associated with better cognitive and social/behavioral outcomes for young children.

The study combines literature review, intensive case studies, systematic naturalistic and timed child observations, interviews with staff/parents/managers, documentary analysis, and a survey of 46 childminders. The main focus is on 14 Foundation Stage settings in England: nursery classes, nursery schools, playgroups, private day nurseries, combined/early excellence centres, a day nursery, and two reception classes, selected because they were judged or shown to be effective. The report emphasizes pedagogical practices such as sustained shared thinking, adult-child verbal interaction, formative assessment and differentiation, parent partnership, discipline practices that involve talking through conflicts, curriculum balance, and the role of qualifications and training.

The authors conclude that the most effective settings balance adult-led and child-initiated activity, use sustained shared thinking more often, differentiate and assess formatively, and combine direct teaching with rich open-framework play opportunities. Higher-quality provision is associated with stronger literacy and mathematics experiences, more challenging cognitive interactions, and better social outcomes when adults help children work through conflicts. The report also finds that reception classes are more teacher-initiated and more focused on literacy/mathematics than pre-school settings, while childminders value play and home–setting continuity but had limited uptake of the new curriculum guidance at the time.

finding.finding_summary: The report finds that the most effective settings provided children with more experience of literacy activities, and that qualified staff spent the greatest proportion of their time with children on literacy. The authors also report that open-ended questioning and sustained shared thinking were associated with better cognitive achievement, but they do not provide a single overall effect size for literacy attainment in this report.
finding.measure: Observed curriculum balance / literacy activities; child cognitive outcomes related to pre-reading and language; staff interaction observations

finding.finding_summary: Adult-child verbal interaction, especially sustained shared thinking, was identified as a key pedagogical feature supporting children’s learning and language-related development. The study reports that effective settings used more verbal extension, modeling, and open-ended questioning, though open-ended questions comprised only 5.1% of questioning overall in these settings.
finding.measure: Observed adult-child verbal interactions; questioning type; sustained shared thinking episodes

finding.finding_summary: The most effective settings provided children with more mathematics activity, and teachers devoted a high proportion of their time to mathematics. The report also states that settings with stronger cognitive outcomes offered more challenging academic experiences, including mathematics, but does not report a numeric effect size for math attainment.
finding.measure: Observed curriculum balance / mathematics activities; child cognitive outcomes related to number concepts

finding.finding_summary: Science appears as part of the curriculum balance analysis, and the report notes that curriculum differentiation and effective pedagogy should support children’s cognitive progress across curriculum areas. However, the paper provides limited direct evidence on science-specific outcomes beyond descriptive observations of curriculum coverage, so the finding is suggestive rather than strong.
finding.measure: Observed curriculum balance / science curriculum coverage

finding.finding_summary: The report finds that the most effective settings offered more physical development activities and, in some cases, more creative development and knowledge-and-understanding-of-the-world experiences depending on setting type and child age. Reception classes were especially heavy on literacy and mathematics, while younger children and those with learning delay experienced more PSE and creative development; these are descriptive curriculum-balance findings rather than outcome effects.
finding.measure: Observed curriculum balance across physical development, creative development, and knowledge/understanding of the world

finding.finding_summary: Social and behavioral development is a major focus of the report, and the authors link better outcomes to staff practices such as talking through conflicts, supporting assertiveness, and maintaining consistent discipline policies. The report reports that effective settings had better social/behavioral developmental outcomes and more sustained shared thinking; no single numeric effect size is given in the narrative text provided.
finding.measure: EPPE social/behavioral outcomes (independence, concentration, cooperation, conformity, less anti-social/worried/upset, peer sociability); observed conflict-resolution practices

finding.finding_summary: The report strongly emphasizes higher-order thinking, including sustained shared thinking, initiative, collaboration, and children’s ability to extend activity with adults or peers. Effective settings were associated with more child-initiated episodes, more adult extension of child-initiated activity, and more challenge, suggesting gains in collaboration and critical thinking, although no formal effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Observed sustained shared thinking; child- vs adult-initiated episodes; cognitive challenge coding

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses how staff qualifications and organization affected the distribution of adult time across curriculum areas, but it does not evaluate productivity or workload as an outcome. The evidence is largely descriptive: qualified staff spent more time on literacy and mathematics, while untrained adults spent more time in creative development; this informs staffing/practice organization rather than efficiency per se.
finding.measure: Observed staff time allocation by curriculum area and qualification level

finding.finding_summary: The report examines the influence of the Curriculum guidance for the foundation stage (CGFS) and transition practices across settings, and concludes that it improved continuity between pre-school and school but had uneven implementation. Childminders and some settings reported limited adoption or concern that the guidance/ELGs were too formal, while others reported changes in assessment and reception-class practice.
finding.measure: Interviews with staff, managers, parents, and childminders about CGFS implementation and transition; documentary analysis

paper_profiles.title: Chatbot to improve learning punctuation in Spanish and to enhance open and flexible learning environments
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a chatbot can improve students’ mastery of Spanish punctuation compared with a more traditional paper-based practice method. The paper is situated in the context of university access coursework at the National University of Distance Education (UNED, Spain), where students need self-regulated, out-of-class practice in a blended-learning environment.

The authors designed a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with control and experimental groups (total n=103; control n=51, experimental n=52). Both groups received the same initial face-to-face instruction; afterward, the control group completed a PDF dossier of punctuation exercises, while the experimental group practiced with two chatbot-based punctuation activities for two weeks without tutorial support. The final assessment included more complex punctuation tasks. The experimental group scored higher on the posttest than the control group (mean 32.1346 vs 28.4706; p<0.001), and the authors report particularly stronger gains for correct use of periods, colons, and commas.

In addition to achievement outcomes, the study analyzed forum posts from the experimental group to understand learners’ perceptions. Students described the chatbot as supportive, interactive, mobile/ubiquitous, and useful for feedback, suggesting positive affective and usability perceptions. Overall, the paper concludes that chatbots can serve as a flexible practice-and-feedback tool for language learning, especially for punctuation and other writing skills that benefit from repeated practice outside class.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group using the chatbot outperformed the control group on the final punctuation test. Posttest mean scores were 32.1346 for the experimental group versus 28.4706 for the control group (n=52 vs n=51), with a statistically significant difference (p<0.001) after two weeks of practice.
finding.measure: Spanish punctuation test / exam performance (correction of text with punctuation errors, multiple-choice questions, punctuation of blank text)

paper_profiles.title: Differentiating anxiety forms and their role in academic performance from primary to secondary school
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how three forms of anxiety—general anxiety, test anxiety, and mathematics anxiety—cluster in students and how those anxiety profiles relate to academic performance. The authors ask whether math anxiety is best understood as a single construct or as part of broader patterns of anxiety that differ by developmental stage, and whether those patterns help explain variation in math and reading achievement.

The study analyzed a large sample of 1,720 UK students in Year 4 (ages 8–9) and Years 7/8 (ages 11–13). Students completed self-report measures of general anxiety, test anxiety, and math anxiety, along with standardized tests of mathematics and reading. The authors used latent profile analysis to identify anxiety subgroups separately by age group, then examined whether profile membership predicted performance beyond math anxiety alone.

In Year 4, anxiety profiles were largely undifferentiated and reflected low, slight, moderate, or high anxiety across all measures. In Year 7/8, more distinct profiles emerged, including a profile with elevated general anxiety, a profile with elevated academic anxiety (test anxiety and math anxiety), and a high-anxiety profile with elevations across all three forms. The main conclusion is that older students show more specific anxiety patterns, and students with high general anxiety performed better than students with specifically academic anxiety at comparable math-anxiety levels. The paper argues for a reciprocal explanation of math anxiety and performance and suggests that interventions may need to be tailored to a student’s broader anxiety profile rather than math anxiety alone.

finding.finding_summary: Reading performance varied significantly by anxiety profile in both age groups. In Year 4, one-way ANOVA showed a significant effect of latent profile on standardized reading performance, F(3,813)=6.22, p<0.001; in Year 7/8, the effect was also significant, F(3,899)=11.00, p<0.001. In the secondary sample, adding latent profile improved prediction of reading performance beyond math anxiety and gender, and the 'High anxiety' profile showed higher reading performance than the 'Academic anxiety' profile at similar math-anxiety levels.
finding.measure: Standardized reading performance (HGRT-II)
finding.study_size: n=1720 overall; Year 4 n=817; Year 7/8 n=903

finding.finding_summary: Math performance differed significantly across anxiety profiles in both samples. In Year 4, profile membership predicted standardized math performance, F(3,813)=25.80, p<0.001; in Year 7/8, the effect remained significant, F(3,899)=13.82, p<0.001. In Year 7/8, adding latent profile significantly improved prediction of math performance beyond math anxiety alone (LRT=21.56, p<0.001), with the 'High anxiety' profile performing better than expected from math anxiety alone and better than the 'Academic anxiety' profile (beta=8.00, SE=2.08, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Standardized mathematics performance (MaLT)
finding.study_size: n=1720 overall; Year 4 n=817; Year 7/8 n=903

finding.finding_summary: The central outcome of the paper is the clustering of general anxiety, test anxiety, and math anxiety into distinct latent profiles. In Year 4, profiles were largely severity-based (low/slight/moderate/high across all three measures), whereas in Year 7/8 more differentiated profiles emerged, including a general-anxiety-only profile and an academic-anxiety profile. The study is descriptive rather than intervention-based, but it shows that anxiety patterns become more specific with age and are meaningfully associated with achievement.
finding.measure: Self-reported general anxiety (RCMAS-2), test anxiety (CTAS), and math anxiety (mAMAS) latent profile analysis
finding.study_size: n=1720 overall; Year 4 n=817; Year 7/8 n=903

paper_profiles.title: ConvoLearn: A Dataset of Constructivist Tutor-Student Dialogue
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a pedagogical gap in LLM-based tutoring: current models often answer too directly and do not support dialogic, knowledge-building instruction. The authors propose ConvoLearn, a semi-synthetic dataset of constructivist tutor-student dialogues grounded in knowledge-building theory and organized around six dimensions: cognitive engagement, formative assessment, accountability, cultural responsiveness, metacognition, and power dynamics.

The dataset contains 1,250 high-quality multi-turn dialogues in middle school Earth Science, created through interactions between human teachers and a simulated student. Teachers were recruited to generate and annotate conversations, and the authors used these dialogues to fine-tune several open-source LLMs with QLoRA. They then evaluated model outputs both intrinsically with an auxiliary classifier and extrinsically through a blinded human study with 31 teachers.

The main finding is that fine-tuning on ConvoLearn substantially improved the pedagogical quality of a Mistral-7B model. In human evaluation, the fine-tuned model scored significantly higher overall (M=4.10, SD=1.03) than both the base Mistral model (M=2.59, SD=1.11) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (M=2.87, SD=1.29), with especially strong ratings on Power Dynamics and Formative Assessment. The paper concludes that knowledge-building dialogue data can improve LLM tutoring behavior, though it does not claim direct student learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on middle-school Earth Science dialogue and shows that fine-tuning on ConvoLearn improved the pedagogical quality of science tutoring conversations. In human evaluation by 31 teachers (148 rated examples), the fine-tuned Mistral-7B achieved a mean effectiveness rating of 4.10 (SD=1.03) versus 2.87 (SD=1.29) for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and 2.59 (SD=1.11) for the base Mistral model, indicating substantially stronger science-tutoring discourse rather than measured student science achievement.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated effectiveness of science tutoring dialogues in middle school Earth Science

finding.finding_summary: The study explicitly operationalizes and evaluates dialogue behaviors tied to durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration/argumentation, and evidence-based reasoning. Teacher ratings suggest the fine-tuned model improved these behaviors overall, with the intrinsic evaluation also showing higher predicted effectiveness for the fine-tuned Mistral-7B (M=4.25, SD=0.65 across 72 seed questions) than Qwen-2.5-7B (M=3.75, SD=0.77) and Llama-3.1-8B (M=3.11, SD=0.90).
finding.measure: Teacher-rated pedagogical effectiveness; model-scored effectiveness of tutoring dialogues
finding.study_size: n=31 teachers for extrinsic evaluation; n=72 seed questions for intrinsic evaluation
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.03 (teacher ratings for fine-tuned Mistral); SD=0.65 (intrinsic mean predicted score dispersion across seeds)

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper does not measure student motivation or persistence directly, it targets interactional features that support engagement, ownership, and constructive participation in tutoring conversations. The fine-tuned model was rated especially highly on power-dynamics-oriented dialogue moves (e.g., student ownership of ideas), with mean teacher ratings of 4.42 for Power Dynamics, suggesting stronger support for engaged and agency-promoting interaction.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings on Power Dynamics dimension in tutoring dialogues

finding.finding_summary: The paper develops and evaluates an LLM tutoring dataset for middle-school Earth Science rather than studying a standard academic content outcome such as literacy or math. The fine-tuned model produced higher-quality curriculum-aligned science explanations and questioning behavior, with domain-generalization maintained across Earth Science and Physics seed questions (teacher-rated means 4.11 and 4.08, respectively).
finding.measure: Teacher-rated effectiveness of curriculum-aligned tutoring dialogues across Earth Science and Physics prompts
finding.study_size: n=72 seed questions; n=31 teachers in human evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes a dataset- and model-building pipeline intended to help developers and educators produce more pedagogically aligned tutoring interactions, but it does not directly measure teacher workload or productivity in practice. Its strongest operational signal is that the fine-tuned model generated more effective dialogues than baselines, implying potential efficiency gains for tutoring-system development, though no direct efficiency outcome was reported.
finding.measure: Indirect improvement in generation/evaluation pipeline quality

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically the Blackboard Learning System, in a university setting. The authors frame formative assessment as a diagnostic, feedback-oriented process that differs from summative testing, and argue that frequent low-stakes assessments can improve learning when paired with timely, detailed feedback.

The intervention proposed is a sequence of weekly or fortnightly online tests delivered through Blackboard, including immediate scoring and explanatory feedback. The paper describes the design of a 10-item Java online test and discusses how Blackboard tools such as discussion forums and virtual classrooms could further support feedback and learner reflection. The study population is Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) students, with a survey of students from Business, Engineering, and IT streams about continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option.

Methodologically, the paper combines a literature-based argument for formative assessment with questionnaire data on student perceptions. Results indicate generally positive student support for frequent internal assessments, especially because they break content into smaller units, provide immediate teacher feedback, and help students monitor strengths and weaknesses. The authors conclude that online formative assessment through Blackboard is workable and may support better learning and potentially improve summative semester results, though the paper does not report direct achievement outcomes from an experimental comparison.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments were helpful and supported learning progress. They valued immediate teacher feedback, which they said helped them identify strengths and weaknesses and check whether they were on track; however, the paper reports perceptions rather than achievement effects.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire responses about continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and attitudes toward Blackboard online tests

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents formative assessment as supporting metacognition and self-monitoring, with students using feedback to reflect on mistakes and understand how to improve. In the survey, students said the online tests helped them study small topics progressively and keep in touch with the subject throughout the semester, indicating gains in reflection and self-regulation rather than measured performance outcomes.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, reflection, and progressive learning through frequent online assessments

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment through Blackboard is useful for supporting course learning and may improve performance on semester-end examinations. The main evidence is student perception: a majority favored frequent internal assessments and believed the approach would help them learn individual topics progressively and perform better on summative semester exams, but no direct test-score comparison is reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of learning support and expected performance on summative semester examinations

paper_profiles.title: Towards digitalisation of summative and formative assessments in academic teaching of statistics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of digitizing complex assessment tasks in university-level statistics courses without losing the pedagogical value of open-ended exercises. The authors argue that common web-based homework and assessment systems often support only simple item formats, limited feedback, or static exercise generation, which is insufficient for higher statistics where students must choose solution strategies and sometimes submit intermediate calculations.

To address this, the paper presents enhancements to the JACK e-assessment system that integrate the R programming environment through Rserve. This allows instructors to generate parameterized tasks, evaluate student submissions, create data-driven plots, and deliver detailed step-specific feedback and hints. The system is designed to support both formative practice and summative tests/exams, with different settings for feedback, retries, and grading.

The paper is primarily a system and design report grounded in use in two large undergraduate statistics lectures at the University of Duisburg-Essen, each with up to 700 students per semester. The authors describe practical usage scenarios, the structure of multi-stage exercises, and implementation details, but do not present a controlled impact study. Their main conclusion is that the approach is feasible and useful for complex statistics instruction, with strong uptake in the courses, while noting that formal analysis of learning effects is left for future research.

finding.finding_summary: The system is reported to reduce manual grading effort and support large-enrollment statistics courses by automating generation, evaluation, and feedback for complex exercises. The paper does not report a controlled effect size, but it states that JACK is used heavily in lectures with up to 700 students per semester and that web-based assessment reduces the need for teaching assistants to grade homework manually.
finding.measure: Instructor grading workload / system usability in large-enrollment assessment; usage volume (#exercises, #students, #submissions)
finding.study_size: n=2 lectures; up to 700 students per semester

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on digital assessment in statistics, including hypothesis testing, cumulative distribution functions, quantiles, and data interpretation tasks. It argues that parameterized, multi-stage exercises with R-based evaluation and feedback preserve the quality of higher-statistics exercises and support learning, but it does not report a formal experimental estimate of student achievement gains.
finding.measure: Performance on statistics exercises and exams; correctness of multi-stage statistical problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The system is described as supporting practice, repeated attempts, hints, and feedback that can help students persist and engage with difficult exercises over time. The paper notes that parameterized exercises encourage students to work on tasks more than once and that students practiced heavily before summative assessments, but these are usage observations rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Student practice frequency / engagement with parameterized exercises

paper_profiles.title: AI instructional agent improves student’s perceived learner control and learning outcome: empirical evidence from a randomized controlled trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an AI instructional agent can improve students’ perceived learner control and academic performance in a lecture-based university course. The authors motivate the study by arguing that many current AI tools in education are either administrative or reactive chatbots, whereas an AI instructional agent that can deliver lectures and answer questions in real time may better support learner autonomy.

The study used a randomized controlled trial with 140 Beijing undergraduates initially enrolled, with 125 retained for analysis. Students were assigned to one of three conditions: a human teacher-led lecture, a self-paced MOOC-style video lecture with chatbot support, or an AI instructional agent delivered through the MAIC system. All groups used the same instructional content; the key difference was how instruction and interaction were delivered. The AI condition allowed students to pause, interrupt, and ask questions in real time.
