Results showed that the AI instructional agent significantly increased perceived learner control relative to both the human teacher and MOOC conditions, and also improved post-test performance. The AI group also showed more interaction with the system and shorter learning duration, suggesting greater efficiency and more active engagement. Regression analyses indicated that perceived learner control positively predicted post-test scores even after controlling for gender, age, self-regulated learning, and pre-test achievement. The authors conclude that AI instructional agents can enhance both the learning experience and short-term academic outcomes when they combine structured lecturing with responsive interaction.

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent significantly increased students’ perceived learner control compared with both the human teacher and MOOC conditions. In the final analytic sample (n=125), the group effect was significant, F(2,122)=12.155, p<.001, with AI-human M difference=0.732 and AI-MOOC M difference=0.416. The study also found that perceived learner control positively predicted post-test performance (β=0.055, p<.05), indicating that students who felt more autonomous tended to learn better.
finding.measure: Perceived learner control scale (4-item self-report)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines learner control as a self-regulatory / autonomy-related construct and reports that the AI condition improved students’ ability to manage pacing, time, and questioning. Perceived learner control was negatively correlated with learning duration (r=-0.30, p<.001), and the AI group completed the task in less time than the human teacher group (F(2,122)=265.168, p<.001). These results suggest gains in time management and self-directed learning behaviors rather than only content knowledge.
finding.measure: Perceived learner control; learning duration; question/feedback frequency

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent improved learning efficiency, with significantly shorter learning duration than the human teacher group and higher interaction frequency than both comparison groups. Learning duration differed strongly across groups, F(2,122)=265.168, p<.001, with AI-human mean difference=-1.860 and MOOC-human mean difference=-1.960; interaction frequency also differed, F(2,122)=21.755, p<.001, with AI-human mean difference=5.410 and AI-MOOC mean difference=7.015. These findings indicate that the AI system reduced time to completion while supporting more active interaction.
finding.measure: Learning duration; feedback / interaction frequency

finding.finding_summary: The primary academic outcome was post-test performance on a 16-item multiple-choice assessment. The AI group outperformed both the human teacher and MOOC groups, with a significant group effect, F(2,122)=7.673, p<.01. Pairwise results showed AI-human mean difference=0.128 (p<.01) and AI-MOOC mean difference=0.112 (p<.01), indicating better immediate learning outcomes under AI instruction.
finding.measure: Post-test scores (16-item multiple-choice test; proportion correct)

paper_profiles.title: Word Embedding for Response-To-Text Assessment of Evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically scoring the Evidence dimension of Response-to-Text Assessment (RTA) essays written by upper-elementary students. The authors focus on improving an existing rubric-based automated essay scoring system that relies on exact lexical matching between student essays and source-text evidence, which can miss student spelling errors, tense changes, and paraphrases.

The proposed approach augments the existing feature extraction pipeline with word embeddings (skip-gram and CBOW trained on the authors’ own corpus, plus two off-the-shelf embedding sets). The embeddings are used to identify non-exact matches between student writing and crafted evidence/topic lists via cosine similarity, with the goal of extracting more relevant evidence features for scoring. The study uses corpora of RTA responses from grades 4-8, including separate lower-elementary and higher-elementary samples, and evaluates automated scoring performance with quadratic weighted kappa against human ratings.

Results show that task-specific skip-gram embeddings trained on the local corpus generally outperform the original exact-match rubric baseline and the CBOW model, especially for the lower-grade corpus, and often outperform or match off-the-shelf embeddings depending on the corpus. The authors conclude that small, task-dependent word embedding models can improve automated scoring of evidence use in student writing, though the models sometimes capture overly broad relatedness and still need refinement for the intended formative-feedback use case.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that adding task-specific word embeddings improves automated scoring of students’ evidence-based writing responses in the Response-to-Text Assessment. On the lower-grade corpus (MV PL), the skip-gram model trained on the authors’ corpus achieved QWK=0.682 versus 0.628 for the rubric baseline, indicating better agreement with human raters for writing quality related to evidence use.
finding.measure: Quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) for automated scoring of the Evidence dimension of RTA essays
finding.study_size: n=2076 (Space), n=1804 (MV PL), n=1166 (MV PH); 4-score rating task

paper_profiles.title: Interim Analysis in Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trials for Survival Outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to do interim monitoring in Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trials (SMARTs) when the outcome is time-to-event (survival) rather than continuous. The motivation is statistical and trial-design oriented: the authors want valid early-stopping rules for efficacy in SMARTs while preserving overall type I error.

The paper develops a weighted log-rank testing framework for comparing embedded dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) in SMARTs, accounting for the overlapping treatment paths and the missingness induced by sequential randomization. It derives the joint distribution of interim test statistics, proposes covariance estimation procedures, and compares two classes of efficacy boundaries: Pocock/O’Brien-Fleming-style boundaries and Lan-DeMets alpha-spending boundaries. The methods are evaluated in simulation for two-stage SMARTs and demonstrated on a neuroblastoma survival dataset.

The study uses simulated SMART data and a retrospective reanalysis of a pediatric neuroblastoma clinical trial. In simulations, the proposed covariance estimation controlled type I error reasonably well, while bootstrap covariance estimation was often inflated. The authors conclude that interim monitoring can be implemented for SMART survival outcomes without inflating type I error, and that OBF- or Lan-DeMets-type boundaries preserve power better than Pocock boundaries while allowing earlier stopping in some cases.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is methodological efficiency for clinical trials: interim monitoring can stop SMARTs early when efficacy is evident, reducing average sample size and trial duration. In simulations, OBF/LD-OBF boundaries reduced expected sample size to about 406-467 out of 500 while maintaining power similar to a single final analysis; for example, under alternative scenarios the expected sample size was 406-467 depending on design and statistic.
finding.measure: Expected sample size, early stopping at interim analysis, power under interim monitoring
finding.study_size: n=500 per simulated dataset; 1000 simulated datasets

paper_profiles.title: How mature are survival data at the time of an interim analysis in a clinical trial with a survival outcome?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how to assess whether survival data are sufficiently mature at the time of an interim analysis in a clinical trial with a time-to-event outcome. The motivation is that early stopping for efficacy can be statistically justified on the basis of an information fraction, yet still be based on immature Kaplan-Meier curves that reflect only early events and may not represent the full population well.

The authors derive asymptotic distributions for Kaplan-Meier and Breslow estimators evaluated at the random calendar time when a prespecified fraction p of events has occurred. They show how to construct prediction intervals for the survival curve at the interim analysis, using the assumed survival distributions in each arm, accrual pattern, sample sizes, the event fraction p, and a closeness parameter δ. The paper includes simulation studies suggesting the asymptotic intervals perform well, and a worked application to the KEYNOTE-204 trial to illustrate how the method could help planners choose an interim-analysis timing that balances power and data maturity.

The study is methodological and is aimed at trial designers and statisticians rather than patients. It is set in adult oncology trials with survival endpoints such as overall survival and progression-free survival. The main conclusion is that information fraction alone is not enough to ensure meaningful interim conclusions; planners should also consider expected survival maturity at the interim analysis.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a planning method that can help researchers choose an interim-analysis timing that yields sufficiently mature survival data, potentially reducing the risk of inefficient or misleading early stopping decisions. In simulation studies across eight settings, the asymptotic prediction intervals were reported to closely match Monte Carlo intervals, suggesting the approach is practically usable for trial design.
finding.measure: Accuracy and width of prediction intervals for interim Kaplan-Meier survival estimates; agreement with Monte Carlo simulation intervals
finding.study_size: n=196 to n=1000 across simulated scenarios; 1000 Monte Carlo replications per scenario
finding.confidence_interval: 95% prediction intervals reported; exact coverage not_reported

paper_profiles.title: On the inclusion of non-concurrent controls in platform trials with an interim analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a statistical problem in platform trials: how to analyze a late-entering treatment arm when the control group includes both concurrent and non-concurrent controls, and an interim analysis has already been conducted for an earlier arm. The authors show that a common regression-based method that adjusts for time using period fixed effects can become biased when the decision to keep or stop the earlier arm depends on interim results, because that decision changes whether non-concurrent controls are borrowed in the final analysis.

To address this, the paper proposes a mean-adjusted estimator for the second arm that subtracts the estimated bias induced by the interim decision in Arm 1. The estimator is evaluated through analytical derivations and simulations under no time trend and several temporal drift patterns (linear, stepwise, seasonal, and random-walk), with continuous outcomes and sample-size settings typical of clinical platform trials. The main conclusion is that the unadjusted model can inflate or deflate bias and type I error, while the adjusted estimator—especially when Arm 1’s effect is estimated via the conditional UMVUE—substantially reduces bias, controls type I error in the studied scenarios, and retains power gains over using concurrent controls only.

paper_profiles.title: Efficacy of a hybrid take home and in class summative assessment for the postsecondary physics classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a hybrid assessment format can reduce test anxiety and improve students’ perceived mastery in an introductory college physics course. The authors are motivated by the idea that traditional summative exams can conflate knowledge with anxiety, and they compare a conventional in-class exam format against a hybrid take-home/in-class format.

In the hybrid condition, students received exam questions one week in advance, discussed and prepared them outside class, and then completed an in-class portion under constrained conditions. The comparison group completed standard in-class summative exams. The study was conducted in three sections of calculus-based Physics II at Lafayette College in fall 2022, with survey data aggregated across multiple exams (control n=31; experimental n=59). Outcomes were based on post-exam student surveys measuring stress, preparedness, and perceived mastery, alongside correlations with exam grades.

The results indicate that the hybrid format produced lower self-reported stress during the exam and higher self-reported mastery of physics topics. Specifically, the experimental cohort reported that completing the exam was less stressful than a typical exam in other classes (pMW=0.019) and endorsed greater mastery gains from both preparation and completion of the exam (pMW=0.031 and 0.035). The authors conclude that the hybrid model may be a promising alternative summative assessment approach in introductory physics, though they note limitations including small sample size, self-report measures, and potential response bias toward higher-performing students.

finding.finding_summary: The hybrid take-home/in-class exam reduced students’ perceived stress during the exam compared with traditional in-class summative assessments. On Q10 (“Completing the in-class exam was more stressful than completing a typical exam in other classes”), the experimental group scored lower stress than the control group with a statistically significant Mann-Whitney result (pMW=0.019; rMW=0.236).
finding.measure: Student survey responses on stress/anxiety items (Likert 1-5), especially Q10 and Q7

finding.finding_summary: The hybrid exam format was associated with higher self-reported mastery of physics topics, which is the closest studied outcome to scientific reasoning/disciplinary understanding in this paper. The experimental group agreed more strongly that preparing for the exam increased their mastery (Q14, pMW=0.031, rMW=0.224) and that completing the exam increased their mastery (Q15, pMW=0.035, rMW=0.214).
finding.measure: Student survey responses on perceived mastery of physics topics (Likert 1-5), Q14 and Q15

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appears to have supported preparatory problem-solving and written solution development, which the authors describe as active learning and succinct written reasoning practice. However, this outcome is only indirectly measured through self-reported mastery and exam-preparation behaviors rather than a direct durable-skills assessment.
finding.measure: Survey items on preparation time and perceived mastery; discussion of group problem-solving and rewriting solutions

paper_profiles.title: eRevise+RF: A Writing Evaluation System for Assessing Student Essay Revisions and Providing Formative Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to support young students’ argumentative writing revisions with automated formative feedback. The authors argue that existing automated writing evaluation (AWE) systems often provide feedback on a first draft but do not adequately assess whether students revise effectively in response to that feedback, especially in text-based evidence use and reasoning.

To address this, the paper introduces eRevise+RF, a web-based system that combines automated essay scoring with revision-classification models to provide two kinds of feedback: evidence-use feedback after the first draft and revision feedback after later drafts. The system uses NLP methods to estimate evidence breadth and specificity (NPE and SPC) and to classify revisions as surface vs. content, evidence vs. reasoning, and successful vs. unsuccessful. It was deployed with 6 teachers and 406 students in grades 4–8 across schools in Pennsylvania and Louisiana, using two RTA argumentative writing prompts about the Millennium Villages Project and space exploration.

The study reports strong NLP agreement with human annotations for most components and shows that students’ essays improved across drafts on word count and evidence-use metrics. The authors also find that changes in student revisions generally align with the type of feedback received: evidence-use feedback is associated with increased evidence breadth/specificity, and revision feedback is associated with additional improvement on later drafts. Because the deployment is pilot-level and lacks a control group, the paper provides promising but not causal evidence that integrated formative feedback on evidence use and revision quality can support young students’ writing development.

finding.finding_summary: The system was associated with improved argumentative writing across drafts. For the 516 MVP essays and 450 SPACE essays, word count, evidence score (ES), number of pieces of evidence (NPE), and specificity (SPC) all increased from draft 1 to draft 3; for example, MVP NPE rose from 2.56 to 3.34 and SPC from 8.81 to 13.98, while SPACE NPE rose from 3.02 to 4.09 and SPC from 6.07 to 8.84. In the annotated MVP subset, NPE improved from 2.20 to 2.93 and SPC from 9.00 to 13.59 across drafts.
finding.measure: Argumentative writing quality metrics: word count, evidence score (ES), NPE, SPC, and annotated NPE/SPC across drafts
finding.study_size: n=516 MVP essays; n=450 SPACE essays; annotated subset n=516 MVP essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that the NLP components can reliably automate parts of essay assessment and revision feedback generation, reducing the need for manual review at scale. On the MVP evaluation set, the evidence-scoring indicators achieved QWK of 0.67 (NPE) and 0.82 (SPC), and the revision classifiers achieved F1 scores of 0.96 (RC-Content), 0.66 (RC-Evidence), and 0.70 (RC-Success), suggesting the system can operationalize formative feedback with reasonable accuracy.
finding.measure: Automated scoring/classification accuracy for essay and revision assessment (QWK, F1)
finding.study_size: n=516 essays for scoring indicators; n=1,525 revision pairs for RC-Content; n=1,046 revision pairs for RC-Evidence; n=1,024 revision pairs for RC-Success

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to support revision quality, self-evaluation, and evidence-based reasoning, all of which are durable skills related to metacognition and critical thinking. The study finds that students’ revisions were largely responsive to the feedback, with draft-to-draft changes aligning with whether feedback emphasized evidence, specificity, or explanation. For example, when students received EF1 (need more evidence), annotated NPE increased by 128% from draft 1 to draft 2, and when they received EF2 (need more specific details), annotated SPC increased by 55.0%.
finding.measure: Changes in evidence use and revision quality aligned to feedback type (NPE, SPC, revision labels)
finding.study_size: n=172 MVP essay sequences for feedback-effectiveness analysis

paper_profiles.title: WFIRST Executive Summary
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an executive summary and interim science-definition report for the WFIRST mission, a proposed space telescope for astronomy and astrophysics. It addresses the mission’s scientific rationale, top-level objectives, instrument concept, and observatory requirements rather than evaluating an educational intervention or student outcome.

The report describes WFIRST’s three cornerstone science goals: surveying dark energy through supernovae, weak lensing, and baryon acoustic oscillations; conducting an exoplanet microlensing census; and producing deep near-infrared sky maps for broader astrophysical discovery. It explains the interim design reference mission, observing modes, and requirement flowdown needed to achieve those goals, and argues that the mission can be implemented with existing technologies.

The document’s main conclusion is that WFIRST is scientifically compelling, technically feasible, and a high-priority space mission according to the decadal survey. It recommends proceeding with development and flight, while preserving the full set of observational capabilities needed to meet its astronomy objectives.

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard, and why such an approach might support student learning. The authors argue that frequent, low-stakes assessment paired with timely, detailed feedback can help students monitor progress, identify weaknesses, and prepare better for summative exams.

The implementation described at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) used Blackboard online tests, initially as a proposed series of weekly or fortnightly assessments and then as a small prototype test format with multiple-choice and true/false items. The paper combines a descriptive account of the online assessment design with a student perception survey (16-item questionnaire) about continuous assessment and Blackboard-based testing. Students generally favored the approach because it broke content into smaller chunks, provided immediate teacher feedback, and offered convenience and flexibility.

The main conclusions are that e-learning tools like Blackboard can make formative assessment more workable and attractive to students, especially when feedback is immediate and specific. At the same time, students expressed some concern that frequent assessments could increase stress and overemphasize learning at the expense of grades. The paper is largely exploratory and perceptual rather than causal, but it concludes that formative assessment supported by digital tools may improve ongoing engagement and potentially support better summative performance.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the Blackboard-based formative assessments were attractive because they provided immediate feedback, helped them track strengths and weaknesses, and kept them engaged with the subject throughout the semester. However, some students also reported stress/pressure from too many tests, so the affective response was mostly positive but not uniform.
finding.measure: Student perceptions from a 16-item questionnaire about continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports perceived gains in metacognition and self-monitoring: students said the feedback helped them check whether they were on track, learn topics progressively, and correct mistakes without delay. These outcomes were based on survey responses rather than performance testing, so the evidence is perceptual but directly tied to reflection and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, progressive learning, and error correction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Blackboard made formative assessment more feasible by enabling weekly or fortnightly online tests, automatic presentation of scores, and detailed immediate feedback. This was presented as an efficiency advantage over classroom-based testing because it reduced delay and improved convenience/flexibility, but no direct workload measure was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived feasibility and convenience of Blackboard online tests; comments on immediate feedback and flexibility

finding.finding_summary: Students generally supported frequent small-topic assessments and believed the formative approach would help them learn individual topics progressively and prepare better for semester-end examinations. The paper does not report achievement test scores, but it presents student perceptions that the approach would improve learning and may improve summative grades.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of learning progress and expected preparation for summative exams

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how science and mathematics teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy that combines classroom response systems (“clickers”) with question-driven instruction, dialogical discussion, formative assessment, and meta-level communication. The authors frame the work as a teacher-change study: they want to understand how teachers adapt to a demanding, technology-supported formative-assessment approach and what kinds of professional development help them do so.

The intervention includes classroom response technology, the TEFA pedagogy, and an intensive professional development program. Teachers receive an initial four-day summer workshop, followed by weekly after-school meetings during the first year and continued support every 2-3 weeks in later years. The project is implemented across four staggered sites in western Massachusetts, involving about 39 middle and high school math/science teachers. Data sources include PD transcripts, journals, implementation logs, monthly surveys, classroom video, student surveys, and interviews.

The main contribution is descriptive and developmental rather than causal: the authors present four teacher narratives showing different learning trajectories, along with cross-case observations. They conclude that TEFA is difficult to learn, but teachers can make substantial progress over time, often first mastering the technology, then question design, and later classroom discourse and adaptive use of formative information. Across cases, teachers increased student discussion and student-student interaction, reduced teacher-dominated interaction, and reported using TEFA/CRS data to adjust instruction. The paper also highlights major implementation tradeoffs, including preparation time, class time, classroom management, fit with student capabilities, and the importance of sustained, responsive professional development.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers used TEFA in mathematics classes to support conceptual understanding and review for state-wide math exams, but it does not provide student achievement test statistics. In the qualitative case narratives, teachers such as Kim and Gina described using TEFA to improve students' mathematical reasoning, identify topics needing help, and prepare for assessment; however, no effect size or direct achievement outcome is reported.
finding.measure: math reasoning / exam review / classroom formative-assessment use

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on science teachers learning TEFA as a way to promote question-driven instruction, discussion, and formative assessment in science classrooms. The authors report that teachers increased discussion time and student-student interaction, and that several teachers used the information gained from TEFA to adjust lessons, which they describe as supporting students' scientific understanding and reasoning, but no student test scores are reported.
finding.measure: science classroom discussion, reasoning-oriented questioning, and formative-assessment-informed instruction
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers across four sites

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported changes in student participation, engagement, confidence, and classroom atmosphere as TEFA was implemented. For example, Kim described students 'boldly' sharing ideas in a discussion that felt like the 'beauty' of TEFA, and Renee reported dramatically increased participation after changing the way she revealed histogram results; the paper also notes increased voluntary participation in discussion across cases.
finding.measure: student participation, engagement, confidence, classroom atmosphere
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers; student survey data collected from classes but no single student n reported

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the development of durable skills such as metacognition, collaboration, critical thinking, and instructional agility. The authors report increased student-student interaction, more varied discussion formats, and teachers' growing ability to interpret student thinking and make real-time adjustments based on formative evidence. These findings are qualitative and process-oriented rather than based on a formal outcome measure.
finding.measure: classroom discourse, student reasoning/discussion, teacher adaptive response to student thinking
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers across four sites

finding.finding_summary: Operational tradeoffs are central to the paper. Teachers repeatedly struggled with the time required to craft good TEFA questions and the class time consumed by discussion, while technology glitches sometimes wasted class time; at the same time, teachers became more efficient with practice and used TEFA to manage classrooms and gather information more efficiently. The paper emphasizes workload, feasibility, and implementation fidelity as key constraints on scaling TEFA.
finding.measure: teacher preparation time, class time use, technology reliability, implementation logs, and teacher reports of workload/feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses scaling, professional-development feasibility, and school/district constraints, including the need for technical infrastructure and the ability to support on-site PD at multiple sites. It reports that some schools could not participate because they lacked infrastructure, and that the project's staggered design was intended to distribute workload and permit mid-course improvements, but no policy-level or institutional outcome effect is measured.
finding.measure: implementation feasibility, school technical infrastructure, PD scalability, district/site participation

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education educators; examples focus mainly on secondary and undergraduate contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can be used to support formative assessment and feedback. The authors are concerned with a pedagogically grounded question: not whether LLMs can generate text, but how they can be aligned with formative-assessment principles such as clarifying learning goals, locating where learners currently are, and helping learners move forward.

The article is a narrative/practical review rather than an empirical intervention study. It synthesizes existing research and illustrates prompt-based uses of generic LLMs, domain-specialized LLMs, and LLM-integrated educational platforms for tasks such as rewriting learning objectives in student-friendly language, generating discussion prompts for co-constructing success criteria, creating sample work of varying quality, and producing formative questions/feedback. Examples are drawn largely from secondary-school and undergraduate settings, including biology, mathematics, and fMRI-related instruction.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can augment, but should not replace, expert pedagogy. The authors emphasize tradeoffs: LLMs may save teacher time and scale feedback, but outputs vary, may be inaccurate or too generic, and require teacher judgment, contextual adaptation, and safeguards against overreliance. They also argue that current evaluation metrics for LLM outputs often miss formative dimensions such as task/process/self-regulation feedback quality, and they call for better assessment frameworks and AI-aware formative assessment designs that promote transferable skills.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or accelerating tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating assessment questions, producing sample work, and drafting feedback. However, this is a conceptual/practical claim rather than an empirically tested effect, and no effect size, sample size, or posttest data are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time saved in creating formative-assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that LLM-supported formative assessment can be used to promote transferable skills, critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation rather than simply producing answers. The authors present examples where students critique LLM-generated exemplars or co-construct success criteria, but these are illustrative and not backed by empirical effect estimates.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation, transferable skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses LLM use for writing-related formative tasks, especially simplifying syllabus language, generating learning objectives, and creating sample writing such as methods sections and essays. The evidence presented is descriptive and example-based, showing potential usefulness for writing instruction, but it does not report direct student outcome data.
finding.measure: Writing quality / student-friendly learning objectives / sample essay and methods-section generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes science-specific examples, especially biology and fMRI tasks, showing how LLMs could support formative assessment in scientific contexts by clarifying concepts, generating prompts, and helping students reason about methods and evidence. These examples are pedagogical demonstrations rather than empirical tests, so no quantitative learning gains are reported.
finding.measure: Scientific reasoning / understanding of scientific methods and concepts

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Primary Teacher Training through Academic Portfolios in Advanced Mathematics Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether academic portfolios can help bridge the gap between advanced mathematics coursework and primary-teacher preparation. The author argues that traditional assessment in teacher education often emphasizes summative exams and rote learning, which may not support future teachers in connecting abstract mathematics to classroom practice. The central question is whether a portfolio-based assessment model can improve engagement, learning, and perceived readiness for teaching among preservice primary teachers.

The intervention was implemented in two advanced mathematics courses (Algebra and Number Systems I and II) in a Chilean primary teacher education program. The portfolio approach included a negotiated learning contract, explicit rubrics, reflection prompts, iterative drafts with detailed feedback, and final presentations/discussion tables; the courses also used Canvas activity logs, attendance records, grades, self-assessments, peer evaluations, and reflective writing as data sources. The study involved 37 female preservice teachers across four cohorts over 2022-2024. Results were largely positive: attendance was above 70%, digital engagement was substantial, grades increased across semesters, and students reported stronger self-study, time organization, understanding, reduced anxiety, and better connections between theory and teaching practice.

The paper concludes that academic portfolios appear promising as a formative and summative assessment innovation in mathematics teacher education, especially for making learners more active, reflective, and motivated. However, the author repeatedly notes that the evidence is preliminary and observational, with possible confounds such as cohort differences, post-pandemic return to in-person instruction, and instructor experience. The paper therefore frames the findings as suggestive rather than causal, and recommends larger, longer-term studies to determine whether the observed benefits persist and generalize.

finding.finding_summary: Portfolio implementation coincided with improved course grades in advanced mathematics courses for preservice primary teachers. In MAT2920, the average grade rose from 4.43 in the prior semester to 5.89 when portfolios were introduced, then to 5.71 and 6.44 in later semesters; in MAT2925, the average grade increased from 5.52 to 5.80 at implementation and then to 6.44. The paper presents these as positive associations rather than causal effects, since the sample was small and multiple confounds were acknowledged.
finding.measure: Course grades in Algebra and Number Systems I (MAT2920) and II (MAT2925) on the Chilean 1.0–7.0 grading scale

finding.finding_summary: Teacher candidates reported stronger engagement, intrinsic motivation, and reduced mathematics anxiety after using portfolios. Attendance remained above 70%, 11 of 12 respondents (91.7%) said alternative assessment methods such as portfolios helped mitigate mathematics anxiety, and the authors describe increased ownership of learning and lower stress than high-stakes exams. These results are based on self-report surveys and attendance records rather than experimental comparison.
finding.measure: Attendance records, self-report survey items on engagement/motivation/anxiety, and reflective responses
finding.study_size: n=37 (survey subsample and activity logs reported across cohorts; anxiety item explicitly reported for n=12 in one semester)

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio process was associated with gains in self-regulation, time management, reflection, and pedagogical transfer. In self-assessment surveys, 85.7% of respondents reported improved self-study and 100% reported improved time organization; the discussion tables and reflective prompts were described as fostering critical thinking, self-regulated learning, and the ability to connect abstract mathematics to teaching practice. The evidence is primarily descriptive and qualitative, but it directly targets durable-skill development.
finding.measure: Self-assessment surveys, peer evaluations, reflective paragraphs, and discussion-table participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that the portfolio model improved assessment efficacy and yielded substantial documented student work, but it does not provide a direct workload analysis for teachers. Digital platform logs showed an average of 185 Canvas page views per week, and the structured rubric, drafts, and feedback cycle were presented as making expectations clearer and assessment more manageable. Because no teacher workload metric was reported, the operational-efficiency finding is indirect.
finding.measure: Canvas page views, implementation process descriptions, and instructor/participant perceptions of assessment clarity

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that academic portfolios can help bridge the institutional gap between theory and practice in primary-teacher education and may improve preparation for future teaching roles. The main institutional evidence is qualitative and program-level: the intervention was embedded in the teacher-education curriculum, and the author claims it improved the alignment of advanced mathematics courses with professional competencies. No policy or governance outcomes were measured directly.
finding.measure: Program-level implementation of portfolio assessment within the Primary Teacher Education curriculum and participant/instructor perceptions of preparedness

paper_profiles.title: Common Problems and Effects of Feedback on Fun When Programming Ozobots in Primary School
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 17th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education (WiPSCE ’22)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates which problems primary school children encounter while programming Ozobot Evo robots and how different types of corrective feedback relate to children’s reported fun. The authors are especially interested in practical implementation features that matter for teachers: common student difficulties, feedback strategies that can address those difficulties, and whether feedback helps or hurts enjoyment.

The study was conducted across seven workshops with 116 third- and fourth-grade students (ages 8–10) working in pairs or individually on seven Ozobot activities. The activities combined pen-and-paper programming with one digital block-based OzoBlockly task. Supervisors recorded student problems and their feedback, while children reported fun after each activity using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table).

The paper identifies eight recurring problem types, including task understanding, wrong color codes, robot-specific concepts, reading directions, U-turns, directionality, the app, and miscellaneous technical issues. Overall fun ratings were high, but feedback on urgent problems or problems that could threaten self-efficacy was linked to lower likeability ratings, and direct instruction was associated with worse fun while hints were associated with better fun. The authors conclude that preparatory materials, clearly explained task constraints, and encouraging hints may help teachers support students without undermining motivation, and that the workshop was similarly enjoyable for girls and boys.

finding.finding_summary: Children reported very high enjoyment overall (mean 1.9/2 on the Again Again Table; mean 3.72/4 on the Smileyometer across activities, n=116). However, having to receive corrective feedback on urgent problems or problems perceived as tied to ability was associated with lower fun ratings; for example, task-understanding problems were significantly linked to worse Smileyometer ratings (p=.001, rpb=0.18), and direct instruction reduced fun while hints improved it.
finding.measure: Fun Toolkit ratings of enjoyment/likeability (Smileyometer and Again Again Table) after each programming activity
finding.effect_size: rpb=0.18 for task understanding; rpb=0.13 for direct instruction; rpb=-0.17 for hints

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines students’ problem-solving during robotics programming, including debugging, understanding robot behavior, and using hints or guiding questions to work toward solutions. Qualitative and correlational results suggest that scaffolds such as hints and explanatory prompts supported independent problem solving better than direct instruction, though no standardized achievement test was used.
finding.measure: Observed problem categories and tutoring feedback types during Ozobot programming tasks

finding.finding_summary: The intervention introduced primary school students to computational thinking and introductory programming with Ozobot Evo robots in both pen-and-paper and block-based digital modes. The authors report that the workshop successfully supported early programming experiences and that students were generally able to complete the activities with teacher feedback and auxiliary supports such as stickers and explanations.
finding.measure: Completion of Ozobot programming activities and observed problem/feedback patterns during introductory computing lessons

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly discusses teacher-support tradeoffs and implementation feasibility, especially how teachers can prepare auxiliary materials in advance to handle common problems. It suggests that white stickers, spare robots, prepared hints, and explanatory sheets can reduce time spent on recurring issues, but also notes that preparing such materials takes time beforehand and that direct instruction can be less motivating even if efficient.
finding.measure: Observed tutoring strategies, problem frequency, and discussion of classroom support/auxiliary materials

paper_profiles.title: An Adapted Cascade Model to Scale Primary School Digital Education Curricular Reforms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to scale a pilot primary-school Digital Education curricular reform and associated teacher professional development (PD) program to an entire administrative region in Switzerland. The core problem is that cascade models are often used to reach large numbers of teachers quickly, but they can suffer from content dilution, weak support, poor alignment to local context, and teacher-trainer turnover. The authors propose an adapted cascade model designed to reduce these risks by limiting cascade depth, training teacher-trainers directly with expert trainers, and maintaining expert support throughout deployment.

The intervention studied is a three-phase deployment of a Digital Education PD program for grades 1-4 teachers, led by 14 teacher-trainers who were current teachers in the region and supported by expert trainers. The model included a prolonged initial trainer PD (about 6 months; 26.5 days total), continuing support during deployment, teacher-trainer pairs, instructional coaches in schools, reflective journals, focus groups, and end-of-session teacher surveys. Quantitative data were collected from approximately 700 in-service teachers in the deployment phase and compared with 350 teachers from the pilot phase, while qualitative data came from teacher-trainers’ journals and four focus groups.

The findings suggest the adapted cascade model addressed many traditional cascade-model limitations. Teacher-trainers reported high motivation and perceived benefits from being rooted in the regional context, though recognition and workload remained issues; one trainer left because of the additional load, and overall retention was reported as 67% (77% excluding personal departures). Teacher survey results indicated that teachers in the deployment phase perceived the PD, workshops, and trainers positively, and their motivation and adoption of Digital Education content were broadly comparable to or at least equivalent to the pilot program delivered by experts. The paper concludes that an adapted cascade model with strong expert support, local trainers, and structured feedback loops can effectively scale Digital Education reforms while maintaining teacher acceptance and implementation quality.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers in the deployment phase reported positive perceptions of the PD content, workshops, trainers, and peer exchanges, and the authors report that teacher-related outcomes for perception, motivation, and adoption were at least equivalent to those in the expert-led pilot. The paper does not report a single overall effect size for motivation, but the survey results and qualitative feedback consistently indicate strong acceptance of the model among participating teachers (n≈700 deployment teachers; n=350 pilot teachers).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of PD richness, difficulty, enjoyment, trainer appreciation, exchanges with peers, autonomous motivation, and willingness to implement Digital Education activities
finding.study_size: n≈700 deployment teachers; comparison group n=350 pilot teachers

finding.finding_summary: The adapted cascade model was designed to improve scalability, deployment efficiency, and support while limiting content dilution and logistical burden on expert trainers. Qualitative results suggest the model helped address many classic cascade-model problems, but workload and retention remained meaningful tradeoffs: one recruited trainer withdrew because of the additional load, and some trainers increased their working load by taking on the new role while continuing classroom teaching (14 trained, 1 withdrew; overall retention reported as 67%).
finding.measure: Teacher-trainer workload, retention, and reported feasibility/logistics of large-scale PD deployment
finding.study_size: 14 teacher-trainers (initial recruitment 15; 1 withdrew; 14 participated in data collection)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates a regional, top-down Digital Education reform and the institutional deployment model used to scale it. The adapted cascade approach is presented as effective for spreading a mandatory primary-school Digital Education curriculum across 93 schools, and teacher-trainer feedback indicates the model improved alignment, credibility, support, and scalability relative to traditional cascade implementations.
finding.measure: Large-scale deployment effectiveness of a regional Digital Education curricular reform and its teacher-PD infrastructure
finding.study_size: 93 schools; approximately 9,000 teachers and 130,000 students in the reform context; deployment phase involved approximately 700 teachers in 17 schools

paper_profiles.title: Using Limited Trial Evidence to Credibly Choose Treatment Dosage when Efficacy and Adverse Effects Weakly Increase with Dose
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to choose an optimal treatment dosage when randomized trial evidence is available for only a limited set of dose levels. The central challenge is that efficacy and adverse effects are both assumed to weakly increase with dose, so observed trial arms provide only partial information about the untested doses. The paper develops a partial-identification framework and uses minimax-regret decision making to guide dosage choice under ambiguity.

The approach is presented in a medical decision-making context, especially oncology and drug development, but the methodology is general to any setting with monotone dose-response relationships. The paper formalizes dose thresholds for efficacy and adverse effects, characterizes the identification region for unobserved dose-response distributions, and shows how additional assumptions such as no adverse effects without treatment, concurrent thresholds, or independence can tighten identification. It then derives minimax-regret rules for both a clinician choosing one dose and a public-health planner allocating doses across a population.

The paper is methodological rather than an empirical study of a K-12 intervention, and it does not examine students, teachers, or schools. Its main conclusion is that even limited trial evidence can support credible dose selection when combined with plausible monotonicity assumptions, and that minimax-regret decisions may recommend doses not directly tested in the original trial. The paper also notes that monotonicity can be useful for finite-sample inference and that future work could extend the framework to richer, dynamic, or multicomponent treatment regimens.

paper_profiles.title: Effects of Hints on Debugging Scratch Programs: An Empirical Study with Primary School Teachers in Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether automatically generated hints about common bug patterns in Scratch programs help primary school teachers in training debug and fix faulty student code more effectively and efficiently. The authors focus on a practical problem in K-12 computing education: teachers often need to understand and repair students’ bugs quickly, but many lack deep programming expertise and time for detailed debugging.

The study used an A/B design with 163 preservice primary school teachers. Participants completed self-study Scratch preparation material and then worked through 14 buggy Scratch tasks over two weeks; for Tasks 1–7, one group received static-analysis-based hints from LitterBox while the control group did not, and for Tasks 8–14 both groups worked without hints to test transfer. Performance was measured by correctness of repairs and time on task, with some tasks validated using automated Whisker tests and LitterBox checks.

Results showed that hints substantially improved immediate debugging performance: participants with hints produced more correct solutions and worked faster on the hinted tasks, though one hint could be misleading for some tasks and sometimes reduced performance. On the transfer tasks without hints, the group that had previously seen hints showed only slight, non-significant advantages overall, suggesting limited transfer of learning from hint exposure alone. The paper concludes that bug-pattern hints are useful for teacher support in practice, but hints need clearer localization and solution guidance, and training may need to better encourage reflection for stronger transfer.

finding.finding_summary: On the hinted tasks (Tasks 1–7), automatically generated bug-pattern hints improved debugging efficiency: participants in the hint group took 5.24 minutes on average versus 8.66 minutes for the control group, a reduction of 3.41 minutes per task set. The paper reports an average effect size of Â12 = .70 across Tasks 1–7, with significant time savings on some individual tasks (e.g., Task 1 p=.044; Task 7 for experienced participants p=.013).
finding.measure: Time needed to debug and submit corrected Scratch programs

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Activity-Based Method of Teaching Mathematics on Nigerian Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an activity-based method of teaching mathematics improves secondary school students’ achievement compared with the lecture method. The paper is motivated by persistent low mathematics performance among Nigerian secondary school students and the need for more effective instructional approaches.

Using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with intact classes, the researcher studied 96 Senior Secondary II students from two government-owned schools in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria. Students were assigned to either an activity-based teaching group or a lecture-method control group, and achievement was measured with a 20-item Mathematics Test covering circle geometry and construction. ANCOVA showed a statistically significant advantage for the activity-based group after controlling for pretest scores.

The findings indicate that activity-based teaching substantially improved mathematics posttest performance relative to lecture teaching. The author concludes that activity-based learning can raise achievement in secondary school mathematics and recommends teacher training, retraining, and provision of activity materials and dedicated mathematics rooms to support implementation.

finding.finding_summary: Students taught with the activity-based method scored significantly higher on the Mathematics posttest than students taught with the lecture method, after controlling for pretest scores. The experimental group improved from a pretest mean of 27.19 (SD=9.56) to a posttest mean of 51.71 (SD=8.84), while the control group increased only from 27.39 (SD=9.73) to 29.56 (SD=6.22); ANCOVA reported a significant group effect, F(1,93)=114.461, p<0.001, partial η2=0.261.
finding.measure: 20-item essay Mathematics Test (MT) on circle geometry and construction; pretest and posttest scores
finding.std_deviation: Experimental pretest SD=9.56; posttest SD=8.84; Control pretest SD=9.73; posttest SD=6.22

paper_profiles.title: Pre-service Teachers’ Perception of using Mobile Devices in Teaching Climate Change in Primary Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether pre-service teachers believe mobile devices can be used to teach climate change in primary schools, and whether they feel competent to use such devices themselves. The authors motivate the study by arguing that climate change education should begin early and that mobile technologies may help children collect, share, and discuss images and information about environmental problems, thereby increasing awareness and supporting emergency response and climate literacy.

The study used a descriptive survey design with 150 second-year pre-service teachers drawn purposively from two Colleges of Education in the South East geopolitical zone of Nigeria. A 20-item Likert questionnaire was administered and analyzed using mean scores. The paper reports that respondents generally agreed that mobile devices could create awareness, support knowledge construction, facilitate information sharing, and help reduce vulnerability during climate-related emergencies. However, respondents’ self-reported competence in using mobile devices for teaching was low, suggesting a gap between perceived educational value and actual preparation.

The main conclusion is that mobile devices are seen as useful for climate change instruction in primary school, but pre-service teacher education in the sampled context is not adequately preparing teachers to use them. The authors recommend integrating mobile technology literacy into the teacher education curriculum and improving institutional support and training so that future teachers can use ICT and mobile devices in teaching and learning.

finding.finding_summary: Respondents believed mobile devices would support climate change learning by helping pupils observe, collect, store, share, and discuss information about erosion, flooding, and gas flaring. The paper reports a grand mean of 3.27 on items about awareness, knowledge construction, sharing information, and technology literacy, indicating strong perceived educational value for climate change understanding rather than a tested achievement effect.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey of perceived usefulness for climate change awareness, knowledge construction, information sharing, and technology literacy

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that mobile devices could make learners active participants, encourage anywhere-anytime learning, and support reflection and collaboration around climate change topics. These perceptions were reflected in the survey means (e.g., 3.29 for active participation and 3.26 for observation/interaction/conversation/reflection), suggesting expected benefits for engagement and participation.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on active participation, anywhere-anytime learning, observation, interaction, conversation, and reflection

finding.finding_summary: The study directly emphasizes collaboration, social networking, communication, and knowledge construction as benefits of mobile-device use in climate change instruction. Survey responses were favorable (e.g., mean 3.08 for collaboration and social networking; mean 3.5 for building and constructing knowledge), indicating perceived support for durable skills such as collaboration and communication.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on collaboration/social networking, knowledge construction, conversation, and information exchange

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests mobile devices could improve efficiency by helping pupils store and retrieve information and by enabling teachers to design lessons, but it also reports that pre-service teachers lacked competence and were not being trained with mobile devices. Item-level results show low means for school provision of devices (1.52), being taught with devices (1.72), learning with devices (1.78), and designing lessons (2.10), indicating a clear implementation/workflow gap.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on device ownership, school provision, learning with devices, and ability to design lessons

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that the respondents support incorporating mobile-device use and ICT literacy into the pre-service teacher curriculum, but current institutional support is inadequate. The grand mean for competence-related items was 2.19, with low ratings on being provided devices and trained to use them, leading the authors to conclude that policy statements about ICT integration are not being fully implemented.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey of institutional preparation, device provision, training, and curriculum incorporation

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as a scalable, low-cost teacher coach by generating useful feedback on classroom instruction. The authors focus on three coaching tasks: scoring transcript segments using classroom-observation rubrics, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses elementary mathematics classroom transcripts from the NCTE dataset, consisting of 1,660 observations collected across 317 teachers in four school districts. The authors evaluate gpt-3.5-turbo in zero-shot mode against expert human ratings for rubric-based scoring tasks and recruit two experienced math teachers to judge the quality of generated feedback for highlights/missed opportunities and suggestions.

Results show that ChatGPT performs poorly on rubric scoring, with low Spearman correlations with human ratings across CLASS and MQI items. It also often produces feedback that is relevant but not especially novel or insightful, and 82% of its suggestions repeat actions the teacher already performs in the transcript. The paper concludes that generative AI has promise as a scalable support tool for teacher coaching, but current models are not yet reliable enough to replace or fully automate expert feedback; future work should focus on reducing hallucination, improving novelty and insight, and better tailoring feedback to teachers’ needs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies the quality of AI-generated feedback on elementary math instruction, using MQI rubric items tied to mathematical reasoning and instructional quality. In Task A, ChatGPT showed low correspondence with human ratings on MQI items (Spearman correlations: EXPL 0.02/0.12/-0.11, REMED 0.05/0.06/-0.06, LANGIMP 0.00/0.02/0.04, SMQR 0.17/0.17/0.06 across DA/DA+/RA), indicating poor performance on math-instruction scoring. In Tasks B and C, feedback was often relevant but not insightful or novel, and 82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did in the transcript.
finding.measure: MQI rubric scores for mathematical instruction quality; human ratings of highlights/missed opportunities and suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning
finding.study_size: Task A: n=100 transcript segments; Task B: n=216 CLASS items and n=288 MQI items; Task C: n=36 suggestions

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly motivates ChatGPT as a cost-effective complement to expert coaching, emphasizing scalability and reduced resource demands relative to manual classroom observation. However, empirically the paper does not measure time saved or workload reduction; instead, it shows that current outputs are often weak, which limits immediate feasibility despite the envisioned efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Perceived scalability/cost-effectiveness of automated teacher coaching; qualitative assessment of feasibility and feedback usefulness

paper_profiles.title: Approximation of Fractional Order Conflict-Controlled Systems
paper_profiles.venue: Progress in Fractional Differentiation and Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a mathematical control problem rather than an educational intervention. The author considers nonlinear fractional-order dynamical systems with Caputo derivatives and develops an approximation method that replaces the fractional differential equation with a retarded functional-differential equation driven by finite-difference Grünwald-Letnikov formulas.

The main theoretical contribution is to prove that the approximating system can closely track the original fractional-order system, first for a single Cauchy problem and then for conflict-controlled systems with disturbances. A mutual aiming procedure based on the extremal shift rule is introduced to coordinate the original and approximating systems and guarantee proximity of their trajectories, with illustrative numerical examples showing the approximation error decreases as the discretization parameter h shrinks. The paper is entirely in applied mathematics/control theory and does not study K-12 learners, teachers, or schooling outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Cost-Aware Logging: Measuring the Financial Impact of Excessive Log Retention in Small-Scale Cloud Deployments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the financial and operational consequences of retaining cloud logs for longer periods than are operationally necessary. The central question is whether reducing log retention windows can lower storage costs without meaningfully harming debugging and incident-response utility.

The study uses a simulation-based approach rather than a live deployment experiment. It generates synthetic log data for a 90-day period, then compares four retention configurations: 7, 14, 30, and 90 days. The analysis evaluates storage cost, the proportion of operational queries that can still be satisfied, and a cost-per-useful-log metric, with query access patterns modeled to reflect common debugging behavior in small cloud teams.

Results indicate that shorter retention windows yield large cost savings with limited loss of practical utility. Reducing retention from 90 days to 14 days lowers storage cost by about 84% while preserving approximately 97% of useful query access; even a 7-day window preserves 95% of operationally useful logs. The paper concludes that modest configuration changes can substantially improve cost efficiency in resource-constrained engineering environments, without requiring new tools or architectural redesigns.

finding.finding_summary: Reducing log retention windows substantially improved cost efficiency and reduced operational overhead in the simulation. Compared with a 90-day baseline, a 14-day window cut storage cost by about 84% while preserving 97% of operationally useful logs; normalized CPUL fell from 1.00 to 0.17.
finding.measure: Storage cost, useful log ratio (query satisfaction), and cost per useful log (CPUL)
finding.study_size: n=10000 synthetic queries; 90-day synthetic log stream totaling approximately 10–20 million log entries

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that routine retention-policy changes can reduce recurring cloud spending for small engineering organizations without compromising reliability. The main institutional implication is that default observability policies may create unnecessary costs, and that deliberate retention tuning can improve resource allocation in constrained teams.
finding.measure: Relative storage-cost reduction and preserved operational usefulness under different retention policies

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the role of formative assessment and asks how it might be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System, in a university context. The authors frame formative assessment as a way to support learning through frequent testing, immediate feedback, and opportunities for students to reflect on errors and improve performance over time.

The proposed implementation involves weekly or fortnightly online tests on Blackboard, with question formats such as multiple choice and true/false, along with detailed feedback after each attempt. The paper also discusses design features that may make feedback more effective, such as individualized targets, criteria-referenced comments, and use of discussion forums or virtual classroom tools to extend correspondence with lecturers.

Empirically, the study uses a student questionnaire to capture perceptions of continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option among university students from Business, Engineering, and IT streams. Students generally supported frequent small-topic assessments and valued immediate teacher feedback, flexibility, and the ability to track strengths and weaknesses, but they also expressed concern that too many tests could create stress and overemphasize learning processes at the expense of grades. The paper concludes that the Blackboard-based formative assessment approach is viewed positively and may help improve summative exam performance, though no achievement outcome data are reported.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that splitting course work into small weekly or fortnightly Blackboard assessments was useful for learning individual topics progressively and preparing for summative semester exams. However, the paper reports only perceptions, not achievement gains; students also worried that frequent assessment could overemphasize learning and increase stress.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard-based online tests

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived frequent formative assessment and immediate feedback as helpful for monitoring their strengths and weaknesses, staying on track, and maintaining contact with the subject throughout the semester. The paper also notes concern about stress/pressure from too many tests, indicating a mixed but generally positive motivational and self-regulatory response.
finding.measure: Survey responses on motivation, tracking progress, and perceived stress/pressure

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes feedback-driven learning, reflection on errors, and checking one's own standing in subject knowledge, which are framed as metacognitive benefits of formative assessment. Students said the detailed immediate feedback helped them correct mistakes without delay and learn topics progressively, supporting self-monitoring and metacognition rather than directly measured skill gains.
finding.measure: Survey responses on understanding strengths/weaknesses, checking whether they are on track, and correcting mistakes

finding.finding_summary: The Blackboard implementation is presented as a more flexible and convenient way to administer repeated formative tests than classroom testing, with immediate automated feedback reducing delay in the learning cycle. The paper does not report workload measures, but it argues that online tools such as Blackboard, discussion forums, and virtual classrooms can make feedback and assessment more workable.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of flexibility/convenience of Blackboard tests and timeliness of feedback

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education educators/students (primarily classroom-focused examples; not a single empirical sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide examining how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can be used to support formative assessment and feedback. The authors organize the discussion around a formative-assessment framework: clarifying where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward. They argue that LLMs can assist with student-friendly learning objectives, co-constructing success criteria, generating exemplar work, creating diagnostic questions, and producing feedback at different levels (task, process, self-regulation).

The paper’s main contribution is conceptual and practical rather than empirical. It provides classroom-oriented prompting examples and implementation ideas, such as using LLMs to rewrite syllabus objectives into student-friendly language, generate discussion prompts for co-constructing criteria, and produce sample work of varying quality for critique. The authors repeatedly emphasize that LLMs can augment but not replace teacher expertise, and that prompts must be grounded in subject knowledge, pedagogy, and classroom context.

The review also highlights tradeoffs and limitations relevant to implementation: output variability, the need for teacher review, risks of overreliance by students, privacy/transparency concerns with plugins, and the fact that existing evaluation metrics often fail to capture formative-feedback quality. The authors conclude that future work should develop better metrics, stronger pedagogy-aligned prompt repositories, and more context-sensitive approaches to using LLMs in formative assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by speeding up tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating formative questions, creating exemplars, and drafting feedback. However, this is a conceptual claim supported by illustrative examples rather than a measured effect; no study-level effect size or sample is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / task efficiency (conceptual discussion of time-saving uses of LLMs)

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that LLM-supported formative assessment can promote transferable skills, critical thinking, and self-regulation when used to prompt reflection rather than provide finished answers. The paper also warns that overreliance on LLMs could undermine these skills, so the overall direction is framed as beneficial when implemented pedagogically and cautiously.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation, transfer (conceptual)

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on improving classroom learning in general through formative assessment supports such as clearer goals, better exemplars, and more actionable feedback. It does not report achievement data for a specific academic domain, but it describes expected benefits for learning quality and understanding across subjects.
finding.measure: General academic learning through formative assessment supports (conceptual)

finding.finding_summary: The authors discuss LLMs as a way to help address systemic barriers to formative assessment, especially in large classrooms, under-resourced settings, and contexts with limited access to specialized educational technology. This is framed as a scalability and access argument rather than an empirically tested institutional outcome.
finding.measure: Access/scalability barriers in formative assessment (conceptual)

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on a five-year research project studying how K-12 science and mathematics teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy that uses classroom response systems (“clickers”) to support question-driven instruction, dialogical discussion, and formative assessment. The paper is framed around a central implementation problem: teacher change is difficult, and the authors want to understand how teachers develop comfort, competence, and pedagogical flexibility when adopting a complex instructional technology and associated teaching practice.

The intervention combines three elements: the classroom response system technology, the TEFA pedagogy, and an intensive professional development program. The PD begins with a four-day summer workshop and continues with weekly after-school meetings in year one, then biweekly support in later years. The program is conducted on-site in schools, uses teachers’ own classroom experiences, and is designed to build five skill areas: operating the technology, crafting good questions, orchestrating discourse, interpreting and responding to student thinking, and integrating TEFA within each teacher’s broader classroom context.

The study follows approximately 39 teachers across four sites in western Massachusetts, using a longitudinal staggered-site delayed-intervention design with multiple data sources including logs, surveys, journals, classroom video, and interviews. The paper presents detailed case narratives for four teachers and synthesizes early cross-case patterns. The main conclusion is that teachers can and do learn TEFA, but the process is slow, personal, and constrained by tradeoffs such as preparation time, class time, classroom control, student participation, and technology reliability. Teachers often begin with narrow, conservative uses of TEFA and then gradually expand toward more flexible, student-centered formative assessment practices. The authors also conclude that implementation fidelity, teacher learning progress, and sustainability are deeply linked, and that scalable impact studies will require better instrumentation and support systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that TEFA created substantial implementation demands, especially around preparation time, class time, and technical reliability. Teachers reported that crafting effective questions could be time-consuming, discussion consumed class time, and glitches or missing software reduced efficiency, although some teachers eventually became more efficient and used TEFA more smoothly (no effect sizes reported; n≈39 teachers across four sites).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported preparation burden, class time use, technical glitches, and implementation logs/interviews

finding.finding_summary: TEFA was associated with increased student engagement, willingness to participate, and teacher-perceived motivation in several cases, though effects varied by teacher and class. The paper reports that some teachers saw more voluntary discussion participation and greater student engagement, while others had to adjust implementation to fit students’ comfort and behavior; no standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student participation, engagement in discussion, teacher reports and student survey perceptions
finding.study_size: n≈39 teachers; student surveys administered across participating classes

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that TEFA supported the development of durable skills such as metacognition, reasoning, and dialogue. Teachers reported that TEFA helped them understand student thinking better and shifted classroom discourse toward more student-to-student interaction and more varied discussion formats, with several teachers changing lessons based on formative information from students (no effect sizes reported).
finding.measure: Classroom discourse patterns, teacher understanding of student thinking, and teacher-adapted instruction from video, logs, and interviews

finding.finding_summary: Math teachers used TEFA to review content, probe misconceptions, and prepare for state-wide math exams, indicating support for mathematical learning and assessment. The paper is primarily about implementation rather than achievement testing, so it does not report standardized math outcome effects; however, teachers described TEFA as useful for identifying topics students needed help with and for solidifying learning through question cycles.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported use of TEFA for math review, conceptual understanding, and exam preparation

finding.finding_summary: In science classrooms, TEFA was intended to develop scientific reasoning through question-driven instruction, dialogical discourse, and formative assessment. The paper reports that teachers increasingly used discussion to explore multiple ideas and reasoning paths, and that formative information from student responses led teachers to adjust instruction; no direct achievement test results are provided.
finding.measure: Science classroom discourse and teacher adaptations to student reasoning, observed through video/interviews

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance for Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as a scalable, low-cost complement to human instructional coaching by generating feedback on classroom instruction.
