The paper proposes an alternative pedagogy centered on purposeful peer assessment as a structured learning activity rather than a routine assessment add-on. Through repeated appraisal of peers’ work, students are expected to develop three foundational concepts: task compliance, quality, and criteria, alongside the tacit knowledge needed for complex judgment. The article is theoretical and conceptual, drawing on prior literature and examples rather than reporting an empirical study of an intervention.

The intended population is higher education students working on complex, open-ended tasks across disciplines such as humanities, sciences, health, and professional fields. Sadler concludes that intensive, well-designed peer appraisal can reduce overreliance on teacher feedback and better support deep learning, self-regulation, and evaluative expertise. However, the article does not provide original outcome data or subgroup analyses; it is an argument for a pedagogical model grounded in assessment theory.

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that purposeful peer assessment can develop students’ evaluative judgment, critical appraisal, and ability to make reasoned quality judgments about complex work. No original empirical effect size is reported; the claim is theoretical, grounded in prior research and examples, and centered on building capability in complex appraisal rather than measuring a treatment effect.
finding.measure: Evaluative judgment / complex appraisal capability (conceptual and theoretical construct; not directly measured in this paper)

paper_profiles.title: Mapping research in student engagement and educational technology in higher education: a systematic evidence map
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate higher education students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broad question of how educational technology research in higher education has studied student engagement, and how that literature is grounded theoretically and methodologically. Rather than testing a single intervention, it maps a corpus of 243 empirical studies published from 2007 to 2016, examining definitions of engagement, theoretical framing, engagement/disengagement indicators, learning scenarios, delivery modes, and technology types.

The review finds that student engagement is often under-defined and under-theorized in the literature, with most studies not providing a definition and many not using a theoretical model. The corpus is dominated by quantitative and mixed-methods studies in undergraduate settings, especially in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Taiwan, and China. Common technologies include learning management systems, discussion forums, videos, recorded lectures, and chat, with social-collaborative learning and blended learning being the most common pedagogical contexts.

The main contribution is descriptive rather than effect-based: it shows what kinds of engagement indicators and technologies are most commonly studied, and where important gaps remain in geography, theory, and methodology. Because this is a systematic evidence map, it does not estimate intervention effects or moderator/subgroup effects on student outcomes in the way an effectiveness study would.

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that educational technology studies in higher education most often report behavioral engagement, followed by affective and cognitive engagement, but these are descriptive frequencies rather than causal effects. Across 243 studies, 117 reported all three engagement dimensions, 54 reported at least two, and 71 reported only one; disengagement indicators were reported less often than engagement indicators.
finding.measure: Reported engagement and disengagement indicators across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The evidence map reports that several durable-skill-like indicators appeared frequently in the corpus, especially self-regulation, confidence, critical thinking, and learning from peers. These are not analyzed as outcome effects of an intervention, but as commonly observed engagement indicators across the 243 studies.
finding.measure: Frequency of coded engagement indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes descriptive analyses of how technology tools were used across delivery modes and study contexts, which can inform research and implementation efficiency, but it does not measure workload or productivity outcomes directly. Some tools were more common in blended and distance education, and assessment tools were more common in some contexts than others.
finding.measure: Distribution of technology tools by mode of delivery and study context

paper_profiles.title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper argues that developing students’ evaluative judgement—the capability to make decisions about the quality of their own work and the work of others—should be a central goal of higher education. The authors trace the development of the term across assessment, feedback, self-assessment, peer assessment, rubrics, exemplars, and self-regulated learning, and they propose a concise definition that emphasizes judgment about quality rather than simply generating grades.

Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes prior higher-education research and theory to show how existing pedagogical practices can be reoriented to better develop evaluative judgement. The discussion focuses on five practices: self-assessment, peer assessment/review, feedback, rubrics, and exemplars. For each, the authors contrast common sub-optimal implementations with more promising designs that emphasize criteria, dialogue, reflection, and transfer to future tasks.

The paper is situated in higher education, with examples drawn largely from undergraduate and professional education contexts, including medical education. Its main conclusion is that evaluative judgement is a distinct, necessary graduate capability that should be deliberately cultivated through curriculum and assessment design. The article calls for more empirical work to test strategies for developing evaluative judgement and to track how these capabilities develop over time and into professional practice.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual/theoretical synthesis, not an empirical study, so it does not report experimental effects. The paper argues that practices such as self-assessment, peer assessment, feedback, rubrics, and exemplars can support evaluative judgement, a durable skill involving critical appraisal, metacognition, and justification of quality judgments.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses how feedback, peer interaction, and self-assessment may support students’ self-regulation, agency, and responsibility for learning, but it does not present original quantitative evidence. Any effects are presented as plausible pedagogical claims rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Sentence-level Feedback Generation for English Language Learners: Does Data Augmentation Help?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the task of generating sentence-level feedback comments for English language learners, specifically for preposition-related errors in writing. The authors study whether data augmentation via pseudo-labeled data improves a T5-based feedback comment generation system.

The approach uses a T5-large encoder-decoder model fine-tuned on the GenChal 2022 feedback comment generation dataset derived from ICNALE learner essays. The paper compares a baseline model with several pseudo-data strategies, including multi-stage fine-tuning and combined fine-tuning, using pseudo data created both from the same learner corpus (ICNALE) and from out-of-domain learner corpora (W&I+LOCNESS). Performance is evaluated with BLEU on dev/test sets and with human evaluation F1 on a subset of outputs.

Results show that the T5 systems substantially outperform the shared-task baseline, and that adding pseudo data yields only small gains overall. In automatic evaluation, combined fine-tuning on in-domain pseudo data performs best, while larger out-of-domain pseudo datasets do not help and sometimes hurt. Human evaluation suggests a modest improvement from pseudo data, but the study also finds that performance is strongly shaped by the narrow topic range of the corpus, the limited error type focus, and the templated nature of many reference comments. The paper concludes that pseudo data can help, but only if carefully constructed and matched to the target domain.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies writing feedback generation for English language learners, a literacy-related task. The best T5-based model substantially outperformed the official shared-task baseline, reaching 47.25 BLEU on the test set versus 33.40 for the baseline, and 61.90 human-evaluation F1 versus 31.16 for the baseline.
finding.measure: BLEU on generated feedback comments; human evaluation F1 of correct/incorrect outputs
finding.study_size: n=215 test sentences; human evaluation reported for 3 systems on the test set

paper_profiles.title: P-VALUE EVALUATION, VARIABILITY INDEX AND BIOMARKER CATEGORIZATION FOR ADAPTIVELY WEIGHTED FISHER’S META-ANALYSIS METHOD IN OMICS APPLICATIONS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses methodological problems in adaptively weighted Fisher’s meta-analysis (AW-Fisher), a p-value combination approach used in omics research to integrate results across multiple transcriptomic studies. The authors identify three practical issues with AW-Fisher: slow and imprecise p-value computation, unstable binary weight estimates, and an explosion in the number of biomarker categories as the number of studies grows.

To solve these issues, they propose an importance-sampling plus spline-interpolation strategy for fast p-value computation, a bootstrap-based variability index to quantify stability of the adaptive weights, and a resampling-based co-membership matrix paired with tight clustering to categorize biomarkers by meta-pattern. They validate the methods in simulations and apply them to two real transcriptomic meta-analyses: mouse metabolism microarray data and HIV transgenic rat brain RNA-seq data. The paper concludes that the proposed methods improve computational speed, p-value accuracy, interpretability, and biomarker categorization in large-scale genomic meta-analysis.

This is a methods paper in statistical genomics, not an education study. It does not examine formative assessment, English language learners, students with disabilities, low-income students, or prior achievement, and it reports no subgroup or moderator analyses relevant to those educational populations.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Creativity: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI (GenAI) improves creative performance, and whether it also affects the diversity of ideas produced in human-AI collaboration. The authors conducted a systematic literature review and meta-analysis of 28 studies (8214 participants) published across arXiv, SSRN, and Web of Science, extracting 127 effect-size estimates and standardizing them using Hedges’ g.

The paper compares three outcomes: creative performance of GenAI versus humans, creative performance of humans supported by GenAI versus humans alone, and creative diversity in human-GenAI collaboration versus humans alone. Overall, GenAI performed about as well as humans on average for creative output (g=-0.048, ns), while human-GenAI collaboration modestly improved creative performance (g=0.273, 95% CI [0.018, 0.528]) but reduced idea diversity (g=-0.863, 95% CI [-1.328, -0.398]).

The meta-analysis also explored heterogeneity by GenAI model, task type, and participant background. It found that results depended strongly on the model and task: GPT-4 was most effective in direct human-vs-AI comparisons, while GPT-3.5 showed the strongest gains in collaborative settings. Laypeople benefited more from GenAI collaboration than academics or business participants, but the collaboration also tended to homogenize outputs. The authors conclude that GenAI can augment creativity, but its benefits are contingent on task and model choice and may come with a cost to diversity.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis directly studies creative performance in GenAI-supported and GenAI-versus-human tasks, which falls under academic/creative output rather than a core literacy or numeracy domain. Across 28 studies (n=8214 participants; 127 effect-size estimates), GenAI performed about the same as humans on average in direct comparisons (g=-0.048, 95% CI [-0.257, 0.161]), while humans working with GenAI outperformed humans alone (g=0.273, 95% CI [0.018, 0.528]).
finding.measure: Creative performance / creativity ratings, originality, novelty, semantic distance, creativity scales, and related creativity measures

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines a durable-skill outcome: creativity/ideation performance and related divergent-thinking processes. In direct human-vs-GenAI comparisons, the pooled effect was essentially null (g=-0.048, 95% CI [-0.257, 0.161]), but in human-GenAI collaboration the pooled effect favored collaboration (g=0.273, 95% CI [0.018, 0.528]).
finding.measure: Creative thinking, ideation, divergent thinking, and creative problem-solving tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses how GenAI may support human creativity by reducing cognitive load and facilitating ideation, which overlaps with motivational/engagement-related mechanisms, but it does not directly measure social-emotional constructs. Because this is not a primary measured outcome, evidence is limited; the closest direct result is the modest positive effect of GenAI collaboration on creative performance (g=0.273, 95% CI [0.018, 0.528]).
finding.measure: Creative performance as a proxy for collaborative support/engagement effects

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper discusses the rationale for formative assessment and reports a student perception survey about implementing formative assessment through the Blackboard e-learning system. The authors frame formative assessment as a way to provide frequent, low-stakes checks on learning with immediate feedback, arguing that this should improve learning and prepare students for semester-end examinations.

The implementation described is a series of weekly or fortnightly Blackboard online tests with immediate, detailed feedback. The study was conducted at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) with university students, and data came from a questionnaire measuring views on continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard-based testing. Results showed broad student support for frequent online formative assessments, especially because they supported learning in small topic units and provided immediate feedback.

The only subgroup analysis reported was by academic stream (Business, Engineering, and IT), where differences in perceptions were statistically significant. Engineering students were more likely than Business and IT students to endorse continuous assessment and rate the Blackboard test option favorably. The paper is primarily descriptive and opinion-driven, with no causal impact analysis of achievement outcomes, and it emphasizes that formative assessment may particularly help low achievers by focusing on specific weaknesses and actionable feedback.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments were helpful because they supported learning in small steps, provided immediate feedback, and helped them monitor whether they were on track. In the survey, a majority supported frequent internal assessments and preferred the Blackboard test option over classroom tests for flexibility and feedback, but no pre/post achievement effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, feedback, and Blackboard test option on a questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and self-monitoring by giving students immediate feedback and helping them reflect on strengths and weaknesses. Survey responses indicate students believed the feedback helped them check whether they were on track, but this was measured as perception rather than a direct skill outcome.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, strengths/weaknesses awareness, and feedback utility

paper_profiles.title: Search for stable hadronising squarks and gluinos with the ATLAS experiment at the LHC
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a search for long-lived, slow-moving, electrically and/or color-charged massive particles at the ATLAS experiment using proton-proton collision data at 7 TeV. The motivation is supersymmetric models in which colored sparticles can hadronize into long-lived bound states called R-hadrons, including sbottom-, stop-, and gluino-based scenarios.

The analysis uses 34 pb−1 of early LHC data and combines two detector-based observables sensitive to particle speed and ionization: pixel-detector specific energy loss (dE/dx) and tile-calorimeter time-of-flight (β). Candidate events were selected with missing transverse energy triggers, track-quality requirements, and mass-based signal regions derived from the two independent measurements. Backgrounds were estimated with a data-driven method, and systematic uncertainties were evaluated for signal efficiency, trigger response, tracking, calorimetry, and ionization modeling.

No deviations from Standard Model expectations were observed. The results are interpreted as exclusion limits on stable R-hadrons, yielding 95% CL lower mass limits of 294 GeV for sbottoms, 309 GeV for stops, and 562 GeV for gluinos under the most conservative model assumptions. The paper’s contribution is a null-search constraint on exotic particle models, not an educational intervention study.

paper_profiles.title: BRIDGE the Gap: Mitigating Bias Amplification in Automated Scoring of English Language Learners via Inter-group Data Augmentation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses bias amplification in automated scoring systems for constructed-response science assessments, focusing on English Language Learners (ELLs). The authors argue that when training data are imbalanced, ERM-trained scoring models can widen disparities by underpredicting high-scoring ELL responses, even when those responses contain valid content. The central research question is whether data-level augmentation can reduce this bias without harming overall scoring accuracy.

To address the problem, the paper proposes BRIDGE, an inter-group data augmentation framework. BRIDGE uses an LLM to synthesize high-scoring ELL-like responses by combining construct-relevant content from high-scoring non-ELL responses with authentic ELL linguistic patterns, and then filters candidates with a discriminator for authenticity. The method is evaluated on five California Science Test (CAST) constructed-response datasets using a BERT-based three-class scoring model, with low-resource training simulated by subsampling 1% of the training data. The paper compares BRIDGE to no augmentation, real-data oracle augmentation, oversampling, and paraphrasing.

The main conclusion is that baseline scoring models consistently amplify disparity for the sparse high-scoring ELL subgroup, while BRIDGE reduces both group-level score gaps and bias amplification, often outperforming simple oversampling and paraphrasing and sometimes matching or exceeding the fairness benefit of adding real data. Overall scoring performance remains essentially unchanged, suggesting the approach can improve fairness without a meaningful accuracy tradeoff. The paper is limited to short-answer science items and focuses specifically on ELL fairness in automated scoring rather than direct student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies automated scoring of Grade 8 science constructed responses on the California Science Test (CAST), using score prediction as the outcome. BRIDGE reduces bias amplification for high-scoring ELL responses (e.g., BiasAmp from 0.0097 to -0.0014 in Dataset 1; from 0.0135 to 0.0050 in Dataset 5), while overall scoring accuracy remains stable (Accuracy changes roughly -0.11% to +0.24%; QWK -0.27% to +0.15%).
finding.measure: Automated scoring performance on CAST science constructed-response items; fairness metrics including BiasAmp and MSG Gap
finding.study_size: 5 CAST datasets; low-resource training simulated with 1% of training data, repeated over 10 random seeds
finding.std_deviation: reported for metrics in Table 1 but not as a single study-level value

paper_profiles.title: How Does COVID-19 impact Students with Disabilities and Health Concerns?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how the early COVID-19 pandemic affected undergraduate students, with a specific focus on students with disabilities or health concerns. The authors ask whether these students experienced different levels of educational concern, adversity exposure, and mental health distress compared with students without disabilities/health concerns.

The study analyzes a survey of 147 University of Washington students collected in late March to early April 2020, shortly after courses moved online. The sample included 28 students with disabilities/health concerns, and a subset of 91 returning students was used to compare Spring 2019 and Spring 2020 responses. Measures included concerns about online classes and degree progress, COVID-related adversities, chronic discrimination, major life events, loneliness, perceived stress, depression, anxiety, and PTSD/distress.

Findings suggest that students with disabilities/health concerns were substantially more worried about the transition to online learning, especially its implications for grades, degree requirements, major admission, and graduation timing. They also reported higher chronic discrimination, more major life adversity, more COVID-related adversities, and significantly higher PTSD/distress scores, while perceived stress, depression, anxiety, and loneliness were not significantly different between groups. Subgroup analyses found no significant difference in online-class concerns between students with vision/hearing impairments and those with other disability/health concerns, and the returning-student analysis suggested distress increased from 2019 to 2020, especially among students with disabilities/health concerns.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that the abrupt shift to online instruction had meaningful institutional consequences for students with disabilities/health concerns, who were much more worried about grades, degree requirements, major admission, and graduation timing than peers without disabilities. The summed educational-concern score was higher for students with disabilities/health concerns (M=13.44, SD=6.17) than for non-disabled peers (M=8.25, SD=6.28), t(145)=3.94, p<.001.
finding.measure: Student concerns about the impact of COVID-19 and online learning on grades, degree requirements, major admission, graduation timing, and financial aid

finding.finding_summary: Students with disabilities/health concerns reported significantly greater COVID-related adversity exposure and higher PTSD/distress, but not higher perceived stress, depression, anxiety, or loneliness. For example, PTSD/distress was higher for the disability/health-concern group (M=22.86, SD=15.99) than for peers without disabilities (M=13.18, SD=11.65), t=3.02, p<.01.
finding.measure: Psychological distress and related mental health scales (PSS, CES-D, STAI, UCLA Loneliness, PTSD/distress)

finding.finding_summary: Although not a workload study in the usual sense, the paper documents that the rapid move online created access and participation barriers that could reduce student efficiency in completing coursework. Students with disabilities/health concerns were especially concerned about courses that could not go online and about whether they could meet academic requirements under the new format.
finding.measure: Concerns about online course accessibility and ability to meet academic requirements

paper_profiles.title: 3rd grade English language learners making sense of sound
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how third-grade English language learners make sense of a sound-related physics activity and how language mediates their conceptual understanding. The authors ask how ELLs use everyday language to understand physical phenomena and how everyday and academic language interact during meaning-making and concept formation.

The study was conducted in a sheltered English immersion third-grade classroom in an urban K-8 school. Thirteen students participated, with multiple first languages represented and short-to-long lengths of residence in the United States; the broader school context included a large ELL population and many students eligible for free/reduced lunch. The lesson sequence focused on sound, especially how string length, tension, vibration frequency, pitch, and volume are related in a guitar-like instrument activity.

Using video data and generative coding, the authors analyzed one discussion episode for students’ use of everyday and academic language. They found that students productively used familiar, onomatopoeic, and descriptive terms such as "tick tick," "toong toong," "loose," and "hard" to reason about mechanisms, and that these terms became shared classroom conventions over time. The discussion also showed students attempting to use academic terminology such as "vibrate," with peers and the teacher helping refine it, suggesting that the science activity created a third space where everyday and academic language supported both English development and scientific reasoning. The paper is primarily conceptual and descriptive, not an effects study, and it does not report subgroup, moderator, or prior-achievement analyses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students engaged in mechanistic reasoning about sound, using everyday and emerging academic language to explain how string length and tension affected pitch and loudness. The evidence is qualitative from a discussion among 13 third graders; no effect size or inferential test is reported, but the authors describe students co-constructing explanations and improving their understanding of vibration-related mechanisms.
finding.measure: Classroom discourse during a sound/physics discussion activity; use of mechanistic reasoning in conversation

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that students used and developed English language resources while discussing science, including everyday terms, onomatopoeia, and attempted academic vocabulary such as "vibrate." The authors argue that the activity supported English language development by allowing ELLs to express ideas, negotiate meaning, and formalize vocabulary in a supportive discourse environment; no quantitative language outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Students’ spoken classroom discourse and uptake of everyday/academic vocabulary

finding.finding_summary: The discussion shows collaboration, peer interpretation, and co-construction of knowledge as students responded to each other’s conjectures and rephrased one another’s statements. The paper characterizes these interactions as evidence of productive peer sense-making and distributed authority within a third-space learning environment, but it does not provide quantitative measures.
finding.measure: Peer-to-peer discussion, turn-taking, revoicing, and collaborative explanation

paper_profiles.title: ExpTrialMng: A Universal Experiment Trial Manager for AR/VR/MR Experiments Based on Unity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the practical barrier researchers face when building and running VR/AR/MR experiments in Unity. The authors argue that existing frameworks are often too heavy, too specialized, or too difficult for non-programmers to adapt, and that experiments can fail mid-run because of headset or tracking issues.

To address this, they introduce ExpTrialMng, a Unity library that manages trial presentation from a pre-generated CSV file, saves results after each trial, and supports resuming an experiment from a specified trial number if an error occurs. The paper describes the library’s design, workflow, and example integration in Unity, emphasizing ease of use and reduced data loss rather than reporting a user study or experimental evaluation.

The paper is a software/tool paper aimed at helping researchers conduct psychological, cognitive, and HCI experiments in immersive environments. It does not evaluate learning outcomes or K-12 education effects, and it reports no empirical comparisons of the library against alternatives.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents ExpTrialMng as a tool to reduce implementation burden, simplify trial management, and lower the chance of data loss during VR/AR experiments. It claims the library lets researchers deliver trial settings from a pre-generated CSV, save results after each trial, and resume from a specific interruption point, but it does not report quantitative evaluation, sample size, or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Tool functionality and workflow support for trial assignment, result saving, and experiment resumption

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether InkSurvey, a free web-based system for real-time formative assessment using pen-enabled mobile devices, appears effective across a range of educational settings. The authors argue that open-format, digitally inked responses allow instructors to see student thinking immediately and adapt instruction before misconceptions become entrenched.

The paper is organized as a set of seven vignettes from physics, mathematics, chemical engineering, food science, and biology courses in the United States and Mexico. Across these contexts, instructors describe learning gains, improved performance on quizzes and exams, better student metacognition and engagement, and useful instructional feedback. The evidence presented is largely observational and descriptive, drawing on class assessments, comparison groups in some cases, and student surveys/comments rather than a controlled experimental design.

The paper also highlights some subgroup patterns. One high school Algebra I vignette reports larger learning gains for female students than for males, and another vignette suggests benefits across different learning styles. Overall, the authors conclude that InkSurvey is a promising tool for real-time formative assessment in diverse educational environments, but they also note that further investigation is warranted for subgroup differences and more rigorous evidence of effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: In a high school Algebra I setting, students exposed to InkSurvey showed greater mastery gains on standards-based assessments than students not exposed to the intervention. The paper does not report a single effect size, but it notes that female students in particular demonstrated much greater learning gains than the control group, suggesting a potentially larger benefit for that subgroup.
finding.measure: Standards-based assessments in Algebra I

finding.finding_summary: Across physics and engineering contexts, InkSurvey-supported formative assessment was associated with improved conceptual understanding and problem-solving. Examples include only 1 of 87 students still showing a triple-integrals misconception on a later summative assessment versus 12 of 103 in a comparison section, and an upper-level engineering physics course showing steady improvement in problem-solving scores over the semester.
finding.measure: Summative exam questions, problem-solving strategy scores, conceptual understanding probes
finding.study_size: n=87 vs n=103 for one physics comparison; other studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: In undergraduate and graduate food chemistry / chemical engineering settings, students using InkSurvey and related interactive simulations improved on topic-specific competence ratings and summative quiz performance. Reported average competence increased from about 1.8 to 2.3 after unguided simulation use, and then to about 3.1 after instructor-guided, InkSurvey-mediated probing on a 4-point scale.
finding.measure: Topic competence ratings and summative quizzes

finding.finding_summary: Student attitudes toward InkSurvey were generally favorable, with survey data showing that 54 of 63 students (86%) felt the tool helped the instructor better understand what they knew, and 48 of 63 (76%) said creating responses helped them better understand the material or recognize what they did and did not understand. Qualitative comments also indicate increased motivation, participation, and classroom engagement.
finding.measure: Anonymous student survey and focus-group comments

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports gains in metacognition, self-assessment, and problem-solving-related higher-order thinking. In one survey of 63 advanced laboratory students, 48 (76%) said InkSurvey helped them better understand what was being covered or what they did and did not understand, and instructors observed improved problem-solving skills over time in an upper-level engineering physics course.
finding.measure: Metacognitive/self-assessment survey items; problem-solving skill ratings
finding.study_size: n=63 for survey; course-specific problem-solving study size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Instructors reported that InkSurvey provided immediate feedback on student understanding, enabling them to identify common difficulties quickly and tailor instruction in real time. The paper treats this as a practical advantage of the system, but it does not provide quantitative workload or time-savings estimates.
finding.measure: Instructor reports of feedback timeliness and instructional adjustment

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment I. Applications in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes InkSurvey, a free web-based system for real-time formative assessment using pen-enabled mobile devices. The authors argue that open-format, ink-based responses can give instructors richer insight into student thinking than multiple-choice clicker questions, allowing them to diagnose misconceptions and adjust instruction immediately.

The paper presents seven implementation vignettes across diverse settings: a university honors calculus class, a high school algebra class, university food chemistry courses in Mexico, an introductory calculus-based physics course, a community college biology class, and upper-level undergraduate/graduate physics and chemical engineering courses. In each vignette, instructors report that InkSurvey helped surface student reasoning, increased participation, and supported timely instructional feedback, but the paper is descriptive and does not present a controlled comparison or formal outcome analysis.

The main conclusion is that InkSurvey is broadly usable across subjects, device types, and educational contexts, and that real-time formative assessment can make student misconceptions visible enough for immediate pedagogical response. The paper emphasizes practical classroom experiences rather than causal evidence, and it notes that a companion paper contains additional data on effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: Across multiple vignettes, InkSurvey is described as helping students justify answers, reveal misconceptions, and engage in metacognitive reflection on what they do and do not understand. For example, in physics and calculus settings, open-format prompts forced students to work through reasoning rather than select an option, and instructors reported that this exposed faulty reasoning that would otherwise have remained hidden.
finding.measure: Instructor observation of student responses and reasoning during class discussions

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that InkSurvey increased participation, engagement, and willingness to contribute in class, including among students who may have been less comfortable with technology or public response. In the creativity vignette, anonymity was said to reduce evaluation apprehension and encourage participation from all students.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported student participation and engagement

finding.finding_summary: In the calculus vignette with 87 first-term college students, InkSurvey was used to probe understanding of triple integrals and regions in space. After a formative-assessment question, 32 of 83 student responses showed a misconception of using constant bounds; after discussion and a follow-up question, all students responded and none provided all-constant bounds, suggesting improved understanding within the lesson.
finding.measure: Student responses to InkSurvey questions on defining regions for triple integrals
finding.study_size: n=87 (87 enrolled; 83 responses to one question)

finding.finding_summary: In physics, chemistry, biology, and engineering contexts, InkSurvey is reported to help instructors probe conceptual understanding and reveal misconceptions in real time. Examples include students explaining stopping-distance reasoning in physics and predicting enzyme activity in biology, with instructors using responses to correct incorrect reasoning immediately.
finding.measure: Open-ended conceptual responses and instructor review of misconceptions

finding.finding_summary: In the high school algebra vignette, students used InkSurvey almost daily to solve problem-solving exercises and receive feedback on algebraic work. The reported benefit was that all 25 students could submit solutions, enabling the teacher to compare approaches and address errors before students practiced independently at home.
finding.measure: Classroom implementation in Algebra I with teacher-reported feedback and student work review

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper discusses formative assessment as a pedagogical approach and explores how it can be implemented through an e-learning platform (BlackBoard) in a university setting. The authors frame formative assessment as frequent, low-stakes assessment with immediate feedback, arguing that it supports learning better than purely summative approaches and can be delivered effectively online.

The paper reports a small survey of university students using a 16-item questionnaire about continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and the proposed BlackBoard online test system. Students generally preferred frequent assessments because they broke content into smaller topics, allowed immediate feedback, and helped them identify strengths and weaknesses. The paper also cites prior formative assessment literature and meta-analyses, but its own evidence is limited to descriptive survey results rather than an intervention study.

A modest subgroup difference was reported across academic streams (Business, Engineering, and IT): Engineering students were more likely than the other groups to rate continuous assessment/open-book assessment and the BB test option as 'very much needed.' The paper concludes that formative assessment, especially when paired with immediate feedback and online delivery, may support better learning and possibly improve summative performance, though no achievement outcome is directly tested in this study.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable perceptions of frequent formative assessment because it provided immediate feedback, helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses, and reduced the fear of losing many marks on a single test. In the survey, a majority supported frequent internal assessments and the BlackBoard test option, but no achievement gains were directly measured.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and BlackBoard test option

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognitive processes by helping students reflect on feedback, track progress, and understand their strengths and weaknesses. Evidence comes from student responses indicating that the assessment format helped them study progressively and check whether they were on track, but these are perceptions rather than direct skill measures.
finding.measure: Student perception survey items about strengths/weaknesses, being on track, and progressive learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a statistically significant difference across academic streams in attitudes toward continuous assessment as open-book assessment (Cramer’s V=0.206, p<0.05) and in rating the BB test option (Cramer’s V=0.236, p<0.05). Engineering students were more favorable than Business and IT students, suggesting that acceptability of implementation may vary by subgroup within the institution.
finding.measure: Comparisons of student attitudes by academic stream (Business, Engineering, IT)

paper_profiles.title: Modernizing use of regression models in physics education research: A review of hierarchical linear modeling
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in physics education research: many studies analyze student data with single-level regression models even when the data are hierarchically structured, such as students nested within courses. The authors argue that ignoring this nesting can bias coefficients, standard errors, and statistical significance, and they review hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) as a better-suited approach for multilevel educational data.

The paper has two parts. First, it presents a conceptual review of disaggregation, aggregation, and HLM, using a small illustrative dataset to show how these approaches can yield different relationships between student SAT verbal scores and Force Concept Inventory (FCI) post-test scores. Second, it reanalyzes a real dataset from 5,959 undergraduate students in 112 introductory physics courses at 17 institutions, comparing multiple linear regression (MLR) with HLM for predicting normalized gains on concept inventories. The authors find that MLR and HLM can lead to meaningfully different conclusions, especially when course-level outliers are present.

The main conclusion is that HLM should be used when analyzing hierarchical education data because it better accounts for course-level clustering and produces more reliable estimates. In the empirical reanalysis, HLM showed that collaborative learning without learning assistants was not significantly different from lecture once course-level clustering was modeled, whereas MLR overstated that effect and produced smaller standard errors. The paper is primarily a methods/review article, not a study of an instructional intervention’s causal effect.

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses concept inventory gains as the outcome for a methodological comparison between multiple linear regression and hierarchical linear modeling. In the real dataset (n=5,959 students in 112 courses), HLM and MLR produced different coefficients for course-type predictors on Force Concept Inventory/Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation gains, showing that analytic method can materially change inferences about student learning. For example, the collaborative-learning-without-LA coefficient was positive and significant in MLR (coef=12.99, p<0.001) but much smaller and not significant in HLM (coef=3.26, p=0.283).
finding.measure: Concept inventory gains (Force Concept Inventory and Force and Motion Conceptual Evaluation; post-test minus pretest, percentage correct)

finding.finding_summary: The central finding is methodological rather than instructional: hierarchical linear modeling is more appropriate than single-level regression for nested education data and can prevent biased conclusions at the institutional/course level. In the reanalysis, the use of HLM changed statistical significance for course instructional categories and roughly doubled standard errors relative to MLR, indicating that the choice of model can substantially affect research conclusions and downstream educational recommendations.
finding.measure: Comparison of regression coefficients, standard errors, and significance across MLR vs HLM for multilevel course data

paper_profiles.title: Inquiry-Based Mathematics Education: a call for reform in tertiary education seems unjustified
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a scoping review and critical commentary on inquiry-based learning, specifically in tertiary mathematics education. The authors examine claims made by proponents of Inquiry-Based Mathematics Education (IBME) that students learn better, achieve deeper conceptual understanding, and benefit more equitably when they discover mathematics with minimal explicit instruction.

Rather than reporting a new intervention study, the paper synthesizes prior cognitive science and educational psychology research, including several experimental studies and meta-analyses, to argue that unguided or minimally guided inquiry is generally less effective than explicit instruction for novice learners. The context is undergraduate mathematics, with discussion of related evidence from elementary and other educational settings when relevant. The authors conclude that the broad reform agenda for replacing explicit teaching with inquiry-based methods is not supported by the evidence, especially for novices and for tasks involving high element interactivity.

The review also argues that claims about equity benefits are not substantiated. It emphasizes that the effectiveness of instruction depends on learner prior knowledge and cognitive load: novices generally benefit more from direct explanation, worked examples, and guided support than from discovery-first approaches. Some evidence is discussed for productive failure and sequencing effects, but the overall conclusion is that explicit instruction should usually precede problem solving in the kinds of mathematical learning targeted by IBME.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that inquiry-based mathematics education is generally less effective than explicit instruction for novice tertiary learners. It cites meta-analytic evidence and experimental studies indicating that unassisted discovery/inquiry tends to produce worse learning and transfer outcomes than guided or explicit teaching, especially for complex mathematical content.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes and transfer performance in mathematics education studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper also discusses broader learning outcomes such as conceptual understanding and transfer in mathematics, arguing that these are not improved by unassisted inquiry relative to explicit instruction. Evidence cited includes studies comparing application and transfer test performance under different instructional sequences.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding and transfer tests

finding.finding_summary: The review frames metacognitive control and self-regulation as prerequisite skills for successful inquiry learning, but argues that novices typically lack these abilities and therefore do not benefit from minimal guidance. The conclusion is that inquiry places heavy demands on executive control and metacognitive monitoring, which can undermine learning for weaker or novice students.
finding.measure: Theoretical and empirical discussion of metacognitive/self-regulatory demands during inquiry learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates the broader reform claim that tertiary mathematics should move toward inquiry-based instruction and concludes that such a reform agenda is not justified by the evidence. It characterizes the institutional push for IBME as widespread but unsupported, especially for improving equity.
finding.measure: Scoping review / critical synthesis of reform claims and evidence base

paper_profiles.title: Contributions from Cognitive Research to Mathematics and Science Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Workshop on Research in Science and Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an invited talk that reviews cognitive science findings relevant to mathematics and science education. Its central purpose is not to test a specific intervention, but to synthesize qualitative research on constructivism, misconceptions, novice–expert differences, cognitive load, and knowledge structuring, and to draw implications for teaching practice.

The talk argues that learning is an active, constructive process and that effective teaching depends on understanding how students organize and use knowledge. It presents descriptive models of expertise, emphasizes the importance of prior knowledge and conceptual structure, and suggests pedagogical practices such as using multiple representations, building links across concepts, extending context, and comparing/contrasting examples.

The population discussed is primarily students in mathematics and science settings, with examples drawn largely from introductory and more advanced physics courses, but the actual audience and intended user group are educators and researchers. The paper does not report a single empirical study of students; instead, it summarizes prior cognitive research and proposes instructional implications for classroom practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that cognitive research supports instructional approaches meant to improve mathematics learning by helping students build structured, transferable knowledge rather than memorizing procedures. It cites studies of novice–expert differences and problem solving, including a study in which novice students shifted toward principle-based problem categorization after brief exposure to an expert-like conceptual analysis constraint, but no effect sizes or sample sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Problem categorization, qualitative problem analysis, and mathematics problem-solving performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes cognitive research on science learning, especially misconceptions and novice–expert differences, to argue that scientific understanding depends on conceptual organization and meta-cognitive reflection. It reports that students can be prompted to adopt more expert-like approaches and that misconceptions are persistent, but the paper does not provide a new empirical science outcome with effect sizes or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Science problem solving, conceptual understanding, and categorization of scientific/physics problems

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies motivation, self-confidence, and self-motivation as important components of successful problem solving and expertise development. It argues that students need reasonable expectations of success to become internally motivated, but this is presented as a conceptual claim rather than a directly tested intervention effect.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-confidence, persistence, and self-motivation in problem solving

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that students should develop metacognitive and structural thinking skills such as reflection, evaluation, pattern seeking, and linking concepts across representations. The paper summarizes research suggesting that expert-like qualitative analysis can be induced quickly and that good students notice and refine implicit patterns, but it does not report a single quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Metacognitive reflection, qualitative analysis, pattern recognition, and knowledge structuring in problem solving

paper_profiles.title: Are Educational Escape Rooms More Effective Than Traditional Lectures for Teaching Software Engineering? A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a virtual educational escape room is more effective than a traditional lecture for teaching software modeling in a software engineering course. The authors motivate the study by noting that prior research on educational escape rooms has often lacked control groups, objective learning measures, or sufficiently robust designs.

The intervention was a fully virtual escape room delivered face-to-face through the Escapp web platform and compared against a traditional 1.5-hour lecture covering the same software modeling content (UML use case, class, sequence, activity, and state machine diagrams). The study used a cluster randomized controlled trial with 326 second-year undergraduate software engineering students at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid: 164 in the escape-room group and 162 in the lecture group. Students completed identical pre- and post-tests, and the experimental group also completed a perceptions questionnaire.

Results showed significant learning gains in both groups, but the escape room group improved more. Using ANCOVA with pretest as covariate, post-test performance was significantly higher for the escape room group with a small-to-medium effect size (r=0.25, p<0.001). Students also reported very positive perceptions of the activity, including high engagement, enjoyment, perceived learning, and strong preference for the escape room over a lecture. The authors conclude that educational escape rooms can outperform traditional lectures for teaching this software engineering topic, while noting that future work should examine long-term effects and whether results vary by student characteristics.

finding.finding_summary: Students who learned software modeling through the educational escape room outperformed those who learned through a traditional lecture on the post-test, after controlling for pretest scores. The difference was statistically significant (p<0.001) with a small-to-medium effect size (r=0.25) in favor of the escape room group, in a sample of n=326 undergraduate software engineering students.
finding.measure: Software modeling knowledge test (10 multiple-choice items; pretest/post-test scores; ANCOVA-adjusted post-test performance)

finding.finding_summary: Students in the escape room group reported very positive perceptions of the activity, including finding it fun, immersive, well organized, and worth recommending to other students. The questionnaire results also indicated strong enjoyment and preference for the escape room over a traditional lecture, though these were self-reported perceptions rather than standardized motivational outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceptions questionnaire (Likert items and closed-ended items)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that the escape room was conducted in teams of 4–6 students and was designed to encourage collaboration, communication, and teamwork. However, these skills were not directly measured as outcomes; the evidence is limited to the collaborative structure of the activity and students’ positive perceptions of the experience.
finding.measure: Team-based participation and questionnaire-based perceptions of the activity

paper_profiles.title: Work from Home and Job Satisfaction: Differences by Disability Status among Healthcare Workers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the ability to work from home is associated with job satisfaction and a set of work-experience perceptions, and whether those associations differ for workers with disabilities versus workers without disabilities. The motivation is to understand whether remote work can function as a workplace accommodation that narrows disability-related gaps in satisfaction and workplace experiences.

The authors surveyed 1,405 healthcare employees from a large state-wide university-affiliated health system in 2023 and analyzed a final sample of 993 respondents after excluding missing data. They used multivariable regression models with interactions between disability status and work-from-home frequency to test whether remote work moderates the relationship between disability and outcomes such as job satisfaction, job autonomy, turnover intentions, organizational commitment, perceived organizational support, inclusion, treatment of people with disabilities, and relations with managers and coworkers.

The main findings are that workers with disabilities report worse workplace experiences on many dimensions, even though direct job satisfaction did not differ significantly by disability status in the descriptive analysis. Working from home is generally associated with more favorable work experiences for all workers, but the benefits are often smaller for workers with disabilities than for workers without disabilities. In particular, remote work does not close disability gaps in workplace experiences because the positive effects are usually larger for non-disabled workers; in some cases, relationships with managers and coworkers are even less favorable for disabled workers who work from home.

finding.finding_summary: Working from home was associated with better work-related functioning for the overall sample, including higher job satisfaction and better job autonomy, especially for those working from home 3+ days per week. In the regression models (n=993), WFH 3+ days/week was associated with higher job satisfaction (b=0.195, p<0.01) and higher job autonomy (b=0.294, p<0.01), suggesting improved perceived efficiency/control at work.
finding.measure: Job satisfaction; job autonomy index

finding.finding_summary: Remote work was generally linked to better work-experience perceptions that reflect engagement and workplace well-being, but the paper's strongest evidence is on turnover intentions and organizational commitment rather than student-like social-emotional constructs. For the full sample (n=993), WFH 3+ days/week was associated with lower turnover intentions (b=-0.162, p<0.01) and higher organizational commitment (b=0.176, p<0.01), while job satisfaction was also higher (b=0.195, p<0.01).
finding.measure: Turnover intentions, organizational commitment, job satisfaction

finding.finding_summary: A central result is that disability status moderates the relationship between work from home and workplace experiences. Although remote work improved many outcomes overall, the benefits were often smaller for workers with disabilities than for those without disabilities, meaning remote work did not close disability gaps. For example, WFH 3+ days/week had a positive base association with organizational commitment (b=0.176), but the disability interaction was negative (b=-0.117), indicating a smaller net gain for disabled workers.
finding.measure: Interaction models of disability status by work-from-home frequency across workplace experience indices

paper_profiles.title: EmoBridge: Bridging the Communication Gap between Students with Disabilities and Peer Note-Takers Utilizing Emojis and Real-Time Sharing
paper_profiles.venue: The 26th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses communication and note-taking challenges in peer note-taking programs (PNTPs) for students with disabilities in higher education. The authors argue that existing PNTP arrangements are often unidirectional: peer note-takers provide notes, but students with disabilities have few ways to give feedback in real time or participate actively during class.

To study the problem, the authors first conducted a formative interview study with 16 participants (8 students with disabilities and 8 peer note-takers) and then designed EmoBridge, a collaborative note-taking web platform that supports real-time shared editing and emoji-based communication. They refined the system through a pilot with 3 pairs and evaluated it in the wild for at least four weeks with 7 peer note-taker/student-with-disability pairs in actual classes.

The evaluation used questionnaire data and interviews. Results suggested that EmoBridge improved students with disabilities’ class concentration, real-time feedback exchange, and perceived advantages of the note-taking process, while also reducing peer note-takers’ sense of sole responsibility and making communication easier. Effects varied by pair relationship and class context, indicating that collaborative note-taking benefits are shaped by social and instructional conditions rather than technology alone.

finding.finding_summary: The study found improved engagement, concentration, and enjoyment for students with disabilities after using EmoBridge. For SWDs, class concentration improved significantly on Q4 (median 4 to 7, p=0.04), and enjoyment of collaborative note-taking increased from median 2 to 5 (p=0.08), suggesting better participation and affect during class.
finding.measure: 7-point Likert questionnaire items on class concentration and enjoyment of note-taking (Q4, Q10)
finding.study_size: n=12 questionnaire respondents in the evaluation study (5 SWDs and 7 PNTs; analyses reported separately by role)

finding.finding_summary: EmoBridge improved collaborative note-taking and real-time communication between students with disabilities and peer note-takers. Post-deployment, both groups reported better ability to share feedback in real time (Q9: SWDs median 2 to 7, p=0.042; PNTs median 2 to 5, p=0.05) and PNTs reported it was easier to ask SWDs about unclear class content (Q7: median 3 to 6, p=0.039).
finding.measure: 7-point Likert questionnaire items on real-time feedback sharing, communication, and collaboration (Q7, Q8, Q9)
finding.study_size: n=12 questionnaire respondents in the evaluation study

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes EmoBridge as a support tool for peer note-taking programs in higher education and argues that such systems can improve the effectiveness of disability support services. In the field study, SWDs reported that EmoBridge was more advantageous than previous note-taking methods after deployment (Q11 median 1 to 5, p=0.041), suggesting institutional value for accessibility services.
finding.measure: 7-point Likert questionnaire item comparing EmoBridge with previous note-taking methods (Q11), plus qualitative evaluation of PNTP practice
finding.study_size: n=12 questionnaire respondents in the evaluation study

finding.finding_summary: The system reduced the psychological burden on peer note-takers by distributing responsibility through real-time feedback and shared editing. Qualitatively, PNTs reported less pressure to capture every word and a reduced sense of sole responsibility, especially when SWDs could monitor and correct notes in real time; this was supported by improved ease of communication and feedback exchange in the questionnaire results.
finding.measure: Questionnaire items on note-taking challenge and reliance, plus interview reports of burden reduction
finding.study_size: n=12 questionnaire respondents in the evaluation study

finding.finding_summary: The main academic effect was improved note-taking experience and understanding of lecture content, especially for students with disabilities. Although note quality and understanding items did not reach statistical significance overall, SWDs reported lower note-taking challenge (Q2 median 2 to 1, p=0.06) and better understanding/tracking of notes through real-time access, while qualitative evidence suggested improved participation in class note-taking.
finding.measure: 7-point Likert questionnaire on note-taking challenge and understanding of note content (Q2, Q3), plus interview data
finding.study_size: n=12 questionnaire respondents in the evaluation study

paper_profiles.title: Complexity in Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual/theoretical chapter; no empirical study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This encyclopedia chapter surveys the role of complexity theory in mathematics education. The authors argue that complexity provides a useful lens for understanding mathematics learning as emergent, adaptive, multi-level, and context-sensitive rather than linear and decomposable.

The chapter organizes its discussion into four senses of complexity in mathematics education: epistemological, historical, disciplinary, and pragmatic. It traces the historical development of complexity science, describes how complexity-oriented perspectives connect with constructivist, sociocultural, embodied, and critical theories of learning, and argues for curriculum and pedagogy that incorporate modeling, simulation, and agent-based computation.

In the pragmatic section, the chapter suggests that classrooms designed around complexity can support collaborative sense-making, interdisciplinary connections, and reflexive forms of learning. However, it is not an empirical study; it does not test an intervention or report participant outcomes, subgroup analyses, or effect sizes.

paper_profiles.title: Development of astronomy research and education in Africa and Ethiopia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad overview of recent developments in astronomy research, education, outreach, and human-capacity development across Africa, with a particular focus on Ethiopia. It argues that astronomy can serve as a tool for education, technological development, socio-economic growth, and progress toward the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

The article describes major infrastructure and institutional developments, including radio and optical telescope projects, postgraduate training programs, public outreach initiatives, and national and international collaborations. In Ethiopia, it highlights the creation of ESSS and ESSTI, the establishment of graduate programs, the development of research groups, teacher workshops, school collaborations, and STEM-for-girls activities.

The paper is primarily descriptive and programmatic rather than evaluative: it does not test an intervention or report quantitative outcome data. Its main conclusion is that astronomy has growing strategic value in Africa and Ethiopia, but sustained investment, collaboration, and policy support are still needed to expand research capacity and educational impact.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports substantial institutional growth in astronomy across Africa and Ethiopia, including new observatories, graduate programs, professional societies, policy roadmaps, and international meetings. These developments are described as strengthening research capacity, collaboration, and human-capacity development, but no quantitative effect sizes or controlled comparisons are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional development activities, observatory establishment, graduate program creation, professional society formation, policy development, and international collaboration initiatives

paper_profiles.title: Classroom assessment and pedagogy
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that formative assessment cannot be fully understood in isolation from pedagogy. Black and Wiliam revisit their earlier work on formative assessment and propose a broader framework in which classroom assessment is embedded within the wider act and discourse of teaching, including curriculum, instruction, dialogue, planning, and summative assessment.

The paper is primarily a conceptual/theoretical synthesis rather than an intervention study. It distinguishes between formative and summative functions of assessment as different kinds of inferences drawn from assessment evidence, while emphasizing that the same assessment instrument or classroom task can serve both purposes depending on how it is used. The authors discuss classroom dialogue, peer assessment, written feedback, the formative use of summative tests, and teachers’ summative judgments as interconnected components of instruction.

The context is general classroom teaching and assessment across school settings, with examples drawn from prior research and policy debates in England, the USA, Australia, Canada, and elsewhere. The central conclusion is that good classroom practice requires integrated attention to assessment for learning and assessment of learning, and that high-stakes accountability systems can distort pedagogy unless summative assessment is designed and used in ways that support learning. The article also argues that teachers should have a meaningful role in summative assessment, provided that validity, reliability, moderation, and support systems are addressed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrating formative and summative assessment can improve the quality of classroom decision-making, but it also notes that teacher-designed summative assessment systems require training, moderation, and support. In the KOSAP example, moderation was described as valuable for rigour, consistency, and confidence, but the text does not report a numeric effect size or sample size for workload or efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, moderation process value, consistency/confidence in summative assessment practice

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is how assessment systems shape pedagogy, especially under high-stakes accountability. The authors argue that externally imposed tests can undermine learning and that summative assessment systems should support valid, reliable, and comparable inferences while avoiding harmful incentives such as teaching to the test; no effect size is reported because this is a conceptual synthesis.
finding.measure: Assessment system design, accountability effects, moderation and validity of teacher assessment, policy implications

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes that formative assessment supports dialogue, metacognition, self-assessment, peer-assessment, and collaboration as part of effective learning. These claims are grounded in prior literature rather than new data, and the paper does not report a study sample, effect size, or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Dialogue, metacognition, self-assessment, peer-assessment, collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Online Diagnostic Assessment in Support of Personalized Teaching and Learning: The eDia System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual analysis introduces the eDia online diagnostic assessment system and argues for its role in supporting personalized teaching and learning in primary school. The paper is positioned as a synthesis of assessment theory, technology-based assessment, and diagnostic assessment practice rather than as a single empirical intervention study.

The authors describe eDia as an integrated platform for reading, mathematics, and science from the beginning of schooling through Grade 6. They explain the system’s three-dimensional assessment frameworks, item banks, automated scoring, feedback mechanisms, and teacher-assembled testing functions, emphasizing how these tools are intended to provide regular diagnostic feedback for students and teachers and to support differentiated instruction.

The paper also reviews prior eDia-based studies and related technology-based assessment developments, including media-effect comparisons, reasoning assessments, foreign language assessments, and longitudinal uses in Hungary and other countries. Its main conclusion is that technology can make frequent, individualized diagnostic assessment more feasible at scale, but that assessment tools alone do not improve learning unless teachers use the feedback to adjust instruction; teacher training and appropriate instructional models remain necessary.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on diagnostic assessment in reading as one of eDia’s three core domains, but it does not report a single intervention effect for literacy outcomes. It describes a large item bank for Grades 1–6 and notes that the system is used to provide regular diagnostic feedback to support personalized instruction, with empirical validation work and related studies referenced rather than fully reported here.
finding.measure: Diagnostic reading assessment dimensions within eDia; reading comprehension and related literacy tasks

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics is one of the three main domains assessed by eDia, and the paper emphasizes that the system provides regular diagnostic feedback for math learning and differentiated instruction. However, the article is primarily conceptual and system-descriptive, so it does not present a standalone quantitative estimate of impact on mathematical achievement.
finding.measure: Diagnostic mathematics assessment dimensions within eDia

finding.finding_summary: Science is a core eDia domain, including diagnostic assessment of scientific reasoning and inquiry-related skills. The paper outlines the framework and use of the system but does not report a direct causal effect on scientific reasoning outcomes; instead it summarizes how the platform is intended to support measurement and feedback in science learning.
finding.measure: Diagnostic science assessment dimensions within eDia; scientific reasoning/inquiry-related tasks

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses several higher-order thinking and reasoning constructs implemented in eDia, including inductive reasoning, dynamic problem-solving, collaborative problem-solving, creativity, and combinatorial reasoning. These are described as measurable through the platform and useful for research and diagnosis, but the paper does not report a single intervention effect estimate for these skills.
finding.measure: Reasoning and problem-solving assessments (e.g., inductive reasoning, dynamic problem-solving, collaborative problem-solving, creativity)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that diagnostic, personalized feedback may reduce boredom and anxiety and support motivation by keeping tasks optimally challenging. It also notes that motivation and self-regulated learning questionnaires have been implemented in eDia, but the article does not provide direct outcome estimates for student motivation or well-being.
finding.measure: Motivation, mastery motivation, learning strategies, and related questionnaire-based constructs

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is that eDia improves assessment efficiency through automated scoring, online delivery, item banking, and rapid feedback for large-scale diagnostic use. The authors present the system as a way to reduce the time and resource burdens that make traditional frequent diagnostic assessment difficult, but they do not report a single summarized effect size in this conceptual paper.
finding.measure: Assessment workflow efficiency, automated scoring, rapid feedback, and test administration capacity

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that eDia supports personalized teaching, differentiated instruction, and broader institutional assessment capacity, and it reports adoption in more than 1,000 schools in experimental mode. The emphasis is on institutional implementation and system-level use of diagnostic assessment rather than on a narrowly defined student-level effect estimate.
finding.measure: Adoption and implementation of eDia across schools; use for school practice and research

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical review that asks how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors frame formative assessment using established theory (e.g., clarifying learning goals, understanding where learners are, and deciding how to move learners forward) and argue that most current AI work in education has not been aligned closely enough with these core pedagogical principles.

Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, the paper synthesizes examples and design ideas for using LLMs in classroom formative practice. It discusses how LLMs might help educators rewrite learning objectives in student-friendly language, co-construct success criteria, generate sample work for critique, create short-cycle assessments and multiple-choice questions, and produce feedback at task, process, and self-regulation levels. The examples are illustrated mainly through classroom scenarios and prompt templates, with special attention to using accessible, cost-free tools and to the limits of LLM-generated output.

The paper is explicitly aimed at educators and researchers interested in integrating AI into classroom assessment. Its main conclusion is that LLMs can augment, but should not replace, expert pedagogy; their value depends on teachers using them with strong instructional judgment, careful prompt design, and attention to formative assessment principles. The paper also emphasizes the need for better evaluation metrics that capture formative qualities of AI-generated feedback and for future work that develops classroom-appropriate, pedagogically grounded prompt repositories and assessment designs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce educator workload and save time in creating student-friendly objectives, generating sample work, drafting formative questions, and producing feedback. These claims are illustrated with examples and prompt templates, but the paper does not report original experimental effect sizes or student outcome data.
finding.measure: Reported or proposed efficiency in generating formative assessment materials and feedback; no standardized quantitative measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that LLM-supported formative assessment may help foster metacognition, self-regulation, and critical thinking by clarifying goals, prompting reflection, and encouraging students to critique exemplars rather than rely passively on AI. However, these are conceptual claims and classroom design recommendations rather than empirical results.
finding.measure: Metacognitive awareness, self-regulation, critical thinking, and reflection as discussed conceptually

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses formative assessment as a diagnostic use of assessment during instruction, contrasting it with summative assessment and arguing that formative assessment can improve learning when paired with timely, specific feedback. The authors frame the problem as how to implement formative assessment effectively in a technology-rich university setting, especially through an e-learning platform.
