The study proposes and pilots weekly or fortnightly online tests using Blackboard Learning System at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus). These online assessments were designed to provide immediate, detailed feedback after student responses, with test formats including multiple choice, true/false, matching, fill-in-the-blank, and essay items. The paper describes the implementation and reports student perceptions from a questionnaire survey about continuous assessment and Blackboard-based testing.

The population was university students in business, engineering, and IT streams. Results suggest students generally supported frequent small-topic assessments and valued immediate teacher feedback, flexibility, and the ability to identify strengths and weaknesses. The paper concludes that e-learning can support formative assessment and that such assessment may help students stay engaged across the semester and potentially improve performance on summative exams, though the evidence presented is based on perceptions rather than learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable attitudes toward frequent internal assessments because they felt learning could happen in steps, the assessments checked on learning, and immediate feedback reduced delay in correcting mistakes. In the questionnaire, students also said teacher feedback helped them measure strengths and weaknesses and check whether they were on track; no achievement effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, immediate feedback, and teacher feedback from questionnaire items

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and self-monitoring by helping students reflect on feedback, understand errors, and evaluate their standing in the subject. Students stated that the approach helped them keep in touch with the subject throughout the semester and learn individual topics progressively, but these were perception data rather than measured skill gains.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, reflection, and staying on track with subject learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students supported splitting course work into 10-12 weekly Blackboard assessments and preferred the online format because it made small-topic study easier and provided detailed feedback on errors. The authors claim this formative approach could help students prepare for summative semester examinations, but the study does not report achievement scores or a causal effect on grades.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment / Blackboard online tests and their perceived usefulness for learning and summative exam preparation

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes Blackboard as a convenient way to administer formative assessments online and notes that students preferred it over classroom tests because of flexibility and convenience. This is an implementation-focused finding based on survey responses, not measured teacher workload or time savings.
finding.measure: Student ratings of Blackboard test option versus classroom test option; perceived flexibility/convenience

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on a five-year research project studying how secondary science and mathematics teachers learn to enact Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy built around classroom response system technology (“clickers”). The central question is not whether TEFA improves student outcomes in this paper, but how teachers change over time as they learn the pedagogy, develop comfort with it, and adapt it to their own contexts.

The intervention combines the CRS technology, the TEFA pedagogy, and an intensive professional development program. Teachers across several western Massachusetts school sites received an initial four-day workshop followed by weekly or biweekly PD sessions, with data collected from surveys, interviews, classroom videos, journals, implementation logs, and meeting transcripts. The sample included approximately 39 teachers in middle and high school science and math classrooms.

The paper presents detailed case narratives for four teachers with different trajectories of adoption and adaptation. Across cases, teachers initially struggled with question design, classroom discourse, and using formative information in real time, but many gradually became more comfortable and more student-centered. The authors conclude that TEFA is demanding but learnable, that teacher change is uneven and highly contextual, and that teachers’ use of formative assessment information can lead to real instructional adjustments. The paper is primarily about teacher learning and implementation, with only preliminary discussion of student-learning impacts and no controlled outcome study of student achievement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on the practical demands TEFA places on teachers, including the time needed to craft good questions, manage classroom discussion, and integrate TEFA into existing curricula. Teachers reported both gains in efficiency and substantial workload strain: for example, several became faster and more comfortable with TEFA over time, but others continued to struggle with the prep time and class time required.
finding.measure: Teacher reports, journals, surveys, and classroom observations of implementation and preparation burden

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports changes in teacher-related student engagement and teacher perceptions of student motivation, participation, and persistence during TEFA cycles. Across cases, students often became more willing to participate and discuss ideas, but some teachers also observed low participation or uneven engagement, leading to adjustments in implementation.
finding.measure: Student participation in discussion, teacher observations, and student/teacher surveys about classroom environment

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that TEFA supports students’ and teachers’ development of durable skills such as metacognition, collaboration, and reasoning. The paper describes teachers learning to elicit student thinking, promote peer discussion, and make real-time instructional adjustments based on formative information, with multiple teachers reporting that students engaged in deeper reasoning and dialogue over time.
finding.measure: Classroom discourse quality, teacher reflections, and observed changes in discussion structure and formative use of student responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes a substantial mathematics subset and one teacher (Gina) explicitly used TEFA to review for a statewide math exam and diagnose topic-level weaknesses. However, the paper does not report controlled achievement gains; instead, it emphasizes TEFA as a formative assessment tool that helped teachers gauge understanding and adapt instruction in math classrooms.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported use of TEFA for math review, state exam preparation, and diagnostic checking of student understanding

finding.finding_summary: Because the project is rooted in science and math classrooms, the paper reports that TEFA was used to elicit conceptual understanding and scientific reasoning, particularly through discussion of response questions. The strongest evidence is qualitative: teachers reported better insight into students’ thinking and sometimes changed lessons based on that information, but the paper does not provide student test-score outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-observed student reasoning in class discussions and formative assessment responses

paper_profiles.title: Calibrated Generative AI as Meta-Reviewer: A Systemic Functional Linguistics Discourse Analysis of Reviews of Peer Reviews
paper_profiles.population: Graduate students in online Education courses (master’s, doctoral, and certificate programs)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how generative AI can support formative assessment by producing “meta-feedback” on peer reviews in graduate online courses. The authors focus on a new CyberScholar workflow in which an AI Assistant reviews students’ peer-review comments using rubric-based criteria, generating a score plus qualitative feedback on the quality of the reviews themselves.

Using a corpus of 120 AI-generated meta-reviews from summer 2025 at a public Midwestern U.S. university, the study applies Systemic Functional Linguistics and Appraisal Theory to analyze the discourse of the AI feedback. The paper asks how calibration via retrieval augmentation and metaprompts shapes the rhetorical and relational qualities of the feedback, and whether the AI can approximate effective human formative feedback in a way that supports students’ feedback literacy.

The analysis finds that the AI’s language often foregrounded student agency, offered concrete and context-anchored suggestions, and balanced praise with calibrated critique. The reviews were highly structured, supportive, and rubric-aligned, suggesting that calibrated GenAI can model effective reviewing practices and help students improve their peer-feedback skills. The authors conclude that AI meta-feedback may be useful as a complementary layer within hybrid human–AI feedback ecosystems, but not as a replacement for human relational feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that calibrated GenAI meta-feedback supports feedback literacy, a durable skill closely related to metacognition and collaboration in peer review. Across 120 AI-generated meta-reviews, the system consistently modeled constructive reviewing moves by balancing praise with critique, making expectations visible, and helping students learn how to improve their future feedback practices.
finding.measure: Discourse analysis of AI-generated reviews of peer reviews using SFL/Appraisal categories; rubric-aligned feedback features

finding.finding_summary: The AI feedback was described as supportive, collegial, and motivating, with frequent positive judgment/appreciation and rare negative affect. The authors report that the discourse was designed to sustain student confidence and engagement by softening critique through hedging, praise, and dialogic openness.
finding.measure: Appraisal features in AI feedback (positive judgment, appreciation, affect, hedging, vocatives)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies formative feedback on peer-review quality in graduate education writing tasks. The AI reviews were found to be rubric-aligned, actionable, and pedagogically meaningful, with 120/120 reviews analyzed for discourse features such as process types, circumstantials, and rhetorical sequencing.
finding.measure: Quality and discourse features of formative meta-feedback on peer reviews

paper_profiles.title: FOUNDATIONS FOR AI-ASSISTED FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT FEEDBACK FOR SHORT-ANSWER TASKS IN LARGE-ENROLLMENT CLASSES
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the practical problem of delivering formative assessment feedback on short-answer tasks in large-enrollment introductory statistics courses. The authors argue that while written responses can promote learning and reveal misconceptions, manually scoring and clustering such responses is too time-consuming for instructors when class sizes are large.

The study evaluates natural language processing (NLP) methods as a human-machine aid for formative assessment rather than as a student-facing instructional intervention. Using de-identified responses from 1,935 post-secondary students across 29 class sections at 15 institutions, four trained human raters scored six short-answer tasks with a detailed rubric, and their agreement was compared with an automated scoring model (SFRN) and an LSTM baseline. The work also pilots clustering of response embeddings to support instructors in interpreting groups of similar student answers for scalable feedback.

Results show substantial agreement among trained human raters (pairwise QWK roughly 0.71-0.83; Fleiss’ kappa 0.62-0.70) and strong agreement between the better NLP model and humans (pairwise QWK roughly 0.74-0.82; four-rater Fleiss’ kappa 0.68). The SFRN model outperformed the LSTM in classification accuracy (83% vs. 72%). Clustering experiments suggested that representation choice matters: the learned SFRN representation was relatively consistent for clustering, but a lower-dimensional static representation (WTMF) produced the highest clustering consistency. The paper concludes that NLP-assisted formative assessment is feasible and promising for reducing instructor burden while preserving reliable scoring, but it does not test student learning outcomes directly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that NLP-assisted scoring can support formative assessment at scale with substantial agreement between human raters and the algorithm, suggesting reduced instructor burden for grading and feedback. The SFRN model achieved 83% classification accuracy versus 72% for LSTM, with pairwise QWK values between humans and SFRN of 0.74-0.82 and four-rater Fleiss’ kappa of 0.68.
finding.measure: Inter-rater reliability (quadratic weighted kappa, Fleiss’ kappa), classification accuracy, clustering consistency

paper_profiles.title: CoTAL: Human-in-the-Loop Prompt Engineering for Generalizable Formative Assessment Scoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of automating scoring and explanation of classroom formative assessment responses in K-12 STEM+C contexts, with an emphasis on making the approach generalizable across science, computing, and engineering tasks. The authors argue that formative assessment scoring is difficult for teachers to do at scale, especially for open-ended responses, and that existing LLM prompt-engineering approaches have mostly been tested in narrow domains without stakeholder feedback or curriculum alignment.

To address this, the paper introduces CoTAL (Chain-of-Thought Prompting + Active Learning), a human-in-the-loop prompt engineering framework that combines Evidence-Centered Design, few-shot chain-of-thought prompting, and iterative refinement from teachers and students. The study evaluates GPT-4 on three SPICE curriculum formative assessments completed by sixth-grade students: a science rules task, a computational debugging task, and an engineering fair-test task. The system is compared against a zero-shot baseline using Cohen’s QWK, and qualitative analyses examine scoring explanations, teacher interviews, and student feedback.

The main findings are that CoTAL improves scoring performance over the baseline on all three tasks, with particularly large gains on the engineering debugging task and strong gains on total-score agreement. The model also produces more transparent explanations by citing student text and rubric criteria, though some logical and context-consistency errors remain. Teacher and student feedback suggests the system is useful and understandable, and the authors conclude that human-in-the-loop prompt engineering can improve both scoring accuracy and feedback quality for formative assessment in real classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: CoTAL improved GPT-4’s scoring of formative assessment responses tied to science, computing, and engineering reasoning tasks. On the Rules Task, average QWK increased from 0.826 to 0.916 and Total Score QWK from 0.930 to 0.968; on the Debugging Task, average QWK increased from 0.567 to 0.706 and Total Score QWK from 0.561 to 0.779. The paper reports these gains on sixth-grade formative assessment responses from the SPICE curriculum (analytic sample varying by task: n=158 Rules, n=166 Debugging, n=161 Engineering).
finding.measure: Cohen’s QWK for rubric subscores and total formative assessment scores on science/computing/engineering tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that CoTAL can reduce teacher workload by automating scoring and generating explanations for open-ended formative assessment responses. Although it does not report a direct time-on-task or workload effect size, the study finds that the system can score responses and provide rubric-linked feedback that teachers judged useful, indicating potential efficiency gains in classroom assessment workflows.
finding.measure: Teacher judgments of scoring usefulness and automated generation of scoring explanations; no direct workload metric reported

finding.finding_summary: Student feedback suggested that the AI-generated explanations were understandable and useful for building trust and confidence in the system. The paper reports a focus group with 23 students who reviewed GPT-4’s scores and feedback and then completed a survey assessing agreement with scoring accuracy, feedback utility, and confidence in the system’s ability to grade future assignments; results are described qualitatively rather than with numeric effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student survey responses and focus group feedback on feedback utility, trust, and confidence

finding.finding_summary: The work suggests that CoTAL supports metacognitive understanding by giving explanations that connect student answers to rubric criteria and by helping students and teachers reflect on responses. The paper’s qualitative findings emphasize explanation quality, self-reflection, and the interpretability of scoring decisions, but it does not report a direct quantitative measure of durable skills.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of scoring explanations, teacher interviews, and student critiques

paper_profiles.title: Towards digitalisation of summative and formative assessments in academic teaching of statistics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to digitalize complex statistics exercises for university teaching without losing the pedagogical value of open-ended tasks. The authors argue that common web-based homework and assessment systems are insufficient for higher statistics because they either lack flexible exercise design, cannot evaluate student input deeply, or do not support rich feedback generation. To bridge this gap, they extend the JACK e-assessment system so it can interact with the statistical programming language R through Rserve.

The proposed approach supports parameterized exercises, multi-step tasks, detailed step-level feedback, hints, and fallback paths for unexpected student inputs. The paper also distinguishes between formative assessment use cases (with feedback, hints, and repeated attempts) and summative assessment use cases (without hints/feedback and with tighter grading constraints). The context is large undergraduate statistics lectures at the University of Duisburg-Essen, with courses enrolling up to 700 students per semester.

The paper is primarily a system/descriptive implementation report rather than an experimental evaluation. It presents examples of digitalized exercises, describes technical integration with R, and reports usage figures from two statistics lectures. The authors conclude that the approach is feasible and widely used in practice, but they do not provide a controlled comparison of learning gains attributable to the system.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the JACK system was used extensively in undergraduate statistics teaching and that exercises supported by R enabled complex, parameterized quantitative tasks with detailed feedback. The authors state that students who worked most during the semester appeared to have the best exam performance, but they do not provide a controlled estimate of learning impact.
finding.measure: Usage in statistics exercises and reported exam performance in undergraduate statistics courses
finding.study_size: Descriptive statistics: 22 students / 398 practice submissions / 51,803 test submissions; Inductive statistics: 40 students / 4 exams / 153 practice / 25,949 submissions

finding.finding_summary: The system is presented as a way to reduce manual grading effort and support large-enrollment courses through automated evaluation, feedback, and parameterized exercise generation. The paper reports substantial usage volumes in two statistics courses, indicating that the approach scaled to large cohorts and reduced the need for manual handling of repeated exercises and some grading tasks.
finding.measure: System usage, automated grading/feedback workflow, and support for large-enrollment instruction
finding.study_size: Descriptive statistics: up to 700 students per semester; Inductive statistics: up to 700 students per semester

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports institution-level adoption of the JACK-based assessment approach in two large undergraduate statistics lectures and describes both formative and summative assessments, including voluntary electronic exams as alternatives to paper exams. It concludes that the concept is feasible and accepted by students, but the evidence is descriptive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Adoption and acceptance of electronic formative/summative assessments and exams at one university
finding.study_size: Two large undergraduate statistics courses at the University of Duisburg-Essen

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that parameterized formative exercises, detailed feedback, and opportunities to retry tasks may help students stay engaged, practice more often, and start learning earlier in the semester. However, these are inferred benefits from usage patterns and design rationale rather than measured outcomes with a causal estimate.
finding.measure: Student practice frequency and reported engagement/acceptance in usage observations

paper_profiles.title: Students’ interaction with and appreciation of automated informative tutoring feedback
paper_profiles.venue: FAME 1 – Feedback & Assessment in Mathematics Education (chapter/conference proceedings)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how 15-to-17-year-old secondary students interact with an online mathematics environment that uses an informative tutoring feedback (ITF) strategy. The authors are interested in whether the design—knowledge-of-results feedback, error-specific feedback, try-again opportunities, optional direct instruction, and worked-out solutions offered later in the task flow—supports fruitful student-environment interactions and whether students prefer specific error feedback or worked solutions.

The study is framed as a response to the tension between offering enough guidance to prevent cognitive overload and uncertainty, while preserving room for exploration and self-guidance. The environment focused on linear and exponential extrapolation tasks, and students worked individually in a single session while screen capture and interviews were collected. The design intentionally delayed worked examples at the start and used model backtracking to diagnose final answers and generate error-specific feedback.

Across 25 students from grade 10 and 11 in one Dutch school, the qualitative analyses showed that students often improved after feedback, especially after direct instruction or reduced-complexity subtasks, but error-specific feedback sometimes still left students uncertain. Only a minority demonstrated self-guidance by checking intermediate results. In interviews, students most often preferred a combination of first receiving error-specific feedback and later viewing worked-out solutions. The chapter concludes that a balanced informative feedback strategy can support engagement and is appreciated by students, but it does not measure learning gains directly.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined students' work on linear and exponential extrapolation tasks in an automated formative assessment environment. Using qualitative interaction analysis, the authors found that students often improved after feedback, with 44/79 transitions resulting in improvement overall; improvement was especially high after direct instruction (13/14) and subtasks (7/7), while error-specific feedback led to improvement in 14/29 cases and sometimes still left students unable to continue.
finding.measure: Student task performance and improvement across extrapolation problem-solving episodes; coded transitions following knowledge-of-results, error-specific feedback, worked examples, subtasks, and direct instruction

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantially studies engagement, uncertainty, and self-guidance while students use formative feedback in the environment. Five of 25 students showed self-guidance by checking intermediate results, and the discussion notes that insufficient feedback could leave some students uncertain or disengaged, as illustrated by cases where students stalled after repeated knowledge-of-results feedback.
finding.measure: Qualitatively coded evidence of self-guidance, inability to continue, uncertainty, and students' interview comments about feedback appreciation

finding.finding_summary: The chapter also focuses on metacognitive/self-guidance behavior as students tested whether intermediate calculations were correct using task values. Five of 25 students displayed this behavior, and the authors interpret it as evidence that the feedback design can foster self-guidance, although it was not common across the sample.
finding.measure: Observed self-checking of intermediate results during problem solving; coded episodes of self-guidance

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a large-language-model (LLM)-based auto-grading and feedback system can support formative assessment in constructive geometry tasks on an online math platform. The authors are especially interested in distinguishing classroom formative feedback from adjacent automated assessment uses, so the system is designed to grade open-ended explanations, evaluate student constructions, and deliver attempt-sensitive feedback rather than simply score quiz responses.

The intervention was deployed on Algeomath, a Korean web-based dynamic geometry platform, in a field study with 79 middle-school students in four classes in South Korea. The task sequence included closed-ended items, constructive geometry tasks, and open-ended explanations centered on triangle circumcenter concepts and applied geometric reasoning. Grading was rule-based for closed-ended and construction tasks, while open-ended explanations were graded by GPT-4 using few-shot prompts; feedback was generated from teacher-authored exemplars and adapted across up to three retry opportunities per item.

Results show high alignment between system and teacher judgments for rule-based items and substantial agreement for open-ended grading overall (Cohen’s κ = 0.737 across 878 explanatory responses). Expert review of feedback found it generally serviceable but variable in quality, with common problems including answer leakage, imprecise terminology, and overly generic or punitive phrasing. Student response patterns suggest that feedback often supported rapid short-term correction: 36.7% of initially incorrect responses became correct on the next attempt (260/708), and most gains occurred after the first retry. However, evidence for longer-term transfer to later tasks was weak and not statistically significant, so the paper mainly demonstrates feasibility and short-term formative utility rather than strong causal learning effects.

finding.finding_summary: The system supported short-term improvement on constructive geometry tasks, but the learning effects were uneven. Across 79 middle-school students and 18 items, 36.7% of initially incorrect responses (260/708) were converted to correct answers on the next attempt, and aggregate cumulative success rose from about 0.60 on attempt 1 to about 0.73 on attempt 2, then leveled off near 0.80 by attempt 4.
finding.measure: Correctness on constructive geometry, closed-ended math items, and open-ended geometry explanations; attempt-level conversion to correct answers

paper_profiles.title: Using Generative AI and Multi-Agents to Provide Automatic Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a multi-agent generative AI system can improve the quality of automatic feedback for student constructed responses in science assessment. The authors focus on a known problem in LLM-generated feedback: over-praise and over-inference, both of which can misrepresent student performance and reduce the pedagogical value of feedback.

The study develops AutoFeedback, a two-agent workflow in which one GPT-4o-based agent generates feedback and a second agent validates and revises it using the item rubric, learning context, and feedback criteria. The system is evaluated on 240 middle school science responses drawn from a larger dataset of 845 responses to an item about thermal energy transfer and particle motion. The comparison is between single-agent GPT-4o feedback and the multi-agent AutoFeedback system.

Results show that the multi-agent system substantially reduced problematic feedback. Over-praise fell from 15.42% to 1.25%, over-inference from 27.20% to 7.08%, and feedback containing both problems from 9.58% to 0.83%, with chi-square tests reported as significant (p < 0.001). The paper concludes that multi-agent architectures may be a promising way to improve automated formative feedback, though some errors still remained and the study did not test student learning outcomes directly.

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that a two-agent GPT-4o system produced more accurate feedback on middle school science constructed responses than a single-agent baseline. On a dataset of 240 responses, over-praise dropped from 15.42% to 1.25% and over-inference from 27.20% to 7.08%, with significant chi-square differences (p < 0.001), indicating improved alignment between feedback and the scientific reasoning embedded in student answers.
finding.measure: Frequency of over-praise and over-inference in automatic feedback for science constructed responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that multi-agent automatic feedback can scale formative feedback production by automating generation plus validation, reducing the need for manual teacher review. However, the study measured feedback quality rather than direct time savings or workload reduction, so the operational implication is inferred from the system design rather than directly tested.
finding.measure: Automatic feedback generation and validation workflow quality

paper_profiles.title: How Well Can You Articulate that Idea? Insights from Automated Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines automated formative feedback for middle school science explanation essays and asks why the accuracy of such feedback varies across ideas and across students. The authors focus on a roller coaster physics curriculum in which students write explanation essays, receive automated checklist-style feedback from PyrEval, and then revise their essays.

The central contribution is an error analysis of the automated formative assessment system rather than a test of a new instructional intervention. The authors compare several semantic vector methods and then analyze feedback accuracy using two manually labeled essay datasets (GT1 and GT2) plus a historical corpus of physics constructed responses. They find that feedback accuracy depends both on the distinctiveness of the science idea itself and on the clarity of students’ writing; some ideas, especially the law of conservation of energy, are detected much more accurately than others because they are more formulaic and less confusable.

The study’s context is a 2-3 week design-based middle school physics unit delivered through a digital notebook with virtual experiments, short-answer questions, explanation essays, and revisions. The paper reports that the system generally performs well, but does not experimentally isolate the causal impact of the feedback on student learning in this paper; instead, it argues that inaccurate automated feedback can still prompt students to reflect on how clearly they articulate their ideas. The authors also note that their separate work reports improved revised essays using the feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies automated formative feedback on middle school science explanation writing and shows that the system can help identify missing or unclear ideas in student essays. On the manually labeled datasets, overall feedback accuracy was 79.50% on GT1 and 74.44% on GT2, suggesting the tool was reasonably accurate for supporting essay revision, though the paper itself does not present a causal estimate of writing improvement.
finding.measure: Accuracy of automated idea detection in student explanation essays; quality of student writing clarity as probed by cosine similarity patterns
finding.study_size: GT1 n=39 essays; GT2 n=120 essays (60 students' essays and revisions); additional analysis on 159 essays overall

finding.finding_summary: The curriculum and essays focus on explaining physics concepts such as potential energy, kinetic energy, energy transfer, and conservation of energy. The automated feedback was most accurate for more formulaic scientific statements, especially the law of conservation of energy (main idea 4 accuracy 89.30% overall), and less accurate for more variably expressed ideas like relations between potential and kinetic energy (main ideas 1 and 2 at 66.66% and 64.77% overall).
finding.measure: Automated detection accuracy for six science main ideas in roller coaster physics explanation essays
finding.study_size: GT1 n=39 essays; GT2 n=120 essays; all analyses on 159 essays

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating GPT- and Reasoning-based Large Language Models on Physics Olympiad Problems: Surpassing Human Performance and Implications for Educational Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how well a general-purpose large language model (GPT-4o) and a reasoning-optimized model (o1-preview) solve advanced physics problems compared with Physics Olympiad participants. The authors are especially interested in whether different prompting approaches change GPT-4o performance and what the detailed solution processes reveal about LLM strengths and weaknesses.

The study analyzes six text-based mechanics problems drawn from recent German Physics Olympiad stages. For GPT-4o, the authors generated solutions under four prompting conditions: no prompting, general prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, and single-shot chain-of-thought prompting. For o1-preview, they used general prompting only. In total, 600 LLM solutions were produced and scored against official Olympiad scoring rubrics that considered not only final answers but also intermediate problem representation and reasoning steps. These scores were compared with student solutions from the Olympiad using simulated exam-level aggregates and problem-by-problem analyses.

The main finding is that both models outperformed the human benchmark overall, with o1-preview performing best and GPT-4o prompting variations making little difference. The paper concludes that advanced LLMs now pose a challenge for unsupervised summative assessment because they can solve high-level physics problems at or above top-student level. At the same time, the authors argue that these capabilities could be useful for formative assessment, where LLMs might help students check and reflect on their own solutions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates physics problem solving on six advanced Olympiad mechanics problems, using official scoring rubrics that credit problem representation, identification of relevant concepts, mathematical execution, and final correctness. Across simulated exam sets, o1-preview substantially outperformed all GPT-4o prompting conditions and the human Olympiad benchmark, with very large to huge effects versus students (Cohen’s d=2.28 for o1-preview vs. participants; d=0.87-1.25 for GPT-4o variants vs. participants).
finding.measure: Olympiad problem-solving scores on six advanced physics problems, scored with official problem-specific rubrics
finding.study_size: n=600 LLM solutions; human comparison from Physics Olympiad participant solutions (exact n not_reported in excerpt)
finding.effect_size: d=2.28 (o1-preview vs. participants); d=0.87-1.25 (GPT-4o variants vs. participants)

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that the results have direct implications for educational assessment policy and practice, especially summative assessment in unsupervised settings. Because advanced LLMs could solve Olympiad-level physics problems at or above elite student performance, the paper concludes that authenticating student work in high-stakes assessment is more difficult and that assessment design may need to be reconsidered.
finding.measure: Implications drawn from comparative performance on advanced physics assessment tasks

paper_profiles.title: Integrating LLMs for Grading and Appeal Resolution in Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can be used to grade computer science examinations, generate feedback, and help resolve student grade appeals. The authors introduce AI-PAT, an AI-powered assessment workflow that compares LLM grading across models, compares LLM grading with human grading, and uses LLMs to respond to student appeals.

The study was conducted in a second-year undergraduate Object-Oriented Programming course at Gebze Technical University. Across nine quizzes, a midterm, and a final exam, the system graded 850+ exam submissions and processed 185 appeals. The authors also collected student feedback and examined inter-rater and intra-rater reliability for human graders and LLMs. Results suggest that LLMs can provide scalable grading and detailed feedback, but scores vary by model and prompt configuration, and both human and AI grading show inconsistency.

The paper finds that appeal resolution frequently changed grades, indicating that initial automated grading was sometimes insufficiently accurate or transparent. Students appreciated the speed and detail of AI feedback, but many expressed concerns about fairness, trust, and the desirability of using AI for future assessment. Overall, the paper concludes that LLM-based grading can support formative assessment workflows, but only with transparent rubrics, human oversight, and structured appeal mechanisms.

finding.finding_summary: AI-PAT scaled grading across more than 850 exam submissions and handled 185 appeal cases, indicating substantial automation of labor-intensive assessment work. The authors report that the system provided faster grading and detailed feedback, though no formal time-savings effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Grading throughput, appeal handling capacity, and perceived feedback usefulness
finding.study_size: n=850+ graded submissions; n=185 appeals; n=49 student survey respondents

finding.finding_summary: Student perceptions of AI-PAT were mixed to negative: 45% of survey respondents agreed the feedback was helpful, but 88% said they would not choose AI-PAT for future assessments. The survey suggests that while the system may support learning-related confidence for some students, trust and fairness concerns limited acceptance.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on satisfaction, trust, fairness, and willingness to use AI-PAT again

finding.finding_summary: The system was intended to support reflective self-assessment during grade appeals, and the authors argue that students were prompted to critically analyze their exam responses. However, the evidence is indirect and largely based on process description and perceptions rather than a measured gain in metacognition or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Appeal explanations and student reflections on exam answers
finding.study_size: n=185 appeals; n=49 student survey respondents

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that an AI-assisted grading and appeal workflow can be implemented at course scale, with 74% of appeals resulting in grade changes after review. This suggests institutional potential for more transparent and scalable assessment processes, although the study also reveals the need for human oversight and rubric calibration.
finding.measure: Appeal outcomes, grade changes after review, and student perceptions of fairness

paper_profiles.title: Students’ Patterns of Interaction with a Mathematics Intelligent Tutor: Learning Analytics Application
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal on Integrating Technology in Education (IJITE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ interaction patterns with an intelligent tutoring system can help explain success in a foundation mathematics course. The author analyzes ALEKS data logs together with survey responses to identify predictors of academic achievement, especially the ratio of topics mastered to topics practiced (mtop), prior knowledge, and students’ sequencing of topics during practice.

The intervention/context is not a controlled instructional treatment but the use of ALEKS, a web-based intelligent tutor that provides practice and frequent formative assessments in a higher-education foundation mathematics course in the United Arab Emirates. The sample includes 58 female students whose data logs were tracked over a 7-week period and triangulated with a Likert-scale survey about perceptions of tutoring/cognitive effects and study habits.

The study finds that prior knowledge and mtop are significant predictors of final exam marks, together explaining 42% of the variance in final exam performance. Students who selected topics sequentially were more likely to retain mastery after the summative assessment than students who selected topics randomly, and cluster analysis suggests that random topic selection is associated with weaker retention even when perceptions of ALEKS are positive. The paper concludes that instructors can use learning analytics to monitor progress, identify at-risk students, and encourage more effective sequencing of practice topics.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the ratio of topics mastered to topics practiced (mtop) and prior knowledge significantly predicted final exam marks in a foundation mathematics course. In the stepwise regression model, these two predictors explained 42% of the variance in final exam scores (R2 = 0.42); mtop had a significant positive regression weight (B = 46.008, p = .015) and prior knowledge was also significant (B = 0.649, p < .001).
finding.measure: Final exam marks in foundation mathematics; course mastery/comprehensive test outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The survey and cluster analysis examined students’ perceptions of ALEKS and their study habits, including whether they felt the system had tutoring and cognitive effects. Students with positive perceptions and sequential topic selection appeared to retain learning better, while students with random topic selection showed weaker retention even when perceptions were positive; however, the paper does not estimate a direct causal effect of ALEKS on motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey of perceptions about ALEKS tutoring effect and cognitive effect; self-reported topic-selection habit

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that sequencing of practice topics was associated with better retention of mastery, which the author interprets as reflecting independent learning and metacognitive organization. Students who chose topics sequentially were able to retain mastery after the summative assessment, whereas students who chose topics randomly were less able to retain mastery; in cluster 3 the difference between mastered topics and CT score was significant (t = -2.233, p = .036).
finding.measure: Retention of mastered topics after comprehensive test; paired-sample t-test comparing number of topics mastered vs CT score; topic-selection pattern

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ALEKS data logs can help instructors monitor students’ progress and detect at-risk students who are not maintaining an effective pace of learning. This is presented as a practical benefit of learning analytics for instructional oversight, but the study does not directly measure teacher workload or operational efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Instructor monitoring of data logs and identification of at-risk students

paper_profiles.title: Socratic Mind: Impact of a Novel GenAI-Powered Assessment Tool on Student Learning and Higher-Order Thinking
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether Socratic Mind, a generative-AI-powered formative assessment tool, can support learning in a large online introductory computing course. The tool uses adaptive Socratic questioning, allowing students to respond by typing or speaking and receiving immediate personalized feedback aimed at helping them explain reasoning, identify misconceptions, and refine understanding.

The researchers used a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design with 171 undergraduate students from a 16-week asynchronous CS1301 course at a U.S. research university. Quantitative data came from system logs, surveys, and course performance records; qualitative data came from 141 open-ended survey responses. Students reported high engagement and positive user experience, and greater engagement was associated with stronger perceived learning. In terms of actual performance, the tool did not significantly improve test scores, but it did buffer the typical decline in quiz scores over time, with a particularly stronger benefit for lower-performing students.

Qualitatively, many students reported perceived gains in problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection, while reported changes in verbal communication were weaker because many students used text rather than audio. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI-mediated Socratic dialogue can serve as a scalable formative assessment approach that promotes deeper engagement and higher-order thinking, especially in online computing education.

finding.finding_summary: The GenAI formative assessment tool was associated with improved course quiz performance relative to the comparison group, especially for lower-performing students. In the DiD analysis, the treatment reduced the typical decline in quiz scores by about 3.30 points (β = .107, p < .05; R² = .303), and the extended model showed a significant treatment-by-pre score interaction indicating larger benefits for students with lower baseline performance (B = -0.217, p < .05).
finding.measure: Unit quiz scores and difference-in-differences regression on pre/post quiz performance

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined perceived changes in higher-order thinking skills after use of the tool. Among 141 open-ended survey responses, 69% reported positive changes in problem-solving, 62% in critical thinking, and 60% in self-reflection, while only 38% reported positive changes in verbal communication. These findings suggest the Socratic questioning design was perceived as supporting metacognitive and analytical skills more strongly than communication.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of open-ended survey responses about problem-solving, critical thinking, self-reflection, and verbal communication

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high engagement and positive user experience while using the tool. Mean engagement ratings were high across affective engagement (M = 3.96, SD = 0.76), behavioral engagement (M = 4.07, SD = 0.61), and cognitive engagement (M = 3.96, SD = 0.68), and UX ratings were also strong (usability M = 3.99, SD = 1.16; effectiveness M = 4.09, SD = 1.08; satisfaction M = 3.88, SD = 1.23).
finding.measure: Engagement and Learning Scale; UX survey; interaction logs

finding.finding_summary: Perceived learning outcomes were strongly and positively associated with use of the GenAI tool. Perceived learning correlated highly with affective engagement (r = .76), behavioral engagement (r = .66), and cognitive engagement (r = .58), and was also positively related to UX measures (r = .45 to .54). In the regression model, affective engagement (β = .445, p < .001) and behavioral engagement (β = .181, p < .05) were the strongest predictors of perceived learning, with the model explaining 68.5% of the variance.
finding.measure: Perceived learning scale and multiple regression predicting perceived learning

paper_profiles.title: Studying physics during the COVID-19 pandemic: Student assessments of learning achievement, perceived effectiveness of online recitations, and online laboratories
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This descriptive survey study examined how physics undergraduates experienced the abrupt shift to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors were especially interested in three areas: students’ perceived learning achievement, the perceived effectiveness of online problem-solving sessions (recitations), and the perceived effectiveness of online physics laboratories.

Data came from a questionnaire administered to 578 physics students at five universities in Germany, Austria, and Croatia. The survey measured self-organization, communication, attitudes toward online learning, study environment, perceived learning achievement, recitation formats, and laboratory formats. The paper reports correlational analyses and group comparisons (ANOVAs/MANOVA), not experimental manipulation.

Main findings were that perceived learning achievement was positively associated with self-organization, communication, and having a good study environment, and negatively associated with less favorable attitudes toward online learning. First-year students reported the lowest perceived learning achievement. For recitations, students rated sessions as more effective when they submitted their own solutions and received graded feedback followed by online discussion, and they preferred live collaborative problem-solving over handouts of worked solutions. For laboratories, students perceived the online labs as more effective when they gathered their own data rather than using simulated or secondhand data.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused directly on physics laboratory learning, especially students’ perceived acquisition of experimental skills and reinforcement of physics concepts. Students rated online labs more favorably when they gathered data themselves; compared with simulated or handed-out data, self-collected data was associated with higher perceived experimental skills, F(2, 198)=14.2, p<0.001, and better content reinforcement, F(2, 216)=3.50, p=0.03.
finding.measure: Perceived acquisition of experimental skills and reinforcement of physics content in online physics laboratories

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examined self-organization, communication, and collaborative work as predictors of perceived learning achievement during remote instruction. Perceived learning achievement was positively correlated with self-organization during COVID-19 (r=0.63), communication (r=0.50), and self-organization in general (r=0.33), with all reported correlations significant under Bonferroni correction.
finding.measure: Survey scales for self-organization, communication, and perceived learning achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined students’ self-organization during the COVID-19 semester as a behavioral/motivational factor tied to remote learning success. Self-organization during COVID-19 was strongly associated with higher perceived learning achievement (r=0.63), suggesting that students who reported better planning, routine, and self-management also believed they were learning more effectively.
finding.measure: Self-organization during COVID-19 semester scale and perceived learning achievement

finding.finding_summary: The recitation portion of the study directly evaluated students’ perceived effectiveness of online physics problem-solving sessions. Students who submitted their own solutions for correction and discussion rated recitations as more effective than those who did not, F(1, 393)=6.74, p=0.01; the perceived effectiveness scale was also positively correlated with perceived overall learning achievement (r=0.66, p<0.01).
finding.measure: Perceived effectiveness of online recitations

finding.finding_summary: Although not a policy study, the paper’s findings are framed as guidance for institutional course design during pandemic-era remote teaching. The results suggest that universities should support self-regulation, communication structures, and online formats that preserve student interaction, such as live recitations with feedback and laboratories where students collect their own data.
finding.measure: Implications drawn from survey-based comparisons of online course formats
finding.study_size: n=578 overall; n=401 recitations; n=220 labs

paper_profiles.title: Learn Like Feynman: Developing and Testing an AI-Driven Feynman Bot
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether an AI-driven study bot based on the Feynman learning technique can improve self-regulated learning outcomes compared with passive review. The authors developed the Feynman Bot, a conversational app that uses a large language model with retrieval-augmented generation to prompt learners to explain material, answer questions, and engage in deeper discussion of lecture content.

The study tested the bot in a controlled experiment over three days with 14 working adults enrolled in an online Harvard course on justice/utilitarianism. Participants were randomly split into a passive study group versus a Feynman Bot group; both completed a formative assessment, two days of learning activities, and a summative assessment, and the bot group also completed a self-efficacy survey. The paper reports that Feynman Bot users achieved higher mean learning gains than passive learners, showed greater comfort with the study material, and generally preferred typing over speech when interacting with the bot.

The intervention is framed as an active-learning support tool for self-regulated learners who lack peer or instructor support, rather than as a formative assessment tool itself. The paper uses formative and summative tests to measure learning gain, but the core contribution is the conversational learning environment. Because of the very small sample and exploratory nature, the findings are promising but preliminary.

finding.finding_summary: In a 3-day controlled experiment with 14 working adults, the Feynman Bot group showed higher learning gains on the course content than the passive-learning group. Mean learning gain was 3.83 for the Feynman Bot group versus 2.17 for the passive group, and mean summative scores were also slightly higher for the bot group (M=6.8, SD=1.3) than the passive group (M=6.5, SD=1.9).
finding.measure: Formative and summative assessment scores on two lecture topics from an online justice course; learning gain computed as summative score minus formative score
finding.std_deviation: FB learning-gain SD=1.32; passive learning-gain SD=1.94

finding.finding_summary: The bot increased learners’ comfort and confidence with the study material. All Feynman Bot users agreed that the tool increased their comfort enough to discuss the material with peers, over 57% said they felt comfortable enough to teach or converse about it with new learners, and 85.7% said it was useful for learning new topics.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-efficacy survey on comfort with the study material and with using the bot
finding.study_size: n=7 (Feynman Bot group only; implied by random split of 14 participants)

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the bot supported deeper explanation and application-oriented responses rather than short recall-only answers. On the open-ended questions, Feynman Bot users were more likely to include scenario- or case-based explanations, indicating stronger elaboration and conceptual understanding than the passive group.
finding.measure: Open-ended assessment responses analyzed qualitatively/thematically

paper_profiles.title: Student engagement with teacher and automated feedback on L2 writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how two Chinese university students engaged with two sources of feedback on second-language writing: teacher written feedback and automated writing evaluation (AWE) feedback. The study asks how the two feedback sources differ, how students respond to them behaviorally, affectively, and cognitively, and what factors shape those responses.

The paper uses a naturalistic case-study approach over a 16-week semester in two EAP courses. One assignment involved multiple drafting through the Pigai AWE system; another involved teacher feedback on a different essay. Data included student drafts, feedback records, submission timestamps, documents, and two retrospective semi-structured interviews with each student. The authors compare a highly engaged learner (Flora) and a moderately engaged learner (David), showing that Flora invested more time, strategy use, reflection, and positive emotion, and also produced stronger revisions and higher AWE scores, while David showed more surface-level revision and greater anxiety or confusion.

The main conclusion is that engagement is a central mediating factor in the effectiveness of formative assessment in L2 writing. The paper argues that both feedback source and learner factors, especially language proficiency and strategy knowledge, shape how students use feedback. It also suggests that AWE can support timely, iterative formative assessment, but teacher feedback remains important for more comprehensive and human-centered guidance.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that the highly engaged student (Flora) made extensive revisions in response to both teacher and AWE feedback, while the moderately engaged student (David) made mostly surface-level changes. Flora resubmitted her AWE draft 13 times and increased her score from 79 to 90; David resubmitted once, spent less than 14 minutes, and showed only a negligible score increase.
finding.measure: Revision operations, draft quality/score changes, and writing development in L2 essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that affective engagement strongly shaped how students responded to feedback. Flora felt motivated, frustrated at first but ultimately encouraged by score gains, whereas David felt shocked, disappointed, embarrassed, and demoralized by the AWE score and feedback load, which reduced his willingness to revise.
finding.measure: Interview-coded emotional responses and affective engagement with feedback

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines cognitive and metacognitive engagement, including planning, evaluating, monitoring, self-regulation, and strategy use. Flora demonstrated strong metacognitive control and strategic revision, while David showed limited processing of implicit feedback and little evidence of deeper planning or monitoring beyond copying or deleting text.
finding.measure: Cognitive and metacognitive engagement with feedback; revision strategies such as planning, evaluating, monitoring, rewriting, and reorganization

finding.finding_summary: AWE feedback improved timeliness and supported repeated revision opportunities, allowing students to work at their own pace and obtain immediate diagnostic feedback. Flora leveraged this flexibility through 13 resubmissions over two days, whereas David’s minimal use suggests the efficiency benefits depended heavily on learner engagement.
finding.measure: Number of AWE resubmissions, time on task, and turnaround/revision pace

paper_profiles.title: Optimising Moodle quizzes for online assessments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This short report examines how Moodle quizzes can be designed and analyzed to support online assessment in a third-year civil engineering course. The authors focus on distinguishing formative quizzes, used to teach and practice concepts with multimedia explanations and unlimited attempts, from summative quizzes, used to grade students and distinguish levels of competency. The paper also asks whether Moodle’s built-in quiz statistics can help instructors judge item quality and improve assessments over time.

The intervention was implemented in Hydraulics and Hydrology at an Australian university across four cohorts (n=169). The course used a database of formative and summative quiz questions with text, images, audio, video, staged problems, and immediate feedback. Formative quiz engagement was evaluated by student attempts and video views, while summative quiz quality was evaluated using Moodle’s facility index (FI) and discrimination index (DI). The study is descriptive and relies on psychometric analysis of quiz items rather than a controlled comparison.

The main conclusion is that Moodle quizzes can support teaching, engagement, and automated assessment in a complex applied engineering course. Formative quizzes were associated with high participation and positive student feedback, and the quizzes were described as helpful for learning concepts in students’ own time. For summative items, combining FI and DI helped identify which questions were too easy, too difficult, or poorly discriminating, allowing instructors to revise items and better separate students by knowledge level. The paper also argues that online quizzes can reduce academic workload through automated marking, prompt feedback, and reduced plagiarism risk via randomization and logging.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Moodle quizzes were effective for teaching and assessing a third-year engineering course involving complex mathematical calculations and Excel-based problem solving. Across four cohorts (n=169), the quizzes were used to develop students’ knowledge and assess competency, but no pre-post achievement effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Performance on Moodle formative and summative quiz questions in applied mathematics / engineering hydrology tasks

finding.finding_summary: Formative quizzes were associated with strong engagement and positive student reactions. In the study, 65% of students attempted all formative questions, embedded videos were viewed 2 to 6 times per student, and student comments described the quizzes as helpful and understandable; no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Formative quiz attempts, embedded video views, and student evaluation/comment feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Moodle quizzes improved academic productivity through automated marking, customized feedback, question randomization, and reduced plagiarism concerns. Although no formal workload measure or effect size was reported, the authors state that grading time and repetitive explanation time were substantially reduced, especially for numerical and short-text items.
finding.measure: Academic workload, marking time, and feedback delivery efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Digital curriculum resources in mathematics education: foundations for change
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual review surveys recent literature on digital curriculum resources (DCR) in mathematics education, including e-textbooks, adaptive systems, repositories, and other digital curriculum programmes. The paper asks how DCR differ from general instructional technology, what theoretical frames have been used to analyze them, and how their design and use are changing classroom instruction, assessment, and teacher practice.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the authors synthesize conceptual and empirical studies presented in recent mathematics education venues. They organize the literature around three design features of DCR—instruction, assessment/reporting, and management—and around teacher/student use in lesson preparation, professional development, classroom instruction, and student learning. The review highlights the growing integration of embedded assessment and reporting, the blurring of distinctions between formative and summative assessment in automated systems, and the expanding role of teachers as adapters and co-designers of digital curriculum materials.

The paper concludes that DCR can transform presentation, problem, and work spaces, but that many current systems remain procedurally focused and only modestly transform pedagogy. The authors also argue that design is increasingly iterative and distributed, yet coherence, educative value, and authoring capacity remain underdeveloped areas needing more research. Overall, the paper positions DCR as a potentially transformative area in mathematics education, while emphasizing that evidence is still emerging and uneven.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature on DCR in mathematics education, the effects on mathematical learning are mixed: some adaptive and intelligent tutoring systems showed modest learning gains, but these gains were usually tied to narrow, procedural content rather than deep understanding. The review reports that such systems often slowed the pace of content coverage and did not address deep learning well when needed; no single pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes / content mastery / procedural performance on digital curriculum tasks and assessments

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that some DCR have the potential to provide motivating opportunities and engaging learning experiences for students, particularly through interactive presentation spaces and personalized learning environments. However, these claims are presented as design affordances and qualitative findings from the reviewed studies rather than as a single quantified effect.
finding.measure: Student engagement / motivation / personalized learning experience

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that DCR and associated learning management systems can streamline assessment reporting and provide teachers, parents, and administrators with performance dashboards and progress data. In the reviewed studies, these systems reduced the administrative burden of tracking student progress and enabled more immediate feedback, but the paper does not report a numerical effect size.
finding.measure: Assessment reporting, dashboards, administrative tracking, feedback timing

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that DCR may loosen the link between curriculum policy and practice by shifting curriculum development toward commercial publishers, philanthropic initiatives, teacher collectives, and researcher-led design teams. It also suggests that these changes can increase diffusion and teacher authoring opportunities, but may reduce coherence and weaken traditional national curriculum control; no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Curriculum governance, curriculum coherence, authoring/dissemination models, policy-practice alignment

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practice-oriented review that asks how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in education. It is explicitly organized around classic formative assessment questions: where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward. The authors aim to separate formative assessment from adjacent practices by grounding the discussion in formative assessment theory rather than in generic AI-in-education uses such as automatic question generation, lesson planning, or summative-style evaluation.

The paper proposes a framework for using LLMs to support three main formative assessment functions: clarifying learning goals and success criteria, helping educators and students locate current understanding, and generating feedback that is task-, process-, or self-regulatory-level. Examples include rewriting objectives in student-friendly language, generating prompts for co-constructing success criteria, creating sample work for critique, and producing feedback or questions for quick checks of understanding. The discussion repeatedly notes that LLM outputs must be aligned with pedagogical intent, and that many existing benchmarks evaluate technical quality rather than formative usefulness.

This is not an empirical evaluation of an intervention with student outcomes; rather, it is a conceptual and practical guide synthesizing prior research and offering prompt templates and classroom examples. The context is broadly K-12 and higher education, but many examples are framed for educators and instructors rather than a specific student sample. The main conclusion is that LLMs may scale and augment formative assessment practices, but they should not replace expert pedagogy, and future research should develop better metrics for formative feedback and classroom-appropriate implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload and make formative assessment more scalable by automating or assisting with tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating questions, creating sample work, and producing feedback. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a narrative review, but the central claim is that LLMs can save time and increase the feasibility of frequent formative assessment in large or resource-constrained classrooms.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time savings in formative-assessment task completion

paper_profiles.title: Common Problems and Effects of Feedback on Fun When Programming Ozobots in Primary School
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 17th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education (WiPSCE '22)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what problems primary school children encounter when learning to program Ozobot Evo robots and whether different kinds of corrective feedback affect how much fun they experience. The authors are especially interested in implementation features and tradeoffs that matter for formative assessment in K-12 computing: the type of problem, the urgency of the problem, the tutoring component used, and whether feedback supports or undermines students’ enjoyment and motivation.

The study involved seven 90-minute workshops with 116 third- and fourth-grade students (ages 8-10) using Ozobot Evo in both pen-and-paper and digital block-based programming modes. During the activities, supervisors recorded students’ problems and the feedback provided, and students completed the Fun Toolkit after each activity using the Smileyometer and Again Again Table. The analysis identified eight recurring problem categories, including task understanding, wrong color codes, Ozobot-specific sensor/actuator issues, reading directions, U-turns, directionality, app use, and miscellaneous technical/organizational issues.

Overall, the workshops were rated very positively on fun, but the paper finds important tradeoffs for formative feedback. Direct instruction was associated with worse fun ratings, while hints were associated with better fun ratings; feedback on urgent problems or issues that students might attribute to their own ability tended to be more discouraging. The authors conclude that teachers should prepare auxiliary materials in advance, use encouraging hints rather than revealing solutions, and sometimes handle technical explanations in front of the whole class. The paper also reports little gender difference in overall enjoyment or problem frequency, though mixed groups needed more support with directional movement.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported very high enjoyment overall (mean Again Again Table = 1.9/2; mean Smileyometer = 3.72/4) across seven workshops with n=116 children. However, feedback on urgent problems or feedback delivered as direct instruction was associated with worse fun ratings, while hints were associated with better fun ratings; for example, Smileyometer ratings were significantly worse after receiving feedback on task understanding (p=.001, r_pb=0.18) and app problems (p=.022, r_pb=0.11), and significantly better when hints were used (p=.001, r_pb=-0.17).
finding.measure: Fun / enjoyment ratings using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table)
finding.effect_size: r_pb=0.18 (task understanding, Smileyometer); r_pb=0.11 (app, Smileyometer); r_pb=-0.17 (hints, Smileyometer)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies whether feedback supports or interferes with students’ problem solving and collaboration during programming with educational robots. It reports that hints, explanations, and guiding questions often helped students continue, whereas direct instruction could reduce enjoyment; the authors interpret hints as preserving autonomy and supporting co-constructed problem solving. The study also notes that some tasks required students to reason from the robot’s perspective, draw codes in reverse order, and debug sequences, indicating an emphasis on spatial reasoning and debugging rather than achievement tests.
finding.measure: Observed problem-solving, debugging, and collaboration during Ozobot programming activities; thematic analysis of supervisor notes

finding.finding_summary: The paper is substantially about implementation and teacher-facing support features, including what problems arise, what kinds of feedback resolve them, and what auxiliary materials can reduce workload. It finds that many common issues could be addressed efficiently with prepared explanations, white stickers, spare robots, and front-of-class instruction for non-individualized issues, but it does not quantify workload or time savings.
finding.measure: Teacher/supervisor notes on problems and feedback types; qualitative synthesis of implementation needs

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the workshop model is feasible for primary classrooms and that Ozobot programming can be used to encourage girls and boys similarly. It reports no overall gender difference in problem frequency or enjoyment, with only one significant difference in directional movement problems for mixed groups (p=.029, η²=0.1), suggesting the intervention is broadly usable across group types and could inform teacher preparation and instructional design.
finding.measure: Gender- and group-constellation comparisons of problem counts and fun ratings
finding.effect_size: η²=0.1 (mixed groups needing more help with direction); overall problem differences η²=0.01, p=.312

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the role of formative assessment in improving learning and argues for its implementation through an e-learning platform, Blackboard Learning System. The authors frame formative assessment as frequent low-stakes checking of learning paired with immediate, individualized feedback, and they emphasize that effective feedback should help students identify strengths, weaknesses, and how to improve.

The specific implementation described is a proposed series of weekly or fortnightly Blackboard online tests, including a small set of multiple-choice and true/false items with detailed immediate feedback after submission. The paper also suggests supporting tools such as discussion forums and virtual classroom features to extend lecturer-student correspondence. Rather than evaluating achievement gains experimentally, the study reports student perceptions from a questionnaire survey about continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option.

The respondents generally favored frequent internal assessments, especially when split into small topic-based tests with immediate teacher feedback. Students reported that the format helped them study progressively, stay in touch with the subject across the semester, and feel more clear about their standing; however, they also expressed concern that too many tests could increase stress and that learning might be overemphasized relative to grades. The paper concludes that Blackboard-based formative assessment is workable and may improve summative performance, but it does not provide direct outcome data on achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments with immediate feedback supported their learning process, helped them stay engaged with the subject throughout the semester, and made it easier to track whether they were 'on track.' However, some also reported stress/pressure from too many tests, so the affective response was mixed even though overall perceptions were favorable.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition because students receive immediate feedback, reflect on errors, and work toward closing the gap between current and desired performance. Students also said the assessment structure helped them learn individual topics progressively and understand their strengths and weaknesses.
finding.measure: Student perception survey and authors' theoretical framing of metacognition/reflection

finding.finding_summary: The Blackboard system was presented as a convenient way to deliver repeated formative tests, with students favoring it over classroom tests because of flexibility and convenience. The paper also suggests the system can reduce delay in feedback delivery and allow lecturer support through Blackboard tools such as discussion forums and virtual classroom features, but it does not quantify workload or efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Student perception survey of Blackboard test option and implementation features

paper_profiles.title: Causal Sets: Discrete Gravity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a set of lecture notes reviewing causal set theory as an approach to quantum gravity. The central question is whether spacetime can be modeled as a discrete, partially ordered set whose causal order and counting measure together recover continuum geometry at large scales. The notes develop the kinematics of causal sets, including definitions, reconstruction ideas, dimension and length estimators, and the relationship between sprinkling, coarse-graining, and manifold approximation.

The paper also surveys proposed dynamics for causal sets, especially sequential growth models constrained by discrete general covariance and Bell causality. It discusses phenomenological applications such as fluctuations in the cosmological constant, horizon entropy, and the emergence of observables. The work is theoretical and does not study educational interventions, students, teachers, or K-12 settings; it is included here because of the retrieval pipeline, but it is not substantively related to formative assessment or AI in education.

paper_profiles.title: Numerical analysis techniques for non-linear dynamics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a lecture-style tutorial on numerical methods for analyzing non-linear dynamics in particle accelerators.
