It explains phase-space dynamics, fixed-point analysis, Poincaré maps, resonance behavior, and the onset of chaos, then surveys chaos-detection techniques such as dynamic aperture estimation, Lyapunov exponents, and Frequency Map Analysis (FMA).

The contribution is not an intervention study in education; it is technical instructional material aimed at accelerator-physics learners and practitioners. The examples are drawn from accelerator rings and beam dynamics systems, including the LHC, HL-LHC, SNS, and CLIC pre-damping rings, to show how numerical analysis tools diagnose resonances, diffusion, and stability limits.

The main conclusion is that frequency-domain and map-based tools are especially useful for understanding how non-linear elements, resonances, and beam-beam effects drive chaotic behavior and reduce dynamic aperture. The paper also highlights how these methods support design choices such as working-point selection and corrector placement, but it reports no educational outcomes, formative-assessment implementation, or K-12 learning effects.

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Signal Processing and Machine Learning: Math Learning Equity for Elementary and Middle School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that strong early mathematics foundations are essential for later success in signal processing, machine learning, and more broadly STEM pathways. The authors frame elementary arithmetic and middle-school algebra as cumulative prerequisites and contend that inequities in access to practice, feedback, and enrichment contribute to widening achievement gaps over time.

Rather than presenting a controlled study, the article is a perspective/review-style discussion of systemic barriers and of three out-of-school math support programs run by universities or external organizations: CyMath, Algebra by 7th Grade (Ab7G), and Math Motivators. The paper describes implementation features such as tutoring frequency, hybrid versus in-person delivery, use of ALEKS adaptive software, parent communication, transportation, mentor composition, and limited tutor training. It also reports a small amount of descriptive student progress data from CyMath and cites a program report from Ab7G indicating gains for students completing a full grade level in ALEKS.

The main conclusion is that early, sustained math support plus family awareness and school partnerships may help reduce later math gaps, but the evidence presented is largely descriptive and anecdotal. The authors emphasize tradeoffs in implementation, including tutor continuity, feasibility of in-person versus hybrid tutoring, parent and transportation supports, and the time costs of homework and classroom game-based activities. They close with broader suggestions for schools, such as more math practice, clearer parent communication, and summer catch-up opportunities.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily discusses mathematics support and reports descriptive progress rather than a controlled estimate. For CyMath, the authors note one student moved from the 40th percentile in Sept. 2023 to the 85th percentile in May 2024 and the 92nd percentile in Jan. 2025, while other students showed smaller gains; for Ab7G, the paper cites a prior report that students who completed a full grade level in ALEKS each year (n=20) showed significant growth in mathematics proficiency and higher likelihood of proficiency or above on Indiana’s ILEARN.
finding.measure: Standardized test percentiles (MAP, iReady), ALEKS grade-level completion, ILEARN proficiency
finding.study_size: CyMath: about 25 students total across 2023-24/2024-25; Ab7G cited study: n=20

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that mentorship, recognition of goals, parent encouragement, and fun-lab activities support student self-efficacy and engagement, especially in Ab7G. However, these claims are qualitative and implementation-focused; no standardized psychosocial effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Observations of self-efficacy, engagement, and participation in tutoring/mentoring activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly discusses workload and feasibility tradeoffs in program delivery. It notes that planning math games takes substantial teacher time and may reduce time for individual practice, while hybrid tutoring improved tutor continuity and outreach but required internet access and scheduling flexibility; no quantitative workload outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Program feasibility, tutor continuity, teacher time demands, transportation/logistical supports

finding.finding_summary: A major focus is on how university-community partnerships, school principal support, transportation, parent communication, and access to adaptive software can expand math support for underrepresented students. The article presents these as implementation enablers and institutional lessons, but without causal estimates of policy or schoolwide impact.
finding.measure: Program partnerships, recruitment/retention, family outreach, access to technology, school support structures

paper_profiles.title: The Association of Opening K-12 Schools with the Spread of COVID-19 in the United States: County-Level Panel Data Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 school counties in the United States
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether opening K-12 schools in the United States during 2020 was associated with increased spread of COVID-19, and whether school mitigation measures such as staff mask requirements moderated that association. It uses county-level panel data combining school opening plans from MCH Strategic Data, foot-traffic data from SafeGraph, county COVID-19 case/death data from the New York Times, and non-pharmaceutical intervention data to examine links between in-person/hybrid/remote school openings, school visits, and subsequent COVID-19 case and death growth.

The authors estimate event-study models and debiased dynamic panel regressions with county fixed effects, state-week fixed effects, lagged cases, testing growth, and policy controls. They find that higher K-12 school visits are associated with higher subsequent case growth, that fully opening K-12 schools in-person is associated with roughly a 5 percentage point increase in weekly case growth, and that this association is stronger when staff mask mandates are absent. Remote openings are associated with lower case growth relative to in-person or hybrid openings. The paper also finds that school openings are associated with increased workplace mobility, suggesting a mechanism through which school reopening may affect community spread. Overall, the authors conclude that opening schools in-person likely increased COVID-19 transmission, partly through both within-school transmission and increased adult mobility, and that mitigation measures such as staff masking appear to reduce risk.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that opening K-12 schools in person was associated with higher county-level COVID-19 spread. In the debiased panel regression, fully opening K-12 schools in person was associated with about a 5 percentage point increase in weekly case growth, and K-12 school visits were associated with a 0.47 increase in case growth (SE=0.07); the corresponding association with deaths was also positive in longer-lag models.
finding.measure: County-level weekly COVID-19 case growth rates and death growth rates
finding.study_size: n=690,297 observations in the main case-growth regression; up to 3144 counties in the panel
finding.effect_size: 0.047 for in-person opening; 0.467 for K-12 visits

paper_profiles.title: Development and validation of the Converging Lenses Concept Inventory for middle school physics education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops and validates the Converging Lenses Concept Inventory (CLCI), a multiple-choice assessment intended to measure middle school students’ conceptual understanding of image formation by converging lenses in optics. The authors position the instrument as useful for both formative and summative assessment, with item distractors designed to reflect common misconceptions about light, refraction, screen placement, partially covered lenses, and related lens-physics concepts.

The study is not an intervention trial but a test-development and validation paper. The instrument was created by a multidisciplinary team and then evaluated using distractor analysis, classical test theory, item response theory, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, student interviews, and an expert survey. Data came from German middle-school students who completed the CLCI as pretest, posttest, and follow-up test around instruction on converging lenses; additional qualitative validation came from seven student interviews and five expert reviews.

Results showed that the final 15-item version had generally acceptable psychometric properties after removing one problematic item (Q2). Students’ scores increased substantially from pretest to posttest (M=11.07 to 17.84 out of 30, p<.0001), and post/follow-up scores correlated better with physics grades than pretest scores (r=-.42 vs. r=-.24). The authors conclude that the CLCI provides a valid, practical instrument for assessing conceptual understanding of converging lenses in middle school physics, with evidence that it can detect learning gains and retain stable measurement after instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The CLCI functioned as a valid measure of middle school students’ conceptual understanding of converging-lens optics, and scores increased significantly after instruction. Using the final 15-item version (max 30 points, excluding Q2), mean total score rose from 11.07 pretest to 17.84 posttest, with a highly significant improvement (p < .0001) in a sample of 318 posttest students.
finding.measure: CLCI total score on conceptual understanding of converging lenses
finding.study_size: n=318 posttest; n=349 pretest; n=72 follow-up

paper_profiles.title: DMP_AI: An AI-Aided K-12 System for Teaching and Learning in Diverse Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents DMP_AI, an AI-aided educational platform designed for K-12 schools that integrates data mining, natural language processing, machine learning, learning analytics, and federated learning. The system is intended to support multiple school functions: predicting academic performance and behavior, generating early warnings, analyzing individualized education plans (IEPs), identifying talented students, and recommending cross-school electives.

The paper is primarily a system description and real-world pilot report rather than an outcome-evaluation study. The authors describe how the platform was built to address privacy, heterogeneous data, and cross-school deployment challenges, and they emphasize teacher involvement in iterative development. The system was piloted in eight local schools (three primary and five secondary) beginning in March 2023, with a user-experience survey administered to 33 users.

Survey results were generally positive: users rated the interface and perceived usefulness favorably, and they expressed interest in continued use. At the same time, respondents reported limited gains in understanding AI and indicated that training and technical support remain important implementation needs. The paper concludes that DMP_AI is feasible to deploy in real schools, but sustained support, clearer training, and further development are needed for broader adoption and long-term sustainability.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot suggests the system may improve educator efficiency by consolidating student academic, behavioral, and IEP-related information into a single platform and by providing predictive dashboards and alerts. However, the paper does not report objective workload or time-savings outcomes; the evidence is based on user perceptions from 33 respondents in eight schools.
finding.measure: User-experience survey items on usability, helpfulness, and willingness to continue using the modules

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily studies real-world implementation feasibility of an AI-aided K-12 system across diverse primary and secondary schools. It reports successful installation and piloting of four AI modules in eight local schools, indicating that cross-school deployment with privacy-preserving architecture is feasible, though the paper does not evaluate policy or institutional outcomes quantitatively.
finding.measure: Pilot implementation in eight schools and survey feedback on feasibility, usefulness, and sustainability

paper_profiles.title: Solutions to Problems at Les Houches Summer School on EFT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a solution manual for problems from the 2017 Les Houches summer school on effective field theory (EFT) in particle physics and cosmology. It is organized around worked solutions to exercises covering renormalization, the renormalization group, EFT power counting, operator classification, field redefinitions, decoupling and matching, anomalous dimensions, and example calculations in QCD, QED, scalar field theory, and the Standard Model EFT.

The document does not study an educational intervention, formative assessment, or K-12 context. Instead, it presents derivations and computational techniques intended for advanced physics students attending a graduate-level summer school. The main contribution is pedagogical: it demonstrates standard EFT methods through explicit calculations and explains why certain identities and matching relations hold.

Because this is not an empirical education study, there are no K-12 outcomes, implementation features, dosage, fidelity measures, or achievement effects to extract. The paper is best characterized as instructional physics content rather than research on AI in education or formative assessment.

paper_profiles.title: Language Diversity: Evaluating Language Usage and AI Performance on African Languages in Digital Spaces
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how three African languages—Yoruba, Kinyarwanda, and Amharic—are represented in digital spaces and how well language-detection tools handle them. The authors compare Reddit data with news-media data, showing that Reddit posts are sparse, heavily code-switched with English, and often not representative of natural monolingual use, while local news sites provide cleaner, monolingual text.

The study evaluates two language-identification approaches: AfroLID, an Africa-focused language identifier, and a general multilingual LLM (Llama 3.3 70B). Using scraped Reddit posts from language-specific subreddits and news articles/comments from BBC Yoruba, Rwanda Broadcasting Agency, and Fana Broadcasting Corporation, the authors find that both tools perform poorly on code-switched Reddit data but near-perfectly on clean news text. AfroLID identified 100% of Yoruba and Amharic news posts and 97.14% of Kinyarwanda news posts correctly; the LLM achieved 100% accuracy on all news data but classified much of the Reddit text as English. The authors conclude that professionally curated news content is a better source for training and evaluating AI models for African languages than conversational platform data, and that future models must better handle code-switched language.

finding.finding_summary: Both AfroLID and the multilingual LLM performed near-perfectly on clean, monolingual news-language data, but struggled substantially on code-switched Reddit text. AfroLID correctly identified 100% of Yoruba and Amharic news posts and 97.14% of Kinyarwanda news posts; the LLM reached 100% accuracy on all three news datasets, but labeled 69.23%-97.45% of Reddit posts as English, indicating difficulty with mixed-language conversational text.
finding.measure: Language identification accuracy on news articles and Reddit posts in Yoruba, Kinyarwanda, and Amharic

finding.finding_summary: The study found that professionally curated news media is a significantly better source of clean, context-rich training data for African-language AI systems than Reddit-like conversational platforms. News sources contained monolingual text and enabled far higher detection accuracy, while Reddit data was sparse, heavily English-dominant, and less representative of authentic language use.
finding.measure: Comparison of digital language presence and suitability of sources for AI training/evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that current data ecosystems disadvantage African languages and that AI development should shift toward community-supported, professionally curated, and better-documented language resources. It recommends using news media, supporting code-switched processing, and building more inclusive language technologies to improve representation in digital systems.
finding.measure: Implications for language-resource development and AI design for low-resource African languages

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the value and practicality of formative assessment, especially the role of frequent low-stakes testing with feedback, and argues that formative assessment should improve learning and eventual summative performance. The authors discuss theoretical support from assessment literature and describe how formative assessment can be implemented through the Blackboard e-learning system.

The implementation described uses Blackboard Learning System (Release 6) at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) to deliver weekly or fortnightly online tests. The proposed assessments include multiple-choice, true/false, and other item types, with immediate detailed feedback, score review, and options such as open-book testing, randomized questions, and supplementary tools like discussion forums and virtual classrooms.

The study also reports a student survey on perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard-based testing. Students generally favored the approach because it broke content into smaller topic-based assessments, provided immediate teacher feedback, and offered convenience and flexibility. However, students also expressed concerns that too many frequent tests could increase stress and overemphasize learning at the expense of grades. The paper concludes that the Blackboard option is a promising way to support formative assessment, but it is primarily a perception/implementation paper rather than an outcomes study with achievement data.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Blackboard-based formative testing can make assessment more convenient and flexible for instructors and students, but it does not measure teacher workload directly. The implementation is described as enabling online delivery of weekly/fortnightly tests, automatic score display, and detailed feedback, which the authors frame as a practical advantage of the e-learning approach.
finding.measure: Perceptions of Blackboard test convenience/flexibility and implementation practicality from student survey and descriptive discussion

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent Blackboard assessments with immediate feedback helped them stay engaged with the subject, check their strengths and weaknesses, and feel on track. At the same time, some students worried that too many tests would create stress and pressure to perform, indicating both positive motivational effects and negative affective tradeoffs.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of motivation, stress/pressure, and engagement with continuous assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes metacognitive benefits of formative assessment, especially helping students reflect on feedback, identify mistakes, and progressively improve topic by topic. Students likewise reported that immediate, detailed feedback helped them correct mistakes without delay and understand their performance, but no direct achievement test of metacognition or transfer was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of feedback usefulness for self-correction, reflection, and tracking learning progress

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that formative assessment, especially when delivered frequently with immediate feedback through Blackboard, should prepare students to perform better on end-of-semester summative tests. This is presented as an intended instructional benefit rather than a directly measured achievement outcome, and no score gains or test statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Perceived preparedness for summative semester examinations and continuous subject learning

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Primary Teacher Training through Academic Portfolios in Advanced Mathematics Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether academic portfolios can improve teacher preparation in advanced mathematics courses for preservice primary teachers. The central problem is the disconnect between abstract mathematics coursework and the practical demands of teaching primary mathematics, which the author argues can weaken engagement, motivation, and perceived relevance of advanced content.

The intervention studied is a portfolio-based assessment model implemented in Algebra and Number Systems I and II at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. The portfolio process included a negotiated learning contract, explicit rubrics, reflection prompts, draft-and-feedback cycles, and final presentations/discussion tables, with supporting instruction and teaching assistant guidance. Data came from attendance records, CANVAS logs, grades, self-assessment surveys, peer evaluations, reflective writing, and instructor observations across 37 female preservice teachers over four semesters.

Findings are presented as preliminary and associational rather than causal. The paper reports higher attendance, increased digital engagement, improved course grades, substantial time investment in portfolio work, and positive perceptions of reduced mathematics anxiety and stronger connections between theory and teaching practice. The author concludes that portfolios may be a promising formative/reflective assessment approach in mathematics teacher education, but notes that larger samples, longer follow-up, and stronger controls are needed to establish causality and long-term effects.

finding.finding_summary: Portfolio implementation coincided with improved course grades in advanced mathematics. In MAT2920, the average grade increased from 4.43 in the prior semester to 5.89 when portfolios were introduced, then rose to 5.71 and 6.44 in subsequent semesters; in MAT2925, the average increased from 5.52 to 5.80 and then to 6.44. The paper reports these as promising associations but does not claim causal effects because multiple cohort and instructional factors may also explain the gains.
finding.measure: Course grades in Algebra and Number Systems I and II

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio approach was associated with stronger engagement, motivation, and reduced mathematics anxiety. Attendance remained above 70%, no absences were recorded for assessed activities, and 11 of 12 respondents (91.7%) said alternative assessment methods such as portfolios helped mitigate mathematics anxiety. Survey and reflective responses suggest the gradual, revision-based process reduced pressure compared with high-stakes exams.
finding.measure: Attendance, self-assessment surveys, anxiety self-report, reflective comments
finding.study_size: n=37 overall; anxiety survey n=12; self-assessment survey n=7 for some items

finding.finding_summary: The study links portfolio use to improvements in self-regulation, time management, reflection, and critical peer evaluation. All surveyed respondents reported improved time organization, 85.7% reported improved self-study, and peer assessments suggested students could identify strengths and weaknesses in portfolio quality and organization. Reflective writing and discussion-table activities were described as supporting metacognition and deeper conceptual connections.
finding.measure: Self-assessment surveys, peer evaluation surveys, reflective paragraphs, discussion table participation
finding.study_size: n=37 overall; self-assessment survey n=7 for some items; peer evaluation n=7 for some items

finding.finding_summary: The portfolio model appears to have increased student time burden while also being perceived as organized and manageable with support. No participant reported spending less than two hours per week; 42.9% reported more than eight hours before deadlines, and 85.7% said the grades matched their effort. The paper reports useful implementation supports—clear rubrics, draft feedback, teaching assistant help, and digital submission—but also notes student requests for more consistent grading, more structure, and more detailed initial instruction, indicating workload/feasibility tradeoffs.
finding.measure: Self-reported time spent on portfolio development, satisfaction with grades, implementation feedback
finding.study_size: n=7 self-assessment survey respondents; implementation context n=37

finding.finding_summary: Beyond grades, the paper reports that portfolios helped teacher candidates connect abstract mathematical content to teaching applications and demonstrate understanding through presentations and discussion tables. Digital interaction with course materials averaged 185 CANVAS page views per week, and peer feedback highlighted neat organization, step-by-step explanations, and effective use of technology as strengths. These outcomes are framed as evidence of improved assessment efficacy and communication of mathematical ideas rather than direct gains on a standardized measure.
finding.measure: CANVAS page views, presentations, discussion tables, peer-rated portfolio quality, instructor observations

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as an automated teacher coach by generating classroom-observation scores and feedback from elementary mathematics classroom transcripts. The authors frame generative AI as a potentially cost-effective complement to scarce expert coaching, and propose three zero-shot teacher-coaching tasks: scoring transcript segments using classroom-observation rubrics, identifying instructional highlights and missed opportunities, and generating actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE transcript dataset, which contains 1,660 fourth- and fifth-grade math classroom observations from 317 teachers across four school districts. For quantitative scoring, the authors compare ChatGPT’s predictions against human expert ratings on selected CLASS and MQI items; for qualitative feedback, experienced math teachers rate the model’s responses for relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty. The model is prompted zero-shot with gpt-3.5-turbo, without fine-tuning, to mimic how teachers might currently use ChatGPT.

Results show substantial limitations. ChatGPT’s score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings across all rubric items, and adding rubric descriptions or chain-of-thought style reasoning does not improve performance. For qualitative feedback, teachers judge many responses as not insightful or not relevant, and model suggestions are frequently redundant with what the teacher already did in the transcript (82% of suggestions). The paper concludes that current off-the-shelf ChatGPT has promise as a scalable feedback tool but is not yet reliable enough to replace expert coaching, especially because it often fails to provide novel, faithful, and context-sensitive feedback.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed weak alignment with expert classroom-observation scores on mathematics-instruction rubrics. On MQI items, Spearman correlations with human ratings were low across prompting methods: EXPL 0.02/0.12/-0.11, REMED 0.05/0.06/-0.06, LANGIMP 0.00/0.02/0.04, and SMQR 0.17/0.17/0.06 for DA/DA+/RA respectively (n=100 segments for quantitative scoring). Qualitative feedback for math instruction was also often judged insufficient: teachers rated many MQI highlights/missed-opportunity responses as not relevant (55% No), not faithful (29% No), and not insightful (71% No).
finding.measure: Spearman correlation with human MQI observation scores; teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, and insightfulness for MQI feedback
finding.study_size: n=100 transcript segments for quantitative scoring; n=288 MQI feedback examples for qualitative evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could provide a cost-effective complement to expert coaching by automating transcript scoring and feedback generation, which would reduce reliance on scarce human coaches. However, the study does not directly measure workload reduction, time savings, or productivity gains, so the evidence is conceptual rather than causal. The main empirical support is that the system can produce outputs at scale, but with substantial quality limitations.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of scalability/cost-effectiveness; no direct workload metric measured

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates whether ChatGPT can produce actionable, insightful feedback that would support teacher reflection and instructional improvement, which overlaps with higher-order coaching-related skills such as reflection and problem solving. Teachers rated many responses as lacking insightfulness (CLASS: 51% No; MQI: 71% No) and noted that 82% of suggestions were redundant, indicating limited added value for reflective improvement. This suggests the model’s feedback was often not sufficiently novel to foster deeper professional judgment.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of insightfulness and novelty/redundancy of feedback and suggestions
finding.study_size: n=504 total feedback examples across Tasks B and C (216 CLASS + 288 MQI + 36 suggestions, with teacher ratings on sampled subsets)

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of providing teachers with timely, scalable, and personalized feedback on classroom discourse practices in K-12 mathematics. The authors focus on “talk moves,” a set of accountable-talk strategies that support student participation, reasoning, and mathematical discussion, and argue that existing human observation approaches are too costly and slow to scale.

The intervention described is TalkMoves, an end-to-end system that uses classroom audio/video recordings, automatic speech recognition, and transformer-based language models to identify teacher talk moves from transcript sentence pairs and generate feedback dashboards for teachers. The model is trained on 501 transcripts of K-12 math lessons (176,757 sentences total) manually coded by expert annotators, and the best-performing model (RoBERTa-Large) achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the held-out test set. The paper also describes a pilot deployment with 21 teachers across two midwestern school districts, where teachers used the system during the 2019–2020 academic year and provided survey/interview feedback.

The study is primarily a technical development and implementation paper rather than an impact evaluation on student learning. Its main conclusions are that transformer models can classify discourse practices more accurately than earlier BiLSTM approaches and that such AI systems can potentially scale expert-like feedback for teacher professional learning. The authors also note implementation tradeoffs, including noisy classroom speech, under-recognition of student talk by ASR, the need for sufficient context windows, and the use of a streamlined model (DistilRoBERTa) in the deployed application to reduce computation time.

finding.finding_summary: The system substantially improves the efficiency and scalability of identifying classroom discourse features compared with manual expert coding. The best model achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set, and the authors emphasize that this automated pipeline can replace time-consuming, expensive human transcript coding for teacher feedback generation.
finding.measure: Model classification performance for identifying talk moves in classroom transcripts (F1, MCC)

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a pilot deployment showing that the application can be used by 21 teachers across two midwestern school districts during the 2019–2020 academic year, suggesting feasibility for broader institutional use. The authors position the tool as a scalable alternative to expert observation systems, with potential to support teacher professional learning at scale, although no student outcome or policy impact is tested.
finding.measure: Pilot implementation with teacher use, surveys, and interviews

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CHI-style ACM venue; exact issue not specified in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers can be engaged as co-design partners to create AI curricula that are integrated into core subjects rather than taught only as standalone computer science content. The authors argue that AI education is often inaccessible to many classrooms because teachers need more scaffolding, clearer implementation supports, and ways to align AI activities with existing subject goals and student needs.

To explore this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from a mix of subject areas and grade bands. The workshop included short presentations on AI, AI tools, ethics, and diversity; a between-session brainstorming assignment; and small-group curriculum co-design with researcher facilitation. Teachers produced draft integrated lesson plans in social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities, and the team analyzed workshop audio, questionnaires, and artifacts using open coding.

The main findings are that teachers emphasized four practical concerns when designing AI-integrated lessons: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. Teachers wanted assessment methods that captured conceptual understanding, preferred engaging hooks and student-driven contexts, needed clearer guidance on tool selection and classroom fit, and valued group work but worried about group size and participation balance. The paper concludes that integrated AI curriculum is more feasible when it includes explicit scaffolding for ethics, data, reflection, and classroom implementation, and that remote co-design can surface useful design tradeoffs even though the study does not test student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that integrated AI curriculum needs explicit supports for logistics, tool selection, and classroom structure in order to be feasible. The workshop surfaced implementation tradeoffs such as whether to use Machine Learning for Kids or Google Quick, Draw!, how much time teachers need between sessions, and how group size affects participation; however, these were design observations rather than measured efficiency effects. The study involved 15 teachers and shows that researchers can reduce teacher uncertainty by providing scaffolds, but it did not quantify workload reduction.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported feasibility, logistics, and implementation considerations from workshop discussions and post-workshop feedback

finding.finding_summary: Teachers emphasized engagement as a core design goal, describing ways to anchor lessons in real-world contexts, student interests, and gamified activities. They believed these features could increase motivation and participation, but the paper reports only teacher perceptions from co-design discussions rather than student engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher discussion of engagement, motivation, anchoring, student-driven learning, and gamification

finding.finding_summary: The co-designed curricula emphasized collaboration, reflection, and conceptual evaluation, all of which are durable skills the teachers thought should be central to AI learning. Teachers described group work, peer discussion, reflection on data and ethics, and oral/alternative assessments as ways to build collaboration and critical thinking, but the study did not measure student skill gains directly.
finding.measure: Teacher-created curriculum drafts and discussion of collaboration, reflection, and conceptual assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies how co-design with teachers may improve the adoption and accessibility of AI curricula in K-12 settings. Teachers identified the need for scaffolding, subject alignment, and ethics supports, and the workshop produced draft curricula that could be implemented in classrooms; the authors argue this collaborative process can increase teacher buy-in and broaden AI access beyond computer science classrooms. No institutional outcome was quantitatively measured.
finding.measure: Teacher buy-in, perceived applicability to classrooms, and production of implementable curriculum drafts

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping high school teachers notice and support collaborative argumentation during classroom discussions. The authors developed Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that uses NLP to automatically code student talk for argument moves, specificity, and collaboration, then presents teachers with visualizations such as annotated transcripts, collaboration maps, and strength/weakness summaries.

The system was evaluated in a real-world deployment with 18 high school English Language Arts teachers from 4 schools. Teachers participated in a workflow where they led and recorded a discussion, had transcripts manually coded, and then used DT in a cognitive interview and survey. The study found that teachers perceived DT as useful for learning about students’ discussion quality and for planning future facilitation, with all 13 usability items receiving positive ratings on average. The NLP classifiers also showed moderate-to-substantial agreement with human annotations (e.g., argument move kappa=0.574, macro F=0.730; specificity kappa=0.727, macro F=0.688; collaboration kappa=0.566, macro F=0.439), though collaboration prediction was weaker for some labels. The paper mainly reports usability and classifier performance rather than student achievement effects.

finding.finding_summary: The system was perceived as helpful for teachers’ workflow around analyzing classroom discussion and planning next steps. In a deployment with 18 high school ELA teachers from 4 schools, all 13 usability items were rated positively on average, including items on ease of use (mean=4.11/5), usefulness of the annotated transcript (mean=4.89), and goal-setting (mean=4.56).
finding.measure: Teacher usability survey ratings of Discussion Tracker features and overall helpfulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on collaborative argumentation, a durable skill involving collaboration, evidence-based reasoning, and discussion quality. Teachers reported that DT helped them recognize students’ strengths and weaknesses during discussion and gave them more insight into student learning than they usually get from reflecting on the discussion alone (mean=4.67), suggesting the tool supports teacher learning about collaborative discourse rather than measuring student achievement directly.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of support for analyzing collaborative argumentation and facilitating discussion

paper_profiles.title: All Together Now: Teachers as Research Partners in the Design of Search Technology for the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that teachers should be treated as central research partners—not just facilitators or participants—when designing and evaluating classroom search technologies. The authors frame teachers as the “expert-in-the-loop” who can connect student needs, classroom practice, and tool design, and they use their own multi-year work on children’s search tools to illustrate why teacher involvement improves the relevance and usability of research.

The paper is not an intervention study or an empirical evaluation of learning outcomes. Instead, it is a reflective qualitative position piece drawing on the authors’ prior collaborations with primary school teachers in Italy, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States. It describes how teachers helped with research agenda-setting, study design, task construction, and classroom implementation, and it argues that this collaboration led to more authentic studies, better alignment with classroom practice, more usable tools, and findings that were easier to interpret in educational terms.

The main conclusion is that teacher partnership benefits both researchers and teachers: researchers get more grounded and realistic studies, while teachers gain opportunities to influence technology design and deepen their use of classroom digital tools. The paper emphasizes process and implementation lessons rather than student achievement effects, and it does not report quantitative outcome data or effect sizes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that involving teachers as research partners improves the practicality and feasibility of classroom technology research, making studies less intrusive and better aligned with regular instruction. It claims that teacher collaboration helps researchers design authentic tasks, capture real classroom interactions, and produce more usable tools, but it reports no quantitative workload or efficiency metrics.
finding.measure: Reported researcher/teacher perceptions of feasibility, authenticity, usability, and alignment with classroom instruction

finding.finding_summary: The paper makes a broader institutional argument that teacher involvement can reduce the disconnect between educational technology design and classroom practice, helping technologies become more widely adopted and better integrated into schools. This is presented as a conceptual and experience-based conclusion rather than a measured policy or system outcome.
finding.measure: Qualitative observations about technology integration, adoption, and teacher partnership

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Blind Video Quality Assessment with Rich Quality-aware Features
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of blind video quality assessment (BVQA): predicting perceived video quality without access to a pristine reference video. The authors argue that existing BVQA models often generalize poorly when moved to unseen social-media videos, especially videos that have passed through modern capture, preprocessing, compression, and enhancement pipelines.

To improve generalization, the paper proposes RQ-VQA, a modular feature-fusion framework that combines a trainable spatial backbone with frozen off-the-shelf quality-aware features from several pretrained models. Specifically, it fuses learnable spatial features from Swin Transformer-B, temporal motion features from SlowFast, spatiotemporal features from FAST-VQA, and spatial quality-aware features from LIQE and Q-Align. The model is trained with a PLCC-based loss and evaluated on three social-media VQA datasets (KVQ, TaoLive, LIVE-WC), with additional participation in the NTIRE 2024 Short-form UGC Video Quality Assessment Challenge.

The paper’s main conclusion is that combining heterogeneous quality-aware features substantially improves prediction accuracy and cross-dataset generalization relative to prior BVQA baselines. RQ-VQA achieves state-of-the-art results on the reported benchmarks and ranks first in the NTIRE challenge. Ablation studies show that each feature source contributes complementary information, higher input resolution improves performance, and PLCC loss yields better correlation with MOS than MSE or MAE. The discussion also notes a limitation: the model can overestimate quality for text-overlaid or synthetic-content videos, suggesting a need for domain-specific encoders in future work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a blind video quality assessment method on three public social-media video datasets and reports strong prediction performance against human mean opinion scores (MOS). On KVQ validation/test and LIVE-WC, RQ-VQA achieves SRCC/PLCC of 0.914/0.918, 0.926/0.924, and 0.955/0.955 respectively, outperforming all compared methods; on TaoLive it is comparable to the best baseline (0.912/0.918).
finding.measure: Video quality prediction accuracy measured by SRCC and PLCC against MOS

finding.finding_summary: The authors explicitly assess deployment practicality and report that the full RQ-VQA system runs with near real-time inference on an NVIDIA RTX 3090, taking 5.30 seconds for an eight-second 1080p video. They also note that the Q-Align branch can be removed in resource-constrained settings to reduce computational cost while preserving competitive performance.
finding.measure: Inference time, parameter count, FLOPs, and architectural efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Scale Guided Hypernetwork for Blind Super-Resolution Image Quality Assessment
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (computer vision / image quality assessment benchmark datasets)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of blind image quality assessment (IQA) for super-resolution (SR) images. The authors argue that existing blind SR IQA models focus mainly on image content and visual artifacts, while ignoring an important piece of prior information: the SR scale factor. They first conduct qualitative and statistical analyses showing that subjective quality scores differ significantly across scale factors, and that scale is strongly associated with perceived quality.

To exploit this finding, the paper proposes a scale-guided hypernetwork (SGH) framework. SGH keeps an encoder-based content-perception stage, but uses the SR scale factor to generate the parameters of the quality-prediction layers, enabling scale-adaptive evaluation rules. The framework is applied to several existing blind IQA backbones (CNNIQA, JCSAN, ResNet50-based IQA, DeepSRQ, HyperIQA) and evaluated on three SR IQA datasets: Waterloo, QADS, and CVIU.

The experiments show consistent improvements over the original backbones on both within-dataset and cross-dataset tests. The paper also compares SGH with a simpler fusion-based approach that concatenates scale and image features, finding that SGH usually performs better and generalizes more strongly. The main conclusion is that incorporating scale information through a hypernetwork meaningfully improves blind SR IQA, especially for generalization across datasets and scale factors.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed scale-guided hypernetwork improved blind super-resolution image quality prediction across all three datasets and multiple backbones. For the ResNet50 backbone, single-dataset SRCC increased from 0.8868 to 0.9530 on Waterloo, from 0.9110 to 0.9432 on QADS, and from 0.8294 to 0.9268 on CVIU; corresponding PLCC gains were also substantial (e.g., 0.9203 to 0.9749 on Waterloo).
finding.measure: Blind super-resolution image quality assessment performance using SRCC, PLCC, and KRCC against subjective quality scores
finding.study_size: Waterloo n=312 SR images; QADS n=980 SR images; CVIU n=1620 SR images

finding.finding_summary: The method is explicitly designed to automate image quality evaluation and reduce reliance on time-consuming, expensive subjective testing. The paper reports that subjective tests are costly and cannot scale to real-world optimization systems, while the proposed blind IQA framework improves automated prediction quality and generalization, making evaluation more feasible in practice.
finding.measure: Automated blind quality assessment feasibility and generalization for SR images

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy that combines classroom response systems (“clickers”), rich question-driven instruction, whole-class dialogue, formative assessment, and meta-level communication. The project is framed as a five-year study of teacher change and professional development rather than a student outcome trial. The authors explicitly focus on implementation features, teacher learning trajectories, and the challenges and tradeoffs teachers experience as they adopt TEFA.

The intervention consists of classroom response technology plus an intensive, multi-year professional development program: an August workshop, weekly after-school meetings in year 1, then biweekly support in years 2-3, with on-site PD at teachers’ schools. The sample included approximately 39 science and math teachers across four sites in western Massachusetts, spanning middle and high school settings. Data sources included PD transcripts, teacher journals, implementation logs, surveys, classroom video, interviews, and student surveys, analyzed through mixed qualitative and quantitative methods.

The paper’s main conclusions are that TEFA is demanding but learnable, and that teachers typically progress through recognizable stages: becoming comfortable with the technology, then with question design, then with classroom discourse, and eventually with using formative information to adjust instruction. The paper reports implementation tradeoffs around preparation time, class time, control of discussion, student participation, and the need to adapt TEFA to local contexts. It does not report causal achievement effects; instead, it provides descriptive evidence that teachers who implemented TEFA more richly often gained better information about student thinking and changed lessons accordingly. The authors argue that TEFA and its PD can change teacher practice over time, but feasibility and scalability depend on support, fidelity, and responsive adaptation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantial implementation burden and time tradeoffs: good TEFA question design required significant preparation time, and classroom use consumed class time that teachers worried would reduce content coverage. At the same time, teachers reported becoming more efficient over time with the technology and question design, and some used TEFA to manage classroom routines more efficiently.
finding.measure: Teacher reports, implementation logs, PD reflections, classroom video, and interviews describing preparation time, class time, and technical/logistical burden

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is to describe a multi-year professional development model and its feasibility across several school sites, emphasizing scalability, on-site support, and implementation fidelity. The authors conclude that the program can support teacher change over time, but that large-scale implementation would require efficient tracking of teacher progress and careful attention to local school context and infrastructure.
finding.measure: Feasibility of multi-site professional development; implementation fidelity; teacher retention/participation across sites

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported increased student participation, stronger engagement, and changes in classroom atmosphere as TEFA was used more effectively, especially when question design and discussion structures improved. The paper also notes shifts in students’ perceived comfort and willingness to participate, based on teacher reports and student survey data, though no causal student-effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Student participation, engagement, and perceived classroom environment from student surveys, teacher logs, and classroom observations
finding.study_size: classrooms taught by approximately n=39 teachers

finding.finding_summary: TEFA is presented as supporting metacognition, reasoning, and collaborative discussion through question-driven instruction, dialogical discourse, and meta-level communication. Teachers reported that TEFA helped them better understand student thinking and adjust instruction in response, and classroom observations indicated increases in student-student interaction and discussion depth. No standardized effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher- and video-based indicators of student discussion, reasoning, and metacognitive classroom talk

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes mathematics teachers and describes TEFA used to review material, assess understanding, and support preparation for state-wide math exams, but it does not report achievement test scores or causal numeric gains. For the math classrooms described, TEFA was used as formative assessment to identify topics needing help and to support conceptual understanding and exam review.
finding.measure: Mathematics formative-assessment use, including exam review and identification of topics needing help
finding.study_size: subset of participating teachers in math classrooms (exact n not reported)

finding.finding_summary: The pedagogy is explicitly grounded in science teaching and is reported to increase opportunities for students to reason through rich questions, explain thinking, and engage in scientific argumentation. Teachers reported gaining better information about how students were thinking about concepts and changing lessons accordingly, but the paper does not provide a student science achievement estimate.
finding.measure: Scientific discussion quality, reasoning-oriented classroom interaction, and teacher reports of understanding student thinking
finding.study_size: subset of participating science teachers (exact n not reported)

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the pedagogical role of embedded formative assessment in undergraduate engineering classrooms and argues that it can improve learning by making student thinking visible to instructors and students. Rather than testing a specific intervention with a controlled design, it synthesizes theoretical rationale and representative examples from engineering education, with a focus on how technology has made real-time formative assessment more feasible and less burdensome for instructors.

The paper emphasizes technology-facilitated approaches such as clickers, cell-phone polling, Google Docs, and especially open-format responses collected with Tablet PCs and InkSurvey. It highlights implementation features that matter for effectiveness: instructor responsiveness to student feedback, question design that reveals reasoning, flexibility to adjust instruction, and tradeoffs between multiple-choice efficiency and open-ended diagnostic richness. The undergraduate examples from an intermediate electromagnetics course (about 60 students) illustrate how open-format questions can expose misconceptions, calculation difficulties, and weak transfer between related tasks.

Overall, the paper concludes that embedded formative assessment can support active learning, metacognition, and improved instruction, but its full potential depends on how well the instructor uses the feedback and on choosing formats that capture student thinking. It also notes practical tradeoffs: technology reduces clerical burden and can enable real-time feedback, but closed-response tools may limit insight into reasoning, creativity, and misconceptions. The paper is primarily a conceptual/illustrative overview rather than an outcomes study, so it does not report causal achievement effects for K-12 learners.

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides illustrative evidence that open-format formative assessment can reveal students’ understanding and misconceptions in a third-year undergraduate electromagnetics course, particularly in reasoning about Gauss’s law, limits of integration, dot products, and symmetry arguments (n=60). However, it does not report a formal achievement effect or posttest comparison; it mainly shows that students’ written/digital responses exposed both correct reasoning and common errors.
finding.measure: Open-format written/graphical responses to conceptual and derivational electromagnetics questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment can increase metacognition and critical thinking by prompting students to reflect on what they know and do not know, and by requiring them to construct explanations rather than select answers. In the example course, students’ responses showed weaknesses in deeper reasoning and helped the instructor target scaffolded guidance, but no formal pre/post measure of metacognition or critical thinking is reported.
finding.measure: Observed student reasoning quality and responsiveness in open-format formative assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that technology-facilitated formative assessment reduces the clerical burden on instructors by streamlining collection and analysis of student responses. The paper describes clickers, texting platforms, online documents, and InkSurvey as tools that enable instantaneous or rapid feedback, making real-time formative assessment more feasible in large classes, though it does not quantify workload reduction.
finding.measure: Instructor burden / speed of collecting and interpreting student responses

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Three Pivotal Concepts in K-12 Science State Standards and Maps of Conceptual Growth to Research in Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks which physics concepts are central in K-12 science standards, foundational for later science learning, and especially difficult for students to learn. The authors compare concept maps of physics content, review the science standards of four U.S. states plus national standards, and synthesize prior physics education research on student misconceptions and instructional approaches.

The paper identifies three recurring conceptual areas: Newton’s laws (force and motion), conservation of energy, and geometrical optics. For each, the authors explain why the concept is pivotal in the K-12 curriculum, how it appears across state standards, and what makes it hard for students to understand, emphasizing robust misconceptions, context dependence, and difficulty transferring knowledge across problem types.

The paper also highlights instructional approaches that have shown some success, such as prediction-then-demonstration activities, interactive lecture demonstrations, and research-based explorations using motion sensors and computer graphs. However, it is not an intervention study with new outcome data; rather, it is a conceptual and literature-synthesis paper intended to inform teacher preparation, curriculum design, and professional development.

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes prior research showing that students have deep and persistent misconceptions about Newton’s laws and conservation of energy, but that targeted conceptual interventions can improve understanding. Examples cited include force-and-motion explorations, prediction-based demonstrations, and research-based energy tasks; however, the paper reports these as literature examples rather than new experimental results, and it does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding of force and motion and conservation of energy as measured by instruments such as the Force Concept Inventory and research-based conceptual multiple-choice tests

paper_profiles.title: Sticky Help, Bounded Effects: Session-by-Session Analytics of Teacher Interventions in K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how teachers decide whom to help during technology-supported K-12 math instruction, and whether teacher help has benefits that extend beyond the current class session. The authors focus on two temporal questions: whether prior help history and momentary student states (especially idle and struggle) predict who receives additional help, and whether help predicts later learning across sessions.

The study combines interviews with nine middle-school math teachers and large-scale log analysis from MATHia classroom use. In the interviews, teachers reported prioritizing learning, engagement, equity, and contextual cues when deciding whom to visit; they also described using digital dashboard signals and trying to avoid repeatedly focusing on the same students. The quantitative analysis used 1.4 million student-system interactions from 339 students across 14 classes in ten U.S. schools, with teacher-logged help events linked to fine-grained engagement detectors.

The main findings suggest that help is "sticky": students who had been helped before were more likely to receive help again, even after controlling for current engagement state. Idle behavior predicted help within sessions, but did not lead to sustained across-session attention, and teacher help did not predict later skill acquisition in subsequent sessions. Help coincided with immediate within-session learning, but those benefits did not persist longitudinally, implying that teacher interventions were largely session-bound. The authors argue that analytics tools should better surface coverage gaps and revisits to support more equitable allocation of teacher attention.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher help coincided with immediate learning within sessions, but it did not predict later skill acquisition across sessions. In the cross-lagged analyses, help in session t-1 did not significantly predict the number of new KCs learned in session t (bK = 0.04, z = 0.64, p = .52), although within-session help and learning were positively correlated (r ≈ .13, p < .001).
finding.measure: MATHia learning outcomes: new knowledge component (KC) acquisition / first mastery estimated from an AFM, plus within-session association between help and learning
finding.study_size: n=339 students; 14 classes; AFM fit on 425,285 first attempts across 827 KCs
finding.effect_size: r≈.13 (within-session correlation); bK = 0.04 (cross-lagged, not significant); gamma = 0.0092 for practice effect in AFM

finding.finding_summary: The paper found strong persistence in help-seeking/attention dynamics and clear associations between current disengagement and teacher intervention, but no sustained effect of help on later idle behavior. Prior idle behavior strongly predicted current help within the mixed-effects model (OR = 2.74, 95% CI [1.83, 4.11]), yet prior help did not significantly predict later idle (d1 = -0.05, z = -1.45, p = .147), and prior help did not significantly predict later disengagement outcomes across sessions.
finding.measure: Idle disengagement state; struggle state; teacher-help likelihood across sessions
finding.effect_size: OR = 2.74 for idle predicting help; OR = 1.32 for prior help predicting later help; cross-lagged b1 = -0.10 for idle -> later help
finding.confidence_interval: [1.83, 4.11] for idle predictor; [1.19, 1.46] for prior help predictor

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined how teacher attention is allocated over time and whether dashboards could support more efficient and equitable orchestration. Help was highly concentrated: in an average session, about 50% of students did not receive a visit while the other 50% received all the help, and prior help history significantly increased the odds of another intervention (OR = 1.32, 95% CI [1.19, 1.46]). The paper argues that session-by-session analytics could improve feasibility and coverage by helping teachers identify under-visited students and avoid repeatedly revisiting the same students.
finding.measure: Teacher intervention likelihood, revisit concentration, distribution of help across students, help-history effects
finding.effect_size: OR = 1.32 for prior help history; Gini = 0.641 for concentration of help

finding.finding_summary: At the classroom-and-school systems level, the paper highlights inequitable concentration of teacher attention and proposes dashboard changes to improve allocation fairness. The empirical pattern of sticky help suggests institutional tradeoffs in orchestration: teachers intended to distribute attention fairly, but logged help events clustered on a subset of students, motivating coverage-aware analytics and reflective supports.
finding.measure: Distribution of teacher help across students; Lorenz-style concentration of intervention coverage
finding.study_size: n=339 students across 10 U.S. K-12 schools

paper_profiles.title: Towards an Assessment-oriented Model for External Information System Quality Characterization
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to characterize and assess external information system quality (EISQ) in inter-organizational settings. The authors argue that existing quality models and assessment approaches often fail to account for the full set of operational aspects involved in quality evaluation, especially when systems operate across organizational boundaries and are affected by contextual, technical, organizational, and usage-related factors.

To address this, the paper proposes RatQual, an assessment-oriented model that classifies 17 external quality characteristics into a three-axis framework and evaluates them through three complementary aspects: internal quality potentiality, external implementation compatibility, and quality in use. The model uses maturity-level mappings, compatibility matrices, and operational performance indicators, and is supported by a Quality Monitoring Tool (QMT) that automates assessment, tracks quality evolution over time, and suggests scenarios for reaching planned quality targets.

The paper is conceptual and methodological rather than an empirical study of a specific intervention in classrooms or schools. It is grounded in information systems quality management and is intended for organizations engaged in inter-organizational collaboration. The main conclusion is that RatQual offers a more complete and actionable way to assess external quality characteristics by combining a priori and a posteriori perspectives and by linking assessment results to improvement planning and monitoring.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes RatQual as a structured model for assessing external information system quality across organizational boundaries and claims it improves quality evolution planning and periodic monitoring. It argues that the model and its accompanying tool can better support inter-organizational collaboration by combining internal readiness, compatibility, and in-use performance into a single ratio metric, but it does not report an empirical evaluation with outcome data.
finding.measure: conceptual quality assessment framework and monitoring capability

finding.finding_summary: RatQual is intended to automate quality assessment and support periodical monitoring, which the authors present as helping improve information system quality management efficiency. The Quality Monitoring Tool is described as reducing manual assessment work and enabling planned-state improvement, but the paper provides no measured workload, time savings, or productivity results.
finding.measure: automation of assessment and quality monitoring workflow

paper_profiles.title: NiCE Teacher Workshop: Engaging K-12 Teachers in the Development of Curricular Materials That Utilize Complex Networks Concepts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the Networks in Classroom Education (NiCE) workshop, a professional-development and co-design event intended to help K-12 teachers learn network science and create curriculum materials that apply network concepts in their classrooms. The authors argue that network science can support cross-disciplinary teaching, alignment with standards such as NGSS, and more connected ways of thinking about subject matter.

The workshop brought together 21 K-12 educators with diverse grade-level and subject expertise for a four-day program at West Point in July 2017. The design combined short pre-workshop videos, presentations, hands-on activities, group discussion, lesson-plan development, feedback cycles, and end-of-workshop presentations. Teachers were organized into grade-band groups and partnered with network scientists to support resource creation.

The paper reports descriptive outcomes from post-workshop surveys and the products created during the workshop. Teachers reported large gains in their knowledge of network concepts and their likelihood of using them in instruction, and they produced 13 publicly available resources, including 10 lesson plans and 3 broader education projects. The paper concludes that collaborative workshops can successfully build teacher capacity, generate curriculum materials, and motivate teachers to bring network science into K-12 education.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop increased teachers’ self-reported knowledge of network science concepts and their likelihood of using them in lessons. Across the post-workshop survey items, participants reported large before/after gains on a 1-6 scale, indicating improved understanding of network concepts and their instructional use, but the paper does not report inferential statistics or standardized effect sizes.
finding.measure: Self-reported ratings of knowledge of network concepts and likelihood of using them in the classroom (1-6 scale)

finding.finding_summary: Participants described the workshop experience in strongly positive terms, using words such as “informative,” “inspiring,” “relevant,” and “thoughtful,” suggesting increased motivation and engagement with network science. The paper characterizes the workshop as fostering creativity and enthusiasm, but it provides descriptive rather than inferential evidence.
finding.measure: Three-word open-ended workshop experience responses; descriptive participant feedback

finding.finding_summary: The workshop was designed and described as supporting teachers’ work by helping them create standards-aligned materials and ease workload through cross-disciplinary network-based lesson design. The paper explicitly states that network science can facilitate collaboration, increase creativity, and ease workload, but these are conceptual claims supported only by participant feedback and resource production rather than direct workload measurement.
finding.measure: Descriptive workshop feedback and production of lesson plans/projects

paper_profiles.title: The effects of teaching strategies on learning to think critically in primary and secondary schools: an overview of systematic reviews
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an overview of systematic reviews examining teaching strategies that may help primary and secondary school students learn to think critically. The authors were motivated by the development of the Be Smart about your Health resources for lower secondary students in East Africa, but they intentionally used a broad scope because many relevant reviews did not measure critical thinking directly and often included multiple education levels and outcomes.

The review mapped 326 systematic reviews published after 1999 that evaluated a wide range of instructional approaches, including didactic strategies, questioning and prompts, assessment and feedback, collaborative learning, problem-based and inquiry learning, e-learning, individual learning, and teacher training. The paper synthesizes review-level findings for 37 strategies judged most relevant, with evidence certainty ranging from very low to moderate. Overall, the authors conclude that many teaching strategies can inform the design of critical-thinking resources, but the evidence base is uneven, frequently outdated, and often limited by weak reporting of study design, risk of bias, adverse effects, and subgroup/moderator analyses.

finding.finding_summary: This overview centrally examines teaching strategies intended to improve students' critical thinking, reasoning, and related higher-order cognitive skills. Across the included reviews, the authors note that 46 reviews reported higher-order thinking outcomes, including critical thinking (11 reviews), problem solving (16), metacognition (8), and argumentation (5), with certainty ranging from very low to moderate; however, the paper does not pool a single overall effect size for critical thinking across the full set of reviews.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem solving, metacognition, argumentation, and other higher-order cognitive outcome measures reported in the included systematic reviews

finding.finding_summary: Although not focused on a single academic subject, the overview includes many reviews on subject-matter learning outcomes such as achievement, retention, transfer, and comprehension across primary and secondary school contexts. The authors report that the included reviews used a wide range of academic achievement and learning measures, but because this is an overview of reviews rather than a single meta-analysis, no unified effect estimate is provided here.
finding.measure: Academic achievement, learning, retention, transfer, comprehension, and related subject-matter outcomes as reported in the included reviews

paper_profiles.title: An Interpretive Phenomenological Analysis Study of the Reading Achievement of African American Boys in Elementary Restart Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines how teachers, multiple classroom leaders, and instructional facilitators in a North Carolina restart school context understand the instructional practices that support early reading achievement for African American boys in kindergarten through third grade. The study is motivated by persistent racial and gender achievement gaps in elementary literacy and the author’s interest in the role of school-based practices in low-performing schools.

Using an interpretive phenomenological analysis (IPA) approach, the author conducted semi-structured interviews with six participants from Thomas County School District. The analysis was framed by Critical Race Theory and sought to surface educator meanings around professional development, explicit instruction, equity-oriented design, student voice, and how to gauge student learning. The study does not test an intervention or estimate causal effects; instead, it identifies themes suggesting that educators believe effective literacy support depends on stronger professional learning, more explicit and multisensory instruction, and greater attention to equity and student agency.

The main conclusion is that successful support for African American boys’ early literacy in restart schools is closely tied to educator capacity and instructional design rather than to a single program. The dissertation argues for ongoing professional development, conceptual thinking about practice, and deliberate use of retrieval practice and multisensory instruction in reading lessons. Because the work is qualitative and interview-based, it offers narrative insights rather than quantitative subgroup estimates or effect sizes.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative dissertation does not report a tested literacy intervention or quantitative gains in reading achievement. Instead, it identifies educator-perceived practices associated with supporting African American boys' early literacy in kindergarten through third grade, including explicit instruction, multisensory instruction, and retrieval practice; no effect size, confidence interval, or sample-based literacy outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about instructional practices supporting early literacy/reading achievement

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on restart-school instructional practice and school-level supports, emphasizing professional development, equity-oriented design, and how educators in low-performing schools make sense of their practices. The evidence is qualitative and interpretive, so it supports narrative claims about institutional improvement needs rather than quantified institutional effects.
finding.measure: Interview themes related to professional development, restart-school context, and instructional leadership

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.population: Elementary, Middle, and High School (U.S. K-12)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) improve learning outcomes for U.S. K-12 students and, importantly, under what conditions their effects are larger or smaller. The authors conducted a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies published from 2011–2021, yielding 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS, and used multilevel meta-regression plus MetaForest to examine heterogeneity across study design, student characteristics, intervention features, outcome measures, and setting.

The intervention category is ITS broadly defined as adaptive software that provides personalized instructional support such as hints, feedback, worked examples, reading materials, and question sequences. The included studies covered elementary, middle, and high school settings, with a substantial focus on math and reading/writing outcomes; several studies also targeted English learners, students in poverty, and low achievers. The review found an overall positive effect of ITS on learning outcomes (g=0.271), with similar effects for elementary and middle school students and for low-achieving students, but smaller effects in rural settings. MetaForest suggested that worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, learning outcome type, and immediate measurement were among the most important moderators of effect size.

The paper concludes that ITS are generally beneficial in U.S. K-12 contexts, especially when implemented as main instructional methods, with worked-out examples, and when outcomes are measured immediately after the intervention. The authors also report that standardized test outcomes show smaller effects than researcher-developed tests, and that effects decline as intervention duration increases. Overall, the study supports broader adoption of ITS while emphasizing that implementation features and context meaningfully shape observed impacts.

finding.finding_summary: Across K-12 ITS studies, literacy-related outcomes (reading and writing) showed a positive pooled effect of g=0.323 (SE=0.039, 95% CI [0.218, 0.428], k=55). The review also reports a very large immediate-posttest effect on learning outcomes overall (g=0.460) and a smaller end-of-school-year effect (g=0.155), indicating stronger gains when literacy outcomes are measured immediately after intervention.
